The Marine Minerals Administration reports that as of Thursday, October 8, 130 production platforms and rigs have been evacuated or moved resulting in production shut-ins of about 1.3 million barrels per day of crude oil and 1.1 billion million cubic feet per day of natural gas. events.title: Europe's answer to SpaceX pops 19% as Ukraine's Starshield limits raise concerns
events.summary: Eutelsat soared again on Friday after competitor SpaceX's Starlink systems came under criticism. Ukrainian officials said the system, which is critical to its defense against Russian attacks, was restricted. Eutelsat is known as Europe's answer to SpaceX and aims to challenge its market dominance. Earlier this week, tensions rose between the U.S. and Ukraine after Kyiv accused Elon Musk's SpaceX of imposing new restrictions on its military-grade Starlink internet service without warning, curbing connectivity and limiting Ukraine's ability to defend itself against Russian attacks. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy criticized the U.S., saying "Starlink was switched off" in the middle of the night, preventing Ukrainian drones from intercepting Russian attacks, and ultimately contributing to civilian deaths. "They knew what they did," Zelenskyy said. "It's not about attack. It's also about defending the lives… People were killed because not enough destroying, not enough interceptors, including interceptors with Starlink, which didn't work." SpaceX CEO Elon Musk responded by shifting blame on the U.S. government and said that Starshield systems were under Washington and President Donald Trump's control. Eutelsat shares rose 19% on Friday, and was up 25% over the past five days following the news of Starlink's struggles in Ukraine. Eutelsat's share move this week is more evidence "supporting the sovereign value of European Satellite networks," Deutsche Bank analysts said in a note Thursday. Markets viewed Eutelsat as "the credible Starlink alternative" amid the disruption, they added. "Whilst we note Eutelsat does offer a global LEO [Low Earth Orbit] constellation, we believe it lacks the scale to offer the number of terminals that Starlink can provide," they added. "We would expect the shares to give up some of the gains." Eutelsat consolidated with satellite internet provider OneWeb in 2023, looking to challenge Starlink's market dominance. However, Eutelsat currently has over 600 satellites in orbit, while Starlink has more than 6,750, the company's websites show. Ukraine's deputy minister for recovery, infrastructure, and transport Serhiy Derkach told CNBC on Friday that Russia had amped up attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, taking advantage of restrictions on military applications, including striking bridges, railway networks, and border crossings. "With U.S. limiting the use of Starlinks on the battlefield, Russia feels that this is their moment to try and inflict even more pain and suffering on Ukraine's civilian infrastructure," Derkach said. "We are definitely moving towards very harsh weeks and months and need our partners' support now more than ever," he said, adding that Ukrainians already experience blackouts lasting 4-12 hours per day.

events.title: AI 'espionage' is a reality that companies need to be 'wary of,' DNI Jay Clayton says
events.summary: U.S. companies and the Trump administration both "need to be wary" of AI-related foreign espionage attempts, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNBC. Clayton was asked how concerned Americans should be in light of the recently revealed case charging Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan with installing a recording device in an OpenAI conference room. Clayton said a White House AI task force at its first meeting built on an accord recently signed by President Donald Trump and tech leaders. U.S. companies and the Trump administration both "need to be wary" of foreign espionage attempts as the race for artificial intelligence dominance continues, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told CNBC on Friday. AI "amplifies" existing cybersecurity risks toward U.S. digital infrastructure, which is interconnected with critical systems related to everything from public goods to the national defense and global communications, Clayton said on " Squawk Box ." It's "why we're focused on hardening those systems" and using "our commitment to continue to lead to stay ahead of those nefarious actors," said Clayton, who leads a new White House AI task force . Clayton was asked how concerned Americans should be with the threat of foreign spying in light of the recently revealed case charging Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan with allegedly installing a recording device in an OpenAI executive conference room. Alfozan has not been charged with espionage; the federal charge involves alleged interception of oral communications. Alfozan, who was an OpenAI employee, had booked a one-way plane ticket to Saudi Arabia with his wife and another family member prior to his arrest, according to federal prosecutors. Trump census plan to cut noncitizens from 2030 count spurs potential legal fight Elon Musk becomes biggest known donor of 2026 midterm election Trump defends Russia diesel deal: 'I made the right choice' "The short answer to your question is espionage, both commercial espionage, and I would say state-sponsored espionage, are realities," Clayton said. "It's something that our private sector companies need to be wary of. We, as a government, need to be wary of," he said. The OpenAI incident "shows the lengths that people will go to try and supplant our leadership in this, or at least stay close to us in this emerging technology," Clayton said. An ex-CIA official, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss non-public information, told CNBC this week that the case is "probably the tip of the iceberg." Clayton, who was appointed AI czar earlier this month, said that the task force's "very good" inaugural meeting at the White House on Thursday built on the accord signed by President Donald Trump and a number of AI leaders at the White House last month. Trump had described the agreement, which includes industry pledges to police AI risks itself, as "morally binding." The task force also established three subcommittees that are focused on different AI-related issues. One is tasked with reporting and response, another with assessing critical infrastructure and working with the private sector, and a third with law enforcement and responsibility, Clayton said. The DNI reiterated to CNBC that the Trump administration is intent on staying ahead in the AI race. "We're not the only ones developing it. There are vectors in this technology that are coming from some of our known adversaries and competitors," he said. "The Chinese, the Russians, the Iranians, the North Koreans all have significant technical capability. We need to stay ahead of them."

events.title: U.S. small-scale solar generation has quadrupled in the last decade
events.summary: U.S. Energy Information Administration - EIA - Independent Statistics and Analysis Browse by tag liquid fuels natural gas electricity oil/petroleum production/supply crude oil consumption/demand generation prices map states exports/imports international coal renewables weather forecasts/projections gasoline capacity steo (short-term energy outlook) Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Annual Electric Power Industry Report We estimate that U.S. generation from small-scale or rooftop solar photovoltaic systems (smaller than 1 megawatt of capacity) has increased from 18,812 gigawatthours (GWh) to 92,979 GWh over the last decade. The four states with the highest generation of small-scale solar in the country—California, Arizona, Texas, and Florida—are in regions with more abundant solar resources . Even though it is in a region with lower solar resources, New York ranks as the fifth-largest rooftop solar generation producer as a result of capacity growth supported by technology improvements and state incentives. The year-over-year change in generation was particularly high in 2022, when total generation grew by 25% compared with the previous year amid record capacity growth . Changes in different programs supporting rooftop solar partly explain this increase in generation. For example, California’s Net Energy Metering (NEM) 2.0 program was available through April 2023. This net metering program offered higher export compensation than the subsequent Net Billing Tariff, or NEM 3.0 . All the capacity built under the NEM 2.0 program was grandfathered in, incentivizing higher capacity installation before the current NEM 3.0 took effect. California accounted for 37% (34,411 GWh) of total U.S. small-scale solar generation in 2025. Between 2024 and 2025, rooftop solar generation in the state grew by 8%, largely due to an increase in capacity. Small-scale solar capacity in California increased from 18 gigawatts in 2024 to 20 gigawatts in 2025. The state with the next largest amount of small-scale solar power generation is Arizona, accounting for over 6% of total U.S. generation, or 5,795 GWh. Year-over-year generation in Arizona grew only 6% in 2025. The largest increase happened between 2022 and 2023 when generation from small-scale solar grew by 22% in the state. Arizona customers can access a 25% state income-tax credit and other incentives for adding rooftop solar to their properties. States such as Florida and Texas have seen rapid growth in small-scale solar generation in the last decade as more capacity has been added. Generation in Texas grew from 391 GWh in 2016 to 5,408 GWh last year. Over the same period, Florida’s generation grew from 205 GWh in 2016 to 5,198 GWh in 2025. These two states provide incentives through property tax exemptions and other programs specific to each state and, in some cases, utility. Programs in states with lower irradiance levels are also supporting growth in rooftop solar generation. New York offers incentives, which have encouraged small-scale solar growth in the state. Other states with similar programs include New Jersey , Massachusetts , and Illinois . Although generation from small-scale solar continues to grow year over year, the rate of growth has declined since 2022. EIA uses its surveys of electric utilities to collect information on the number of customers with small-scale solar systems and the aggregated capacity. Electric utilities do not necessarily know how much electricity is generated by rooftop solar on their distribution systems, so generation must be estimated. To develop estimates of generation, we rely on tools such as the National Renewable Energy Laboratory's System Advisor Model and PVWatts . Data on commonly used tilt angles and orientations for small-scale solar systems in California were used as inputs to be representative of tilt angles and orientations in other states. events.title: Veritas expands its anti-counterfeit chip to jewelry, trophies, and fragrance bottles
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Counterfeits of luxury goods are a major problem for fashion houses. Counterfeiters are getting better at replicating brands’ marks and passing off dupes, known as “ superfakes ,” as genuine items. A startup called Veritas wants to tackle the problem with its own chip that verifies goods. Veritas was founded by Luci Holland, a former Tesla technical product manager who also has a background in design and art. Its chip is built to be easily inserted into products without damaging them. Brands can use it to verify whether a product is the real deal, and customers can show a certificate of ownership through the company’s app. Holland said other approaches are easier to defeat, because a digital record can be reproduced through a copied QR code or static NFC link. “Our approach combines secure, authenticated chip responses with integration into the product itself. Our chip generates a secure response with each tap and includes a tamper-detection wire. We make the connection between the object and its digital identity part of the proof,” Holland said. The Veritas founder told TechCrunch over email that the company has just introduced the second version of its chip, which works on metal surfaces and can be scanned through glass. “The next-generation chip is ready for production and supports a broader range of applications, including jewelry, trophies, hard-surface products, and glass objects such as fragrance bottles,” Holland said. “Alongside our garment integrations, this gives brands more ways to incorporate authentication directly into their products.” This week, the startup announced a partnership with ATHLOS, a women’s track-and-field competition founded by Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian, who is also an investor in Veritas. As part of the partnership, all 18 championship crowns will include Veritas’ chips so they can be verified. The company also embedded a chip into a pair of LeBron James’ first Nike shoes, reimagined by artist Adam Port. Tapping a phone to the shoe brings up its history and story. The company has so far raised $1.75 million in pre-seed funding led by Ohanian’s venture firm Seven Seven Six, with participation from DoorDash co-founder Stanley Tang; Gloria Zhu, co-founder of skincare brand Reys; and former TechCrunch editor Josh Constine. Since its February fundraise, the company has shipped an iOS app for consumers and a brand portal that lets companies manage product records and build owner experiences. Through the app and the portal, brands can offer experiences such as clubs, event check-ins, and segmented early access to product drops. Veritas competed in this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt Startup Battlefield, which ran Tuesday through Thursday. A winner was announced Thursday afternoon . events.title: I'm not scared of aging. I'm having more fun in my 60s than I did in my 20s.
events.summary: I'm having more fun in my 60s than I did in my 20s. Krista Buckner; Visuals By Christina I'm in my 60s and I'm enjoying life more than I did in my 20s. At this point in my life, I'm more confident in my fashion choices and friendships. Plus, I've finally stopped questioning whether I'm where I'm "supposed to be" in life. At 62, my life looks almost nothing like the one my 20-year-old self pictured. It's better. Sure, I'm divorced and don't have grandchildren , but I have adult children I adore and friendships with decades of history. Plus, I'm doing something I never imagined: building a career on social media. Every day, I talk to over 200,000 followers on TikTok and 135,000 on Instagram about hope, finding your purpose, and remembering that life doesn't have an expiration date. At an age when many people are winding down, I seem to just be getting started. And I wouldn't change a thing. I dress for myself, not my age I love experimenting with bold fashion choices. Visuals By Christina I've always loved fashion, from jeans and flip-flops to high heels and designer gowns. But these days, I have more confidence in my choices and a lot less interest in anyone else's opinion of them. When I look at clothes, I don't see an age requirement. I see something I either love or don't. Whether it's a bold print , an unexpected silhouette, or a statement piece, my decision on what to wear comes down to how it looks and feels on me, not how old I am. Fashion has always been a form of self-expression for me, and getting older hasn't changed that. I don't think women should have to trade their sense of style for something more "age-appropriate" every time they celebrate another birthday. Plus, my goal isn't to look 30. It's to make 30-year-olds excited to turn 60. After all, why would I want to turn back the clock? I've spent six decades learning who I am. I wouldn't trade that wisdom just to have younger-looking skin . My friendships don't require me to be anyone but myself My friends and I are there for each other during life's best and worst moments. Krista Buckner One of the most beautiful parts of getting older is having friendships that have stood the test of time. There's something special about sitting across from someone who knows the chapters of your life you'd rather forget and realizing you have absolutely nothing to prove. My friends and I have stood by one another through divorces, financial struggles , challenges with our children, and some of life's most difficult moments. But we've also shared incredible joy, deepened our connections, and celebrated the love, wisdom, and experiences that make growing older such a gift. In my 20s, I was still figuring out who I was. Now, there's no pressure to perform, impress, or constantly please the people closest to me. We don't take everything personally, either. If someone is busy or life gets complicated, we understand. We know that a friendship isn't measured by how often you see each other. That kind of freedom doesn't happen overnight. It's built through years of showing up, forgiving, laughing, and sometimes simply giving each other grace. I've stopped questioning whether I'm where I'm supposed to be One of the greatest gifts of aging is being able to spend time with my adult children. Krista Buckner When I was younger, I spent so much time wondering whether I was on the right path. I had a very specific picture of what my life should look like, and when things didn't go according to plan, I questioned myself. At 62, I can look back and see that even the experiences I never would have chosen were my greatest gifts of all. Every path is the right path. Loss taught me gratitude. Starting over taught me courage. Being told I wasn't enough taught me to recognize my own worth. And through it all, I've developed a resilience that allows me to face whatever life brings with confidence and hope. And perhaps that's the biggest difference between 22 and 62: I know that my life is happening for me, not to me. I spent so much of my younger years thinking about what my life would become. Now I'm actually living it, and I still have so much I want to do. I know aging is inevitable. But spending decades dreading it isn't. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Tesla unveils long-delayed Roadster developed with SpaceX, fueling merger speculation
events.summary: Tesla revealed its next-generation Roadster from a SpaceX test site in Texas on Thursday. CEO Elon Musk first debuted the Roadster refresh concept in 2017 but Tesla has since missed every targeted delivery date. Tesla said the new Roadster, equipped with SpaceX thrusters, can accelerate from zero to 60 miles per hour in less than a second. Tesla showed off its long-delayed next-generation Roadster on Thursday, almost a decade after Elon Musk's company started taking deposits for the electric sports car. The event was livestreamed from a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, near Waco, starting at 7:55 p.m. local time, or 8:55 p.m. ET. In attendance along with Musk were design leader Franz von Holzhausen and Lars Moravy, vice president of vehicle engineering. "You're going to see some crazy stuff tonight," Musk said. "You're going to see the results of what happens when you have a collaboration with the world's best car company and the world's best rocket company." Tesla's original Roadster, designed and engineered by a team led by founding CEO Martin Eberhard, was based on a Lotus Elise chassis and was first delivered in 2008, selling for roughly $100,000 in small volumes until 2012. The next-generation Roadster is expected to be a high-end, low-volume model that relies on SpaceX technology to enable it to hover. While Musk fanatics expressed their excitement on social media, the Roadster isn't likely to have any material financial impact on the company. At the event, Musk and his team showcased a white sports car that raced up a curved ramp, then clung to it upside down and vaulted off it, flipping in mid-air and hovering slowly before landing on the ground. The two-seater can go from zero to 60 miles per hour in under a second, according to Tesla's timer, a feat Moravy demonstrated for the live audience. Musk said the next-generation Roadster would enter production in 2028. The price wasn't announced, and the company didn't disclose specifications about other performance-level variants of the new Roadster. It was unclear whether the vehicle would be street-legal, with Musk saying on stage that "This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car." The Roadster unveiling has added to speculation of a possible merger between Tesla and SpaceX. For years, Musk's companies have worked with and paid each other, even sharing some personnel. The collaboration has increased in 2026, with speculation about a possible SpaceX-Tesla merger swirling since the aerospace and defense company went public in June. SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell told CNBC ahead of the IPO that a merger "might make Elon's life a little easier." Barclays analyst Dan Levy predicted in a note out this week that such a merger could happen before the end of 2026. Tesla reopened reservations for the refreshed Roadster in recent weeks, accepting $50,000 deposits from prospective buyers in the U.S., Canada and China. Musk first promoted the refreshed Roadster concept at an event in November 2017 , and the following June in a series of tweets. He wrote at that time, "SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car." The engines would improve speed and braking, and may "even allow a Tesla to fly." The prototype Tesla showed on Thursday is built to be as lightweight as possible with a steer-by-wire system, steering yoke, and an array of technologies developed by SpaceX, including thrusters, carbon overlay pressure vessels and diffusers, and powerful fans that enable the car to do some gymnastics. One feature Tesla left out of its forthcoming Roadster is the company's "FSD" or automated driving system. Musk said the new Roadster will be the last vehicle the company produces that's intended to be controlled by a human driver. Tesla started taking $50,000 deposits for the revamped Roadster in 2017, but has since missed every targeted delivery date. As recently as last October, Musk was hyping a Roadster demo that he hoped would happen before the end of 2025. That didn't take place either. Musk's former friend and OpenAI co-founder Sam Altman mocked the Tesla CEO in posts on X last year over the extreme delays, showing screenshots of his reservation and refund requests. "I really was excited for the car! And I understand delays," Altman wrote. "But 7.5 years has felt like a long time to wait." Altman got his refund, and the two ended up in court earlier this year over a separate matter related to OpenAI's governance and ownership structure. Others have kept their reservations. Lawrence O'Connor, founder and CEO of Other World Computing in Austin, Texas, told CNBC ahead of the event that he reserved a Founder's Edition of the new Roadster in November 2017, effectively giving the company what he called an "interest-free loan" of $250,000. O'Connor wrote in a message that he would be attending the show and was "excited to see what has been 9 years in the making.

events.title: Here's how the CoreWeave sell-off is affecting OpenAI vs. Anthropic valuations
events.summary: The spread is widening between AI leaders OpenAI and Anthropic as a sell-off in CoreWeave leads neocloud stocks lower. OpenAI's valuation is down more than 4% the past 24 hours after briefly slipping under $1.5 trillion, according to perpetual futures pricing on decentralized exchange Hyperliquid. Meanwhile, Anthropic perps are up 2.4% over the same time period, recovering an overnight dip and indicating a valuation of just over $2 trillion. OpenAI's valuation is down more than 4% the past 24 hours after briefly slipping under $1.5 trillion, according to perpetual futures pricing on decentralized exchange Hyperliquid. Meanwhile, Anthropic perps are up 2.4% over the same time period, recovering an overnight dip and indicating a valuation of just over $2 trillion. Perpetuals are bets that never expire. They maintained by "deployers" on Hyperliquid's blockchain infrastructure that determine a funding rate for going long or short the futures based on a spot "oracle" price that uses third-party data like private funding rounds and secondary market transactions to estimate private-market prices. Open interest, defined by Hyperliquid as the sum of long and short positions on a contract, is more than five times bigger in Anthropic than OpenAI — more than $41 million, compared to less than $7 million in OpenAI. Right now the deployer behind these pre-IPO contracts – the developer building the exchange – is Entropy IO. TradeXYZ, the most prominent developer on the platform, typically does not list pre-IPO perps until S-1s are public, according to David Schamis, CEO of Hyperliquid Strategies , the publicly traded treasury company that invests in the HYPE token that powers the exchange. "Liquidity will probably be deeper once TradeXYZ lists these companies," Schamis said in a call. "Generally these will trade at a premium to the IPO price but they do a good job predicting where it will be post-IPO." The bigger price drop in OpenAI perps reflects the company's closer ties to GPU rent-a-center CoreWeave, whose shares touched a new one-year low Thursday, extending a decline over that period to 54%, as concerns mount over the company's debt-financing strategy. In April, CoreWeave announced a deal with Anthropic to power the company's Claude products, but did not disclose the value of the deal. The company's relationship with OpenAI stretches back further, and as of September 2025 was worth at least $22 billion including a 5-year agreement to provide datacenters and technology. While OpenAI perps are falling more than Anthropic the past 24 hours, the two are both down about 15% from highs last month, according to Hyperliquid pricing.

events.title: IMF suggests UK should cut spending rather than raise taxes on banks, as Healey prepares budget raid – business live
events.summary: IMF: UK should cut spending rather than raise taxes on banks Heather Stewart is the Guardian’s economics editor, reporting from Bangkok this week: We’ve just been in the IMF’s Europe press conference, where the topic of bank taxes in the UK came up [following our report that the chancellor is poised to tax Britain’s banks]. Asked about the possibility at John Healey’s upcoming budget, Helge Berger , the economist who is deputy director in the IMF’s European department, suggested there might be better places to look to balance the books. Berger pointed out that Healey’s predecessor, Rachel Reeves , had raised taxes in her budgets, saying: “The last two budgets involved increasing government revenue, and ultimately there’s a moment where this becomes less productive but there’s still areas where Britain can make additional headroom available: modernising the property taxes or VAT, these are good examples. We wouldn’t recommend labour tax.” “Ultimately, with taxes roughly at 40% of GDP - historically, for Britain, a high number - then of course balancing these measures on the fiscal side, doing a bit more there, makes good sense.” He pointed to cost-cutting measures including removing the pensions triple lock , and “better targeting social benefits,” adding, “so I think that’s where you would put the emphasis, rather than the tax that you mentioned.” 31m ago CoreWeave shares down again amid AI debt worries 2h ago Bloomberg: UK banks warn Healey’s tax plan will curtail economic growth 3h ago IMF: UK should cut spending rather than raise taxes on banks 4h ago XTB: Bank tax could hurt FTSE 100 6h ago Worst week for South Korea's stock market since the financial crisis 7h ago IG: UK bank tax risk is now a base case 7h ago Bank shares drop as budget tax hit looms 7h ago BoE's Bailey: seeing 'quite subdued' evidence of second round inflation effects 8h ago Warsh: Super intelligence driving 'massive investment surge' 8h ago CBI: Chancellor should avoid 'further sector-specific taxation' 8h ago Introduction: John Healey poised to raise taxes on banks in budget CoreWeave shares down again amid AI debt worries Over on Wall Street, shares in AI company CoreWeave have tumbled again at the start of trading, as concerns grow over its borrowing levels. CoreWeave are leading the fallers on the Nasdaq index, down 7%. Yesterday, the cost of protecting CoreWeave bonds against default rose to the highest intraday level on record. CoreWeave runs AI datacentres, funded by issuing high-yield debt. Fawad Razaqzada, market analyst at StoneX, says: CoreWeave was among the names caught up in the recent sell-off, although the stock recovered yesterday after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the company’s financial position was improving and its cost of capital was falling. That is hardly an impartial endorsement, given Nvidia’s sizeable interest in CoreWeave, so the more important question is whether the recovery can be sustained once the immediate reassurance fades. More broadly, this week’s price action suggests the market debate is beginning to shift. The question is no longer simply how large the AI opportunity can become, but how profitable the enormous investment required to realise it will ultimately be. The head of ⁠the IMF on Friday isued an appeald to global leaders to cooperate in the face of multiple economic risks, such as rapid advances in AI and the Iran war. Kristalina Georgieva said the sheer speed of technological change added to the long list of challenges, including disruptions to the global trading ​system, high food and energy prices and lingering wars, all of which threatened to widen the ‌gulf between advanced economies and the world’s poor. Bond markets, ‌she said, were clearly sensing the risks, with US, German and Japanese 10-year sovereign yields reaching their highest levels in decades. “The need of the hour is for urgent and practical international cooperation,” Georgieva told at a plenary session today. Audit, tax and business advisory firm, Blick Rothenberg argues that increasing the bank corporation tax surcharge from 3% back to 8% might backfire. Artur Vorobyev , a director at Blick Rothenberg, says: Although this may sound like a reversal of a tax cut, when the surcharge was reduced in 2023, corporation tax increased from 19% to 25%. The combined rate on bank profits went up from 27% to 28%. Increasing the surcharge to 8% now would bring the combined rate to 33%. This is a significant rise and is counterproductive if the Government wants banks to invest and lend more to aid growth.” Bloomberg: UK banks warn Healey’s tax plan will curtail economic growth Bloomberg are reporting that the UK’s banking industry has “ramped up lobbying” against extra taxes planned by Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey. They are apparently warning that a hike could shrink economic output by £6bn over five years and hit areas outside London the hardest.

events.title: Zuma’s illness raises questions for South Africa opposition
events.summary: The News Concerns over the health of former South African President Jacob Zuma have raised questions about the future of uMkhonto weSizwe (MK), the populist party built around him that has redrawn the country’s political landscape. The 84-year-old was taken to hospital two weeks ago. Since then, MK officials and the Zuma Foundation have circulated conflicting accounts about his condition. The party initially described Zuma as healthy and undergoing routine checks before returning home. That claim was later contradicted by the foundation, which said he remained in hospital and declined to provide regular updates. In a sign of the impact on the party, MK canceled its flagship Siyathatha rally less than three weeks before South Africa’s municipal elections. The uncertainty has become a political issue because of Zuma’s central role in the party he publicly launched nearly three years ago, after switching from the African National Congress (ANC) ahead of a general election. MK emerged from the 2024 poll as one of the biggest forces in South African politics, winning nearly 15% of the vote on promises to scrap the constitution, expropriate land without compensation and nationalize banks, insurers and strategic mines. Its performance accelerated the slide of the ANC, once led by Nelson Mandela, which lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since the end of apartheid and was forced to form a coalition government. Still, the MK’s rise has been punctuated by leadership turmoil, internal purges, and recurring disputes over candidate selection. Zuma’s absence from public campaigning has heightened questions about whether the movement can maintain its momentum without him. Natasha Marrian, a political analyst at the Bureau for Economic Research, a South African think tank, said the MK party, launched as a breakaway outfit for Zuma supporters who opposed the ANC leadership of President Cyril Ramaphosa, was a Zuma project from the outset. “He is the party’s central drawcard,” she said. “There’s no clear center holding it together in his absence.” Know More Zuma’s son, Duduzane, serves as the party’s first deputy president and is widely regarded as a potential successor, but analysts question whether he can replicate the appeal of his father, who led South Africa from 2009 to 2018 before being ousted amid corruption allegations and a wider state capture scandal. “Duduzane is a completely unknown political figure,” said André Duvenhage, a political analyst at South Africa’s North-West University. “He comes from a business background.” The ANC may benefit from Zuma’s absence, said Musa Xulu, an independent political analyst, adding that if he remains largely absent from the campaign trail, some ANC voters who followed him could drift back. “The ANC is becoming the biggest beneficiary of Zuma’s current disappearance from public politics. The MK party is Jacob Zuma and Jacob Zuma is the MK,” Xulu said. Notable The ANC secured a legal victory ahead of the 4 November 2026 local government elections when the Constitutional Court ruled in its favour, ordering the electoral commission to reinstate 181 disqualified candidates onto the ballot papers.

events.title: As a Texas local, I skip the crowds in Austin and head west to a charming nearby city with amazing wineries
events.summary: Fredericksburg, Texas, and its surrounding areas have some incredible scenery and wineries. Malachi Jacobs/Shutterstock I've lived in Texas for many years, and Fredericksburg is one of my favorite places to visit . Fredericksburg has incredible wineries, and I like that it isn't too far from Austin or San Antonio. The small city has a charming, walkable Main Street with some great shops and restaurants. After more than 15 years of driving between San Antonio and Austin as a longtime Texas local, I've found my favorite detour: Fredericksburg. Part of the scenic Texas Hill Country, it's a walkable city with German roots, popular for its array of wineries, boutique hotels, and lively downtown. Although I love Austin and San Antonio , Fredericksburg provides a small-town feel that the aforementioned cities — with populations close to a million each — could never quite achieve. In my opinion, Fredericksburg's small population of about 12,000 people only lends to its charm. It's a great break from bigger Texas cities, as it's less than a two-hour drive from Austin or San Antonio. Here are a few reasons I visit Fredericksburg twice a year and highly recommend it as a travel destination. In this area, wine is a huge draw Main Street has restaurants, wine-tasting rooms, coffee shops, and bars. Little Vignettes Photo/Shutterstock Fredericksburg is situated in the heart of Texas wine country , so visiting without enjoying one of its many wineries is like a crime in Texas. (Another crime? Dry brisket.) In Fredericksburg, you can either stop by a multitude of tasting rooms on Main Street or drive out past a ranch or two to find Tuscan-style wineries hidden in plain sight. One of my favorite wineries is Augusta Vin Winery — and it's worth the extra drive. I always enjoy sipping reds in the spacious tasting room, with large open windows perfect for taking in the Texas sunshine. A few other wineries worth visiting in Fredericksburg include the Rhinory for the unique experience of drinking at a rhino reserve, Slate Theory for a touch of modernity, and Grape Creek Vineyards or Barons Creek for classic experiences with beautiful views. There's no shortage of great places to grab a meal in Fredericksburg The Restaurant at The Albert Hotel is beautiful. Kat Stinson Consider leaning into the city's German heritage at The Auslander, one of the many locally owned restaurants on Main Street. Reminiscent of a classic Bavarian beer hall, it has beer, a whole section of schnitzel entrées, sausage plates, and German sandwiches. For a guest more partial to upscale fare, try The Restaurant at Albert Hotel. It's fairly new and a great place for date night . Led by Michelin-starred chef Michael Fojtasek, The Restaurant pays homage to seasonal Texas Hill Country-inspired cuisine with fresh local ingredients (like peaches) and spins on German dishes. For good Texas barbecue , stop by Junebug's BBQ. Its menu is filled with smoked meats — the pulled pork is especially impressive — and all the fixings. Other notable local bites include Vaudeville's famous gumbo that's only available on Saturdays, Otto's decadent cinnamon rolls, and Alstadt Brewery's ice-cold beer and tasty Reuben sandwiches. I've tried brisket and pulled pork at Junebug's BBQ. Kat Stinson Main Street is also home to several nice coffee shops — and the Old West-themed Java Ranch is my go-to for a perfect iced latte. I also suggest checking out Kaffee Haus and Caliche Coffee and Roasters. Lastly, if you want to visit an Instagram-worthy spot with lots of bubbly, head down Main Street to the all-pink paradise that is Brooke's Bubble Bar. It's a very cute place to snap photos and enjoy a drink. There's so much to do and try here, and I know I'll keep coming back I find it's often easy to find parking in downtown Fredericksburg. Main Street in Fredericksburg I often switch up which vineyards, cafés, and eateries I visit, and Fredericksburg's variety of accommodations makes it easy to change up where I stay, too. I can sleep in one of several boutique hotels, go for a more rustic stay at the Onera treehouse resort near Main Street, or enjoy a cozy guest cabin at Cross Mountain Vineyards . Hotels and eateries aside, Main Street also has tons of art galleries, antique shops, clothing boutiques, jewelry stores, and more. I appreciate that I can spend a whole day exploring downtown without ever moving my car. (Plus, I've always been able to find ample free parking on Main Street). If you want to enjoy a big Texas city, check out Austin or even San Antonio. However, if you're looking for a quieter alternative with a small-town feel, Fredericksburg is a great choice. After each visit, I know I'll be back soon. This story was originally published on September 30, 2025, and most recently updated on October 16, 2026. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: African energy's 'Big Bang' moment
events.summary: Alexis’s view The Iran war is shaping up to be the catalyst of a seismic shift in Africa’s energy sector. And, in the case of the continent’s richest man Aliko Dangote, the conflict has proven the old adage that luck is what happens when preparation meets opportunity. Dangote’s mega-refinery on the outskirts of Lagos State has revealed the scale of a West African market underserved by locally refined fuel, while upending conventional thinking by showing African refineries can supply markets in Europe and Asia. At the same time, disruption in the Strait of Hormuz has exposed the vulnerability of nations that are heavily dependent on fuel imports: South Africa and Kenya have hiked prices, which runs the risk of driving inflation. Meanwhile, President Bola Tinubu’s removal of Nigeria’s subsidy three years ago has allowed prices to skyrocket, turning the cost of fuel into a key campaign issue ahead of January’s election. Policymakers have been quick to react to the altered energy dynamics. South Africa announced plans to increase its strategic oil reserves for the first time since the end of apartheid to mitigate supply shocks, Angola wants to implement faster exploration concessions while urging southern African governments to help finance a new refinery , and plans to build refineries in Uganda and Tanzania have gathered pace. Fola Fagbule, who heads the Kenya regional office of multilateral lender Africa Finance Corporation, which helped to finance Dangote’s Lagos refinery, called the impact of the Nigerian billionaire’s project a “Big Bang” moment. He told me various projects are being developed across the continent “as a result of the new realities in the energy market.” The shift has potential pitfalls. Daniel Evans, global head of fuels and refining research at S&P Global Energy, acknowledged the increased appetite for downstream investment across Africa, but warned difficulties remain around projects that require high levels of capital expenditure. But a new generation of refineries has the potential to transform economies, not only protecting countries from future energy shocks but providing the baseload power needed to ramp up manufacturing. As Fagbule put it, the legacy of this paradigm shift could be how it triggered “massive, large-scale industrialization in Africa that nobody expected.” Notable Dangote Refinery is pushing to extend the sale of its shares to Egypt , indicating that Africa’s largest IPO is likely to take a more pan-African shape .

events.title: Demand for AI experts brings deepfakes and chatbot impostors
events.summary: AI experts are coming — and the pretenders too. “Anybody who knows anything about AI” is in high demand from investors trying to play the AI trade, said Gemma Postlethwaite, CEO of expert network GLG. And there are plenty of deepfakes and people using AI chatbots willing to play the part. “We have to be able to deliver experts that not only are who they say they are, but know what they say they know,” Postlethwaite tells Semafor. To test for authenticity, GLG is doing additional screening and ID verification — increasingly on camera with questions designed to trip up AI avatars. It’s also parsing transcripts to find “situations where somebody’s expertise is going off-piste,” she said. “Think of it like a digital fingerprint of knowledge.” Verify, then trust. GLG is also connecting frontier AI labs with subject-matter experts to help train models in sensitive subjects, such as child psychiatrists who can craft responses to kids in crisis and nuclear or bioweapon experts to respond to bad actors looking for instruction manuals. — Liz Hoffman

events.title: Congo Basin deforestation nears Amazon levels
events.summary: Forest clearing in the Congo Basin nearly matched losses in the Amazon for the first time in a decade of monitoring, even as deforestation slowed worldwide, a new study found. The destruction releases vast stores of carbon, adding to climate change that is already contributing to drought and forest fires across the tropics. Expanding farming, timber, and mining activities are driving the clearances in the basin, which is home to the world’s second-largest tropical rainforest, the Forest Declaration Assessment group said . In DR Congo, where most of the forest is situated, decades of conflict — along with poor oversight — have fueled uncontrolled logging, driving up the rate of tree loss in central Africa this decade. Meanwhile, there has been a steep decline in deforestation in Latin America and the Caribbean, leaving the two regions almost on a par. — Ruben Nyanguila

events.title: Palestinians, US journalist attacked in West Bank pogrom: What we know
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians harvesting olives and severely beat Washington Post photojournalist Heidi Levine. Israeli settlers brutally attacked Palestinian olive pickers and a photojournalist working for The Washington Post in the occupied West Bank on Friday, beating villagers and setting olive groves ablaze. The attack was among several targeting Palestinians trying to gather their olive harvest, with further assaults and arson reported in nearby communities as well. list 1 of 4 Malaysia’s welcome for Min Aung Hlaing undermines its stand on justice list 2 of 4 Why is China buying up gold? list 3 of 4 Pakistan orders school inspections following deadly roof collapse list 4 of 4 Fuel tanker fire engulfs market in southern Nigeria These incidents are just the latest in weeks of intensifying pogroms on local communities in the West Bank by Israelis from illegal settlements who are largely protected – or at least unrestricted – by Israeli forces. Veteran journalist Heidi Levine, 64, was taken to hospital after the assault on Friday in Abu Falah, northeast of Ramallah. A Palestinian man was also shot in the thigh by Israeli soldiers, according to a witness who spoke to Al Jazeera and the Palestinian news agency Wafa. Dozens of masked settlers attacked Palestinian farmers harvesting olives, throwing stones, using slingshots and setting trees on fire. Levine, an American freelance photojournalist who works for The Washington Post, fell to the ground during the attack before she was set upon, witnesses said. “We looked and saw that there was a journalist … on the ground with people surrounding her, beating her, clubbing her, robbing her, pulling her up, beating her again and kicking her,” Jasper Nathaniel, an independent journalist who witnessed the attack, told Al Jazeera. Levine later told reporters that her attackers “just kept kicking me and kicking me, like probably 50 times”. Levine was wearing a protective vest marked “PRESS” on the front and back. Her cameras and phone were taken from her during the assault, the Washington Post reported. Nathaniel said he and others managed to reach her when the settlers briefly backed away, but she struggled to stand. “She was in very, very bad shape. She couldn’t really get up off the ground,” he said. As they helped her towards paramedics, settlers charged again, throwing more stones, he added. Levine was eventually taken to hospital in Ramallah. Nathaniel said Israeli soldiers arrived after the settler assault and opened fire and used tear gas against Palestinians, shooting a man in the leg. “They do nothing to stop the settlers, and they speed into town and start firing their guns and tear-gassing, and they shoot a Palestinian man in the leg,” he said. “They’re pointing their guns at the paramedics who are helping him, shoving journalists, including myself,” Nathaniel said, adding that the man was eventually taken away in an ambulance. “We are outraged by this unwarranted attack on a journalist doing her job and urge a thor ough investigation and follow-through from authorities,” Matt Murray, executive editor of The Washington Post, said in a statement. Wafa also reported that Israeli forces fired live ammunition and tear gas at Palestinians during the attack. After the soldiers left, Palestinians returned to harvesting their olives, Nathaniel added. Where else have olive pickers been attacked? There was violence in other parts of the occupied West Bank on Friday, as well. In Burqa, east of Ramallah, four Palestinians were reported to have been injured in a settler attack on olive pickers. In nearby Turmus Aya, settlers assaulted farmers and burned vehicles and olive trees. A civil defence volunteer was also injured, according to Wafa. The attacks follow the killing of Ali Hassan Yasser al-Bazzari, 44, during an assault on Palestinians gathering olives near Burqa, northwest of Nablus, on October 7. Witnesses reported that settlers and Israeli soldiers attacked the harvesters. Journalists documenting the violence have also been targeted. On October 6, armed settlers beat Palestinian AFP photographer Jaafar Ashtiyeh, 58, with rifle butts near Aqraba, south of Nablus. He was taken to hospital with injuries to his head and torso, according to witnesses, relatives and colleagues. The Israeli settler pogroms have been going on for many weeks, and have stepped up as the seasonal Palestinian olive harvest gets under way. The Israeli rights group Yesh Din has recorded at least 170 pogroms since September 27, around the start of the annual olive harvest, Reuters reported. The violence threatens Palestinian livelihoods and access to their land. Farmers endure assaults, the destruction of trees and the theft of crops, while settlers have also begun stealing olives from Palestinian-owned groves themselves.

events.title: Singapore-listed firm faces Indonesia's probe over suspected land clearing by burning amid haze
events.summary: Several Singapore-listed plantation and agribusiness companies have faced scrutiny over fires in Indonesia that have contributed to the haze in Singapore. Indonesia has opened a preliminary probe into suspected land clearing by burning in a Kencana Agri subsidiary’s North Kalimantan concession, after fires and haze spread across the region. Kencana Agri, Wilmar, GAR, Bumitama Agri and First Resources said fires affected some concession areas, but many started outside their land or in community areas before spreading. Singapore’s National Environment Agency will issue preventive notices to seven Indonesian firms, mostly in timber and pulpwood, as authorities step up action over the haze risk. SINGAPORE – Indonesian authorities have started a preliminary inquiry into suspected land-clearing fires in a concession area operated by a subsidiary of Singapore-listed palm oil producer Kencana Agri. The company disclosed on Oct 16 that investigators had inspected the affected area in North Kalimantan in September and that the inquiry was ongoing. Kencana acknowledged that fires had affected approximately 62 ha within concession areas operated by its subsidiaries in North and East Kalimantan, although it maintained that the fires had spread from adjacent land rather than originating from its operations. The disclosures came in response to queries from Singapore Exchange Regulation (SGX RegCo) over recent forest and peatland fires in Indonesia and the resulting transboundary haze affecting Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia. Kencana is among several Singapore-listed plantation and agribusiness companies that have faced scrutiny over fires in Indonesia in recent days, with some acknowledging fires within their concessions but disputing that they had started them. The company, which has plantations and mills in Sumatra, Kalimantan and Sulawesi, said the affected area was small compared with its total planted area of around 67,862 ha. Its firefighting teams had worked with local authorities and communities to contain the fire, using drones and fire observation towers to identify active fire fronts and to direct ground crews. “The incidents are under control, with ongoing monitoring and precautionary response measures being maintained,” it said. Agribusiness giant Wilmar International also acknowledged on Oct 16 that fires had been detected in small areas of some of its Indonesian concessions, but said they had originated outside its concession boundaries or on land farmed by local communities within them. The group said its field verification indicated that the fires had subsequently spread into areas under its management. Wilmar said its firefighting teams, working with local authorities and communities, had extinguished all such fires quickly. It also said it had not undertaken any new oil palm planting at its company-owned plantations in Indonesia since 2013. Its field activities since then have been limited to replanting existing cultivated areas, which it said was carried out mechanically without the use of fire. Wilmar added that it had maintained a strict no-burning policy since 2006, covering its subsidiaries and third-party suppliers. Suppliers that breached the policy could have their commercial relationships terminated. Meanwhile, Golden Agri-Resources (GAR), said on Oct 16 that the recent forest and land fires had not materially affected its operations. GAR, which operates oil palm plantations across Sumatra, Kalimantan and Papua, said it had received enquiries from various stakeholders about the fires and whether its concessions or activities were connected to the incidents. However, it said that, to the best of its knowledge, there had been no allegations, claims or findings that its operations had contributed to the recent fires and haze. The company also said neither it nor its subsidiaries had received any formal notice of investigation, enforcement action or allegation from regulatory or government authorities in connection with the fires. Its Indonesian-listed subsidiary, Sinar Mas Agro Resources and Technology (SMART), had separately responded to queries from the Indonesia Stock Exchange on Oct 15. SMART said the fires had not materially affected its operations, 2026 production targets, revenue, profit or asset values. Indofood Agri Resources also disclosed on Oct 16 that its Indonesian-listed subsidiary, Salim Ivomas Pratama (SIMP), had responded to queries from the Indonesia Stock Exchange over forest and land fires. SIMP, which operates plantations across Java, Sumatra, Kalimantan and Sulawesi, said it is monitoring hotspots using satellite data, and any detected hotspots would be addressed promptly to prevent fires. It did not specify whether any hotspots had been detected within its plantation areas. Bumitama Agri, which requested a trading halt on Oct 16, said fires had damaged some areas within or adjoining its Indonesian concessions, particularly community-managed and unplanted land.

events.title: Spain punished by FIFA for Islamophobic chants during Egypt friendly
events.summary: Spain sanctioned by FIFA after incidents at Espanyol’s stadium in Barcelona, which staged the friendly with Egypt. Spain have ‌‌‌‌been fined $20,000 and ordered to partially close their stadium ⁠⁠⁠⁠for their ⁠⁠⁠⁠next friendly after supporters twice chanted Islamophobic slogans during the game against Egypt in March, FIFA said ⁠⁠⁠⁠in a statement. The sanctions relate to incidents at the RCDE Stadium near Barcelona, home of LaLiga club Espanyol, ⁠⁠⁠⁠where some Spain fans chanted, “Who doesn’t jump is a Muslim” during a World Cup warm-up match which ended in a 0-0 draw. list 1 of 3 Man Utd veering towards crisis as Man City cloud hangs over Premier League list 2 of 3 Man United’s Martinez apologises for outburst after talks with Carrick list 3 of 3 What led Manchester United’s Martinez to meltdown in Madrid – all to know After the second occurrence of the chant, the stadium announcer ‌‌‌‌issued a warning and the scoreboard displayed a message against discriminatory behaviour. Spain winger Lamine Yamal, who is Muslim, condemned the chants at the time, describing them as disrespectful and intolerable and calling those responsible “ignorant and racist”. Spanish police launched an investigation the following day, while world governing ⁠⁠⁠⁠body FIFA later started disciplinary proceedings against ⁠⁠⁠⁠the Spanish football federation (RFEF). It argued that the word ‘Muslim’ was “neither insulting nor pejorative”, adding that the fans’ conduct should be assessed under FIFA’s Article 17, ⁠⁠⁠⁠which covers political, ideological, religious or offensive messages, rather than Article 15, which deals ⁠⁠⁠⁠with discrimination and racist abuse. However, FIFA’s disciplinary ⁠⁠⁠⁠committee rejected that argument, saying Article 15 does not require the explicit use of a slur and that a term can be discriminatory when ‌‌‌‌used in context as “an insult, taunt, or marker of inferiority”. FIFA fined the RFEF and ordered the closure of at least ‌‌‌‌15% ‌‌‌‌of available seats for Spain’s next friendly. Al Jazeera has contacted the RFEF for comment.

events.title: South Africa tightens rules on weight-loss drugs
events.summary: South Africa is planning to tighten the rules around pharmacies making their own compound versions of medicines, including the popular weight-loss and diabetes treatments Ozempic and Mounjaro, Reuters reports . The move is likely to be welcomed by pharmaceutical giants such as Novo Nordisk and Eli Lilly as they seek to curb the pharmacy-made products competing with their blockbuster GLP-1 drugs. South African Pharmacy Council CEO Vincent Tlala said his organization was working with the industry regulator to update standards governing the compounding of medicines because they are worried that some pharmacies have become, in effect, “small-scale manufacturers,” producing large quantities of treatments in advance, rather than for specific patients. The discussion on new guidelines, expected to be published around March next year, follows June’s court victory for Novo Nordisk against local compounding pharmacies making unauthorized copies. With the highest adult obesity rate in Africa , at 30%, the drugs are in high demand in South Africa, but the cost of the trademarked version puts them out of reach for most people. — Tiisetso Motsoeneng

events.title: South Africa’s Black firms face $45B funding gap
events.summary: South African Black-owned businesses face a funding shortfall of $45 billion, a new report shows, citing “explicit investor bias” alongside barriers such as limited collateral and governance concerns. The findings come three decades after the democratic government introduced a raft of measures — known as Black Economic Empowerment (BEE) — aimed at reversing the dispossession suffered by Black people under apartheid and colonialism. Despite the efforts to redress the problem, South Africa remains one of the world’s most unequal societies. The study, published by British International Investment and Sweden’s Swedfund, both state-owned development finance entities, lands as Washington steps up pressure on Pretoria to dismantle BEE. US Ambassador Leo Brent Bozell III has put scrapping the policy on a list of demands tied to improving the investment climate. Pretoria has refused, despite disagreements within the coalition government. Instead the policy conversation has moved to creating a $60 billion fund to help scale up small Black-owned businesses. — Tiisetso Motsoeneng

events.title: Wee Hur enters Singapore student housing market with 1,398-bed NTU project
events.summary: A hall of residence at Nanyang Technological University. The new development will mainly house postgraduate students. Wee Hur Holdings is entering Singapore’s purpose-built student accommodation market with a 1,398-bed Y-Suites project at NTU. NTU issued a Letter of Award after a competitive process. The award covers design, construction, financing, operation and maintenance. The project may become Singapore’s largest privately developed and operated student housing on an autonomous university campus. Construction is due in Q3 2027, with operations by the start of the 2029-30 academic year. Wee Hur says the project will grow its pipeline and regional Y Suites platform. SINGAPORE – Wee Hur Holdings is entering Singapore’s purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA) market with a 1,398-bed Y-Suites development at Nanyang Technological University (NTU). The Singapore-listed property and construction group said on Oct 16 that NTU had issued it a Letter of Award for the project, following a competitive expression-of-interest and request-for-proposal process. The award covers the design, construction, financing, operation and maintenance of the accommodation facility. The parties are working towards finalising an agreement, with the award subject to its terms and conditions. Upon completion, the project is expected to be Singapore’s largest privately developed and operated student accommodation facility within an autonomous university campus, Wee Hur said. The development will mainly house postgraduate students, with a limited number of beds allocated to undergraduates. It will also be Wee Hur’s first Y Suites-branded asset in Singapore. Construction is targeted to begin in the third quarter of 2027, with operations scheduled to start by the beginning of the 2029- 2030 academic year, subject to approvals from NTU and the regulatory authorities. The project will be undertaken through a special-purpose vehicle, with Wee Hur responsible for the development from design and construction through to operations and maintenance. The roughly 6,000 sq m greenfield site is located next to 30 Nanyang Link within NTU’s main campus. The project vehicle will be granted an initial 20-year land lease, with options for two five-year extensions, subject to the definitive agreement. Wee Hur Property chief executive Goh Chengyu said the award will add to the group’s development pipeline and provide greater visibility for its construction activities. He added: “By developing the PBSA from the ground up and operating it over the long term, we can apply our experience across the full real estate life cycle – from design and construction through to operations.” The project also expands Wee Hur’s student accommodation business into a third market, after Australia and Hong Kong, as the group builds out its Y Suites platform across the Asia-Pacific. Goh Wee Ping, Wee Hur Holdings’ chief investment officer and chief executive of Wee Hur Capital, said bringing Y Suites to Singapore was “an important step” in the group’s ambition to build a regional PBSA platform. “Working with NTU allows us to bring our experience to our home market while further scaling a platform that we believe can create long-term value for the group,” he said. events.title: Neet rates higher in England’s smaller cities and towns than in biggest cities
events.summary: Initiatives to address youth employment crisis and offer training are being launched in towns such as Telford Smaller cities and towns across England have higher rates of young people not in employment, education or training than the nine largest cities, analysis shows. The Centre for Cities, an independent thinktank dedicated to improving the economies of the UK, used 2021 census data to work out the rates across 41 cities and towns in England. Of those places, 10 of the smallest cities and towns had higher rates of 16- to 24-year-olds out of employment and education – an average of 15.7% of their youth population, compared with an average of 13.9% across the nine largest cities . It comes amid a national debate over chronic youth unemployment in the UK, with the latest ONS data showing just under 1 million young people are not in employment, training or education (Neet). An interim report published by the former Labour cabinet minister Alan Milburn in May found that the UK was “at risk of a lost generation”, with young adults facing a “perfect storm” of challenges. His final report is expected soon after the budget on 28 October. The Centre for Cities analysis shows London (117,095) and Birmingham (44,995) have the highest number of Neets in absolute terms, representing rates of 13.1% and 15.9% respectively. The average Neet rate across England is 12.6%. In Blackpool , 2,660 of young people are not in education, employment or training, a rate of 21.2%. In Slough, 2,170 young people are Neet (14.1%). The Shropshire town of Telford has 2,780 Neets (15.1%). Rob Johnson, a senior analyst at the Centre for Cities, said the higher rates of Neets in smaller towns and cities were often a reflection of their general economic performance. In particular, he said such areas could be affected by their proximity to larger cities, but the figures could also be a reflection of the weakness of bigger city economies in the north and Midlands. “A big root cause of higher rates of Neets in these places is because we know these are cities that have weaker economies,” he said. “The big headline [is] of 1 million Neets across the country but it’s actually more important to understand where those people are. The scale is important, but you just need to know the extent of the variation across the country.” Johnson said the picture was mixed across smaller cities and towns. “Somewhere like Slough, which is actually quite a productive economy, does have a relatively high rate of Neets. There’s an issue there about connecting those people to the local economy.” For some in Telford , 30 miles north of Birmingham, the answer to the UK’s chronic crisis of youth unemployment may lie in its local shopping centre. The Skills Shop, a new youth employment hub opened by Telford College in partnership with the Department for Work and Pensions, aims to connect young people with education, local employers and mentors to tackle the high Neet rates in the region. Sarah Davies, the executive director of employer engagement and partnerships at Telford College, said there were multiple drivers for the Neets crisis, including the Covid-19 pandemic, mental health disorders and changes in the job market, and there was no “one size fits all” solution. “It’s a national concern because young people are our future. If you’re out of work, you’re more likely to stay out of work,” she said. “If you ask any young person, they’d rather be working than sat at home. Nobody wants to sit at home on TikTok all day.” Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning One of those benefiting from courses at the college is George Bate, 21, who is learning to become a HGV driver after graduating from university with a degree in games design. He said he had been unable to pursue a career in gaming due to a lack of opportunities and so embarked on the HGV course after he was signposted by the jobcentre. “I’d applied to most of the stuff around the area and just didn’t get a response, so that was the disheartening part. I couldn’t find anywhere that was willing to take me,” he said. “A lot of the time, it’s not even a person who reviews any of your [applications].” When asked about narratives surrounding young people being “lazy”, Bate said there was a lack of employment opportunities as well as an absence of career progression. “It makes it so much more stressful to find a career when you know that some of them don’t have the correct amount of upward mobility,” he said. Charlie Pryce, 19, is also taking the HGV course and said he had applied for other jobs but faced several barriers to further training and employment. “People our age, we’ve got a long life ahead of us and we actually want to do work. We might not start off the best but I think we can grow into the role,” he said. “It’s not nice sitting around not doing anything. It’s nice to get out there and do stuff and feel like you’re actually providing something and just working hard.

events.title: The ultra-rich are spending one million dollars a day fighting California’s proposed billionaire tax
events.summary: Tech billionaires have raised more than $340m to defeat Prop 40, a one-time 5% wealth tax that will fund healthcare and education Tech billionaires have been dumping hundreds of millions of dollars into the fight against a wealth tax in California . They’ve raised more than $340m, and the campaign they’re funding is spending more than $1m a day to defeat the measure, according to state financial disclosures. With the election less than a month away, those funds are being spent at a stepped-up pace. During the first 19 days of September, according to the most recent campaign filings, the opposition campaign plowed through at least $21.2m to fight the billionaire tax – surpassing $1m per day. Voters are being inundated with robotexts, mailers and advertisements that warn a tax on billionaires would “expose all Californians to higher taxes”, as one ad reads. Californians will vote on the ballot measure, Proposition 40, in early November. If passed, it would require a one-time 5% tax on the state’s billionaires, with the proceeds mostly funding healthcare programs, along with some education and food assistance. The measure has divided Democrats in the state, with some giving enthusiastic support and others rejecting the proposal because it’s just a one-time levy and the bulk of it would only fund certain healthcare programs. The state’s major unions and progressive politicians like the Vermont senator Bernie Sanders and California congressman Ro Khanna back Prop 40. But both the Democratic and Republican candidates for governor, as well as organizations like Planned Parenthood Affiliates of California, a lobbying branch of the healthcare group, oppose it. Among its fiercest critics, however, are the tech billionaires it would most directly apply to. The donors to the no campaign are a who’s who of Silicon Valley , including the Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, DoorDash CEO Tony Xu, Stripe CEO Patrick Collison, crypto magnate Chris Larsen and several prominent venture capitalists. The biggest donor, by far, is the Google co-founder Sergey Brin , who has contributed at least $102m to fight the tax, according to campaign finance filings. The runner-up is Schmidt, who has donated more than $42m. For comparison, the yes on 40 campaign has raised a total that’s just shy of $33m, mostly from the healthcare union sponsoring the measure. Proponents and opponents alike are casting the billionaire tax as a potential first step toward wealth taxes in more states. While those against the measure see it as populist contagion , those in favor connect it to the top issue of the midterms – affordability. And with California having more billionaires than any other state, Prop 40 is seen as setting the stage for more referendums on wealth inequality throughout the country. “There’s a lot of volatility among the electorate surrounding a pushback against Marie Antoinette and her tech friends,” said David McCuan, a political science professor at Sonoma State University who studies ballot measures. “And that’s what the ‘yes’ forces are relying on.” Recent polling on Prop 40 shows that it’s favored to pass, but its lead has shrunk over the last few weeks as the opposition campaign has increased spending. A late-September poll by the University of California shows 45% of voters likely to vote yes on the tax with 42% voting no. Just a month earlier, the proposal enjoyed a 7% lead . Complicating matters are two separate countermeasures that Prop 40’s opponents successfully placed on the November ballot, Proposition 41 and 42. Prop 41 directly targets the billionaire tax, while Prop 42 is more of a general proposal to protect individuals from certain new taxes. If either of these measures receives more yes votes than Prop 40, they will stop the billionaire tax from taking effect – even if it passes. “Props 41 and 42 have poison pills in them to destroy 40,” McCuan said. “And when voters are confused, when they are uncertain … it’s much easier to get a no vote.” Earlier this month, the campaign fighting the billionaire tax placed an ad on television, digital and streaming platforms across the state. It starts with quiet, foreboding music and the president of the California Medical Association, René Bravo, dressed in a white lab coat, saying: “The people pushing Prop 40 say it’s supposed to improve healthcare. That’s not true.” The campaign has debuted similar ads saying teachers, carpenters and firefighters also oppose the wealth tax, saying it’s “a dangerous experiment”. The messaging around the campaign centers on how the tax would hurt “doctors, teachers, small businesses, working families and public safety”, without mention of the state’s billionaires. The no on Prop 40 campaign calls it “an everyone tax”. Likewise, the campaigns for the two measures that would pre-empt the billionaire tax argue these proposals promote transparency and have the backing of small businesses and taxpayers.

events.title: For restaurants Covid-19 was a crisis – pandemic loans are proving a disaster
events.summary: Low-interest loans kept many eateries afloat. But the industry never recovered enough for them to repay the debt F or almost 20 years, Jai Mazumdar has served vegetarian curries, samosas, gulab jamun and other Indian delicacies at Spice N Curry, a cafe and grocery nestled inside a modest strip mall near Florida International University (FIU) in Miami. When the Covid-19 pandemic devastated his business, as it did with so many restaurants, Mazumdar took out a $370,000 economic injury disaster loan (EIDL) from the federal government in early 2021. At the time, it provided a desperately needed lifeline. He was confident that once business returned to normal he could begin repaying the 30-year loan, which came with a low 3.75% interest rate and a 30-month deferment period. But when his business didn’t recover, the disaster loan turned out to be a disaster of its own. The Spice N Curry cafe relied heavily on traffic from FIU. Since many students and faculty were studying and working remotely both during and after the pandemic, Mazumdar’s lunch business took a major hit. As the losses mounted, he applied for additional EIDL funds and was extended another $87,000 loan the following year. Borrowers with EIDLs totaling more than $200,000 were required to personally guarantee the loan, which meant that if they default, the government would be able to seize their personal assets. Five years later, Mazumdar is struggling to make his monthly payments, and he’s losing faith that he’ll ever be able to fully repay the loans. Since Congress passed the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (Cares) Act in March 2020, the federal government has issued 3.9m Covid-related EIDLs totaling $378.4bn to businesses that faced hardship as a result of the pandemic. The Small Business Administration (SBA) was tasked with administering the loans – up to $2m per individual applicant. Despite the attractive rates and flexible terms, according to a congressional report released earlier this year, EIDL defaults have steadily risen to over 30%, resulting in $75.2bn in charged-off loans as of last June. “Covid was an extinction event for tens of thousands of restaurants,” said Erika Polmar, executive director of the Independent Restaurant Coalition, a non-profit advocacy group for independent bars and restaurants in the US. “The ones that survived, if they didn’t receive [restaurant revitalization fund] grants, had to pay off all that debt from small businesses loans or EIDLs. Local initiatives that promised rent relief or eviction moratoriums often fell through. So they moved through 2022 and beyond trying to pay off their debt and weren’t able to reinvest in their businesses.” Mazumdar says his business is worse off today than it was during Covid – a sentiment echoed by other operators whose businesses have been negatively affected by rising food, labor and energy costs. “There is a tsunami going on right now,” he said. “Rents are very high. The average population doesn’t have spending power. There is a lack of qualified labor. Tourism has also declined here. Everyone is just nervous about when the next leg of the stool is going to collapse.” Five years after he took the loans, Mazumdar says the EIDL money is gone. Initially, he used the funds to refurbish the space and upgrade equipment, installing new refrigeration and freezer units to increase his retail inventory. He used the rest to cover operating expenses. After finally reopening the cafe in 2022, sales declined so badly that he decided to close the dining room permanently after just a year and a half. “My monthly EIDL payment is $1,900, and my home mortgage is $1,600,” he said. “I had to rent out a room in my own home so I could have extra income to cover part of the payment.” His business has lost money every year since Covid, yet he’s managed to stay current with his loan payments. “I’ve been working seven days a week, 12 hours a day for the last three years. It’s become a completely hand-to-mouth existence.” When borrowers exceed 120 days past due on their EIDL payments, the loans are transferred to the US treasury department for collection. That results in additional fees and penalties that typically amount to about 30% of the principal. When the loans are personally guaranteed, the IRS can garnish the delinquent borrower’s wages, tax refunds or a percentage of their social security benefits. Randy Barnette, founder of the Virginia-based Ornery Beer Company, is almost two years past due on a $500,000 EIDL he took out in February 2021. Before Covid hit, he was actively searching for a space to open a second location of the Ornery Beer Company Public House, his restaurant and bar that features Ornery brand beers.
