events.title: Stock fixing scandal could see Turkish companies frozen out of global indexes
events.summary: MSCI froze certain index-related changes for Turkish equities on Oct. 15, citing concerns about free-float reliability and market integrity. MSCI said that if sufficient progress is not evident by June 2027, it may consider a consultation on moving Turkey from Emerging Market to Frontier or Standalone status. Turkey’s regulator has ordered 131 funds managed by seven portfolio companies into liquidation after redemption defaults and turmoil in thinly traded stocks. A market manipulation scandal is continuing to rock Turkey, with the country's emerging market status coming under threat and the country's listed companies now at risk of being frozen out of global indexes. Allegations began swirling in the fourth quarter of 2025 that investment management firms were artificially inflating stock prices by piling into small, illiquid listed companies with low free float rates. Turkey's Capital Markets Board (SPK) later said the investments in the stocks "could not be explained by economic realities or by the financial fundamentals of the companies concerned." In September, Pusula Portföy became the first asset manager ​to report a fund default, with rival Tera Portföy saying in the following days that two of its funds had also defaulted. Turkey's benchmark BIST 100 stock index plummeted 16.7% in the month of September. Deep losses and redemption pressure at a swathe of investment funds saw SPK step in and order the liquidation of 131 investment funds days later. The funds ordered to liquidate collectively oversaw assets worth around 1 trillion Turkish lira ($20.2 billion). On Sept. 21, Borsa Istanbul announced that dozens of stocks that had been at the heart of the scandal would be removed from the BIST 100 at the start of October. On Thursday, index provider MSCI threatened to revoke Turkey's status as an emerging market in the wake of the scandal. It said it was applying a freeze on certain index-related changes for Turkish equity securities, effective immediately and until further notice. "As part of the MSCI 2026 Market Classification Review, MSCI highlighted serious concerns raised by institutional investors about possible coordinated trading through fund holdings closely affiliated with certain smaller listed companies, which undermines the reliability of free float estimates and market integrity," the company said in a statement. "MSCI noted that it would look for tangible and credible progress, including granular and timely disclosure of beneficial ownership, robust surveillance and enforcement against coordinated trading behavior, and a transparent rules-based framework for identifying and treating securities with structurally distorted free float." The equity freeze means Turkish companies won't be added to certain MSCI indexes or moved into larger-company indexes. Existing companies won't receive higher index weightings as a result of changes to their share counts or the proportion of shares available to foreign investors. "Should sufficient progress not be evident by June 2027, MSCI will consider additional measures, including a consultation on a potential reclassification of the MSCI Turkey Indexes from Emerging Market to Frontier or Standalone Market status," MSCI added on Thursday. Turkey wasn't the only country in MSCI's firing line on Thursday. The index provider said it was also launching a proposal to reclassify the MSCI Indonesia Indexes to "Standalone Market" status, effectively downgrading Indonesia from emerging market status. MSCI said it had reported in June that market participants were raising "significant concerns regarding the investability of the Indonesian equity market." These included "persistent opacity in shareholding structures and suspected coordinated trading behavior," it added. "While the Indonesian authorities have announced reforms, including enhanced disclosure of shareholders with ownership above 1%, more granular investor classification disclosure, High Shareholding Concentration (HSC) reporting, and a roadmap towards a minimum free float requirement of 15%, institutional investors have emphasized the need for consistent implementation and evidence of sustained material impact from these announcements," MSCI said. "Market participants have indicated to MSCI that, to date, sufficient progress has not been observed consistently across the Indonesian equity market. Despite the announced reforms, significant concerns remain around market dysfunction, including continued suspected coordinated trading behavior and lack of evidence of meaningful enforcement." It said an existing freeze on Indonesian securities in MSCI Indexes would remain in place until further notice.

events.title: How UN chief Antonio Guterres tests the limits of quiet diplomacy
events.summary: Portugal's Prime Minister Antonio Guterres called President Bill Clinton from Lisbon on August 30 and September 8, 1999, to discuss the growing crisis in East Timor. The small Southeast Asian territory, which had endured a brutal Indonesian occupation since 1975, was again engulfed in violence after voters overwhelmingly chose independence in a referendum. Pro-Indonesian militias responded to the vote for independence by unleashing a so-called "scorched-earth" campaign, destroying infrastructure, displacing up to half a million people and killing thousands. The crisis resonated in Portugal, where linguistic, Catholic, and historical ties to its former colony helped fuel a solidarity movement. An estimated 10,000 demonstrators, dressed in white, formed human chains through Lisbon’s city streets. Guterres had raised the issue before. At a 1996 summit in Bangkok, he met Indonesia’s President Suharto and broached the politically sensitive topic of East Timor, offering to restore diplomatic relations (severed since the 1975 invasion) in exchange for the release of Timorese resistance leader Xanana Gusmao. The proposal was met with an awkward silence. This time, Guterres was asking the United States to support a UN mission in East Timor, but Washington was reluctant to confront Indonesia. Guterres recalled in his 2022 biography, “Honest Broker”, that he warned Clinton during the second call that Portugal could reconsider its Balkan deployments if the international community failed to intervene. Portugal’s contribution to NATO was small but politically well-placed, with its troops serving in the alliance’s prominent post-Cold War missions in Bosnia and Kosovo. Guterres offered Clinton a choice: risk a public falling-out with a founding NATO ally, or use Washington’s influence to make Indonesia accept an international force in East Timor. The next day, amid growing international pressure, the White House stated that Indonesia “must” allow international assistance. For Guterres, it was an early test of multilateral crisis diplomacy, a skill set he would later bring to his post as UN secretary-general in 2017. East Timor, also known as Timor-Leste, finally won its freedom in 2002. For spearheading diplomatic efforts during the 1999 crisis, Guterres was awarded Timorese citizenship in 2024. “Antonio Guterres pushed a lot for what we now call the referendum, and when violence broke out he was one of the people calling for a UN intervention,” said Christine Cabasset, a teacher at Lille Catholic University and an expert on East Timor, reflecting on how the East Timor crisis foreshadowed Guterres’s later career. “Guterres had a critical role all along the way,” she added, noting how he later pushed for the creation of the UN Transitional Administration in East Timor. “There is also a kind of love story with the UN, I mean, that strong link between Timor-Leste and the UN… Multilateralism, which is still really the purpose of the UN, has been critical in the independence of Timor-Leste. And Guterres [himself] became very important in the UN starting from 2005.” Guterres’s response to the East Timor crisis reflected an approach shaped by his Catholic faith, his early work with Portugal’s poor and his political coming of age after the fall of a dictatorship. He carried those experiences into a career built on finding common ground and helping people caught in crises. But as UN secretary-general, he has faced the limits of that approach, struggling to turn appeals for peace into action when the world’s most powerful countries are at odds. Antonio Manuel de Oliveira Guterres was born in Lisbon on April 30, 1949, to Ilda Candida de Oliveira Guterres and Virgilio Dias Guterres, a senior employee of the Lisbon gas and electricity company. He spent summers and extended periods in the countryside with his grandparents in the small village of Donas. His childhood friend Vitor Dias told the newspaper Publico that Guterres’s grandmother stressed the importance of education and by “three or four years old, he already knew how to write his name.” The grandparents’ house was right next to the church where “Little Toni” often served as an altar boy. Portugal was then under the rule of dictator Antonio Salazar, whose Estado Novo regime closely resembled Italian fascism, but with less emphasis on brute force, personality cults and revolutionary zeal, and more on Catholic conservatism. As a result, the country was politically and culturally cut off from much of democratic Western Europe. “As dictator, [Salazar] was very much marked by corporatism, the idea of an organic society without conflict and also by Roman Catholic conservative values,” said Antonio Costa Pinto, a historian at the University of Lisbon. “But especially in the late 60s and early 70s … it basically became a Cold War dictatorship, an anti-communist one.

events.title: Replit’s CEO says the future of work is the ‘self-driving company’
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Replit CEO and co-founder Amjad Masad has seen how AI is impacting the workplace firsthand, with businesses adopting his company’s AI coding tools to develop and launch their own software. At TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco on Thursday, Masad shared what Replit has learned about what that means for the future of work in the AI age, including how humans will still play key roles as AI agents come to work alongside them. He described his vision of a “self-driving company,” referring not to robotaxi makers, but how agents will come to do much of the grunt work at companies while people become more valued for their judgement and taste. “The reality is, all of our jobs — perhaps everyone in this audience, especially — changed over the past year,” he said, addressing the audience at Disrupt. “But a big part of America and the world, they still don’t know that that change is coming, and it’s going to be surprising to a lot of people,” Masad said. He said Replit’s team had been reflecting on how AI technology impacted their own workplace over the past year, particularly after AI agents became more reliable sometime earlier this year. “Our company entirely changed how we operate, and I would say the closest analogy is a ‘self-driving company’,” Masad said. “The company is sort of self-improving, so a lot of the work that’s going on is driven by agents.” Illustrating the shift, Masad said that when support tickets come in at Replit, they’re first examined by an agent, which performs the initial triaging by looking at GitHub issues, the codebase, and Linear tickets. By the time the support request reaches a person, they have all the additional information that helps them decide how best to proceed. And when that support person decides to submit a patch to apply a fix, it’s just a click to deploy another agent. “You have an entire loop where agents did most of the work, but crucially, there’s human judgment in the middle, and we don’t think that’s going away anytime soon. You need human judgment; you need taste,” Masad explained. The end result is that instead of taking jobs from people, agents are changing what people work on. “We’re spending a lot more time figuring out what to work on,” Masad continued. “I go around the company, I see a lot more discussions, a lot more whiteboarding. We spend a lot more time on architecture, how to build things. And so I think the future of work — the self-driving company idea — is really trying to discover what AI transformation means.” He also noted that when Replit talks with other businesses, the conversations are more about how AI can help people become more productive and happier at work. (The latter because the AI agents make work less boring and more creative, he said.) “There’s a positive vision of the world that Silicon Valley is not really putting out, and we’re hoping to do that,” Masad added. events.title: Pro-Nazi chants before Hajduk Split-Ajax UEFA Europa League match slammed
events.summary: Croatia’s Hajduk Split hosted Ajax on Thursday, but chants for pre-World War II regime precede UEFA Europa League game. Croatian leaders have slammed pro-Nazi and anti-Semitic chants by Hajduk Split football fans before their UEFA Conference League match against Ajax, while Israel’s embassy voiced shock. Groups of Hajduk Split fans, known as the Torcida, marched through the coastal town of Split before Thursday’s match chanting: “Crush the Jews”, “Rise up Adolf (Hitler)” and “Let’s go Ustasha”, referring to the country’s World War II pro-Nazi regime, local media reported. list 1 of 4 Man Utd veering towards crisis as Man City cloud hangs over Premier League list 2 of 4 Man United’s Martinez apologises for outburst after talks with Carrick list 3 of 4 Man United’s Martinez takes to social media to defend his criticism of club list 4 of 4 What led Manchester United’s Martinez to meltdown in Madrid – all to know Dozens of fans were detained before Thursday’s match for violence. During the match, Torcida fans set off flares and other pyrotechnics in the stands, forcing more than a 10-minute stoppage. An investigation was opened into the pro-Nazi chants and suspects are being detained, police said. President Zoran Milanovic in a Friday statement condemned the incident as “unacceptable and shameful”. He urged swift action against the perpetrators to “show that there is no place in Croatia for the glorification of Nazism and Ustasha ideology”. Israel’s embassy in Zagreb said on X it was “deeply shocked by the serious antisemitic incident that took place in Split and condemns it in the strongest possible terms”. Conservative Prime Minister Andrej Plenkovic also condemned “messages of anti-Semitism … completely at odds with the values we want to uphold in Croatian society”. Hajduk Split, who won the game 2-1, in a statement apologised to UEFA and Ajax who “witnessed scenes which we do not want Europe to remember”, while the Croatian football federation also condemned the incident. Croatia’s ultra-nationalist hardcore supporters have tainted the country’s image for years, notably by chanting pro-fascist slogans and displaying Ustasha symbols. The Ustasha regime killed and persecuted hundreds of thousands of ethnic Serbs, Jews, Roma and antifascist Croatians. Croatia were docked a point by UEFA after their fans painted a swastika on the pitch in Split in 2015, before a Euro 2016 qualifier with Italy. In recent years, the country has seen a growing tolerance for its pro-Nazi past, and critics accuse authorities of failing to sanction the use of Ustasha emblems.

events.title: Houthi strikes expose Saudi Arabia's vulnerabilities
events.summary: The deadliest week for civilians in the Gulf marks a turning point in the US-Iran war that has engulfed the Middle East from Beirut to Aden, and from Irbil to Salalah . Saudi Arabia stepped up strikes on Yemen’s Houthis after the group hit Riyadh’s airport 20 times this month, killing 17 people and injuring 333 . Despite Riyadh’s considerable air defenses and vast military spending, the militants have been able to outsmart the systems using relatively cheap drones and missiles. Iranian attacks on the Gulf have brought the region closer together, and the latest strikes by Tehran’s allies in Yemen have galvanized support for Saudi Arabia. Authorities in the region are reinforcing this message of unity: In today’s Friday prayer sermons in Kuwait, imams were instructed to praise the kingdom’s support during Iraq’s 1990 invasion and condemn the Houthis . Similar expressions of support were also voiced in Bahrain, Qatar, and the UAE. While security is by far the most pressing priority, new projections from the IMF have revealed the war’s deepening economic toll. Jihad Azour, the fund’s regional director, told Asharq Bloomberg that the Gulf’s financial reserves, diversified export routes, and government interventions have cushioned the shock . But the IMF now predicts a deeper contraction than previously expected, with GDP trailing pre-war forecasts even after energy production and trade recover. — Mohammed Sergie

events.title: Fed's Warsh withholds rate signal, praises recent global tightening
events.summary: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh, in his speech Friday in Bangkok, declined to offer clues on whether there will be an interest rate hike again this month. He acknowledged a "synchronous tightening" by central banks around the world, saying there are "no free riders." He expressed optimism that artificial intelligence will make economies that use it well more productive and wealthier, warning the road there will be “very bumpy.” BANGKOK — Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh refrained from signaling whether there will be another interest rate hike again this month, while acknowledging a "synchronous tightening" by central banks around the world. "I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year," Warsh said, reiterating his opposition to the use of forward guidance for markets that should rely on interpreting data. He also acknowledged that stance may disappoint anyone who had hoped for a steer ahead of the central bank meeting later this month. "It's a new chapter at the Fed [and] we're not in that business anymore," he said. Warsh spoke at a fireside chat with the International Monetary Fund's managing director, Kristalina Georgieva, as part of the weeklong IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Friday. "Alongside other recent comments from FOMC participants, Warsh's comments indicate that the FOMC is set to pause in October," Goldman Sachs economists led by Jan Hatzius wrote in a note. "We continue to expect a second and final hike in December." S&P 500 and Nasdaq futures edged higher following the speech, while stock market indexes in Asia and Treasury yields were largely stable. Warsh described the global shift toward tighter monetary policy as a common fight on prices. Central banks made their own choices under their own mandates, he said, but the result was "a synchronous tightening in monetary policy in most places around the world," which means "there's no free riders." Surging energy costs stemming from the Iran war and artificial intelligence investment boom are stoking inflation and pushing up borrowing costs around the world, just as global public debt is on pace to exceed 100% of the world's GDP, a level last breached in the aftermath of World War II. The U.S. government has insisted that strong growth would be the best way to grow out of its rising debt pile, dismissing IMF's warning that the plans of relying solely on growth won't work as something that needs to be taken "with a grain of salt." Warsh also expressed optimism about how AI will make economies that use it well more productive and wealthier, while warning the road there may be "very bumpy," and its near-term effect on employment is still uncertain. "I want you to hear from me optimism, but optimism leavened by the seriousness of purpose," Warsh said. A decade from now, he said, people will look back on the developments and "say this was hugely consequential." The Fed raised rates to a range of 3.75% to 4% last month, its first hike since 2023 . Traders see a 72.3% chance for the Fed to keep the interest rate unchanged at the Oct. 27-28 meeting, according to CME FedWatch, while the majority expect a 25 basis point hike at the December meeting.

events.title: British food and drink exports to EU collapse by more than a third since Brexit
events.summary: NFU analysis of official data shows falls in exports to UK’s largest trading partner since 2019 include 70% for sugar and 74% for egg products Exports of British food and drink to the EU have collapsed by more than a third since Brexit with eggs, chicken and potato producers badly hit, new figures show. Analysis by the National Farmers’ Union (NFU) of HMRC data shows a sharp fall in exports in the year to July compared with the same period in 2019, with sugar dropping the most, down 70%. Data for the first seven months also shows poultry exports fell 53%, with eggs and egg products sold for confectionary and baking industries down 65% for the same period. Full-year data from 2019 to 2025 showed an even deeper impact since Brexit with exports of eggs and egg products down 74%. The NFU president, Tom Bradshaw, said: “The EU is our largest trading partner for agri-food products, accounting for 68% of agri-food exports last year, but trade volumes have fallen over a third since 2019.” Boris Johnson’s government signed a deal on the UK’s future trading and security relationship with the EU in late 2020, after the UK’s formal exit earlier that year. Andy Burnham is reconsidering Labour’s red lines on EU membership under pressure to repair the economic damage of Brexit. Economists estimate the cost to the UK economy has been up to £240bn so far. Food exporters have long complained over the added paperwork that Britain’s exit has brought. Since Brexit all food exports are required to have customs paperwork with different codes for every single product. This includes, for example, every variation of an egg product, whether it is fresh, dried, steamed, shelled, or contains added water or sugar. The paper pulp used in egg cartons as well as the eggs also need health certification to show they are free of disease. Also hit hard by Brexit is the horticultural sector with seed potatoes from Britain, mainly Scotland, banned from the EU after trade negotiators failed to agree on equivalent standards in the Brexit trade and cooperation agreement in 2020. Horticultural exports fell more than 50%. Pre-Brexit, Scotland exported around 20,000 tonnes of seed potatoes, worth almost £11m, to Europe each year. Speaking in parliament earlier this week Andy Burnham said that Brexit trade barriers meant “entire truckloads of plants or fresh product can be destroyed because of a single missing stamp or minor paperwork delay”. He hoped to “land a positive outcome” in the upcoming UK-EU reset talks with a new agreement removing many of the sanitary and phytosanitary checks on fresh farm produce exports that came in after Brexit. Burnham told MPs: “Our largest food export, Scottish salmon, faces a 100% rate of document checks at the border, costing us around £100m in lost exports. “British burgers and other fresh meat products cannot be sold in the EU. Seed potatoes from Scotland and shellfish from Wales are banned. This is having a real impact on businesses and the agreement on the table could reverse some of that damage.” A deal to ease sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) checks was largely agreed in May giving food producers time to prepare for changes expected to come in next summer, but key details remain to be finalised. The NFU is calling for “transition arrangements” for some UK crops that have been grown with fungicides or breeding techniques not yet approved in the EU. This is to allow those harvesting this autumn and winter to make use of the new export freedoms when they come in next year. Bradshaw said: “British farmers and growers must retain access to precision breeding technologies that will help to strengthen food resilience to extreme weather and to science-based plant protection products that help protect food being grown for 29m households from pests and diseases. “Any changes must also provide an appropriate transition period to minimise disruption for farm businesses and we will continue to make this case to government while we await the final agreement.”

events.title: 26% of Americans say influencers have swayed their vote. Political campaigns are racing to win them over.
events.summary: YouTuber Jake Paul joined President Trump for an Ohio rally ahead of the midterm elections. Aaron Schwartz/Stringer/Getty; BI The battle for voters in the 2026 midterm elections is playing out on the TikTok For You Page. One in four Americans say creator content has influenced who they voted for. Political candidates are scrambling to connect with more creators in order to reach voters. Content creators are influencing much more than our coffee orders and skincare routines. About one in four Americans (26%) say influencer content has affected who they've voted for, according to a survey of around 2,000 US adults conducted by Morning Consult in September, commissioned by Business Insider. Creator content is an "underestimated avenue" for political campaigns, said Nicole Dunger, a founding partner at the marketing firm People First, which works with candidates and advocacy groups on their creator strategies. "It is a real player and a big player in this space now." If 2024 was the podcast election , 2026 is shaping up to be the influencer one. Instagram and TikTok creators have joined Fox News hosts and personalities like Joe Rogan as go-to sources of information for voters. Influencers like Jake Paul and Hasan Piker have emerged as main characters in politics this year. Paul recently joined President Donald Trump in Ohio for a midterm rally, posting TikTok clips of his Air Force One flight. Piker, meanwhile, has become a campaign ally for progressives like Michigan's Abdul El-Sayed and a negative talking point for Fox News commentators. As online attention has become a key asset in politics , influencers are helping candidates break through the noise. A little over half of US adults (56%) told Morning Consult that creator content had affected their views on political or social issues to some degree. That figure jumped among Gen Z respondents, where close to three in four respondents said their views had been swayed by influencer posts. For campaigns, the challenge is identifying the right creators to work with, particularly when many influencers don't regularly talk about politics. "You have to have your base of people, your core supporters, and then you have to have a broader cultural space of people who don't always talk about politics," said Parker Butler, a managing partner at the digital strategy firm Luminary Strategies, which works on social strategy with Democratic candidates like James Talarico. "It's worth having different pockets of creators for different purposes." Reaching creators with smaller followings than Piker (about 3 million Twitch followers), or Paul (around 21 million YouTube subscribers) is a focus in 2026, Butler said. He said the goal is to shift the creator outreach strategy from "this person has a million followers" to identifying influencers who work in a particular niche a campaign is trying to reach. Political chatter is moving from TV to YouTube More and more, political discussions are playing out on digital platforms, whether that's podcasts, YouTube videos, or Twitch streams. YouTube was the top source for political and election news among US adults in September, narrowly beating out TV, print, and X (formerly Twitter), according to a survey from Syracuse University. About one in five Democrats and Republicans said podcast appearances could make them "more likely to support a candidate," according to a July through August survey of likely midterm voters from the podcast industry group Sounds Profitable. A smaller share of Independents (11%) said podcasts could make them more likely to back a candidate. While campaigns see attention moving online, they're still spending the bulk of their ad budgets on TV . Part of that may be because they're accustomed to buying TV spots . They're also reckoning with the fact that influencer marketing is harder to predict and measure, particularly as social-media feeds become more personalized and algorithmically driven . "It can be very challenging, but you see the results in the end," Dunger said. "It's the same with door knocking. We know door knocking somehow works and has worked for so long, but it's not like we have those direct measurements." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: RIP, neoliberalism. Its ghosts live on
events.summary: Neoliberalism is over. Around the world, the populist left and right are rejecting it. As a political term, it’s a dead man walking, even as its market-based policies still shape major economies. This isn’t a eulogy for free enterprise, which Americans strongly support. It’s a eulogy for a word that has lost its meaning and stands in the way of a real debate about markets and the role of government. In the Wall Street Journal , James Lloyd Dusenbury recently argued that our political vocabulary, including communism and capitalism, is obsolete. Neoliberalism belongs on the list, too. Start with the obvious: no one agrees what it means. Even Stanford’s Encyclopedia of Philosophy doesn’t offer a single definition. To its defenders, it’s the belief that markets work better than governments, which have a limited role in regulating capital and distributing wealth. To its detractors, it’s shorthand for whatever they dislike about global capitalism: billionaires, technocrats, Silicon Valley, immigration, even Pete Buttigieg. In short, it’s a zombie word.  Second, no one identifies with it. There are socialists, libertarians, progressives, and conservatives. Where are the neoliberals marching in the streets? Like neoconservatism, it’s a label used in academia, media, and think tanks, not real life. Third, it’s a Frankenstein word, and at seven syllables, a long one. “Neo” means new. Liberalism can mean anything from Adam Smith to LBJ. New Liberalism? No wonder people are confused. So, what are we really talking about? When the populist left says neoliberalism, it usually means high prices, billionaires, and corporate power. When the populist right says it, it usually means trade, immigrant labor, or technocrats.  Look at France. Emmanuel Macron, long the face of French neoliberalism, is leaving office very unpopular, and polls say voters are looking to the far left and right for his successor. Even Canada’s Mark Carney, a hero to many Democrats for standing up to President Trump, has been tarred by the left as a neoliberal .  What does neither side mean? Free enterprise. According to Gallup, 77 % of Americans view free enterprise favorably . Just 55% say the same of capitalism. The gap suggests Americans distinguish between the two. The distinction is especially sharp among Democrats. Despite all the talk of their socialist turn, 65% view both socialism and free enterprise positively, while only 35% view capitalism that way. They don’t see the first two as mutually exclusive. Big business, however, stands at just 35%, behind socialism at 43%. Small business, by contrast, scores 95%. This suggests the public’s real objection is corporate power, not enterprise itself. Even Gallup concludes the numbers don’t point to a “wholesale movement away from markets and toward socialism.” Here, socialism and neoliberalism share the same brand problem . Many Americans support policies associated with socialism, like expanded health coverage, while most oppose it as an economic system. Although they’ve cooled a bit on capitalism in recent years, they still associate free enterprise with choice, innovation, and personal advancement . So, are Americans closet socialists or closet neoliberals? Economic swingers, perhaps? The truth is these labels don’t describe what they really want. As Dusenbury points out, words change. During the Reagan-Thatcher and Clinton-Blair years—neoliberalism’s apex—it meant deregulation, international trade agreements, or the Washington Consensus. Now it’s a pejorative, a way to signal “this is bad” without saying what or why. That’s a problem, because there are real policy questions that need answers. Do Americans want free enterprise with bigger guardrails, a Nordic-style welfare state, or state-directed industry? How open should trade be? Those are choices voters can debate. They can’t debate a word that means billionaires to one group and Uber Eats to another. So, say what you mean . If you want to criticize corporate power, call it that. If you oppose data centers or H-1B visas, explain why. If you want better health care, advocate for it. Neoliberal policies will continue, whatever we call them. Even as some Americans look fondly to Canada and Western Europe, with their generous welfare states, these countries have market economies with plenty of private enterprise. Where, exactly, is this magical, market-less world on a map?  As a word? Neoliberalism is history. events.title: 3 fine-print disclaimers from Musk and Tesla about the new flying Roadster you should probably know about
events.summary: Tesla's Roadster fires its cold-gas thrusters. Tesla Elon Musk unveiled Tesla's flying, thrust-powered Roadster with a jaw-dropping demo. Tesla fans about to shell out as much as $250,000 to reserve it should probably read the fine print. Tesla said it can't guarantee the Roadster will be delivered, and it's unclear if the rocket-powered version is street-legal. Where Tesla's going, you might not need roads — but you still need to read the terms and conditions. Tesla's thruster-powered, midair flip-kicking, flying supercar was a wow moment even by the standards of the company's famously off-the-rails product unveilings. But Tesla fans lining up to pay as much as $250,000 to reserve the new Roadster , which can do 0-60 mph in under a second thanks to a system of cold-gas thrusters, should probably take a close look at the fine print. Tesla's Roadster executes a gravity-defying flip. Tesla The company's T&Cs make it clear that the final price of the bleeding-edge EV — which comes in Performance, Thrust, and Rocket variants — has yet to be determined and state that there are no guarantees the Roadster will ever be delivered. Meanwhile, it is unclear whether the two thruster-powered versions of the Roadster will actually be road-legal. After combing through the Roadster's reservation agreement and Musk's comments at its unveiling, here's what you should know before splashing out on Tesla's most outlandish vehicle yet. 1. It's not clear where you can actually drive it As the dust cleared on the jaw-dropping Roadster showcase , one key question remained unanswered: where exactly will you be able to drive it? At the event, Musk said the cold air thruster-powered flying Roadster would be an actual "car that someone can own," not just a one-off concept demonstration. But the Tesla CEO added that he was "not sure it's necessarily legal in all jurisdictions," and when an audience member asked if it would be street-legal, Musk was vague. Elon Musk said the Roadster would enter production in 2028. Tesla "Depends on your street. But it'll be a viable car," the billionaire said. The flying Rocket variant shown in the demo is invite-only. It's listed on Tesla's website with the caveat that it is "not approved for public road use." The gravity-defying stunts, flips, and barrel rolls shown off at Thursday's unveiling were performed without a driver in the car for safety reasons, and Musk described the vehicle as "not necessarily a safety-optimized car." By contrast, Tesla describes the Performance variant — which costs $50,000 to reserve — as "road ready" with its fan-suction system providing "next-level performance on and off the track." That suggests the goal is for the base version of the Roadster, at least, to be road-legal. The limited-edition Thrust variant, meanwhile, is described as "race ready," implying that this version might be exclusively for driving on race tracks. That would not be unusual for a high-end hypercar, with Ferrari , Pagani , and Bugatti all selling track-only supercars that don't adhere to normal vehicle regulations. 2. It could cost more than you signed up for Shelling out up to $250,000 for a Roadster reservation by no means guarantees that you will get one at that price. According to the terms and conditions of Tesla's Roadster reservation agreement, the fees for the Performance and Thrust variants are only an estimate, as the company is still "working on what options, features and hardware the vehicle will have." Tesla unveiled a less science-fiction version of the next-generation Roadster in 2017. Tesla The final purchase price will be confirmed closer to the start of production, the document said, with the (fully refundable) reservation payment going toward the actual cost of the car. 3. Delivery is not guaranteed The T&Cs also advise reservation holders that the Roadster is still "under development" and Tesla "cannot guarantee when your vehicle will actually be delivered or if it will be delivered." This will likely bring back bad memories for Tesla fans who paid $50,000 to reserve the next-generation Roadster when it was first unveiled in 2017 . That version of the Roadster, a more conventional supercar that could still hit 0-60 mph in 1.9 seconds, languished in development for years and ultimately never entered production. The delay caused some long-suffering reservation holders like Musk's  arch-rival, Sam Altman,  and tech YouTuber  Marques Brownlee,  to cancel their orders in frustration after waiting nearly a decade for a car that never arrived. Tesla fans will be hoping that history doesn't repeat itself. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: Phoenix Suns owner Mat Ishbia predicts team will win opening round playoff series — and the NBA season hasn't even started
events.summary: Phoenix Suns owner Mat Ishbia told CNBC Sport his team will make the playoffs — and win its opening round series. The team was ousted in the first round last season. Ishbia said he's working with NBA Commissioner Adam Silver on bringing a new contest to All-Star weekend. Ishbia, CEO of United Wholesale Mortgage, said the company's 80% share decline in the past 12 months won't lead him to sell the Suns. Get the CNBC Sport newsletter directly to your inbox The CNBC Sport newsletter with Alex Sherman brings you the biggest news and exclusive interviews from the worlds of sports business and media, delivered weekly to your inbox. Mat Ishbia says owning the NBA's Phoenix Suns and the WNBA's Phoenix Mercury isn't enough — winning is what he really wants. Ishbia has owned the Suns and the Mercury since 2023. He and his brother, Justin, own a minority stake in MLB's Chicago White Sox. Justin will take over as controlling owner of the Sox in the coming years . But unlike billionaires such as Stan Kroenke, Josh Harris and John Henry, who all own multiple teams, Ishbia says he's not interested in building a sports conglomerate. He's only interested in buying teams if he thinks he can move the needle on winning. "I have different goals. Those guys are obviously doing great things. But my view is not to be some sports empire," Ishbia told CNBC Sport in an exclusive interview. "I'm not making investments in sports. I'm buying a team that I can impact and help win and help compete and do some cool things with the fans." That's not a common message among many sports investors these days, who seem to be desperate for ways to put their money into live sports teams even as valuations climb higher and higher. Ishbia said that as the owner of both the Suns and the Mercury he's extremely hands-on. "I'm very active in the Phoenix Suns and Phoenix Mercury at a high, high level right now, and I get very much in the weeds," he told me. "If I can't impact it in a positive way, I'm not going to do it. So I'm not just making investments here and there." That puts pressure on Ishbia to deliver. The Mercury made the WNBA Finals in 2025 but fell back to 16-28 this year, making them one of the worst teams in the league. The Suns shipped All-Star forward Kevin Durant off to the Houston Rockets and still managed to make the playoffs last season (where they were swept in the first round by the Oklahoma City Thunder). But this season the Western Conference is stacked with teams with credible championship ambitions, including the Thunder, the San Antonio Spurs, the Denver Nuggets, and the Minnesota Timberwolves. That said, Ishbia isn't shying away from making concrete predictions about this season for the Suns. "You should be thinking that we're going to be better than we were last year," he said. "As in, we're going to make the playoffs. We're going to win the first playoff series." Ishbia bought the Suns and the Mercury for a combined $4 billion. Less than four years later, CNBC values the two teams together at just shy of $7 billion. Ishbia told CNBC he recently turned down an offer for a small minority stake in the team ("a couple percent") that would have valued the two teams together at more than $8 billion. "I think most people will put my basketball teams, the Suns and Mercury, at between an $8-and-$9 billion valuation right now, and I think that that's going to continue to grow," Ishbia said. Mark Walter, CEO of Guggenheim Partners and TWG Global, agreed to sell his majority stake in the Lakers in August, less than a year after acquiring control of the team. Prior to the transaction, there had been a flurry of media reports about federal criminal and civil investigations into the accounting and disclosures involving Walter's insurance businesses. In August, TWG Global issued a statement saying, "despite what has been reported, there has been no fraud." Ishbia says the Walter sale has put more attention on his outside businesses — primarily United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM), the nation's largest mortgage lender. Ishbia and his family control the company, and Ishbia is the CEO. UWM shares are down about 80% in the past 12 months amid a weak housing market. In 2024, Hunterbrook Media investigated UWM's alleged practice of turning independent mortgage brokers into non-independent funnels for billions of dollars of mortgages. "Litigators and mortgage experts say UWM's conduct could constitute fraud and run afoul of laws passed after 2008 to protect borrowers," Hunterbrook reported . At least two lawsuits were filed against the company in the wake of Hunterbrook's analysis. Some of the claims are ongoing and some have been dismissed by a judge. In August, UWM suspended its dividend. Hunterbrook wrote another story questioning the hedging practices of the company.

events.title: Remote work made these colleagues more open with each other, not less
events.summary: Many employees see having the freedom to work from home as a benefit. DigitalVision/Getty Images If you need to participate in video meetings for work, you’ve probably experienced more than one disruption, whether it’s kids darting around or home renovation noise. Meetings that use Zoom and similar software are a fixture of remote work, which surged during the COVID-19 pandemic and remains prevalent. As of August 2026, 36% of American workers in management, professional and related occupations did at least some of their work from home, according to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. I’m a management scholar who studies how, when and where people work . Before the pandemic began, I was studying a professional services company. That made it possible for me to follow how its staff transitioned from primarily working in person to mostly remote through 2024, which gave me more insight into how remote work has changed people’s lives. The study included 275 interviews and about 330 hours of observation. Most people in the groups I followed ended up working from home four or five days a week, joining meetings by video. What I found was the opposite of what I expected. Learning more about colleagues Rather than pulling colleagues apart, remote work brought them closer and made them more willing to be open with one another. The findings were peer-reviewed and will be published in an upcoming issue of the management journal Organization Science. Before the shift to remote work, I assumed – consistent with the predictions made by many prominent researchers of workplace relationships – that moving people out of the office would break down social connections. But I was wrong. In the office, before the shift to remote work, I found that people primarily viewed one another as work colleagues rather than whole people. Reflecting this relationship, workers sometimes said they felt uncomfortable sharing with one another aspects of their lives that might limit their ability to do work. For example, one worker I interviewed, Patrick, was afraid to tell his colleagues he could not work late one night because he was helping his mom. All the names I’m mentioning are pseudonyms to protect the privacy of the people involved and their employer. “Even though you didn’t sleep last night, you’re expected to show up and smile and be fine,” said Tamara, an exhausted parent with two young children, when she was still commuting regularly to the office. Surprisingly, people told me that they learned a lot more about one another once they began to work remotely instead of being together in an office. During my research, I heard about children yelling in the background and pets wandering in front of cameras. A spouse arriving home from work stopped to say hello on screen. In team chat channels, people posted photos of their children, their animals and the meals they had cooked. “Everyone has noises in the background, or they have something going on or whatever, and so we get to know each other quicker and on a deeper level than we would otherwise,” Tamara told me. In some cases, this increased sense of closeness happened to people who had known each other for years prior to switching to remote work. When you’re a remote employee, you may get more quality time with your pets. Moment/Getty Images Growing psychological safety Psychological safety is the sense that you can take an interpersonal risk at work, such as admitting a mistake, asking for help or raising a problem, without being judged negatively. Decades of management research tie psychological safety to important outcomes for both workers and organizations, including learning, creativity and speaking up . Over time, working remotely seemed to improve psychological safety for many of these co-workers. People became “less afraid to talk about the interface of their personal and professional lives,” Leah said. Before, she added, no one would have volunteered that a breakup was affecting them and that they needed a day off to decompress. After the company went remote, people told me they felt more comfortable sharing their own challenges as they tried to juggle their work and the challenges they faced in their personal lives. Supporting work and nonwork activities And as people started sharing these problems with their co-workers, they also told me they felt as if they could then better support one another. When one worker’s father fell ill, his colleague, Brooke, took over the tasks the two had planned to do together. “I’m just going to take this over for you right now,” Brooke told him. “And then, whenever you can, come back and swoop in.” The colleague was able to dedicate time to caring for his father. And importantly, because help circulated this way, Brooke said, a task no longer “stopped dead in the water” when one person could not get to it. This deeper collaboration did not seem to come at the expense of getting tasks completed. As an employee I’m calling Charles explained, having co-workers sharing details about their personal lives has “helped us to work more effectively in a lot of ways.” Crucially, these improvements were experienced by people with many different living arrangements – young and old, those with and without kids or partners, men and women. And these benefits were positively reinforcing. For instance, sharing more meant learning more about others, which further reinforced psychological safety. My findings suggest that remote work can be a benefit that employers and employees may overlook. Rather than treating time out of the office as a cost to social connection among employees, they might treat it as a way to grow personally and get to know co-workers better. Vanessa M. Conzon does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

events.title: Pakistan orders school inspections following deadly roof collapse
events.summary: Families demand justice for the 35 people killed; relatives say they had warned that the roof was leaking. Authorities in Pakistan have ordered inspections of regional schools after the collapse of a classroom roof killed at least 34 children and a teacher. Reports on Friday said that the government has ordered the administration of the northeastern province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to launch the checks after the deadly incident at Al-Khair school on Thursday. list 1 of 3 Imran Khan’s PTI braces to fight federal takeover of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa list 2 of 3 Violence in Pakistan over emergency rule in Imran Khan stronghold list 3 of 3 School roof collapses in northwestern Pakistan, killing at least 35 people At least 34 students aged 13 or younger, as well as a teacher, were killed in the roof collapse. There are conflicting reports about whether the inspections will cover both public and private schools or only private schools. The province’s education department has been given three days to report its findings, according to The Associated Press news agency. Schools are to be classified as safe, in need of repairs or improvements, or potentially unsafe. Various structures will be assessed, including roofs, ceilings, walls and staircases. Police arrested Mohammad Khan, the owner of Al-Khair school, shortly after the roof of mud and bricks collapsed. The building was structurally weak, according to Peshawar Police Chief Saeed Ahmed, who also said that Khan had told officers that recent rains had weakened the structure. Bereaved families are demanding justice, with some of the victims’ relatives maintaining that they had warned Khan about rainwater repeatedly seeping into classrooms. Dozens of mourners gathered outside the school on Friday to remember those who died. Pakistan’s construction standards are widely reported to be poor and builders commonly use substandard materials. The roof of a private tutoring centre in the eastern city of Lahore collapsed in June , killing 14 people.

events.title: We spend 7 months a year near our grandkids in Texas. The other 5 are for us in Florida.
events.summary: Valerie and Glenn Cherry split their time between Tampa and Florida. Courtesy of Valerie Cherry Valerie Cherry was thrilled when her first grandchild was born. She wanted to be a hands-on grandma. The mom-of-one yearned to be closer to the young family but was reluctant to leave her hometown. With 1,000 miles between them, she found a "middle ground" by renting nearby for half of the year. This story is based on an interview with Valerie Cherry, 68, a clinical psychologist from Tampa, Florida. It has been edited for length and clarity. My husband, Glenn, 68, and I were delighted when our first grandchild — a little girl —was born four years ago. Our son, Jamal, is an only child, and we are a very close-knit family. We rushed from our home in Tampa to help him and our daughter-in-law, Sierra, who had settled 1,000 miles away in Houston, with the demands of a baby. Do you have an interesting arrangement for caring for your grandchildren? Please send details to Jane Ridley at jridley@businessinsider.com if you'd like to share your story. Our trips lasted between a month and six weeks, and there was a lot of to-ing and fro-ing between the two cities. We'd either stay with the family or rent Airbnbs to give everyone a bit of space. The Cherrys enjoy an active social life in Tampa. Courtesy of Valerie Cherry. It felt great to be hands-on and useful, especially because Jamal and Sierra work very hard in finance and forensic psychology, respectively. Back home in Florida, though, we lived life to the full in our gated, suburban community. Glenn, a relief veterinarian , and I had meaningful friendships there. We knew lots of people, particularly fellow alumni from our colleges in Georgia . There was always something going on, like book clubs and fundraising activities. Then our grandson was born two years ago. We continued our long visits to care for him and his sister, flying between the two cities. We started to look at places in Houston Soon after his birth, Jamal and Sierra approached us about what it felt like when we weren't there. They were a bit nervous and wanted to know whether we'd consider moving close by. We were torn. As much as we wanted to be with our grandchildren, we valued our time in Tampa. Still, we started to look at places in Houston. The trouble was that if we were to purchase something in Houston, it would have had to be in the suburbs . Traffic is terrible, so it would have been around a 40-minute drive to my son's. The Cherrys dressed as superheroes last Halloween to trick-or-treat with their grandkids in Houston. Courtesy of Valerie Cherry Another factor was that we didn't want to be tied down by taxes, insurance, and all of that in Texas because we didn't want to give up our home in Tampa. I Googled other options and came across a building called Landing right in downtown, a little over 10 minutes from the family. It was different from other arrangements because you could stay there for as long or as short a period as you liked. We paid a membership fee and secured a two-bedroom apartment that was already furnished. The only things we brought were a couple of pots for the kitchen. We found a middle ground It now works out that we spend around seven months a year in Houston and five in Florida. However, the 4,800-square-foot house in Tampa is classified as our main residence. The apartment is much smaller at 1,600 square feet, but we like it very much. There are two swimming pools in the building, playrooms, and a basketball court. I feel like we have found a middle ground. We can spend quality time with our grandkids, especially when their parents are on a date or away for the weekend. We're busy planning for Halloween this year as it's a big thing for us all. We haven't lost our identity as grandparents Meanwhile, if one of the children gets a fever at day care or school, Glenn or I can pick them up. It's an extra pair of hands. We haven't lost our identity now that we're known as Nana and Papa. We regularly fly back and forth to Florida to enjoy the company of longtime friends. Our neighbors keep an eye on the house while we're away, too. It's reassuring. I know we're privileged to be in this position, but it really is the best of both worlds. events.title: Elon Musk cash infusion helps GOP Senate super PAC raise record $273 million
events.summary: The Senate Leadership Fund, the GOP’s main Senate super PAC, entered the final stretch before the Nov. 3 midterm election with more than $155 million in cash. Elon Musk's $158 million boosted SLF to raise a record $272.9 million in the third quarter. As the election map tightens, SLF has shifted money from North Carolina to Republican-held states including Kansas, putting more resources into defense. The Senate Leadership Fund , the Republican Party's leading Senate super PAC, posted the largest quarterly haul in its history and entered the final weeks before the Nov. 3 midterm election with more than $155 million in cash, according to a new Federal Election Commission filing Thursday. The SLF brought in $272.9 million from July through September, including $209.7 million from donors — including. Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk , who supplied the bulk of that money Musk poured $158 million into the SLF in September through an affiliated Texas PAC created to support Republican Ken Paxton. His two contributions of $75 million and $83 million are among the largest political donations ever. Musk's contribution alone also exceeded the Democratic Senate Majority PAC's entire third-quarter fundraising. That super PAC reported raising a record $151 million during the period and ended September with $111.8 million in cash, which the group said was its third-quarter record. The super PAC's FEC filings are not yet available. The SLF's haul shattered its own previous records. The group brought in nearly $116 million in the third quarter of 2024 and $111 million in 2022. In 2020, when it filed monthly reports , SLF took in roughly $157 million from July through September . Its previous quarterly high was roughly $216 million in the final three months of 2020, according to a CNBC review of FEC filings. The record influx gives Republicans a sizable financial cushion as they fight to preserve their 53-seat Senate majority across the country that has become increasingly defensive in the closing weeks of the election. The SLF paused additional advertising in perennial battleground North Carolina this month after spending more than $30 million there — according to AdImpact data — and redirected resources toward Kansas , where Republican Sen. Roger Marshall faces an unexpectedly competitive challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton. In Nebraska, SLF has committed $15 million to defend Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts, including $7 million through the affiliated Cornhusker Majority, The Wall Street Journal reported this week. Trump carried Nebraska by more than 20 percentage points in 2024. The super PAC has also been central to the Republican intervention in Texas, where Democrat James Talarico has turned what had been expected to be a safe GOP Senate contest into one of the most expensive races in the country. Republican groups spent roughly $122 million in Texas in September alone and had another $66 million in advertising reserved through Election Day as of the beginning of October, according to AdImpact data. Talarico announced Thursday that he raised $64 million in the third quarter, the largest third-quarter haul on record for a Senate candidate. Paxton raised $10.2 million , according to a FEC filing.

events.title: Anthropic’s IPO could be the biggest ever. Your AI budget helps explain why
events.summary: Good morning. Anthropic hasn’t filed its S-1 yet, but one of its early backers is already predicting the biggest IPO ever. A longtime Anthropic investor, who asked not to be named, told Fortune’s Shawn Tully that he expects the shares to be priced at around $1.8 trillion—below the company’s reported $2 trillion target. He predicts a post-IPO trading value of $2.3 trillion to $2.4 trillion , surpassing SpaceX’s $2.1 trillion market cap at the close of its first trading day. He argues that figure reflects Anthropic’s underlying worth, not a short-lived first-day pop. For finance professionals, however, the more consequential story may be the economics of enterprise AI. About 80% of Anthropic’s revenue comes from corporate customers, compared with roughly half of OpenAI’s sales, Tully reports. One reason the investor backed Anthropic, he told Fortune , was that it was “more of an enterprise play” than a consumer business. That enterprise focus makes his prediction about AI spending especially worth watching. He expects prices to fall as open models gain ground, even as usage continues to explode. For CFOs, that creates a familiar budgeting challenge: AI costs per unit may decline even as total spending keeps climbing. Lower prices don’t necessarily mean lower budgets when adoption is accelerating. Then there’s the valuation. A debut near $2 trillion would require enormous profit growth to justify it. The investor isn’t fazed, calling Anthropic “the fastest-growing company in history” and arguing that it can afford to slow down and still deliver substantial value. That’s his conviction, not yet a verdict from public markets. Read Tully’s full story here . Have a good weekend. events.title: I believe in AI. But my AI assistant gave me more work than it could finish
events.summary: I opened my daily to-do list and found 156 items. “Daily” was doing some ambitious work in that sentence. I’m a writer, publisher and entrepreneur. I expect a certain amount of chaos. There are manuscripts, emails, projects, follow-ups and the occasional administrative mystery that arrives disguised as a perfectly ordinary Tuesday. Still, 156 items suggested that my productivity system had developed career ambitions of its own. It was building a department. Soon it would need an org chart. Some of the work was already underway. Some items overlapped. Some were reminders about other reminders. Tasks that belonged together had become separate obligations, each carrying the emotional weight of an unfinished thing. I had asked for help getting work done. I was getting very good at maintaining evidence that work existed. I use AI, and I remain a big believer in what it can do. It helps organize ideas and get thoughts onto a page. Technology that makes expression and work more accessible matters to me. That is why I want to be honest about the less glamorous part: an assistant can generate work faster than it can finish it. Ask it to help with a project, and it may produce a plan. Ask it to improve the plan, and it may produce a checklist. Ask it to make sure nothing gets missed, and the checklist may develop subcommittees. Every item can sound reasonable on its own. Collectively, they can turn help into a second job. The problem starts with an easy confusion: identifying the next step feels like progress. Sometimes it is. A clear plan can get a stuck project moving. But a plan also has a comforting property: it can be created without confronting the hardest part of the work. A draft can sit there looking polished. A calendar can fill up with preparation. A task can be checked off because someone wrote instructions for completing it. Meanwhile, the email still needs sending. The application still needs submitting. The client still needs the finished file. A productivity system earns its keep when those things happen. After the 156-item surprise, I started insisting on a more useful question: What would “done” look like to the person who asked for this? For an article, that could mean a finished draft, if a draft was requested. If the request was to pitch it, “done” includes an actual pitch. If the request was to publish it, a document called FINAL_FINAL_REALLY_FINAL does not quite complete the journey. The distinction sounds obvious. It gets surprisingly slippery once work passes through several tools, checklists and assistants. Here are the changes I’m making. First, I want a daily list that reflects available capacity. For assistant execution, I’m aiming for roughly 25 meaningful entries on a weekday, while preserving real deadlines and necessary daily operations. The number is a working limit for my system, rather than a productivity prescription for everyone. Its purpose is to force a choice. If everything is due today, the list has stopped helping me decide what to do today. Flexible work can live in a backlog with a reasonable checkpoint. Waiting for someone’s response deserves a waiting status. A genuine deadline deserves space that has not already been occupied by 40 vaguely urgent reminders. Second, related work needs a home. A campaign may involve research, outreach, tracking and follow-ups. Those requirements still matter. Putting them under one clear execution item can preserve the work while reducing the number of separate things shouting at me. The details should remain available when they are useful. I don’t need every detail to greet me at the top of the stairs. Third, I want proof attached to completion. If an assistant says an email was sent, I should be able to see it. If it says something was published, I need the live link. If it says a file was delivered, I need the usable file and the delivery record. That proof also helps prevent duplicate work. A system that remembers what actually happened can stop proposing the same action with slightly different punctuation. Fourth, a blocker needs to be specific. “Unable to complete” gives me another mystery to manage. “The form requires an answer only you can provide” gives me a decision. “This browser session cannot access the account” identifies an access problem. The next question is whether anything else can move forward. One missing answer should not freeze every unrelated part of a project. Finally, I want the system to count outcomes. How many pitches actually went out? Which replies need an answer? What has been accepted? Which deliverables reached the client? What remains unfinished? I care about those numbers because they describe the work I was trying to accomplish. A magnificent list of possible actions describes the system’s imagination. These changes require judgment. Some days have more real deadlines. Some tasks take minutes; others need uninterrupted hours. A short list can still be unrealistic, and a long checklist can be useful inside a complicated project. The goal is a system that helps me see the difference. AI can be extraordinarily helpful here. It can reconcile records, find overlaps, preserve context and handle routine steps. But it needs instructions that reward finishing, checking and communicating honestly about what remains. It also needs permission to stop manufacturing another plan when the next useful action is already clear. I still want an assistant. I still want technology to make work easier and possibilities bigger. I would just like my to-do list to stop recruiting. events.title: The Download: failed social media bans, and extending pets’ lives
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Kids are outsmarting social media bans. That’s not a problem we need to solve. —Michal Luria, Aliya Bhatia, and Danah Boyd Social media bans are stacking up. In July, France joined Australia in restricting minors from accessing social media—barring children under 15 from major platforms, before the ban was blocked by the country’s top court on human rights grounds.  The UK aims to forbid kids under 16 from accessing Facebook, TikTok, and other platforms in early 2027, and the EU has announced its own plan to prohibit social media for kids under 15. But early lessons from Australia, which enacted a ban in 2024, show that these sorts of age restrictions are easily circumvented.  Here’s what we ought to do instead to keep kids safe . Can’t bear to say goodbye to your pet? Biotech’s got you covered. —Jessica Hamzelou I don’t remember much about Peppy, my first and only pet cat. What I do vividly remember, though, is the day she went missing. I was 10 years old, and I searched everywhere for her, scouting nearby fields and woods until sunset. I made posters. We never found her. I was devastated. Almost 30 years later, pet owners have an expanding set of options to potentially prolong their years with their furry companions. The possibilities include drugs, cloning, and even cryonics. But is that a good thing? Read the full story on the promises and pitfalls of pet life extension . This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday. 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Form Energy and its iron batteries Form Energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s  10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026 , available  exclusively to subscribers . As wind and solar power grow, utilities need cheaper ways to store electricity for longer periods. Form Energy aims to meet that need with batteries that can store energy for 100 hours. The company has developed a new type of battery using iron, a far more abundant and cheaper metal than those used in many existing batteries. It uses a process that Form calls “reversible rusting,” in which iron turns to rust as the battery discharges and back to iron when it charges. See how Form Energy hopes to make renewable power more reliable . —Jonathan W. Rosen Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch , spanning everything from electric buses to portable rubber dams . events.title: Influencer marketers are leaning into FOMO to cut through the noise
events.summary: Substacker Erika Veurink hosted a pop-up vintage sale for her readers at Rothy's. Courtesy of Rothy's A version of this post appears in the CMO Insider: Creator Brief newsletter. Sign up for Business Insider's marketing newsletter . The latest hot marketing KPI: RSVPs. Creators ranging from Substackers to "SNL" stars are jumping off the screen to in-person events — and marketers can't get enough. "IRL is the No. 1 brand equity builder of all the channels," said Justin Thomas-Copeland, CEO of the American Association of Advertising Agencies (4As). As it becomes harder to reach customers online, in-person events offer a way for brands to connect with their biggest fans — and hopefully inspire a flurry of social content. One night last month, Snapple turned a decommissioned Staten Island Ferry into a floating comedy club featuring Colin Jost and Pete Davidson. Lindsay Burstein , a top marketer at Snapple parent Keurig Dr Pepper, said the night resulted in about 200 pieces of user-generated content. "It is the buzziest thing that the brand has done in a very long time," she said. Snapple threw a "Snapple Island Ferry" event with comedians Colin Jost and Pete Davidson. Snapple Events aren't a new phenomenon, but interest from marketers is surging. In its annual survey of marketers, Linqia found that 53% said they planned to work with influencers on events in 2026, up from 34% in 2025. "We've seen an uptick in both custom brand pop-up experiences and brand activation at large events," Linqia's chief strategy officer Keith Bendes said. Influencer marketers are becoming event planners IRL activations and events can also help brands gauge the depth of a creator's connection with their audience — and how valuable partnering with them might prove. Substack creators, for instance, have "rabid fans and followers" who are hungry to connect in person, said Rothy's VP Anna Doré. After Substacker Erika Veurink's article for New York Magazine featuring Rothy's shoes went viral, Rothy's struck a partnership with the writer that included a vintage pop-up experience at a Rothy's in New York City. The Rothy's pop-up drew over 200 people and grew the store's foot traffic by 75% that day. There can be category-specific reasons some brands are going all in on events. Flushable wipes maker Goodwipes, for one, leans on IRL experiences, said SVP of marketing Meredith Diehn, "partially because it's an intimate category, but there's a lot of questions around flushability and why should I leave toilet paper for Goodwipes." Still, it can often be harder to measure success from an IRL event and prove it's an efficient use of marketing dollars. Beverage brand Poppi is also a fan of IRL events and pop-ups. Courtesy of Poppi "Live experiences is not an efficient business," Bilt CMO Zoe Oz said. "It's like the most inefficient, unscalable thing you can possibly do. But we found those to be 10 times more effective than the other ways we used to spend money." Events also aren't a foolproof strategy, Copeland of 4As said. There's a lot that goes into an experience, and if one part goes wrong or a creator is involved in an inauthentic way, criticism can spread quickly. They present practical challenges as well, sometimes forcing marketers to wear yet another hat: event planning. Burstein said that planning Snapple's comedy event — despite its eventual success — took her "blood, life, sweat, and tears." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: How to dress a tech oligarch: The Social Reckoning’s costume designer on Zuckerberg’s style evolution
events.summary: Susan Lyall worked with actor Jeremy Strong to research the Meta CEO’s favorite Nikes and luxury sweaters The first Aaron Sorkin Facebook movie, 2010’s The Social Network, helped cement the early aughts image of Mark Zuckerberg rebelling against corporate norms in rumpled hoodies and T-shirts. The follow-up, The Social Reckoning, is carbon-dated from 2019 to 2021. This is “post-hoodie”, as the movie’s costume designer, Susan Lyall, describes it, “post-thumbing his nose” to formality. It is also peak robot. Zuckerberg’s reserved wardrobe of suits or interchangeable long-sleeved shirts echo his chilling composure throughout, even as fury simmers under the surface. The costume was based on deep research by Lyall and also by actor Jeremy Strong who, she says, is “very into costume”. Having worked together before, on the Sorkin movies Molly’s Game and The Trial of the Chicago 7, they would text a lot during the preparation process. “He reaches out before I even get to reach out to him. It’s my third movie with him, so I’m pretty used to it. He’s very proactive. He’s one of my favourite actors because of that. He would know exactly where [Zuckerberg] wore what. He wanted the exact Nike shoe – the footwear was very important to him – and the exact Brunello Cucinelli T-shirt and sweater, and so on,” she says. Strong has become notorious for method acting, and method dressing, too, seems to be part of his process. “It’s sort of the first step in the performance. That and the haircut,” says Lyall. The conversations went deep. “It’s actually kind of nerdy, you know, to sit there and talk about the color of the shoelaces. There aren’t that many people who want to talk about that. I always joke with him, if the acting thing doesn’t work out, you can have a position in my department!” she says. Lyall found those Nikes – to be specific, the 2018 Nike Flyknit trainer in black anthracite – on Grailed. For the sweaters, it was Strong, she says, who worked out how to reach the eye-wateringly expensive Italian luxury brand Brunello Cucinelli, in order to buy specific pieces, “because we don’t want the latest. We want stuff from five or six years ago, and they were very helpful at procuring it. And that was because of him. He was really proactive.” Lyall has spent a lot of hours thinking about how tech oligarchs dress. Not only Zuckerberg but Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos and others too, who were partial inspiration for another of her recent credits, the 2025 Jesse Armstrong movie Mountainhead about four devilish plutocrats. They, too, wore a lot of Brunello Cucinelli. That brand sells cashmere cardigans for $16,500 and ribbed sweaters for $4,600. Amusingly, it currently has the Immanuel Kant quote “beauty is the symbol of the morally good” in prime place on its website homepage. In Lyall’s view, Brunello Cucinelli is a “safety net for people like Mark Zuckerberg. If they’re not sure about what they’re wearing, if they pay a lot for it, they feel a little better about it. You know, if this little sweater is $2,000, it must be good. It’s kind of a security blanket, or just an affirmation of your own success. You’re going to be OK if you’re wearing this tasteful thing.” The Zuckerberg of The Social Reckoning had moved on from the earlier antifashion stance that prompted him to declare, in 2014, that he was “not a cool person”, and only wore grey T-shirts because he wanted to make “as few decisions as possible … I feel like I’m not doing my job if I spend any of my energy on things that are silly or frivolous.” By the period captured in the movie, says Lyall, “I believe Zuckerberg was trying to be relatable, but also starting to understand Silicon Valley’s obsession with taste and the cost of things.” He was also more buff than he had been. In her interpretation, he seemed to be thinking: “My fit physique looks very nice in this clingy but expensive sweater. And ‘if you know, you know’ – I think there’s a bit of that. But I also think, he’s nouveau riche without being gaudy. It’s not without taste.” Since then, Zuckerberg’s outward presentation has graduated to outright peacocking. For the tech billionaires, in general, says Lyall: “I think something happened. I think they have discovered a new way to flex. And it’s not quiet luxury. It’s loud.” For Zuckerberg specifically – whose makeover came suddenly with ostentatious gold chains, Loewe shorts and Alexander McQueen suits embellished with dragonflies in around 2024 – it could not feel much more strategic. Dabbling with fashion allows Zuckerberg to look like a different guy from the one we have seen so many times sweating in a suit in front of Congress. It also provides a distraction from the reality of his products and work, giving him something soft and harmless to talk about. Zuckerberg has even used the classic fiction writer’s trick of embedding backstory within his jewellery.
