events.title: NVIDIA RTX Spark PCs Available Today — A New Beginning for Windows PCs
events.summary: News Summary: NVIDIA RTX Spark laptops are available today from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI — with additional systems to follow — bringing RTX acceleration and NVIDIA’s full-stack AI platform to slim, premium Windows PCs for creation, gaming and local AI. RTX Spark delivers up to 1 petaflop of AI compute and up to 128GB of unified memory — enabling AI developers, creators and gamers to run frontier AI models locally, render 90GB+ 3D scenes and play AAA games at 1440p at over 100 frames per second, all on a slim, portable device. Day-one support across local AI agents, creative apps and major games helps users put RTX Spark to work immediately — from editing with Adobe Photoshop and Premiere to running Hermes and OpenClaw agents and playing titles including Gears of War: E-Day and NBA 2K27 with NVIDIA DLSS 5. NVIDIA today announced the availability of  NVIDIA RTX Spark ™ laptops, bringing together RTX graphics and NVIDIA’s full-stack AI platform in slim, premium Windows PCs for accelerated creation, immersive gaming and powerful local AI — rolling out from ASUS, Dell, HP, Lenovo, Microsoft and MSI. Combining decades of NVIDIA innovation into a single superchip, RTX Spark delivers up to 128GB of unified memory and 1 petaflop of FP4 AI performance to run large language models and AI agents locally. On a single device, creators, developers and gamers can move seamlessly between their everyday workflows and emerging AI agents on the familiar Windows platform. “RTX Spark brings the power of NVIDIA AI, RTX graphics and CUDA together with Microsoft Windows in one PC for creating, gaming and running personal AI agents,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “Together with Microsoft and our PC industry partners, we’re bringing creators, developers and gamers a new generation of Windows PC, built for the work they do today and the personal AI agents they’ll work with next.” “We’re building Windows to be the platform for hybrid intelligence, where AI can run locally when it makes sense and reach the cloud when needed,” said Yusuf Mehdi, executive vice president at Microsoft. “Windows PCs powered by RTX Spark unlock powerful new local compute for creators and developers, expanding what they can create, build and run on Windows.” A New Beginning for Windows PCs RTX Spark brings NVIDIA’s accelerated computing platform to a new generation of portable Windows PCs. At its foundation is a single superchip combining an NVIDIA Blackwell RTX GPU and an NVIDIA Grace CPU with up to 128GB of unified memory and up to 1 petaflop of FP4 AI performance. That shared memory allows demanding creative projects and local AI models to run simultaneously and efficiently. MediaTek collaborated with NVIDIA on the custom CPU design, contributing to its best-in-class power efficiency, performance and connectivity. All of NVIDIA’s platform innovation comes together in RTX Spark — NVIDIA CUDA ® , DLSS, OptiX™, Reflex, G-SYNC ® , TensorRT™ and hardware-accelerated video — in a device that fits in a messenger bag. Slim, efficient designs and all-day battery life bring these capabilities wherever users create, develop and play. From Tool to Teammate RTX Spark gives users the capabilities to deploy local AI agents that turn the PC from a tool into an everyday teammate that can complete tasks, generate assets and write code. Users can put agents to work immediately. Guided setup and easy installers help users get started with agents, including GitHub Copilot, Hermes, OpenClaw, Perplexity, Pi and WorkBuddy, without requiring a command line. “Personal AI becomes more useful when it can work with your tools and help get things done,” said Dillon Rolnick, CEO at Nous Research, creators of Hermes Agent. “We brought Hermes to RTX Spark so people can put open AI models and agents to work locally on a Windows laptop, with greater control over their data and the freedom to shape AI around their own workflows.” NVIDIA’s models and tools build on that ecosystem. Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB, a 74-billion-parameter model optimized for tool calling and multistep tasks, brings more capable local AI to supported RTX Spark configurations. The NVIDIA OpenShell ™ secure runtime and Microsoft Execution Containers help users control agent permissions, while NVIDIA agent skills let compatible agents work with tools including NVIDIA Broadcast , RTX Remix and Omniverse ™ libraries. For example, compatible agents can adjust Broadcast effects during a stream or batch-process recorded clips, all on a local PC. That experience extends across devices with NVIDIA PAIR , letting RTX Spark serve AI inference to compatible Windows, Linux and macOS computers on a home network while keeping other PCs free for creating and gaming. Create, Innovate, Play RTX Spark helps creators move from an idea to finished content wherever they work, with the ability to edit 8K 4:2:2 video and render large 3D scenes up to 90GB, even when unplugged. With the arrival of RTX Spark, Adobe is enhancing its industry-leading creative applications, including Photoshop, Premiere and Substance 3D, with NVIDIA TensorRT acceleration in AI-editing features. In Premiere, creators can work faster across some of the most intensive parts of post-production, from playback and rendering to effects, color grading and more. Photoshop and Premiere offer native RTX Spark support through beta releases available at launch, with Substance coming soon. “Creatives are pushing the boundaries of what’s possible across image, video, audio and 3D, and they need tools that can keep up with their ambitions,” said Deepa Subramaniam, vice president of product marketing for creative professionals at Adobe. “By combining NVIDIA’s advanced computing technology with Adobe’s industry-leading creative applications, we’re delivering enhanced experiences that empower creatives to bring their ideas to life with greater power and speed.” For enhancing recorded content, NVIDIA Broadcast 2.3 lets creators remove background noise from existing recordings and shape their voice with Studio Voice Mic Profiles. Beta RTX Video features enable up to 4K super resolution and 4x frame generation. In ComfyUI, new RTX Video nodes can turn 15 frames-per-second (fps) AI-generated video into smoother 60 fps footage and convert it to high dynamic range without requiring per-use cloud inference charges. Code, Test and Deploy With One Machine As AI shifts software development from writing code to directing agents, work often spans a laptop, a cloud AI model and a cloud virtual machine for testing. events.title: Glassdoor President: finding the right job shouldn’t feel like winning the lottery
events.summary: Finding a job right now feels like a fool’s errand. Tailoring resumes, customizing cover letters, retyping the same work history into an endless stream of application portals, and then, more often than not, hearing nothing back. The problem isn’t that the search takes effort, it’s that the effort so rarely produces anything in return. The sense that a resume goes straight into a black box isn’t imagined – applications per job have more than doubled since 2022, and the average company now has 56% fewer recruiters to review them. Fifteen plus years ago, job seekers had a different kind of  problem. Workers had almost no visibility into what a company was actually like before saying yes to a job: the pay, the culture, how a manager treated people, whether what got promised in an interview held up once someone started. The information ran one way only. Glassdoor entered the picture to level the playing field for employees and job seekers with an infrastructure around workplace transparency. Anonymous employee reviews and ratings that let people see inside a company before applying worked because it gave job seekers something they’d never had: an honest, firsthand account of what they were walking into, from current employees with no reason to lie about it. That was an important starting place, but it was incomplete. Knowing what a company is like doesn’t tell a job seeker, or an employer, whether a specific person and a specific role are actually right for each other. A resume is a highlight reel and a job description is a wish list; neither says much about whether someone will thrive in the day-to-day reality of a job, or whether a company will deliver on what it promised. Get that match wrong and the costs compound in ways that are easy to miss: people end up in roles that don’t fit, their confidence and engagement erode, which costs the business too, and because leaving means stepping back into the same broken search, many just stay. Over the past two years, our data shows that burned-out workers are less likely to apply for another job compared to workers giving similar ratings. Employers are feeling that same gap. As part of Indeed, Glassdoor is also working to solve this problem from the other side of the hiring equation. Our CEO, Hisayuki “Deko” Idekoba, called the hiring process a “vicious cycle,” and the numbers back him up: 96% of people who changed jobs last year did it without a recruiter ever reaching out. Nobody designed a hiring process this broken on purpose. It’s the result of a decades-old assumption that more is better –  apply to more jobs and the odds improve, recruit more candidates and the right one turns up, compare enough resumes to enough job descriptions and a match reveals itself. None of that holds up anymore. Artificial intelligence is pouring fuel on that fire. When it’s used mainly to generate and process more applications, it doesn’t fix a broken hiring process – it accelerates it, making the experience worse for everyone, on both sides of the desk. Confidence is cratering alongside it: our most recent Employee Confidence Index showed that workers’ outlook on their employer’s next six months just hit a record low. Professionals are feeling it most acutely, and not because there’s a shortage of jobs. Software postings are actually up roughly 20% year over year, even with tech employment still 3.8% below its 2022 peak. The jobs are there – what’s missing is the confidence and right tools to go after them in a targeted way. For someone weighing a move, uncertainty raises the stakes, and a longer list of openings offers little reassurance that the next job will be a better match. What people need is a clearer picture of what they’re actually moving into. I think what more than a decade of that data points to is a narrower, more useful question than the one hiring has been asking. The question was never really “can this person get this job?” It’s “is this a place where this person is likely to do well?” A resume and a job description alone can’t answer that. Firsthand accounts of what it’s actually like to work somewhere can get much closer, and that’s the real opportunity sitting inside all the information the first wave of transparency generated but never fully put to use. That’s the idea behind Glassdoor Recruiter , which we launched this month; instead of asking people to sort through thousands of listings and guess which ones might be right, it surfaces a much smaller set of roles most likely to align with their experience, goals and the realities of the workplace, drawing on workplace insights rather than a resume and job description alone. Paired with the reach of Indeed’s hiring marketplace, people also get more say in how visible they are to employers, turning the search into a two-way conversation rather than a one-way application funnel.  The future of hiring is about helping more people find work that fits and more companies find people who can thrive there. It’s a problem worth solving, and fixing it is bigger than any one company or platform and will take more than better technology. It will take an industry willing to admit that giving people information was never going to be enough on its own. Because finding a job that fits shouldn’t feel like winning the lottery. events.title: Samsung Electronics exec: The investments that last build more than factories
events.summary: In Taylor, Texas, Samsung is preparing to open a new advanced semiconductor manufacturing facility. It began as the largest investment we had ever made in the United States. But the most important thing about Taylor is not the size of the facility or the dollar figure attached to it. It is what is being built around it. Samsung began manufacturing semiconductors in Central Texas nearly 30 years ago. Taylor builds on the workforce, institutional knowledge and supplier relationships developed through decades of operating in Austin. Hundreds of employees began working from the Taylor campus last year, some bringing years of experience from Austin, while Samsung prepared a new local workforce and expanded partnerships with schools and colleges across the region. Taylor illustrates a broader principle: Long-term investment is not a succession of disconnected announcements, but a sustained commitment in which each phase strengthens the foundation for the next. Samsung was founded in Korea, but we have been investing, manufacturing and hiring in the United States for nearly five decades. During that time, Samsung has invested more than $100 billion here, and our U.S. facilities generate more than $40 billion in economic impact and support more than 175,000 jobs. That experience has taught us that putting up capital is not the same as putting down roots. A facility can be built in a few years, but becoming part of a local economy takes much longer. It requires skilled workers, suppliers that can grow alongside the investment and institutions that prepare people for new opportunities. What that looks like will differ from one community to another. In Newberry, South Carolina, Samsung opened its first U.S. home appliance manufacturing facility in 2017. Since then, the facility has generated more than $900 million in economic impact for the region. Its longer-term value, however, also depends on whether the surrounding community is equipped to participate in and sustain the opportunities it creates. Companies should not wait until a position needs to be filled to invest in that capacity. As the skills required across manufacturing and technology change, workers will need more accessible pathways into new careers—and young people will need earlier opportunities to see themselves as innovators and problem-solvers. That is the idea behind Samsung’s Solve for Tomorrow program, which asks middle and high school students to use STEM to address problems in their own communities. In Newberry, for instance, students at Newberry High School developed a pollinator garden and composting system in response to a local sustainability challenge, connecting classroom learning with community problem-solving and career exploration. That project is part of a much broader effort. Since 2010, more than 620,000 students have participated in Solve for Tomorrow, with Samsung providing technology and classroom resources to more than 4,300 schools nationwide. The projects vary widely, but they begin with the same question: What is a problem in my community, and how can I help solve it? Giving students the tools to answer that question is different from building a manufacturing facility, but both can leave a community better prepared for what comes next. This is why global scale and deep local roots are not competing ideas. The strongest global companies measure success not only by what an investment produces today, but by what workers, institutions and communities are equipped to do tomorrow. As the United States marks its 250th anniversary, much of the conversation about its economic future is focused on what the country must build next. Communities receiving new investments have every right to ask a related question: What will remain after the announcement is made and the ribbon is cut? The answer should be more than a facility or a dollar figure. It should be people with new skills, stronger pathways into emerging industries, suppliers prepared to grow and institutions equipped to support future opportunities. Capital can build a factory. Durable investment builds the capabilities that allow companies and communities to keep moving forward together. events.title: Indonesia’s Danantara pledges $5 billion to home-grown companies as MSCI once again threatens a downgrade
events.summary: Indonesia’s sovereign wealth fund Danantara plans to invest $5 billion in Indonesian businesses over the next six to nine months, its chief investment officer said, a commitment made before MSCI proposed downgrading the country to standalone status, a move that has since sent the Jakarta Composite Index down 11.6%. “We’re encouraging our guys to focus on the fundamentals of Indonesian businesses because they’re growing healthily,” Pandu Sjahrir, Danantara’s chief investment officer, told Fortune on the sidelines of the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference in Singapore on Oct. 12. “Why wouldn’t we be buyers of these types of businesses? It’s our job to look at, support and buy great companies.” This comes as the sovereign wealth fund , launched by Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto in 2025, steps up as a stabilizer for the country’s stock market, currently under scrutiny from global index providers like MSCI. On Oct. 15, days after Fortune ’s interview with Pandu, MSCI proposed downgrading the country from emerging-market to standalone status . This would remove Indonesian stocks from MSCI’s emerging and frontier-market indices and prompt investment funds to consider reducing their exposure to the country. The country has until April 2027 to enact reforms. (Indonesia recently preserved its Secondary Emerging status in FTSE Russell’s annual count) That news sparked an 11.6% plunge in the benchmark Jakarta Composite Index. The index is now down just over 40% for the year —showing just how much Indonesia still needs to do to convince global investors to back its companies, and why Danantara is stepping in. “Once there’s a shift in perception, even if the fundamentals are good, the stocks will see a downturn,” Pandu admitted. “Overall, Indonesian consumer stocks are down over 20%, and that isn’t even as bad as those related to mining or energy.” ‘Economic value,’ not necessarily ‘commercial value’ Pandu, who made his name in the private sector, now has to focus on different metrics than a straightforward return on investment. “The idea is to create economic value, and not necessarily commercial value first—that’s an important distinction,” Pandu explained. “If the projects serve as a significant economic multiplier and remain within the cost of capital range, we’ll most likely fund it.” Danantara has four arms: asset management, investment management, the Danantara Development Management Fund (DDMF) and Danantara Resources Indonesia. The fund’s asset management wing supervises and corporatizes more than 1,000 of Indonesia’s state-owned enterprises, while its investment management segment seeks to maximize returns via bonds, public markets, and domestic and foreign equities.  The DDMF is Danantara’s arm with the strongest social mandate. It deploys long-term capital toward national infrastructure projects with high social yield but lower immediate commercial returns. Among them is the Giant Seawall Project , a multi-segment complex along the Northern coast of Java set to take up to 20 years to build, and a coal gasification program . A fourth unit—Danantara Resources Indonesia—fully launches next January. In Pandu’s telling, it’ll serve as a single digital platform that centralizes the exports of Indonesia’s natural resources, starting with its top three: coal, palm oil and ferroalloys. (The country is the world’s top exporter of nickel products , contributing over 60% of global supplies, according to Reuters.) “We’ll be using a lot of technology to ensure we do the reporting well,” Pandu said. “We’ll try to do those three [commodities] really well first, and then we’ll go from there.” Yet the snap decision to have Danantara take over exports— announced by Prabowo in May —has unnerved analysts who worry about encroaching state control of the economy, as well as at the sovereign wealth fund.  “Under normal conditions, investors might take more time to assess the policy details,” Dedi Dinarto, the associate director at strategic advisory FGS Global, told Nikkei Asia in May, when the proposal was first announced. “But when the rupiah is under pressure, and the equity market is already weak, introducing a new layer of state control mechanism over strategic assets can quickly become a confidence issue.” ‘Get paid to learn’ Pandu wants Danantara to double down on partnerships and human capital next year. On Oct. 6, Danantara announced it was investing $250 million in HighPeak Energy, a Texas-based oil and gas producer. “The collaboration is a way for us to learn about shale technology, which isn’t often seen in Indonesia,” Pandu said. “What we want to do is to learn about new technologies, how to de-risk them, and bring that knowledge back.” “If we are able to have some good downside protection, we get paid to learn,” he added. The sovereign wealth fund is also making strategic hires. In 2025, Danantara hired two executives from Singapore’s GIC, Daniel Lim and Weihan Wong, to lead its global private market coverage . Danantara now has around 500 employees.  “The way we look at it—at least during my time—is how we can bring the best human capital [to Indonesia], and encourage the transfer of knowledge for the benefit of Indonesians,” Pandu concluded.  And despite the challenges of running a sovereign wealth fund in a country scruntiny, Pandu said he still gets “butterflies” at work. ”I wouldn’t trade it for the world, man.” This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Current price of oil as of October 16, 2026
events.summary: At 7:45 a.m. Eastern Time today, oil was priced at $108.51 per barrel with Brent serving as the benchmark (we’ll explain different benchmarks later in this article). That’s a rise of $1.84 compared with yesterday morning and around $47 higher than the price one year ago. Oil price per barrel % Change Price of oil yesterday $106.67 +1.72% Price of oil 1 month ago $109.73 -1.11% Price of oil 1 year ago $61.23 +77.21% Will oil prices go up? It’s impossible to forecast oil prices with detailed precision. Many different elements affect the market, but ultimately it boils down to supply and demand. When worries about economic recession, war, and other large-scale disruptions increase, oil’s path can shift fast. How oil prices translate to gas pump prices Gas prices at the pump don’t only track crude oil. They also include what it takes to refine and move that fuel, the taxes layered on top, and the extra markup your local station adds to stay in business. Since crude oil generally makes up a majority of the per-gallon cost, changes in its price have an outsized impact. When oil surges, gas prices typically rise in tandem. But when oil retreats, gas prices often lag on the way down, a trend sometimes described as “rockets and feathers.” The role of the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve In case of emergency, the U.S. has a store of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its primary purpose is energy security in case of disaster (think sanctions, severe storm damage, even war). But it can also go a long way toward softening crippling price hikes during supply shocks. It’s not a long-term answer and is more meant to provide temporary relief, assisting consumers and keeping critical parts of the economy running, like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, etc. How oil and natural gas prices are linked Both oil and natural gas are key sources of the energy we use every day. Because of this, a big change in oil prices can affect natural gas. For example, if oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, which increases demand for natural gas. Historical performance of oil To gauge oil’s performance, we often turn to two benchmarks: Brent crude oil , the main global oil benchmark. West Texas Intermediate (WTI) , the main benchmark of North America Between these two, Brent better represents global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. And, it’s often the best way to track historical oil performance. In fact, even the U.S. Energy Information Administration now uses Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook. Looking at the Brent benchmark across several decades, oil has been anything but steady. It’s seen spikes due to factors such as wars and supply cuts, and it’s also seen crashes from global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example: The early 1970s brought the first big oil shock when the Middle East cut exports and imposed an embargo on the U.S. and others during the Yom Kippur War. Prices dropped in the mid-1980s for reasons such as lower demand and more non-OPEC oil producers entering the industry. Prices spiked again in 2008 with increased global demand, but it soon plummeted alongside the global financial crisis. During the 2020 COVID lockdown, oil demand collapsed like never before—bringing prices below $20 per barrel. All to say, oil’s historical performance has been anything but smooth. Again, it’s hugely affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more. Energy coverage from  Fortune Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage: Infrastructure and the grid needs to scale with AI—or else ‘Forget all the frontier models’ Chevron CEO warns oil buffers that cushioned the Iran war shock have been ‘drained’ Trump: Massive oil, gas and mineral exploration set to begin in ‘our new and beautiful’ Greenland Frequently asked questions How is the current price of oil per barrel actually determined? The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic. How often does the price of oil change during the day? The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing. How does U.S. shale oil production affect the current price of oil? In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply. How does the current price of oil impact inflation and the broader economy? When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf. events.title: Tesla's new flying Roadster did exactly what Elon Musk said it would in a post 8 years ago
events.summary: Elon Musk may have been years late on his Roadster deadline, but the tech Tesla showed off was just as described eight years ago. Win McNamee/Getty Images Musk described his plans for the Tesla Roadster during a 2019 exchange with YouTuber MKBHD. On Thursday, the Roadster did exactly as Musk promised nearly eight years ago, leaping into the air. While Musk missed his own deadline by years, the technology on display was just as he described it. It's been a long time coming. Almost eight years ago, in January 2019, Elon Musk shared plans on Twitter for Tesla's Roadster to lift off using cold-gas thrusters and ultra-high-pressure air. On Thursday, the much-anticipated Roadster did exactly that. Musk's 2019 assertion came in response to a user sharing a GIF of the DeLorean from "Back to the Future" hovering in midair. "The new Roadster will actually do something like this," he wrote. Tech YouTuber Marques Brownlee responded: "The thing is I feel like you’re not joking." "I'm not," Musk said. I’m not. Will use SpaceX cold gas thruster system with ultra high pressure air in a composite over-wrapped pressure vessel in place of the 2 rear seats. — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) January 9, 2019 He then described a SpaceX-made cold-gas thruster system that uses high-pressure air stored in a composite pressure vessel. At a SpaceX test site in Texas on Thursday, almost 8 years later, a Roadster climbed a curved ramp, dropped, rolled through the air and landed on its wheels. It used the same basic technology: cold-gas thrusters fed by high-pressure air stored in composite pressure vessels. The 2019 exchange was not Musk’s first mention of thrusters. In June 2018, he said the Roadster would include roughly 10 of them and suggested they might allow the car to fly. Using the config you describe, plus an electric pump to replenish air in COPV, when car power draw drops below max pack power output, makes sense. But we are going to go a lot further. — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) June 9, 2018 When another user proposed compressed-air cold-gas thrusters, Musk said that configuration made sense and described a pump to replenish the air. Musk's account of the technology has proved more consistent than his production timetable. Tesla unveiled plans for the second-generation Roadster in 2017 and originally targeted production for 2020. After repeated delays, Musk said in the reveal that production will begin in 2028. The Roadster is not Tesla’s only vehicle to miss an ambitious release target. When Musk unveiled the Cybertruck in 2019, he said Tesla expected production to begin in late 2021. The first customer deliveries took place two years later, in November 2023. While Musk has missed plenty of deadlines, many of his more improbable technology plans have made it beyond the drawing board. In December 2020, he said SpaceX would try to catch a returning Super Heavy booster with its launch tower. We’re going to try to catch the Super Heavy Booster with the launch tower arm, using the grid fins to take the load — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) December 30, 2020 Nearly four years later, the tower’s mechanical "chopsticks" caught one for the first time. The tower has caught the rocket!! pic.twitter.com/CPXsHJBdUh — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 13, 2024 Musk has a habit of promising the improbable well before it is ready, but eventually, the improbable part arrives. events.title: Lowball retention bonuses doomed Perella-Piper Sandler merger
events.summary: The Scoop A merger between two Wall Street boutique firm collapsed after senior bankers balked at their retention bonuses. The deal between advisory firm Perella Weinberg Partners and investment bank Piper Sandler envisioned paying Perella’s highest producers $2.5 million in shares of the combined company to stay on for as long as three years, according to people familiar with the matter. The rest of its partners were split into tiers and offered bonuses of between $500,000 and $1.5 million. Perella CEO Andrew Bednar called some partners individually to describe their retention packages and gauge their reaction, the people said. They were almost uniformly negative, with the offers deemed “offensively low,” in the words of one banker, compared to the millions that top dealmakers at the firm make per year. That opposition led to the talks ultimately falling apart, some of the people said. The Financial Times earlier reported that the deal had collapsed . A spokesperson for Perella did not respond to requests for comment. Perella Weinberg went public in 2020 and had seen its shares lose half their value since early last year. Bednar had sought a deal with at least one other bank earlier this year, although talks only progressed with Piper, some of the people said. Rohan’s view Expect to see a wave of departures from Perella in the coming weeks and months. Recruiters at rival banks are already fielding calls and making their own, I’m told. Bankers don’t want to work at troubled businesses, and seeking a deal signaled just that. Perella, the junior partner in these talks, had been seeking some kind of deal for months before alighting on Piper. Bankers, especially rainmakers, have healthy egos. It’s difficult enough to lock them up, but it’s a critical step in talent-driven mergers like this. Failing to do so highlights exactly the risk that companies take when they try to strike deals.

events.title: ‘Trying to dominate’: In Cyprus, some fear Israel’s growing influence
events.summary: Shackled, bleeding, raped: Abuse in Israeli prisons Does Trump have real leverage over Netanyahu? Israel now reaches into Cyprus’s water, gas, health and defence and a number of Cypriots fear their island is losing control. Nicosia and Limassol, Cyprus – Heavily bearded and wearing a loose shirt, Christos Achniotis speaks about the history and demographics of Cyprus and runs off dates from memory. He was 16 when Turkish troops landed in Cyprus in mid-1974. At one point, Limassol has long had a large Russian community, he said, but that revolved around property investments. list 1 of 3 Why has Greece signed a $3.5bn missile deal with Israel? list 2 of 3 Deep-sea search begins for 20 people missing in Cyprus ferry disaster list 3 of 3 ‘Each country goes its own way’: How Balkan politics shape ties with Israel Now, he believes there is pressure from Israel, which he says is “trying to dominate as much as possible, land-wise, company-wise”, as well as politically and militarily. Israel’s reach in Cyprus now runs through the state’s most vital systems. Mekorot, Israel’s state water company, helps supply the island’s water. Israel Aerospace Industries, a state-owned arms maker, is supplying its new air defences. And Israeli firms run a growing hospital network and hold a stake in the country’s largest gasfield. Israel’s economy is about 15 times Cyprus’s, according to the World Bank, and Israel’s military spending is about 73 times that of Cyprus. Cyprus’s government presents the ties as a security alliance against Turkiye, but several Cypriots interviewed by Al Jazeera said they feared their country is handing another state control of systems it cannot live without. Israel is “a small area with big money and a big military”. Cyprus is strategically placed in the Mediterranean and, just a 35-minute flight away, is an attractive piece of land, said Achniotis. Cyprus gets about 80 percent of its drinking water from the sea. With its dams just 21 percent full in March, desalination plants supply most of what comes out of its taps, according to the Water Development Department. Agriculture Minister Maria Panayiotou said in June that desalination would cover almost all domestic demand by next year. Mekorot has joint ventures with Cypriot firm Netcom that run two of the island’s five permanent plants, at Larnaca and Episkopi, according to the Water Development Department. In August, Mekorot expanded its cooperation with Cyprus, signing a memorandum with the Nicosia District Water Board to help manage water and sewerage in the capital. For Danae Laou, who works in hospitality in Limassol, the water deals crossed a line. “It’s terrifying to see, but at the same time, we have no power,” she said. Today’s occupation of Palestine is in part facilitated by control of vital resources. “I can see the same thing happening here”, she said. In the occupied West Bank, the company is on the United Nations list of businesses linked to illegal Israeli settlements. Najla Abdellatif Vallander, a Swedish-Palestinian environmental advocate who founded Zero Waste Palestine, has tracked Mekorot’s work in Palestine and abroad and told Al Jazeera that its operations in the West Bank are akin to “water theft”, diverting Palestinian sources to illegal Israeli settlements. “Israeli settlers are able to enjoy almost unlimited amounts of water while Palestinians are not allowed to use their own water sources,” she said. Palestinians “have to buy back their own water sources from Mekorot”, and are mostly barred from digging their own wells. “This is water apartheid,” she said. At the time of publishing, Mekorot had not responded to Al Jazeera’s request for comment. Israel’s economic footprint has grown fast. Investors in Israel held 5.1 billion euros ($5.7bn) of investment in Cyprus at the end of 2024, more than six times what they held in 2017, according to the Central Bank of Cyprus. The true figure may be higher as the data excludes Israelis living in Cyprus or elsewhere, and may miss money routed through companies whose owners are hard to trace. The Tel Aviv Stock Exchange is also weighing a bid for the Cyprus Stock Exchange, which the government is privatising, Cyprus Mail and the Israeli business daily Globes reported this month. The Cypriot exchange’s European Union licence would give Israel “greater access to the Eurozone market”, a source close to Cyprus’s Ministry of Finance told the Cyprus Mail. Hadassah Medical Centre Limassol, the Israeli hospital group’s first centre in Europe, began seeing patients in July and was formally opened on Thursday. Its opening was ratified in Israel by Hadassah’s governing bodies, including the Hadassah Women’s Zionist Organization of America. Offshore, Israel’s NewMed Energy owns 30 percent of the Aphrodite gasfield, according to its filings to the Tel Aviv Stock Exchange. The two governments are also negotiating over the field, which Israel says extends into its waters.

The billionaire, who hosted a demonstration of the Tesla Roadster 2 at the SpaceX rocket development and testing facility in Texas, said the sports car could go from 0 to 60mph in a record time of less than a second and had thrusters. A video of the event shows the Roadster, which he said was controlled remotely “to make sure we don’t kill anyone”, driving up a curved ramp using suction to grip upside down, before using thrusters to flip, fly and land . Later in the demonstration the Roadster is seen using the jets to leap over a line of Tesla’s existing models and then accelerate to 60mph in record time. “Turns out the future does have flying cars,” Musk said in a post on his social media site, X, accompanying a video from the event. Speaking at the event on Thursday, Musk said: “Flying cars are real. It’s got altitude controls, thrusters and main thrusters in the rear. So it can basically fly like a rocket, it can do rolls, crazy gymnastics.” “I’m not sure it’s necessarily legal in all jurisdictions,” Musk said, adding that the prototype was “not necessarily a safety optimised car but it takes the fun meter to 11”. In 2014 Musk expressed his scepticism about a future with flying vehicles . However, three years later he announced the development of the Roadster 2, which will go into production in 2028 and priced in excess of $200,000, (£150,000), to create an electric sports car “to give a hardcore smackdown to gasoline cars”. events.title: New details about Khaby Lame's $975 million deal deepen the mystery
events.summary: Khaby Lame has been pursuing other partnerships as his big payday remains in question. Simon Galloway/LAT Images Khaby Lame's splashy $975 million deal is still on ice nine months after it was announced. Lame's plan to merge his business with a publicly traded firm was celebrated by creator economy insiders. The public company's stock price has fallen 99% since its January high. A new financial filing provides fresh details — and more questions — about a mysterious $975 million deal struck by TikTok's top star, Khaby Lame . On January 9, Lame — who has over 160 million followers — entered into an agreement that would theoretically net him a major payday and take his company public. The mechanism: a merger with the publicly traded Rich Sparkle Holdings , a financial printing firm based in Hong Kong. Then, in late January, Lame went silent on the merger. Now, we have an update: the deal is still on ice. A Rich Sparkle financial filing on September 30, its first since March, described the deal as conditional on a due diligence process, a minimum valuation of Lame's company, and stock exchange approval. That's the same language that has appeared in previous filings. While the deal has been in limbo, Rich Sparkle's stock has plummeted 99% from its peak. In the wake of the announcement of the deal with Lame's company in January, the stock shot up to a high of about $180. On Thursday, it closed at $1.93. Several prominent brokerages had restricted or blocked trading in the stock , Business Insider exclusively reported in April. The original deal announcement was celebrated throughout the creator economy , since such rich valuations are rare among influencer-founded companies, and it would give everyday investors an unusual opportunity to directly bet on a creator. The high profile of Lame, a Senegalese-Italian creator who rose to fame from dialogue-free comedy videos, means the outcome of the deal could impact how investors assess the viability of backing businesses centered on individual creators. The January deal terms promised Lame's company 75 million shares, which would be worth about $145 million at Thursday's closing share price. The initial agreement had valued that stake at $975 million. Rich Sparkle and Lame did not respond to multiple requests for comment. At the time of the original announcement, Rich Sparkle said that it planned to create an AI avatar of Lame to do brand deals and sell products on social media. It projected this business could drive more than $4 billion in annual product sales. An unusual stock detail The new filing contains another intriguing detail: Rich Sparkle issued nearly $39 million in stock to its staff as part of their compensation during the six months ended March 31, resulting in an operating loss of almost $40 million. In the year-earlier period, it issued no share-based compensation. This new share issuance means some employees could have benefited from the stock's massive spike following the Lame deal announcement. The filing doesn't indicate which staffers received shares or exactly when they got them within that six-month period. Paul Nary, a management professor at Wharton, said the size of the share issuance was unusual relative to the company's valuation and revenue. If the deal is in motion, we haven't heard a peep from Lame, who removed Rich Sparkle's stock ticker, ANPA, from his social-media bios in late January. The content creator continues to post for brands, recently making a cameo in the James Bond-inspired video game "007 First Light," signing on as a brand ambassador for travel eSIM company Holafly, and promoting the Dakar 2026 Youth Olympic Games. events.title: Anthropic and General Catalyst: the market is mispricing resilience
events.summary: In 2001, Amazon’s stock had fallen roughly 95% from its peak and many of its dotcom peers were in liquidation. But Amazon had spent 1999 building fulfillment capacity far ahead of demand, expanding from 300,000 square feet to more than five million. When the crash came, that excess capacity gave Amazon optionality. It opened its network to other retailers and independent sellers, turning idle warehouse space into a platform business. Resilience is a growth asset that markets still price as an afterthought. For most of the last century that was defensible: resilience meant surviving disruption, a defensive property rewarded only in hindsight. But as disruption becomes more frequent and varied, the companies that absorb shocks fastest are the ones that grow while competitors retrench. AI accelerates this divide. It threatens incumbent business models while giving companies a powerful instrument for absorbing shocks. Organizations running on AI-enabled processes are cheaper to operate and have more room to act when conditions change. One of the most expensive mistakes in markets is confusing “still growing” with “structurally sound.” Recurrence is not the same thing as durability. Yet markets price the risks of disruption more accurately than the businesses built to withstand it. The qualities that make a company resilient are visible in advance. The challenge is measuring durability before disruption makes its value obvious. That gap shows up in four places. Demand resilience. AI is exposing how conditional some recurring SaaS revenue really is. Software embedded in core processes and compounding on proprietary data has held up better than software sold by the seat for work AI can now do. Yet investors have historically screened by sector label rather than depth of entrenchment. Healthcare, defense and energy sit at the other end. Regulatory barriers and institutional trust make them harder to displace digitally, while demand for essential services can rise when conditions deteriorate. A hospital becomes more vital to its community during a crisis — the same conditions under which a SaaS business may see customers pull back and growth falter. Defense and energy can behave the same way. Aramco spent years building flexibility into its system, including the East-West Pipeline and multiple pipeline and storage options. Those investments paid off within days of the Iran war and disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, helping it remain one of the world’s most reliable oil suppliers. Supply-chain resilience. Markets punish disruption, yet give little comparable credit to companies that spend to avoid it. TSMC pays a significant near-term cost to diversify manufacturing beyond Taiwan. Its overseas factories are more expensive to build and operate, weighing on margins as they come online. Markets see that cost immediately and the protection only later. TSMC’s Arizona factories have run at yields matching Taiwan since late 2024. The option paid off; it simply took longer than a quarterly model tolerates. Capital-stack resilience. Private-equity sponsors bought hundreds of software companies in 2021, often borrowing heavily on the assumption that recurring revenue would remain predictable enough to service the debt. But not all recurring revenue is equal. The duration of that debt is fixed. The duration of the revenue underneath it is variable, and AI is shortening it unevenly. Software that genuinely sits inside a customer’s operations has proved more durable. The difference was visible from the start, but investors focused on recurring revenue rather than what made it recur. System resilience. A company can appear resilient while consuming resilience from the system around it. Electrical grids are built with spare capacity to absorb shocks. AI data centers increasingly draw on that capacity, transferring risk from individual companies to the broader system. The North American Electric Reliability Corporation has sharply raised its forecast for peak electricity demand and in May issued its highest-severity alert after a sudden, massive swing in computing demand. The most resilient companies will invest in the systems they depend on rather than treating spare capacity as theirs to consume. The principle extends beyond infrastructure. JPMorgan has built resilience through a balance sheet designed to absorb financial shocks and a business diversified well beyond investment banking. That structure has helped it withstand periods of stress that left less diversified peers exposed. Building resilience carries a cost. Redundant capacity, stronger balance sheets and operational flexibility all require investment before they are needed. But those investments buy optionality and the ability to keep moving when conditions change and competitors cannot. That is the market’s blind spot. Companies can spend years building resilience that weighs on near-term returns while its value remains invisible until conditions deteriorate. The result is a market that prices the cost of resilience before it prices its value. Amazon in 2001 was that kind of company. There are many more of them now. events.title: China plans AI export curbs to exert control over key tech
events.summary: Restricted technologies would include model weights and source code for products exceeding certain performance thresholds. China proposed adding advanced artificial intelligence technologies to its export-control list, potentially restricting overseas transfers of AI models and chip designs in an effort to tighten control over homegrown advancements in a strategically important sector. The draft proposal covers 23 AI technologies, including large language models, agents, chip designs and computing clusters. Restricted technologies would include model weights and source code for products exceeding certain performance thresholds. Chinese AI startups have in summer 2026 made significant progress in closing the gap on US industry leaders. Models like Moonshot AI’s Kimi K3 and DeepSeek’s latest editions offer better pricing and Chinese companies also favour the approach of sharing the weights – used to steer an AI system toward finding an answer – of their models to encourage developers to build on top of them. They are also increasingly looking for markets beyond China, with the likes of Z.AI making their wares available on US cloud service providers like Amazon Web Services. The proposal forms part of a broader effort to control 40 technologies across industries where Chinese companies have become increasingly competitive. It would also cover five biomedical technologies and 12 solar technologies, including proprietary cell and gene-therapy platforms and production technology for certain advanced solar modules. “This is more than routine maintenance,” said Ryan Etzcorn, a senior director at Ankura China Advisors. “By targeting AI, solar and biotech – industries where China holds a growing edge – Beijing is signalling that steadier relations with the West do not mean it will stand still.” China regularly updates its catalogue of technologies that are prohibited or restricted from export. In 2020, Beijing added algorithms to the list, after the first Trump administration threatened to ban TikTok unless the app sold its US assets to an American company. The proposed AI export curbs are aimed at ensuring “the safety and controllability” of the technology, a spokesperson for the Commerce Ministry said, citing the risk of misuse for attacking critical infrastructure, defense industries and core government systems by non-state actors or malicious entities. “The Chinese government’s necessary management of these technologies aims to solidify the security baseline, prevent misuse and abuse, ensure that AI remains under human control, and promote international governance of AI,” the spokesperson said in a statement. The proposal would restrict exports of core technology for models trained on “important data” and containing at least 2 trillion parameters – like Kimi K3 or Alibaba Group Holding’s Qwen3.8-Max – or ranking among the world’s top 10 on measures including performance, usage and safety. China’s cyberspace regulator broadly defines such data as information that, if leaked, may endanger national security, economic operation, social stability or public safety. The new Chinese guidelines are likely to stoke uncertainty in an AI industry already grappling with strict content controls, a licencing regime and potential US sanctions. The proposed restrictions against shipping mega-parameter models abroad are likely to hamper development given AI labs are training ever larger platforms: in September , Alibaba declared plans to develop models with between 5 and 10 trillion parameters, far larger than what’s common today, for longer and more complex tasks. Open-source technology and research already in the public domain would not be covered, and the government will provide streamlined procedures, such as automatic licensing, to exports involving open-source AI technologies. Deploying a covered model overseas would constitute a technology export, according to a statement. Deployments on overseas infrastructure owned by the Chinese provider could qualify for automatic licencing. Companies that allow overseas customers to use restricted AI models through apps, websites or online services would not be subject to the proposed controls, the Commerce Ministry said. Beijing said the measures were not aimed at any particular country, region or entity. The ministry also proposed to restrict the export of design technologies for AI chips built using 14-nanometer or more advanced techniques or employing 2.5D or 3D advanced packaging. The proposed restrictions also cover design technologies for certain advanced memory chips. China simultaneously imposed a temporary registration requirement for exports of the technologies covered by the proposal. events.title: Why is China buying up gold?
events.summary: Beijing’s gold purchases reflect a shift away from reliance on US dollar assets, experts say. China is increasing its gold reserves in a bid to reduce its dependence on US dollar assets and protect against financial and geopolitical risks, analysts say, while households are turning to the precious metal amid uncertainty over the domestic economy. The People’s Bank of China reported buying gold for a 23rd consecutive month in September, when the country’s central bank also made its largest monthly purchase in nearly three years. The sustained buying points to a longer-term effort to spread risk associated with its vast reserves, experts say. Among concerns is high US debt and Western governments’ freezing of assets, which has highlighted the inherent risk in holding money overseas, particularly for emerging market and Global South economies. Gold bought and stored domestically offers protection against that risk because access does not depend on the will of another government. But central bank buying and household demand for gold in China have different drivers. While Beijing is managing its financial exposure, private investors are seeking somewhere to preserve their savings. Here is what we know. China’s central bank added approximately 23 tonnes of gold in September, bringing its reported holdings to about 2,410 tonnes, according to the World Gold Council. That was its largest monthly purchase since October 2023. Gold accounted for 8.5 percent of China’s total official reserves at the end of September, compared with 5.5 percent at the end of 2024. Reserves are assets central banks hold to ensure they can meet international payments and respond to financial disruption. They usually include foreign currencies, foreign government debt and gold. Private demand for gold within China has also risen, with purchases of gold bars and coins 28.4 percent higher in the first half of 2026 than during the same period last year, according to the China Gold Association. The buying of gold has continued amid falling prices, with gold down around 8.5 percent over the month. The World Gold Council attributed the decline in gold prices partly to a stronger dollar and higher returns on US government debt. With interest rates going up in an attempt to curb inflation, these investments are attractive for buyers as they pay interest, making them more attractive to private investors than gold, which does not. A key objective is to reduce dependence on US government debt, known as Treasuries, according to Thu Lan Nguyen, head of commodity research at Commerzbank in Frankfurt. China holds substantial reserves in dollar-based assets and, therefore, buying gold reduces its exposure to decisions taken in Washington. “China’s gold purchases are part of a broader effort to make its reserves more resilient,” Nguyen told Al Jazeera. The freezing by Western countries of roughly $300bn in Russian Central Bank overseas assets following Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022 demonstrated how reserves held abroad can quickly become inaccessible. The concern for China may be that a future confrontation with Washington could expose some of its overseas assets to similar restrictions. “Gold held domestically has a crucial advantage in this respect: it does not represent a claim on another country and is therefore much less exposed to sanctions or asset freezes,” Nguyen said. “I would interpret it primarily as risk management,” she added, pointing to increased geopolitical tensions and economic and fiscal risks. America’s rising debt, which hit $40 trillion for the first time in history earlier this year, adds another source of uncertainty. In February, the US Congressional Budget Office projected that federal debt held by the public would rise from 101 percent of the size of the US economy in 2026 to 120 percent in 2036. That provides context for concerns about Washington’s ability to repay that debt going forward should an economic crash occur. Much of this debt is held by China. Gold, therefore, offers a less volatile and risky asset to hold. Chinese households have different motivations for buying gold. When confidence in other investments weakens, gold can become more attractive as a way to hold savings. “Strong demand for gold can partly reflect a search for alternative stores of value,” Nguyen said. The World Gold Council has identified weak Chinese share markets as one factor supporting domestic demand for gold, while its property market is burdened by heavy borrowing and overbuilding, contributing to a fall in housing prices, making it a poorer investment. Analysts warned that China’s increased buying of gold does not signal an imminent end to the dollar’s global dominance. “I would be cautious about describing this as a major shift away from the dollar,” Nguyen said. “The dollar remains by far the dominant global reserve currency.

events.title: I watched Nvidia's Jensen Huang work the room in London. He brought big checks — and a blunt message
events.summary: Nvidia boss Jensen Huang took to the stage in London on Wednesday, as part of a tour of Europe ahead of GTC Berlin next week. Huang announced the chip giant was taking stakes in five U.K. startups. "We're not your largest investor, but we are your best investor," he proclaimed. Nvidia has a near monopoly over the most powerful AI chips and Huang courts tech execs and world leaders with ease. This report is from this week's The Tech Download newsletter. Like what you see? You can subscribe here. Nvidia's Jensen Huang draws a crowd wherever he goes. In an old converted church in West London on Wednesday night, Huang stood on a pop-up stage in front of politicians, investors, tech execs and journalists, announcing the chip giant was taking stakes in five U.K. startups. "We're not your largest investor, but we are your best investor," he proclaimed. "I'm gonna invest in you, I'm gonna invest in you," he shouted, pointing at the founders. His appearance in London was part of a European tour ahead of Nvidia's GTC event in Berlin next week. Earlier, he'd searched out U.K. neocloud Nscale CEO Josh Payne in the crowd, declaring, "last year you were zero." "Now look at them," he said. "We invested in you, I attracted a whole bunch of investors to you." Nscale could be the most valuable British company in a decade, Huang said to cheers from the crowd. The Nvidia boss certainly doesn't lack for confidence. The warm reception Huang regularly receives is a sign of just how much sway he holds in the AI industry. Nvidia has a near monopoly over the most powerful AI chips and Huang courts tech execs and world leaders with ease. He's a near constant presence at U.S. President Donald Trump's side at state dinners and visits. In London, after the pomp and ceremony of Huang's speech, he emerged around 40 minutes late to a media huddle outside the front of the church. "The Prime Minister [Andy Burnham] and I had a nice whiskey together. He's a whiskey man," he told reporters. Later, Huang said he'd be meeting German Chancellor Friedrich Merz "in a couple of days." Huang spoke to journalists for nearly an hour that evening — a fair effort considering he'd only eaten a "quarter of a quarter" of a sandwich that day — dishing out praise and criticism to Europe with a bombastic assuredness. "Nothing pains me more, frankly, than to see one of the most technologically advanced countries to be left so far behind in technology," he said, referring to Germany. And the U.K. didn't escape scot-free. "If you tell an entrepreneur there's one in a million chance they can succeed, that entrepreneur says, 'So you're telling me there's a chance?' But in the UK, somehow there's 999,000... reasons to fail." The CEO was also bullish on Europe's chances of succeeding with AI, not least, presumably, because Nvidia now has stakes in so many of the region's most promising startups. On Wednesday those lucky startups were biotechs Prima Mente and Boltz, project delivery platform Foresight, algorithm discovery startup Hiverge and quantum company Riverlane. Those companies, alongside others in the U.K. that Nvidia isn't naming, will be the recipients of $1.16 billion of Nvidia cash. Earlier in the week the chip giant announced it was taking stakes in a number of French startups. It's all part of a major push by Nvidia to build out holdings across the AI stack. Among the recipients of funding from Nvidia have been the likes of OpenAI, Anthropic, Intel and XAI. The chip giant has participated in 116 investment rounds in 2026 so far, according to Dealroom, up from just 12 in 2022. Anthropic's third-quarter revenue is said to hit $16.8 billion ahead of IPO , according to people familiar with the matter. Apple and Meta team up to make Muse AI model run on Mac computers. CoreWeave credit default swaps hit distress levels as investors soured on AI debt. TSMC posted record profit for a sixth straight quarter , beating estimates . ASML says it's getting order interest through 2030 as profit smashes expectations . SpaceX's military satellite system, Starshield, has drawn renewed attention this week as Ukraine has grappled with restrictions on the tech. My colleague Elsa Ohlen has written this must-read explainer on how it works and differs from Starlink.

events.title: Malaysia’s welcome for Min Aung Hlaing undermines its stand on justice
events.summary: As the US attacks the ICC, Kuala Lumpur welcomes a leader the court’s prosecutor wants arrested. Middle powers must defend international justice. Executive Director, The Initiative to Promote Tolerance and Prevent Violence (INITIATE.MY). On October 8, Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim received Myanmar’s President Min Aung Hlaing in Putrajaya with a guard of honour and an official luncheon, in the military chief’s first visit since the 2021 coup. Nine days earlier, Malaysia sent 1,476 Myanmar nationals back by sea in the first phase of a plan to return 5,000 people. Kuala Lumpur calls this pragmatic diplomacy. In reality, it lends a middle power’s credibility to the Trump administration’s retreat from international accountability, weakening the laws and institutions smaller states rely on most. Since May, a surge of online hate speech and misinformation has targeted the Rohingya, Malaysia’s largest refugee community. By late July, at least nine Rohingya community schools had closed or faced closure orders, and more than 100 Rohingya told UNHCR that residents of their Penang village had driven them out. The hostility ignores the facts: Malaysia’s police chief says Rohingya account for 0.02 percent of crime. Yet research by INITIATE.MY and the Center for the Study of Organized Hate found AI-generated content amplifying anti-Rohingya disinformation across Malaysia, Indonesia, India and Bangladesh, casting refugees as a threat and legitimising vigilante violence. Electoral politics plays a part. After heavy losses in three state elections, and with a general election due by February 2028, Anwar’s coalition may see a hard line on Rohingya returns as a show of control, though voter disillusionment and right-wing rivals make any electoral gains uncertain. Malaysia is not acting alone. Mongolia hosted Vladimir Putin in 2024 despite an ICC arrest warrant, and Hungary welcomed Benjamin Netanyahu in 2025 despite another. Kuala Lumpur denies this is recognition, yet Anwar says Malaysia will work towards Myanmar’s full reintegration into ASEAN, and Min Aung Hlaing wants a seat at the bloc’s November summit in Manila. Each welcome makes the next easier and tells leaders accused of atrocities, from Netanyahu to Min Aung Hlaing, that diplomatic rehabilitation is possible without accountability. ASEAN has tried this before. In April 2021, Min Aung Hlaing agreed to the Five-Point Consensus, then ignored it: The violence continued, the ASEAN special envoy never met Aung San Suu Kyi, and inclusive dialogue never began. The bloc’s one real lever was excluding military leaders from its summits. Myanmar Specialist, Arkar Hein, said “Welcoming him back with nothing asked in return rewards that defiance and tells Naypyidaw that time and a staged election can achieve what compromise would otherwise require. Each handshake abroad also makes the regime less willing to offer its opponents real concessions, and convinces them that only the battlefield will decide Myanmar’s future.” Malaysia has spent decades building its credibility as a regional peacemaker, a hard-won reputation it now puts at risk. It has facilitated the Bangsamoro peace process since 2001, helping negotiate a landmark peace agreement in the southern Philippines, and has facilitated talks in southern Thailand since 2013. In November 2024, Anwar welcomed the ICC’s arrest warrants for Netanyahu and his former defence minister, saying they “should be arrested even if they are visiting other countries”. That same month, the ICC prosecutor sought an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing for alleged crimes against humanity targeting the Rohingya, and an Argentinian court has since issued its own. The Gambia’s genocide case against Myanmar at the International Court of Justice centres on the 2016-17 operations Min Aung Hlaing commanded, which killed thousands of Rohingya, included mass rapes and burned hundreds of villages, driving more than 700,000 people into Bangladesh. UN investigators called for him to face genocide charges. Malaysia is not a party to the Rome Statute and has no legal duty to arrest him. But its credibility as a peacemaker and on Palestine rests on applying one standard to everyone. The returns rest on assurances no independent body can verify. UNHCR says it was not involved in the returns and had no access to verify that they were voluntary, and that safe conditions do not exist. Those returned reportedly included 27 children. Though not a party to the Refugee Convention, Malaysia is bound by the customary principle of non-refoulement, and the UN Special Rapporteur on Myanmar has warned of substantial risks. Naypyidaw says no Rohingya are involved because it does not recognise them as citizens, but other returnees also risk arbitrary detention, prosecution and forced recruitment. The military does not even control Rakhine State, where the Arakan Army holds more than 90 percent of the territory.

events.summary: Trump, Netanyahu and the Iran question How Iran war fallout may shape US elections The US and Russia each have more than 4,000 warheads. China is set to catch up with them within five years, Trump says. The United States is engaged in talks with Russia and China regarding nuclear disarmament, President Donald Trump has announced. Trump said on Thursday that China – which lags behind the US and Russia in terms of the number of warheads it has – is racing to catch up. He added during an interview with US broadcaster Newsmax that Washington is discussing with its peers a route to “denuclearise”. list 1 of 3 Russian nuclear-capable bomber plane crashes, killing six people list 2 of 3 What is the ‘Mother of All Bombs’ US could use in Iran? list 3 of 3 Russia, China veto UN mandate to monitor Iran sanctions China’s nuclear stockpile of about 620 warheads is dwarfed by those of the US and Russia, which each have more than 4,000, but Trump said he thinks China will “catch up” within five years. “The whole thing is a shame because I’d love to denuclearise if possible,” Trump said. “We’re actually talking ⁠to Russia about that, and ⁠we’re talking to China about that denuclearisation.” China doesn’t seem willing to disarm, he noted, but said talks have continued. events.title: Banking tax raid fears hit London lenders' shares ahead of crucial budget
events.summary: The bank surcharge is reportedly expected to rise to 8% from 3% in Finance Minister John Healey's budget later this month. A higher surcharge could reduce U.K.-focused banks' earnings and add to concerns about London's tax competitiveness. Lloyds Banking Group led losses, sliding 1.8%, while NatWest was 1.51% lower by 11:30 a.m. in London (6:30 a.m. ET). Barclays moved 0.13% higher, reversing earlier losses. London-listed shares of HSBC and Standard Chartered — which both derive much of their profits overseas — added 1.2% and 0.71%, respectively. Finance Minister John Healey is expected to raise the sector-specific surcharge on banks' profits to 8%, up from 3%, when he delivers his first budget as Chancellor, scheduled for Oct. 28. The levy, which sits on top of corporation tax, was earlier cut to 3% from 8% under Rishi Sunak's Conservative government in 2023. While the hike could raise £2 billion ($2.67 billion) per year for the U.K. Treasury, it could also slice 6% off lenders' earnings, KBW analysts said in a note Oct. 12. Healey on Thursday described banks as the "jewel" in the U.K.'s economic crown in an interview with Bloomberg. However, the proposed levy has revived wider concerns about the Labour government's approach to financial services, and how the sector may be treated as ministers seek to fund public services and meet fiscal targets. Amanda Blanc, CEO of Aviva , said the financial services sector is one of the U.K.'s "core industries". "What you need to do is to encourage financial services to be successful," Blanc told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Friday. "My urge would be if you really believe that financial services is important, don't make it difficult for people to invest in the U.K., and for those businesses in the U.K. to invest in the U.K." U.K. banks operate with a total tax rate of more than 46%, according to PwC data. That compares to 38.9% for banks in Frankfurt and about 27% in New York. While the tax hike could overshadow lenders' upcoming third-quarter earnings and weigh on shares, analysts at Citi said the budget could act as a "clearing event," resolving uncertainty among lenders. "Fears of a tax & spend (anti-growth) budget, combined with broader geopolitical events, have driven gilt yields higher," Citi said in a note Oct. 14. "This is beneficial for the banks' structural hedge roll benefit to NII, but also serves to increase CoE, which has driven a multiple de-rating and explains why U.K. banks trade at a discount." Analysts led by Andrew Coombs, Citi's head of European financials equity, said U.K. bank fundamentals remain healthy, pointing to corporate releveraging, with lenders' net interest income growth among the highest in Europe. Citi expects mixed third-quarter results, with adjusted pretax profit above consensus at Barclays and NatWest, but below at HSBC, Lloyds and StanChart.

events.title: AI's need for data could breathe new life into a once-buzzy corner of Wall Street
events.summary: Personal AI agents like Instinct are taking over the tech world. Dado Ruvic/REUTERS This post originally appeared in the Business Insider Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . The future of AI might rely on getting your Slack DMs. It's not just your DMs, to be clear. It's internal memos, transaction records, contracts, and even that onboarding guide you probably didn't read when you started your job. Basically, if it's work-related and has been documented, AI companies are interested. The rationale is straightforward: If AI tools are going to automate work, they need a deep understanding of what the work is. BI did a deep dive on AI companies' race to scoop up as much data as possible in its series " The AI Data Grab ." BI's Charles Rollet, Tom Carter, and Stephen Council first unpacked the wild market that's sprung up for this data. Things move quickly, including "exploding offers." Others are figuring out how to leverage their databases. Law firms, which often have detailed archives, are a great example. BI's Melia Robinson has more on that . And sometimes it's about actually creating the data yourself. That's the case in robotics, writes BI's Rya Jetha. Companies are shelling out big to have people record everyday tasks like cooking and cleaning . AI's data push could renew interest in a space that's already navigated an info-hungry industry. Alternative data, unstructured datasets such as satellite imagery and card transactions, became a hot commodity on Wall Street in the mid-2010s. These non-traditional datasets are supposed to give investors an edge. Want to know if Home Depot will beat earnings estimates? Analyze satellite images of its parking lots to see whether foot traffic is rising or declining. When I covered the space closely with my colleague Bradley Saacks, the data providers often highlighted that the real market opportunity was selling into big corporates . Hedge funds might be rich, but there are only so many of them to go around. The market also has a ceiling. If too many people are trading off the same datasets, you lose your potential edge. AI's data needs can fill the gap alt-data providers hoped corporates would. And unlike hedge funds interested in real-time, market-relevant data, these firms benefit from a wider, deeper catalog. Some players already see an opportunity. When former Point72 data wizard Kirk McKeown launched a data startup last year, he told Bradley it aimed to package data in an easily accessible way for AI models to scoop up . It's promising, but there are no guarantees. Alt data faced real growing pains as providers struggled to scale their offerings while maintaining data quality. AI companies' needs might differ, but their expectations won't be any easier. And in some cases, money managers might find the most useful data in their own backyard . In the meantime, follow Bradley here for more coverage on how alt-data providers are navigating the AI era. And keep an eye out for a hedge-fund-focused newsletter from him later this year.
