events.title: ‘It was fake’: Indian villagers allege forgery behind Adani mine project
events.summary: Forged signatures and thumbprints – even of dead and fictitious people – allegedly used to get land for bauxite mine. Koraput, India – Raghunath Khara was shocked to look at his thumb impression on a piece of paper that declared he had consented to a government proposal to mine his village’s pristine forest land for bauxite. He says he never gave that thumb impression. list 1 of 4 Who is Gautam Adani and why is he controversial? list 2 of 4 US federal judge questions DOJ decision to drop Adani charges list 3 of 4 Modi govt allowed Adani coal deals it knew were ‘inappropriate’ list 4 of 4 India’s mining boom threatens tribal people “I always sign in English. It was someone else’s thumb,” alleged Khara, a shopkeeper in Balda village in the tribal-dominated Koraput district of Odisha state in eastern India. Khara is among hundreds of people from Indigenous tribes in Balda and neighbouring Bannur village who have lost their lands to the new bauxite mine. It is being developed by Kalinga Alumina Limited, a subsidiary of Adani Enterprises Limited, a conglomerate owned by Gautam Adani, India’s second richest businessman and close to Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The $24m project will consume a large chunk of the tabletop Balda Hill – home to forests, grasslands and caves that are considered sacred by at least 10 tribal villages surrounding it. To push the project, the purported signatures and thumb impressions of nearly 600 tribals were allegedly collected during village council meetings in Balda and Bannur held on October 9 last year. Bannur is 5km from Balda. Khara says he never attended the meeting at Balda and was instead protesting against the proposed mine with his wife, sister and other villagers about 100 metres from the village council office. “It [thumb impression] was fake. We didn’t attend the village meeting at all. We were all busy protesting outside,” he told Al Jazeera. India’s constitution recognises the rights of Indigenous communities over their traditional lands. Forest laws and laws granting autonomy to tribal areas dictate that village council resolutions are mandatory for any diversion of such lands for other purposes. A resolution passed in a village council meeting is valid only if 50 percent of all the adults in the village consent to it in writing. Government documents claim all the 580 adults – 360 in Balda and 227 in Bannur – agreed to give up their land for the Adani mine. But the elected village heads in both villages denied any signatures were collected and called the two meetings “invalid”. Even photographs taken by villagers at both council meetings show a combined attendance of about 100 people – nearly 40 in Balda and 68 in Bannur – far below the minimum 50 percent quorum required to pass a valid resolution. Moreover, the villagers allege that most signatures on the resolution documents are fake, forged or impersonated. They also claim the documents contain signatures of fictitious persons and even the names of people who died years ago. Some even said their signatures from a previous, unrelated village council meeting were fraudulently pasted onto the bauxite mine document. Al Jazeera emailed the Adani group and its communications chief on August 18 seeking responses to the accusations of forgery and fraud. Then we followed up with a second request for comments on September 25, but did not receive any response. Al Jazeera also sought responses from Manoj Satyawan Mahajan, the district magistrate — the most senior bureaucrat in Koraput – to the concerns raised by villagers but did not receive a response. Rohit Varma, the superintendent of police for Koraput district, also did not respond to Al Jazeera’s queries. Many of those who attended the meetings said they were opposed to the mining project. “We were told that if mining was allowed, the village would get roads, jobs, drainage and water connections and a school built,” said Madhav Kuntili, a farmer in Bannur. Koraput is one of India’s least developed districts and similar promises often have a significant sway. Kuntili said a document was passed around, seeking signatures. “I said if the forest was being diverted, then I would not sign it. They took the paper away from me,” he told Al Jazeera. Across Balda and Bannur, Al Jazeera met many villagers who said they were shocked to find their signatures or thumb impressions on the resolution. Rama Hantal sat motionless by the doorway of his rusted tin-and-wood hut. The 60-year-old has been paralysed for several years and is unable to talk. “There is no chance he could have attended the meeting or even signed,” said Chandrama Hantal, his daughter-in-law. While Hantal had apparently signed the consent form in Odia, Odisha’s official language, Chandrama saw a thumb impression against her name. She also denied attending the meeting. Among the signatories are three Gurubari Kharas – their purported thumb impressions in support of the mining project.

events.title: Microsoft president warns Trump's immigration crackdown could drive top AI talent abroad
events.summary: Brad Smith, the president of Microsoft, defended the company's use of visas and green cards. Paulo Nunes dos Santos/Bloomberg via Getty Images Microsoft President Brad Smith warned that US immigration policies could drive AI talent overseas. "Let's not put that at risk," Smith said. The Trump administration recently suspended Microsoft and other tech firms from a green card program. If America wants to win the AI race, sending the world's brightest engineers packing might not be a winning strategy. That's the warning from Microsoft President Brad Smith, who said the Trump administration's immigration crackdown risks driving the next generation of AI talent away from the United States. "I think we should all be worried about sending intentionally or inadvertently or otherwise, signals that send the most talented next wave of AI software engineers to other countries rather than the United States," Smith said in an episode of Politico's "The Decoded Podcast" that aired on Thursday. His comments come after the Trump administration announced last week that it was suspending Microsoft, Adobe, and several other technology companies from a federal program that  sponsors foreign workers for permanent residency. Vice President JD Vance accused Microsoft of abusing the Permanent Labor Certification, or PERM, program by laying off American employees while hiring lower-paid foreign workers. Smith, who Business Insider reported was recently put in charge of Microsoft's communications , pushed back against those allegations, saying the administration had presented a misleading picture of Microsoft's hiring practices. US Vice President JD Vance has criticized Microsoft's use of visa programs. Daniel Heuer-Pool/Getty Images "What was presented as Microsoft replacing 6,000 people who lost their jobs with 9,000 foreigners was frankly completely off base," he said. Smith said most of the company's visa and green card applications concerned existing employees rather than new hires, adding that Microsoft had hired 9,200 American workers in its last fiscal year. "That was left out of the narrative," he said. He also rejected suggestions that Microsoft pays foreign workers less than their American counterparts, saying employees are compensated under the same system regardless of immigration status. The American dream, on hold The dispute comes amid growing uncertainty for skilled foreign workers in the US. As part of our ongoing H-1B Fallout series , Business Insider previously reported that the Trump administration's shifting immigration policies have prompted some international workers to explore opportunities abroad , including in countries like the UK, Germany, and Canada. An analysis of federal data by Business Insider found that certified H-1B applications fell 10% in the first nine months of fiscal year 2026 compared with the same period a year earlier. Applications for data scientists, however, rose 22.5%, highlighting continued demand for specialized AI talent . Read more about the impacts of the Trump administration's shifting immigration policies in Business Insider's H-1B Fallout series . The winners and losers of the new H-1B era The hidden sacrifices of chasing an H-1B career in America They planned their lives around the H-1B dream. A year of turmoil has some looking beyond America. Watch: Getting my H-1B on the first try felt like 'pure luck.' 4 years later, a layoff meant I had to leave the US. On the Politico podcast, Smith cited immigrants' economic contributions as evidence of what America stands to lose. He said that five of the six technology and science medal recipients recently honored by President Donald Trump had immigrated to the United States. President Donald Trump awards tech execs and founders some of the country's highest scientific honors. Win McNamee/Getty Images According to Smith, the companies associated with those five individuals collectively represent more than a quarter of the S&P 500's market value. Their contributions, he said, benefit not just technology employees but ordinary Americans whose retirement savings and pension funds are invested in those businesses. "Think about what those five individuals have done for the well being, even the wealth and standard of living, of Americans across the country," Smith said. "Let's not put that at risk." events.title: KFC to switch to Coca-Cola beverages in U.S. restaurants for the first time in decades
events.summary: KFC is switching from PepsiCo to Coca-Cola as its beverage supplier for U.S. restaurants. The fried chicken chain has served Pepsi drinks ever since the food and beverage giant acquired KFC in 1986. KFC is trying to win back U.S. diners who have ditched its buckets for rivals such as Chick-fil-A. KFC's U.S. restaurants will ditch PepsiCo and switch to Coca-Cola beverages next year, marking the first time in decades that the Yum Brands chain has changed its drink supplier, the restaurant company said Thursday. Some of KFC's international markets serve Coke products, but the chain's U.S. restaurants have stuck with PepsiCo drinks ever since Pepsi bought KFC in 1986. At the time of the acquisition, KFC was Coke's second-largest fountain account, trailing only McDonald's. Pepsi later spun off KFC, along with sister chains Pizza Hut and Taco Bell — but even as the combined Yum Brands, the company stayed loyal to its previous owner. Without Pepsi, Taco Bell would not serve its iconic Mountain Dew Baja Blast. The change comes as KFC aims to win back U.S. diners, who have ditched the fried chicken chain for rivals such as Chick-fil-A or Popeyes. "This decision is a critical step in the Kentucky Fried Comeback," KFC U.S. President Catherine Tan-Gillespie wrote in a memo to franchisees and employees obtained by CNBC. "A new beverage offering, with a new partner in Coca-Cola, gives us a platform to innovate, meet changing tastes and give customers more reasons to choose us." For many fast-food chains, beverages have become a critical way to attract consumers. A number of restaurants, including McDonald's and Taco Bell, have broadened their drink offerings with options such as refreshers or "dirty soda." For its part, KFC recently unveiled new drinks, including iced coffees and shakes, at Open House , its innovation restaurant in McKinney, Texas. Coke told CNBC earlier this year that the company has helped many of its restaurant partners create new drinks. KFC expects to be pouring Coke beverages in all of its U.S. restaurants by the end of the first quarter of 2027, Tan-Gillespie said. Tan-Gillespie also said that Pepsi remains an important partner for KFC's parent company and the chain's international markets. For decades, Coke and Pepsi have tussled over important restaurant partners, which represent both a sales opportunity and the chance to grow the visibility of their beverage brands. It is unusual for large restaurant chains to switch beverage providers, but not unprecedented. In 2024, Pepsi poached Subway , the largest U.S. restaurant chain by number of locations, from Coke. Besides KFC, Coke has wooed away a number of notable Pepsi customers in recent years, including Culver's, Arby's and Panda Express.

events.title: The world reacts to Elon Musk’s flying car
events.summary: Tesla unveiled a new iteration of the Roadster that can travel upside down. Tesla Elon Musk's Tesla unveiled its new car, the Roadster, on Thursday. In its demonstration, the car took flight using thrusters and performed kickflips. Here's what smart people in tech and business have to say about it. Tesla’s long-delayed Roadster finally made an entrance — by flying off a ramp. At a livestreamed event Thursday night, the sports car climbed a curved ramp until it was upside down, launched into the air, flipped, and landed on its wheels, apparently aided by thrusters beneath the vehicle. “Well, it worked,” Elon Musk said during the livestream. Musk said Tesla and SpaceX engineers collaborated on the car, which uses high-pressure air and thrusters to lift itself off the ground. Tesla also showed a recorded demonstration in which the Roadster reached 60 mph in 0.81 seconds. While the legality of such a device on public roads remains in question, the tech world is reacting to Musk's new creation with awe. Here is what the leading voices in business and tech are saying about the new Roadster. Jason Calacanis Bloomberg/Getty Images Angel investor Jason Calacanis said in an X post that the videos of the flying car looked like "science fiction," and they're real, although they don't seem to be. He seemed enthused by the demonstration, asking that while the car was only airborne for a couple of seconds, "what if it could keep you in the air for five minutes? Or ten? Or 30?" Gene Munster Brian Ach/Getty Images for LocationWorld 2016 Gene Munster , the managing partner at Deepwater Asset Management and a longtime tech analyst, wrote his two takeaways from the Roadster event on X. First, that "it was an engineering flex with no commercial value beyond embarrassing traditional car makers." And the second was that it signaled Musk's ambition to merge his two publicly traded companies, SpaceX and Tesla. John Carmack John Carmack said he's happy to get the Roadster without the thrusters. credit should read GABRIELLE LURIE/AFP via Getty Images John Carmack , the former CTO of Meta's virtual reality division, politely rejected the flying car. "That demo involved a non trivial chance of embarrassing failure!" he wrote on X. He added, "I'm only going for the baseline model. At this point in my life, rocket bunny hops are out of my comfort zone." Marques Brownlee MKBHD Chance Yeh/Getty Images for HubSpot Tech YouTuber Marques Brownlee , better known as MKBHD, appeared incredulous at Tesla's claims about the new Roadster. "They really just got on stage and said this newly designed 4000+ pound car can do flips and go half the speed of sound (380+mph) and will ship in 2028," he wrote on X. "This is a prank, right?" Alexandr Wang Alexandr Wang, Meta's chief AI officer, has been trumpeting Muse. Bloomberg/Getty Images Meta's chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang , had one burning question after watching Tesla's Roadster demonstration. "wait who the hell was driving the tesla," Wang wrote on X, sharing footage of the car speeding down a dark track. Dan Ives Dan Ives. Astrida Valigorsky/Getty Images Dan Ives , an analyst at Yorkville Ives and a longtime Tesla bull, said the Roadster reveal was "a statement about where the Tesla and SpaceX engineering stacks are headed together." He wrote that the car's SpaceX-developed hardware was "a small example of the synergies between Tesla and SpaceX." Still, he said, "The Roadster will not move the volume or revenue needle," but would "restore the brand halo at the top of the market." David Marcus David Marcus. Bloomberg/Getty Images David Marcus , the former PayPal president and Meta executive, credited Musk with bringing a sense of awe back to technology. "The thing I’m most grateful to Elon for is bringing back an age of wonder and excitement to humanity," Marcus wrote on X, sharing Tesla's Roadster demonstration. "That was jaw-dropping awesome! Screams and mouths wide open in the audience. Nuts." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: ‘We should all be worried’: calls grow to limit London rollout of robotaxis
events.summary: Protest planned at Wayve HQ as Uber drivers fear for their future and city’s politicians demand TfL should have power over licences For passengers in Britain who want to try the latest ride, robotaxis are eagerly awaited: more than 100,000 are on Uber’s waitlist in London after the first UK services started in September. Others view them with trepidation. “I think we should all be worried,” said Florentina Ghiuzan, an Uber driver from Essex. “I was shocked TfL approved it so soon . I knew change would come. But I thought it would come with a solution for us.” London’s rollout is facing mounting opposition, from drivers fearing for their future and the capital’s politicians, with a critical report demanding Transport for London (TfL) is given full powers to permit or suspend operations. Drivers will this weekend protest outside the headquarters and depot of Wayve, which has partnered with Uber to supply London’s first autonomous cabs for hire . The direct action marks the latest salvo between unions and the global tech companies, whose driverless cars trials expanded this week to Manchester, with fears that hundreds of thousands of driver jobs could be lost. Although only a handful of driverless cars now ply the streets, Uber has announced plans to deploy 100,000 Nvidia robotaxis worldwide starting next year, and its senior executives have talked about all new cars being autonomous by 2040. In San Francisco, Waymo’s fully autonomous cars already operate more than a quarter of all rides. The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, and bosses at TfL have expressed unease, and the London assembly’s transport committee has called for the government to devolve authority over autonomous taxi services. In a report published this week, the committee said there was “considerable uncertainty around many of the claimed benefits of autonomous passenger vehicles”, and fears over the impact on public transport and congestion, as well as safeguarding and accessibility for disabled passengers. The chair, Caroline Russell, said they were not convinced that London should welcome robotaxis. “Rather than just accepting the autonomous passenger service model proposed by operators, London should be looking at the transport problems it is trying to solve and then considering what solutions this technology could provide,” she said. TfL is understood to see little benefit in the addition of robotaxi services to its crowded city streets , even if the numbers turn out to be relatively few in comparison to the wider traffic. For the robotaxi companies, London is a tempting challenge to crack. Commercially, it is one of the biggest private hire markets in the world and a foothold in Europe; logistically, it is a tricky test bed to prove their vehicles are viable anywhere. Compared with the grid system of US cities in particular, it presents narrower, twisting and unruly streets, without the kind of rules on jaywalking that give cars priority on the road. Under current rules, TfL licenses passenger services, but the government decides whether autonomous vehicles can operate. TfL has approved the start of Uber and Wayve’s limited robotaxi services, which retain a human safety driver in the front seat. As it stands, when it comes to fully autonomous passenger services, the Department for Transport would issue permits for robotaxis with TfL only able to grant or refuse consent, rather than regulate their usage on London’s streets. That has alarmed TfL, which sees parallels with when Uber first started business in London, creating problems few had considered, and was twice rebuffed in licence renewals as not a “fit and proper” operator. Quite how driverless cars will affect the capital’s transport ecosystem is unknown – and TfL wants to retain the power to intervene. City hall is also concerned about the social implications of more than 100,000 licensed drivers losing income or a living. Those at the frontline in the App Drivers and Couriers Union (ADCU) are planning protests outside Wayve’s London base from this Saturday. Their members include Ghiuzan, 42, who started working as a driver four years ago after going back to college. She said: “Our earnings are the same or even lower since I started – and with the robotaxis on the market it could get even worse.” Ghiuzan said she was notified of the start of autonomous services as an Uber customer – but received no notification as a driver. She thinks people will switch to robotaxis: “Young people like them, it’s new, and you don’t have to pay the driver … I might have other skills, but for lots of drivers who are older and have done it their whole life, it’s going to be quite a challenge.” Faisal Osman, 51, from east London, has been an Uber driver for 12 years, after switching from a long commute to an IT engineering job to allow him to work nights when he had children. He knows four other engineers who joined Uber: “We all used to talk about AI taking our jobs in IT.

events.title: Nike's India campus is a long-term growth bet amid turnaround
events.summary: Earlier this month, Nike announced it is expanding into India, a move it said will help widen its global reach and tap into the growing market. Nike has experienced a yearslong slump and a sustained decline in China. Experts say it's uncertain whether the retailer's long-term bet will be enough to offset the short-term pressures. The retailer, which has been struggling to revive its business and regain momentum under CEO Elliott Hill, is hoping the world's most populous country can help it turn the page on its performance. As it reported its fiscal first-quarter earnings on Oct. 1, the company announced it will create a new global campus in Bengaluru, India, as part of its growth strategy. Hill wrote in a letter to employees that the new facility would be a "long-term investment" to help position Nike for success. "India is already an important growth market and manufacturing hub for Nike, with strong capabilities and access to talent," Hill wrote. The new campus is expected to open in the next few years and span corporate roles across the organization, including the namesake Nike brand, Jordan Brand and Converse. Nike plans to discuss its India campus in detail at its investor day next month. In a statement to CNBC, a Nike spokesperson said expanding into India is a "natural" next step for the company as it looks to grow its global presence. "As participation in running, basketball, football, fitness and other sports continues to grow across India, we see an opportunity to better serve athletes through stronger local capabilities, consumer insights, and innovation," the spokesperson said. India will be the world's third-largest retail market by 2030, according to Indian conglomerate Reliance Industries. Its e-commerce market was valued at $159.25 billion in 2026 and is projected to reach $332.94 billion by 2031, according to IBEF, a business advocacy organization created by the Indian government. Nike has endured a yearslong slump and is trying to right its business under Hill's turnaround plan. Nike also announced this month that it would lay off workers across the company as part of what it has dubbed its Pace strategy, which includes supply chain changes and reorganization of the company's geographic segments. Nike expects the effort to deliver approximately $2.5 billion in savings through fiscal 2031. Nike's decision to invest further in India as part of its comeback comes as the sportswear company sheds revenue in another critical international market: China. Though its fiscal first-quarter North America revenue came in just above Wall Street expectations, Hill said that performance wasn't enough to offset pressures abroad. Nike has been particularly struggling in the Greater China market , where its revenue dropped by 26% in its fiscal first quarter. It's part of what experts have said is a broader trend of American companies losing relevance and traction to domestic brands as the once-lucrative market matures. On a call with analysts earlier this month, Hill said the company was taking "deliberate actions" to strengthen its China business, though he said those effects will take time to materialize. Hill said the company plans to refresh its physical retail, spearhead a digital cleanup and create higher quality experiences for consumers. The Nike spokesperson told CNBC the company is "deeply committed" to China and sees the region as one of its "most important long-term growth markets," even as Nike expands its presence in India. "China remains a long-term priority for Nike, while India represents another important opportunity to invest in the future of sport and the next generation of athletes," the spokesperson said. The company's expansion in India may be coming at both an opportune and inopportune time, according to experts. Investing in a growing international market does not guarantee higher sales — it also requires persuading Indian consumers they want the Nike brand, a challenge the company has struggled to overcome in China. "What Nike, I think, is doing right now is going region by region and working to reestablish what the brand stands for," Simeon Siegel, a senior managing director at Guggenheim Securities, told CNBC. Siegel said part of the dissonance for Nike is that each region and segment of the business is at a different stage of its turnaround. He said investing in India may set the company up for a more sustainable future if the China business continues to lag, but Nike needs to have a compelling product, solid storytelling and extensive distribution in the region to be successful there. "I think the company needs to look inward and figure out what is the right way to reestablish profitability," he said. "And that involves, in certain instances, shrinking and saving and cutting, and, in certain instances, investing and looking toward the future, because the goal here is not to shrink to oblivion; it's to shrink to stability, and then ultimately growth.

Time: 3pm – 4pm | Location: Bank of England, Threadneedle Street, London, EC2R 8AH and MS teams The Chair opened the meeting by welcoming Members and outlined the purpose of the meeting. Namely, to consider the results of the 2026 banknote imagery consultation in light of the Bank’s objectives to support counterfeit resilience, and to consider which four animals to recommend to the Governor to feature as the central imagery on the next series of banknotes. The Chair reminded Members of the Bank’s obligations under the Public Sector Equality Duty throughout the imagery selection process. Decision: Members agreed to sign off the updated Terms of Reference adding the Banknote Innovation Programme Director as a new Core Member. Members were reminded of the key milestones in the imagery selection process, including the recent consultation asking for the UK public’s views on a shortlist of animals which could feature as the central imagery on the next series of banknotes. Respondents were able to choose up to two animals from each of three different categories: Mammals; Birds; and Amphibians, Insects and Fish. Members discussed the response to the public consultation, which received nearly 500,000 responses via an online survey, post, emails and phone calls. Members were pleased with the level of public engagement and suggested it showed that the theme resonated with the public. Item 4 – Choosing which animals should feature on Series H banknotes Members were asked to consider the Bank’s objectives that the chosen imagery supports counterfeit resilience, reflects public preference and celebrates the breadth of UK nature. Members were encouraged to consider the four proposed animals as a set to ensure they are sufficiently varied in their forms, movements and habitats to maximise differentiation between each denomination, thereby aiding counterfeit resilience. Members considered the results of the June 2026 public consultation and agreed on the importance of reflecting the public’s views on banknote design alongside the Bank’s wider objectives to ensure secure and resilient banknote design. Members discussed the proposal to feature the Atlantic puffin, barn owl, buff-tailed bumblebee, and European hedgehog as the central imagery on the next series of banknotes. The Atlantic puffin would bring a marine environment that would not be possible with the fox or kingfisher, which had received more selections in their respective categories. This set would include the most popular animal from each of the three categories as well as the most popular marine animal in the shortlist. Members considered how each of the proposed animals’ forms and habitats could be differentiated to help the public easily identify each denomination, as well as how the proposed animals’ movements could be incorporated into security features to support authentication. It may also be possible to include some of the other animals from the shortlist as secondary imagery in the final designs. This would be subject to further engagement with the members of the Banknote Imagery Expert Panel about the animals’ habitats and note design decisions later in the process. Members concluded that the proposed set of animals met the Bank’s objectives for counterfeit resilience and took into account the outcome of the public consultation.

events.title: Norway's $2 trillion wealth fund was frozen out of major defense companies. That may be about to change
events.summary: Proposed changes to Norway's sovereign wealth fund ethics rules could open the door to investments in more Western defense companies. The fund is currently barred from investing in companies including Lockheed Martin and Boeing because of their involvement in nuclear weapons production. Norway will consult on the proposals before the government puts forward a new ethics framework, with parliament expected to vote on the changes in mid-2027. Norway's $2.3 trillion oil fund could soon invest in Western defense companies after years of being frozen out of much of the sector by state ethics guidelines. The sovereign wealth fund is currently worth around 21.8 trillion Norwegian kroner, or $2.3 trillion, making it the largest fund of its kind in the world. With stakes in around 1.5% of the world's publicly listed companies, the fund is one of the biggest investors in the stock market worldwide. In November 2025, a review was ordered into the ethical guidelines governing how Norges Bank invests, following controversy over divestments from some Israeli and American firms. On Thursday, the independent Gjedrem Committee submitted the review's findings to the Norwegian Ministry of Finance. It included a recommendation for radical change to the fund's approach to defense investments, arguing that "Norges Bank must be prepared for situations where conflicts escalate into war." Current ethical rules prohibit the fund from making investments in companies including Airbus , BAE Systems , Boeing , BWX Technologies and Lockheed Martin , as they contribute to the manufacturing of nuclear weapons. The fund does hold some defense stocks, including a 2.3% stake in Germany's Rheinmetall , and a 1.5% stake in Italy's Leonardo . The Gjedrem Committee said Thursday that although the nuclear weapons criterion should be retained, "its scope should change." "The Fund is not to be invested in companies that produce nuclear weapons, unless the company is domiciled in a nuclear-weapon state under the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) that is allied with Norway," it said in its report. "Several European and American companies that produce components for nuclear weapons can therefore be reincluded." It added that potential investment should include companies producing weapons that Norway needs for its own defense, and proposed removing the requirement for arms-makers to be assessed for whether their products are being used by nations in accordance with international humanitarian law. The committee noted that alongside rising geopolitical instability, wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, and energy security concerns, the fund's capital and influence meant it was "timely to reassess the ethical framework." "The Fund's size and reach give better access to company management and boards than the Fund had in 2003," it said. "In a time of a more demanding political situation abroad, this provides opportunities of which the management should make use." "The liberal, rules-based international order is in decline," it added. "Economic policies are increasingly used as instruments of foreign policy. Cooperation between countries has become more transactional and negotiation-driven in recent years." It warned that in this environment, other governments can "more readily perceive ethically motivated exclusions as the policy of the Norwegian government." Norway's oil fund was set up in the 1990s to invest revenues from the country's oil and gas industry. While Norway's finance ministry and central bank are involved in the governance of the fund, investment decisions are made by Norges Bank Investment Management (NBIM), with exclusion recommendations historically put forward by its independent Council on Ethics. "There have been reactions and threats of countermeasures," the Gjedrem Committee said in its report on Thursday. "Retaliatory measures could hit the Fund and other Norwegian interests." In September last year, the U.S. State Department told CNBC it was "very troubled" by NBIM's decision to exit positions in American machinery manufacturer Caterpillar and five Israeli banks, accusing the fund of basing its decision on "illegitimate claims." NBIM had cited "unacceptable risk" that the companies were contributing to rights violations in Palestinian territories when it divested. Norway's finance minister, Jens Stoltenberg – former secretary general of NATO – said at the time that it was "not a political decision." The Gjedrem Committee noted on Thursday that the risk of further backlash to NBIM's investment choices was also rising as public finances came under greater pressure in many countries. "High government debt can jeopardize economic stability in countries, but can also give an incentive to look to foreign investors' interest and dividend income as a revenue base for the state," it warned.

events.title: Poland scrambles fighter jets as Russia strikes western Ukraine
events.summary: Countries along NATO’s eastern flank are growing increasingly concerned about the risk of escalation of the war in Ukraine. Poland has scrambled its defences once again as Russian attacks overnight hit western Ukraine close to Poland’s border. Poland’s armed forces said on Friday that they had scrambled fighter jets during the attacks and no violation of the country’s airspace was recorded. list 1 of 3 Russia attack hits Kyiv after reported intelligence lapse list 2 of 3 Trump slams Zelenskyy as Ukraine resumes strikes on Russian oil refineries list 3 of 3 Russia accuses Ukraine of contradicting US brokered deal It was just the latest such alert as Poland and other countries along NATO ’s eastern flank grow increasingly concerned over the risk of escalation of the war in Ukraine as Russia appears to be accelerating its tests of regional defences. Later on Friday, Bulgaria’s defence minister said Sofia has requested help from NATO to bolster its defences. During air attacks across Ukraine overnight, numerous strikes hit the Volyn region, cutting electricity to 370,000 people across the western district, which sits on the border with Poland. Governor Roman Romaniuk reported that two people were injured. In the eastern city of Kharkiv, a drone attack killed three people and injured five, the regional governor said. In central Ukraine, police said strikes on an apartment block in Uman injured a similar number. Private power company DTEK announced on Friday that it had implemented emergency power cuts across Kyiv due to ongoing strikes. In Russia, officials said air defences had blocked a Ukrainian drone attack against a heating plant in the Vladimir region. Ukraine has had significant success in attacking Russia’s energy infrastructure and its oil refineries in particular. However, that strategy has provoked anger from United States President Donald Trump, who has blamed Ukraine for pushing up global oil prices. Russia said it shot down 644 Ukrainian drones overnight, 94 of them headed for Moscow. Reporting from Moscow, Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova said the capital’s four airports and St Petersburg’s Pulkovo Airport had suspended operations. Ukrainian attacks killed two people in the Russian-controlled ‌Luhansk region of eastern Ukraine, the Russian-installed ⁠governor said. Concern over Russian activity near NATO territory has grown since the summer as Romania, Moldova, Poland and the Baltic states reported numerous intrusions of drones into their airspace and waters. That activity appears to be becoming more bellicose. In recent weeks, drones have struck at least seven cargo ships off the Black Sea coasts of Romania and Bulgaria, leaving 25 people dead or missing. Drones hit two ships off ⁠Romania’s coast this week. A hit on a commercial vessel that sank off Bulgaria’s coast on Tuesday prompted Sofia to summon Russia’s ambassador. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said on Friday that while the evidence pointed to Russia, his government does not have proof. Shortly afterwards, Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov told reporters that Bulgaria ‌has formally asked NATO to deploy combat ⁠aircraft and ⁠antidrone systems to bolster its defences. “We have sent letters and a request to the NATO ⁠Secretary General and the Supreme Allied Commander, ⁠urging them to strengthen our capabilities, which also means deploying additional forces on our territory. We are awaiting their decision,” Stoyanov said. NATO did ⁠not immediately respond to a request for comment, the Reuters news agency reported. Stoyanov said he plans to ⁠meet his Romanian and Turkish counterparts ⁠soon to discuss coordinating action and a common approach to the situation in the Black Sea. Bulgaria, which has proposed a moratorium ‌on attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea, also expects to join a NATO antidrone initiative by ‌the ‌end of October. Romania’s president has also said that his country has asked for additional equipment.

events.title: ‘Clean air is not a favour’: Indonesia’s neighbours fed up with acrid haze as Singapore threatens to prosecute
events.summary: Millions affected by smoke from wildfires as schools close, respiratory illnesses soar and diplomatic tensions rise S ingapore is threatening to prosecute companies responsible for some of the worst fires in years in neighbouring Indonesia, as the region grows increasingly frustrated with a persistent, acrid haze that could result in diplomatic relations fraying. Lawrence Wong, the Singaporean prime minister, said his government was distributing masks to vulnerable citizens and working with countries in the region to deal with the smoke. “At the same time, we are looking into which companies may be responsible for the fires,” he said in a Facebook post on Thursday, adding that he was exploring the idea of “joint action with other countries”. Singapore has no plantations or forests of its own, but several companies with concessions in Indonesia are reportedly based in the city-state. Haze is a persistent problem in Indonesia, but drier-than-usual conditions mean the thick smoke has been drifting into nearby Singapore, Malaysia , Brunei and Timor-Leste, and as far afield as the Philippines and Vietnam. Millions are affected, with school closures, respiratory illness spiking and air pollution indexes reaching unhealthy levels. Malaysians and Singaporeans have been sharing images online of their cities, with skyscrapers disappearing into the smog, and frustration with the region’s most populous country is boiling over. “Year after year, the haze comes back. It affects our health, closes schools, hurts businesses, and costs us billions,” a veteran Malaysian social activist and former politician wrote in a public letter this week. Lee Lam Thye said that real enforcement and “not just polite words” were needed. “Those responsible must be named, investigated, and punished. Clean air is not a favour. It is a basic right.” While Indonesia regularly battles wildfires in the dry season, these blazes are the most intense in more than a decade and exacerbated by slash-and-burn practices to clear land for agriculture, including palm oil, of which Indonesia is the world’s largest producer. Regional diplomats have offered to help Indonesia, but their offers have not always been immediately accepted. On Monday, an Indonesian official said the country was “still capable of handling it”. By the end of the week, Jakarta said it would accept assistance . Such delicate diplomacy is routine among the region’s Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean), which is built on ​quiet engagement and non-interference. A meeting of regional foreign ministers in the Philippines is due next month, but that might be too late. Nerves are fraying. In remarks that went viral on social media, Syahganda Nainggolan, the head of Indonesia’s government communication agency, hit back at the criticism on Saturday. “We don’t only send haze,” he said, “the oxygen in Singapore and Malaysia comes from our forests.” Rare strong words came earlier this month from Anwar Ibrahim, the Malaysian prime minister. He said he had been in contact with Indonesia’s president, Prabowo Subianto , “who agreed to take the necessary steps, and this commitment must be followed by immediate and effective action from the Indonesian side to tackle the root causes of the haze”. At the same time, pressure is growing on Jakarta to declare a national disaster, first from civil society groups but now also from Indonesian politicians and neighbours. According to the Jakarta Post, Indonesian students have been holding protests across Kalimantan and Sumatra, demanding accountability and government action. In one video posted online , a child in a mask stands outside under a dark orange sky and calls on the local and national government to help. He holds a sign that says: “Save our little lungs”. The country has dispatched firefighters and announced a crackdown on arsonists, but declaring a disaster would unlock funds and help thousands with medical expenses. On Friday, the Indonesian forestry ministry said four firefighters were killed in a national park in Java. Longtime onlookers say the issue is not just firefighting, but targeting the companies involved. In recent years, several attempts to take legal action against the companies exacerbating “transboundary haze” have failed, both locally and internationally, and posed a diplomatic minefield. Haze is complex for Singapore and Malaysia, as they host companies working in Indonesia. A Greenpeace report published this month identified businesses based in Singapore and Malaysia that it claimed were linked to burning land in Indonesia. Ultimately, Indonesians bear the brunt of the blazes. The health ministry has reported nearly 280,000 people in the country with respiratory infections linked to the fires, with children under five accounting for more than 60,000.

events.title: SNEF names Poon Hong Yuen as next CEO
events.summary: SNEF chief executive Hao Shuo (left) will be replaced by Poon Hong Yuen, who takes over as chief executive on Dec 1. PHOTOS: SINGAPORE NATIONAL EMPLOYERS FEDERATION SNEF has named Poon Hong Yuen as its next chief executive. He starts as chief executive-designate on Nov 1 and takes over on Dec 1. Poon is now deputy secretary at the Ministry of Digital Development and Information. He also held senior roles at MOM and Spring Singapore, giving him strong policy and digital economy experience. Outgoing chief executive Hao Shuo will leave for a new public service role. Under him, SNEF grew to over 4,000 corporate members and ran transformation programmes for more than 3,200 employees. SINGAPORE - The Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF) has named Poon Hong Yuen as its next chief executive, replacing Hao Shuo after a two-year tenure. Poon will join as chief executive-designate on Nov 1 and take over formally on Dec 1, SNEF said on Oct 16. He is currently deputy secretary at the Ministry of Digital Development and Information. He previously served as deputy secretary (workforce) at the Ministry of Manpower (MOM) and chief executive of the former Spring Singapore. SNEF president Kuah Boon Wee said Poon’s experience would position him well to lead the federation through technological and economic change. “His leadership experience and contributions to workforce policy, enterprise development and the digital economy will be invaluable as SNEF champions employers’ interests, strengthens tripartism and helps businesses harness emerging technologies for workforce transformation and sustainable growth,” he said. Hao, who joined SNEF as chief executive in December 2024, will leave to take up a new appointment in the public service. SNEF did not disclose his next role. Before joining SNEF, he was divisional director for manpower planning and policy at MOM, where he oversaw workforce planning, labour market policies, foreign workforce policies and HR sector development. Under him, SNEF strengthened its policy, research and communications capabilities, while membership grew to more than 4,000 corporate members employing about 900,000 workers. More than 700 employers have taken part in workplace and workforce transformation programmes administered by SNEF in the last two years, benefiting over 3,200 employees. Kuah said Hao also worked with MOM and the National Trades Union Congress on policy reviews, including the Employment Act review and tripartite work on senior employment. events.title: Coffee’s coming glut may not be enough to calm volatile prices
events.summary: The 2026-27 season is widely expected to produce the biggest surplus in years, helped by a potential record crop in the world’s top grower. Coffee supplies are rising after years of shortages, but exchange-certified stocks are still at their lowest since 1999, keeping arabica prices near US$3.50 a pound. A 2026-27 surplus, led by Brazil, could boost private inventories, but traders doubt enough beans will reach exchange warehouses to stabilise futures. Low exchange stocks may keep prices volatile and risk a short squeeze, which could raise costs for roasters and consumers, including latte prices. After years of shortages, the world is finally getting more coffee. The question is how much of it will reach the exchange warehouses that underpin prices across the industry. The market for arabica coffee has been unusually volatile in 2026, due in large part to a deeply depleted repository of beans available to settle expiring futures. Exchange-certified stockpiles have fallen to their lowest point since 1999, helping push prices close to their highest levels this year, near US$3.50 (S$4.50) a pound (454g). Those stockpiles need to rebuild for prices to become more stable. Otherwise, coffee roasters – and ultimately consumers – could remain exposed to sharp price swings even as global supplies improve. There should be plenty of beans to go around: The 2026-27 season is widely expected to produce the biggest surplus in years, helped by a potential record crop in top grower Brazil. But traders and analysts are unsure whether current futures prices offer enough incentive to send those beans into exchange-managed warehouses rather than private stocks. Exchange deliveries were a “slam dunk” when the premium for delivering coffee sooner rather than later was higher, said Judy Ganes, president of J. Ganes Consulting and a veteran commodity analyst. “The math changed, and all of a sudden it didn’t make sense to deliver as much of that.” That distinction matters because exchange warehouses act as a backstop for the coffee industry. They absorb beans when other buyers show little interest and provide a readily available reservoir when supplies become scarce. Roasters have drawn heavily on that reservoir and are now actively buying beans in the physical market at higher prices, intercepting supplies that might otherwise reach the exchange. Growing private inventories would still be good news for roasters and consumers after years of shortages and record prices. But without a significant recovery in exchange stocks, futures could remain volatile. Prices may have to rise to encourage more deliveries, potentially forcing traders with short positions to buy back futures and amplifying the rally. “There’s the possibility that someone gets squeezed,” Ganes said. That can ultimately feed through to the price of a latte. Futures serve as a basis for the prices that many roasters pay for beans, with their final cost typically based on the futures price plus a premium or discount for quality. Consumers are still feeling the pinch of a historic run-up in coffee costs two years ago, and Folgers maker JM Smucker has cited elevated futures as a reason for delaying plans to cut prices. Oliver Broster, senior manager of coffee analysis at Expana, said the looming surplus creates the risk of a steep decline in prices, meaning the exchange should already be an attractive destination for some beans. Some beans are starting to arrive. More coffee from Brazil entered certified stocks in September than in each of the prior 18 months. But the sudden influx of tens of thousands of bags sent futures plunging, and arrivals have since slowed. The fact that around 72% of Brazilian coffee bag arrivals passed an exchange quality test that month – an unexpectedly high rate in line with past years – also pressured prices, since heavy rains had raised fears about potentially widespread damage to the crop. “It’s a huge crop. So in comparison with last year, there’s still a large quantity of excellent-quality Brazil,” Broster said. Still, Brazilian growers have little reason to rush. Flush with cash from record coffee prices in previous harvests, producers have been able to hold beans for longer than usual while waiting for higher offers. Brazilian coffee likely to meet the Intercontinental Exchange’s quality standards is also good enough to be “really getting a premium in some markets” beyond what the exchange can pay, said Marcelo Moreira, a Brazil-based analyst with Archer Consulting. A surge in Brazil’s currency in October on election results may further discourage farmers from selling unless the dollars they receive for exports also rise. Beans from sought-after origins like Colombia are likewise commanding higher premiums, making near-term deliveries to the exchange a less profitable option, according to StoneX senior trader Tomas Araujo.

events.title: I took a 20% pay cut for 8 months so I could spend an entire summer with my kids. It was worth it.
events.summary: The author took a 20% pay cut for more time off with her kids. Courtesy of Natalia Costa As my maternity leave after having my fourth child was ending, summer was starting. I wanted to spend the summer with my kids, and I looked for a solution. I ended up taking a 20% pay cut for 8 months for another 73 days off. Our fourth child was a happy surprise, and arrived on the scene when we were busy putting out metaphorical fires with our 4-year-old twins and our 2-year-old daughter, who seemed to spend most of their time playing and fighting. We felt like we already had a lot of kids. Not too many, but enough. When I learned I was pregnant, we asked ourselves, what was one more? As my maternity leave was ending, I still wanted more time Nine months later, the real party began. My maternity leave started coming to an end just as we were facing a very long summer: 12 weeks, from June 20 to September 8, with no school. We live in Spain, and were about to face one of those eternal Spanish summers I remember so well from my own childhood: long, hot days full of sand, sea, salt, swimming pools, and, yes, boredom. Our monthly expenses were already higher than ever (diapers, onesies, baby food, and all those brand-new baby things I'd previously gotten rid of because I thought we were done having kids). Still, I decided to take a 20% pay cut in exchange for more time, simply so I could get us through the summer. That decision meant more time with the baby, obviously, but also with the rest of my kids, who are still just older than babies themselves. The difference is that 40 years ago, in many families, one salary — usually the man's — could support a household . Today, both parents often need full-time jobs and want to have professional lives of their own. This is the case for us, and it's not particularly compatible with looking after four very young children for 12 weeks. Taking a pay cut gave me an extra 73 days off By agreeing to a 20% pay cut for eight months, I was able to combine my reduced working hours into 73 full days off instead of working shorter days each week. Together with my maternity leave, weekends, and public holidays, those extra days allowed me to stay home with my children much longer than I ever expected. I didn't have to return to work until my baby was 10 months old. It was a financial sacrifice, but it gave me something I couldn't put a price on: more time with my children. Face to face. It sounded stressful when I thought about it. In reality, it turned out to be a dream. I've had the best summer of my life, and I'm afraid I may never get another one quite like it. Since June, the weeks have passed slowly, as we looked for activities to fill the days: painting, drawing, gluing things together, doing yoga or gymnastics, trying to get everyone to nap at the same time, and, obviously, spending hours by the pool and at the beach. There were moments when the baby wanted to breastfeed while my little girl needed a diaper change at the pool, with me sitting on the edge, trying to manage both. Or one kid suddenly needed to pee while the others were happily playing in the water. It has been a crash course in patience, caregiving, and motherhood. But the interesting part isn't just how much fun we had. It's how much money we saved by doing it this way. We saved so much on childcare that it didn't make much of a difference I lost €10,000 (about $11,200) by taking the pay cut, which is a lot of money when you have this many kids. But I also avoided paying for the baby's day care , which costs around €700 a month. Over three months, that's about €2,100. Summer programs for the other three children would have cost around €200 per child a week. Over 12 weeks, that comes to €7,200. Put it all together, and we would have spent about €9,300 on childcare over the summer anyway. So, in practical terms, we gave up roughly €700 so I could spend an entire summer with our four kids. It a good trade. Then there's everything that doesn't fit neatly into a spreadsheet: everything we learned together about being a family, sharing things, expressing ourselves, respecting each other's rhythms, and simply waiting for things to get done, something you do a lot of when there are four small children involved. Financially, it turned out to be a good decision for us. Emotionally, it was even better. The question now isn't really how much we saved or lost. It's what we're going to do next summer. We'll see. events.title: India vs West Indies: Fifth T20 International – teams, start, lineups, Hope
events.summary: India host West Indies in the final match of the tour on Saturday with an all-time classic T20 series level at 2-2. Who: India vs West Indies What: Twenty20 International cricket series Where: M Chinnaswamy Stadium, Bengaluru, India When: Saturday, October 17, at 7pm (13:30 GMT) How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will have all the build-up from 11:30 GMT before our live text commentary stream India host West Indies in the decisive T20 International series finale on Saturday after one of the most compelling white-ball tours in recent memory. list 1 of 4 Asian Cup in Saudi Arabia still on, organisers say, but golf tour postponed list 2 of 4 DR Congo protests Formula 1’s ‘indefensible’ decision to race in Rwanda list 3 of 4 Infantino apologises to FIFA council but critics remain unhappy list 4 of 4 French football body urges fans and students to keep politics out of stadiums The five-game series is level at 2-2 before the match in Bengaluru after record-breaking feats by the tourists that have pushed the T20 World Cup holders to the limit. Al Jazeera Sport takes a look at what has become a must-not-miss showdown. How did West Indies tour of India begin? The teams played a three-match One-Day International to begin the white-ball tour, which saw India take an unassailable lead after opening eight-wicket wins in Thiruvananthapuram and Guwahati. After posting a mammoth 351-7 off their 50 overs – thanks largely to KL Rahul’s 129 off 87 balls – in New Chandigarh, India would have felt they had enough on the board to claim the third match, too. Enter West Indies captain Shai Hope. The opener hit 162 off 143 balls in an unbeaten knock that led his side to a five-wicket win . It was the West Indies highest ODI run chase. How did the India-West Indies T20 series begin? India put the disappointment of the closing defeat in the ODI series behind them by claiming an eight-win win, with 5.2 overs to spare, in the first T20 of the series. Despite fifties from Hope and Sherfane Rutherford, West Indies were bowled out for 171, with Naman Dhir taking three wickets for the hosts. Hope then hit an unbeaten 102 off only 45 balls in the second match to lead West Indies to their highest successful Twenty20 run chase . Hope hit nine sixes and six boundaries as the West Indies finished with 252-4 in reply to India’s 249-5. India restored their series lead in the third match, but only via a narrow 14-run victory. After being bowled out off the last ball of their innings, India posted 223 – led by Abhishek Sharma’s 69 off 30 balls. Arshdeep Singh claimed three wickets as West Indies were restricted to 209-7. What happened in the last India-West Indies T20? It was time for the Hope show again in the fourth game of the T20 tour, as the wicketkeeper-batter hit his second century of the series . The tourists struck 247-3, having been put in, with Hope hitting an unbeaten 102. His nine sixes and four fours were a record tally for a West Indies batter in a T20 International. The total was the second-highest first innings score in T20s against India, trailing England’s 257-3 in Southampton this year. Opener Sanju Samson’s 56 off 23 balls set India off to a good start, but Keemo Paul’s five-wicket haul led West Indies to a 24-run series levelling win. What did Shai Hope joke about his Player of the Match awards? Hope joked after the fourth T20 that he was worried he may ⁠have to fork ⁠out excess baggage fees after picking up his third Player of the Match award on their tour of India. “To be honest, they are a bit heavy, and we have got to look at the luggage weight,” he quipped after the win. “I think we are going to have some problems going back home.” Abhishek Sharma, Sanju Samson (w), Ishan Kishan, Shreyas Iyer (c), Tilak Varma, Naman Dhir, Nitish Kumar Reddy, Axar Patel, Prince Yadav, Mayank Yadav, Arshdeep Singh Shai Hope (c and w), Jewel Andrew, Shimron Hetmyer, Rovman Powell, Sherfane Rutherford, Romario Shepherd, Roston Chase, Shamar Springer, Keemo Paul, Shamar Joseph, Gudakesh Motie

events.title: The UAE’s ‘Zero Hormuz’ strategy runs through Fujairah
events.summary: The Scene From the deck of one of the large tugboats used to guide giant crude tankers into Fujairah’s port, the UAE’s race toward its “Zero Hormuz” strategy is visible in every direction. A carrier capable of moving two million barrels of oil was loading at the port’s lone jetty able to handle such vessels. Smaller ships occupied other berths, and one tanker was loading at an offshore mooring, with a UAE naval corvette standing guard nearby. On the horizon, in the haze, several more tankers lay anchored, engaged in ship-to-ship transfers, taking on oil shuttled through the Strait of Hormuz under US protection for delivery to customers around the world. Fujairah — one of the UAE’s poorer emirates better known for its low-cost resorts and mountain escapes — is at the center of a regional push to reduce Iran’s leverage over Gulf trade through the Strait of Hormuz. Geography has become its biggest asset, and it’s not alone. Saudi Arabia is expanding its pipeline network, and Kuwait is in talks with Riyadh and the UAE to move crude through their respective links. Oman is also a likely beneficiary of the Hormuz disruption, with separate pipeline plans for its ports to safely ferry fossil fuels trapped in the Gulf. For Fujairah, this race to bypass the strait could lead to a new liquefied natural gas plant, a refinery, and “a much bigger port,” Fereidun Fesharaki, chairman emeritus of energy consultancy FGE NexantEC, told Semafor. “This wretched war has created for Fujairah a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity.” Kevin Zweerink/Semafor Know More Fujairah had been preparing for this opportunity long before the US-Iran war erupted on Feb. 28. Abu Dhabi opened a pipeline to the port in 2012 with a daily capacity of 1.8 million barrels of crude, giving itself an outlet beyond Hormuz, just in case. Photos of the port and coastline in the late 1990s show minimal oil storage and loading infrastructure. Today, tank farms line both sides of the coastal highway near the port, and a network of pipes moves products among terminals and to ships. A rail link from Abu Dhabi moves goods and recently began carrying passengers. Glancing at a map of the UAE makes shifting assets east to the Gulf of Oman seem a relatively simple feat for a wealthy country dependent on exporting its resources. But the topography is a challenge: Craggy mountains press against the coastline, making land reclamation the only way to expand. And while the opportunity is clear and few doubt the UAE government’s ability to execute, the territory is still subject to the same risks affecting the region. Being outside Hormuz provides some protection for ships, but the vessels, tank farms, and port infrastructure remain vulnerable. Iran has attacked them all. War insurance has always been an issue for operators in Fujairah, and insurers have indicated they would need to see six months of stable peace before lowering premiums, according to two people familiar with the matter who have negotiated with insurance companies. Thus far, Fujairah’s port has focused on the most valuable trade, leaving the import and re-export of building materials, consumer goods, and machinery to the much larger facilities in Dubai and Abu Dhabi. That is changing. Cargo trucks now line the highway for some 10 miles, waiting for a chance to enter the ports. Ship-to-ship transfers are rising rapidly, from just a handful before the war to 80 in August and 120 in September, according to a person familiar with port operations. They mostly involve crude, but also aluminum, bauxite, and steel. At a dinner during the Energy Markets Forum, organized by Dubai-based consultancy Gulf Intelligence, the word “resilience” was overused, but in this setting, it was appropriate: These are the people who have helped move oil consistently from one of the world’s most volatile regions for almost a century. The business’s boom-bust cycle also came up. Fujairah’s historic advantage was as a link for ships coming through the Strait of Hormuz, but there are other ports to call at in Oman, which has friendlier relations with Iran than anyone else in the Gulf, and the question no one could answer was whether the boom during a crisis would carry on once shipping companies could return to their old routes. For the people of Fujairah, though, the vacant plots of reclaimed land near the port that may soon accommodate an LNG plant and other productive assets may be enough to help them catch up to their wealthier compatriots in Abu Dhabi and Dubai. Mohammed’s view Iran has been threatening to close Hormuz for decades, and while Gulf states didn’t necessarily ignore the threat, they largely operated as if freedom of navigation through the waterway would remain the norm. Saudi Arabia’s and the UAE’s investments in pipelines were prescient. But like their neighbors without outlets beyond Hormuz, they concentrated most of their investment in cities and industrial zones inside the Gulf, within reach of Iranian missiles, opting to prioritize domestic economic development. Today, the direction of travel in the region is redundancy and resilience. Gulf states don’t have much of a choice other than to invest in different routes and use whichever works best. If there’s peace, some pipelines and ports could lie dormant at times. That’s the price of keeping energy and goods flowing when enemies strike at the lifeblood of their economies. All these contradictions are evident in Fujairah’s boom, where its geographic blessing offers no immunity from conflict. Iranian attacks there and on other pipelines in the region signal a future where Gulf states may also need alternatives to their alternatives. Room for Disagreement Fujairah and Oman are beneficiaries of efforts to keep oil and other exports flowing. But making the Strait of Hormuz, in US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent’s words, a “worthless piece of water,” has always been hyperbole. It’s true that crude flows have largely recovered thanks to pipelines and US military escorts of tankers. But liquefied natural gas, fertilizer, metals, helium, and other exports, as well as all the imports that more than 60 million people rely on, can’t all move efficiently through alternative routes. Qatar’s energy minister, meanwhile, has been emphatic in rejecting gas pipelines and relocating processing facilities to other countries, committing instead to LNG expansion in Ras Laffan. For other exporters, the trucking math doesn’t work: The CEO of Fertiglobe, one of the world’s largest exporters of urea and ammonia fertilizers, told me a typical ship carries 50,000 tons of fertilizer. Replacing it would take some 2,000 truckloads . Notable Fujairah’s wartime role reflects years of investment in pipelines, ports, and trading capabilities , energy expert Robin Mills writes in The National. events.title: U.S. Starlink curbs embolden Russia to intensify attacks on Ukraine, minister tells CNBC
events.summary: A Ukrainian infrastructure official warned on Friday that intensified Russian strikes on bridges and energy systems could make the coming winter especially difficult. "With U.S. limiting the use of Starlinks on the battlefield, Russia feels that this is their moment to try and inflict even more pain and suffering on Ukraine's civilian infrastructure," Serhiy Derkach, Ukraine's first deputy minister for recovery, infrastructure and transport, told CNBC. It comes as tensions between the U.S. and Ukraine have flared up after the Starlink service was reported to be restricted in Ukraine earlier this week. Ukraine is bracing for a difficult winter as restrictions on military applications of Starlink have emboldened Russia to intensify attacks on civilian and energy targets, a senior Ukrainian official told CNBC on Friday. Serhiy Derkach, Ukraine's first deputy minister for recovery, infrastructure and transport, said Russian forces had stepped up strikes on bridges in Kyiv, threatening to isolate nearly 2 million residents on the eastern bank of the Dnipro River, while also targeting railway networks and border crossings in an effort to disrupt transport and sow panic among civilians. "With U.S. limiting the use of Starlinks on the battlefield, Russia feels that this is their moment to try and inflict even more pain and suffering on Ukraine's civilian infrastructure," Derkach said. "We are definitely moving towards very harsh weeks and months and need our partners' support now more than ever," he said, adding that Ukrainians already experience blackouts lasting 4-12 hours per day. His warning came as President Volodymyr Zelenskyy on Friday called for support from European leaders in Brussels to help Ukraine prepare a winter support package, including energy assistance, air defenses and funding. Zelenskyy praised Europe's "real leaders" for standing by Kyiv on Friday, as his strained relationship with U.S. President Donald Trump clouds a summit focused on securing further support for Ukraine. "I'm so thankful that we have such huge support from EU Council Commission and leaders – real leaders," Zelenskyy said, emphasizing Europe's backing since the beginning of the war. His remarks come as tensions between the U.S. and Ukraine have flared up after SpaceX's Starlink service was restricted in Ukraine earlier this week, slowing down the connectivity Ukraine relies on to defend against Russian attacks. Zelenskyy is also reportedly facing increasing pressure to tone down public criticism of Trump. Three officials familiar with the EU summit preparations told the Financial Times that they plan to privately urge Zelenskyy to tone down his rhetoric when they meet him in Brussels on Friday. According to Politico , some EU leaders are also concerned about Zelenskyy's handling of his strained relationship with Trump, with one EU diplomat saying Zelenskyy's public criticism of the president was "not helpful." "We want to end this war as quick as possible. We don't see now signals from Russia side that they are ready for this to end this war," Zelenskyy told reporters in Brussels on Friday after he on Wednesday lamented that Russia didn't respect the "energy ceasefire" announced by Trump. Trump last week surprised both Russian and Ukrainian officials by announcing the countries had agreed to stop attacking each other's power infrastructure, in an apparent attempt to ease prices of oil and diesel ahead of the U.S. midterm elections in November. Zelenskyy later welcomed the proposal and said Ukraine had held off strikes on Russian energy targets for three days to abide by Washington's wishes, but he described the deal with Russia to supply diesel to global markets as "weak." Russia hasn't confirmed it agreed to an energy ceasefire, saying only that talks are "ongoing." Russian authorities didn't respond to multiple CNBC requests for comment. — CNBC's George Bextor contributed to this report

events.title: Warsh signals steady Fed outlook despite inflation jump
events.summary: Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh said Friday that the economy has largely performed as expected since September's rate hike, hinting that little has changed in the central bank's outlook. Why it matters: The Fed is weighing another interest rate increase later this month as inflation heats up and the economy remains strong. What they're saying: "Over the month or so that's transpired since then, the world has broadly conformed to our expectations," Warsh said at the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, referring to the Fed's September meeting. Warsh, interviewed by IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva, offered no explicit signal about October: "I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year." His remarks come just before the Fed's standard pre-meeting blackout period ahead of the Oct. 27-28 policy meeting. "It's hard to be in a discussion with central bankers and not compare notes and hear the same thing about the surge in prices," he said, alluding to conversations with international counterparts in Bangkok. State of play: The Fed raised rates last month for the first time since 2023 to contain inflation fueled by the Iran war. Minutes showed most officials expected another hike this year, though the timing remained unclear. Vice chair Philip Jefferson, New York Fed president John Williams and governor Christopher Waller have signaled that the Fed could hold off in October, with Waller noting that rate hikes need not come at consecutive meetings. Friction point: Fresh data this week showed inflation accelerated in September, with signs of price pressures extending beyond energy into services. Odds of an October hike jumped to 50% from 22% after Wednesday's hotter-than-expected inflation report, before retreating to 28% Thursday afternoon, per CME FedWatch. Between the lines: Warsh acknowledged that AI is boosting spending before its longer-term productivity benefits materialize, while investment beyond AI is also strengthening the economy. Warsh said AI was contributing to a "massive investment surge" in the U.S., calling the investment boom "probably the most important thing that's happening in the global economy on the upside." Warsh said AI could ultimately make economies more productive and generate greater wealth. But he said the AI transition was "likely to be a very bumpy one." What to watch: Warsh announced that the Fed will hold the first field hearing of its productivity and jobs task force on Nov. 16 in the Bay Area, bringing together outside experts to examine how AI and other technologies are reshaping the economy. The task force is one of five Warsh launched shortly after becoming Fed chairman to rethink how the central bank approaches monetary policy.

events.title: Trump rules out using a nuclear bomb on Iran: Why that matters
events.summary: It is the first time the president has definitively addressed nuclear weapons, but he did not deny US could use ‘mother of all bombs’. United States President Donald Trump has for the first time explicitly ruled out the use of a nuclear weapon against Iran, but has not denied US media reports that his administration is considering deploying the US’s most lethal non-nuclear munition , nicknamed the “mother of all bombs” in the near future. In an interview published on Thursday by right-wing American news site Newsmax, Trump suggested he does not plan to use nuclear weapons, but also clarified that the devastating aerial weapon, the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast Bomb (MOAB – ‘mother of all bombs ) “is not nuclear”. list 1 of 4 At least two security officials killed near Iran’s critical Chabahar port list 2 of 4 Suspected Israeli online operations cause alarm in Iran and Lebanon list 3 of 4 What is the ‘Mother of All Bombs’ US could use in Iran? list 4 of 4 US sanctions leave Iranians facing flight cancellations and soaring costs “I wouldn’t use nuclear. We don’t have to. We’re the greatest nuclear power in the world,” he told Newsmax. The comments marked Trump’s first definitive statement on the nuclear topic following speculation about a possible atomic conflict earlier in the US and Israel’s war on Iran. They also appeared to confirm speculation that another phase of the war is imminent, likely after the US midterm elections on November 3. Trump told Newsmax that the US might indeed launch another strike on Iran’s nuclear sites, particularly on Pickaxe Mountain, where Tehran is believed to be hiding a nuclear facility deep under layers of granite. He ruled out using a nuclear weapon or a tactical nuclear weapon. “I wouldn’t use nuclear. We don’t have to. We’re the greatest nuclear power in the world,” he said. He also clarified that the MOAB, which CNN reported the US government is considering using, “is not nuclear”. Responding to a question about whether the MOAB is “tactical nuclear” – meaning smaller nuclear munitions – Trump reiterated that it is not. “Well, the mother of all bombs is not nuclear,” Trump said. “It’s not nuclear at all. This is just an extremely large bomb.” Trump declined to say whether he had authorised its use in Iran. Trump also suggested renewed attacks are likely in the near future. The US cannot end the war now because it has to ensure Iran cannot produce a nuclear weapon, he argued, saying he believes that “if they had it, they would use it, in my opinion, instantaneously”. Trump also reiterated that the war would end “very soon” whether by force or diplomacy and that oil prices would then drop. When asked if he would put “troops on the ground”, Trump said: “No, I don’t see that, I don’t see it.” Earlier in the war, Trump had made comments regarding sending in troops, a move analysts said would be devastating for US soldiers because of Iran’s mountainous territory. The MOAB carries a massive payload of about 8,500kg (18,000 pounds or 8.5 tonnes) of high explosives. It weighs 9,800kg (21,605 pounds or nearly 10 tonnes) – about the same as four cars – and is just over nine metres (about 30 feet) long. Stealth bombers are too small to carry it, so it has to be deployed by larger, Lockheed C-130 Hercules transporters. It is designed to explode a few metres above the ground, sending out intense fireballs that can blast buildings and other hard-surface structures within a 1km radius, experts have told Al Jazeera. It is so powerful that a mushroom cloud from its blast has been seen 32km (20 miles) away in tests, the US Air Force has said. “Its large explosive charge can produce devastating blast effects against exposed personnel, equipment and vulnerable structures,” Brussels-based military and weapons analyst Elijah Magnier said. “Its purpose is to generate an exceptionally powerful blast across a surface area.” However, Magnier said there is doubt about whether using the massive surface explosive would be effective against deeply buried nuclear installations in Iran. He added that the terrain in Iran could be difficult for larger cargo aircraft to access. What has Trump previously said about nuclear weapons? Trump has never explicitly mentioned using a nuclear weapon, but he has also never ruled it out. Speculation regarding whether Washington might use nuclear weapons was rife in the early days of the conflict, largely because of the extreme nature of Trump’s numerous threats against Tehran. In April, for example, as Iran enforced a blockade on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, Trump posted on his Truth Social site that “…a whole civilisation will die tonight, never to be brought back again”, if Iran did not agree to a peace deal and reopen the strait. He also threatened to destroy Iran’s infrastructure, saying a bombing campaign “will be Power Plant Day and Bridge Day, all wrapped up in one”, in Iran.
