events.title: I embraced girlboss culture in my 20s. It didn't take long to realize I wanted out.
events.summary: The author leaned out of hustle culture and said she enjoyed a more relaxed, but still fulfilling, life. Courtesy of Catherine Work. I spent my 20s believing that working hard and making money were the keys to independence. I realized I was working so much that I had no time or energy to enjoy the life I was building. Years later, being an ambitious woman looks different to me. I work less and have time for myself. I thought making a lot of money and working hard would make me happy. In my early 20s, I got great grades and finished my undergrad in three years. By my mid-20s, I had finished my graduate degree in law while frequently working 70-hour weeks. I leaned into the idea of being a girlboss , often working weekends or through my lunch, and focusing on making lots of money. It was a habit I saw modeled by my parents. It worked for them, and I thought it would work for me, until it didn't. I thought hard work was the point At 26, I worked long days at my home desk after making "hard worker" and "responsible'"my identity for years. I thought this was what an independent woman was: someone who worked constantly and optimized all of her time. The author said she spent so much time working in her 20s that she barely had time to enjoy the money she made. Courtesy of Catherine Work. Sure, I was saving lots of money and networking, but I was often too tired on my day off to do anything. I often chose to work on Saturdays and didn't even have time to spend my hard-earned money. Two things made me realize this wasn't a sustainable lifestyle: I once told a friend I couldn't take a 15-minute lunch break to call her, and another time I struggled to lift my full duffle bag for an upcoming trip after not working out for months. Something had to give. I didn't want to just recover from burnout I was clearly burned out. I could have taken some time off to recover and come back, but then the cycle would have continued. It helped that I spent my early 20s in Cameroon and Costa Rica, two places where work-life balance looks a lot different than it does in the US, and people live with their parents much longer. Looking back on those years when I was truly happy helped me to question what I was focusing on in my life. I came to a new conclusion. I didn't want to simply recover after burning out. I wanted to reject the premise that burnout was the price of being an ambitious woman. I stopped hustling toward anything In 2022, as the COVID restrictions were lifted more and a relationship I had been in ended, I decided to travel while working a few hours per week. As a then single, childfree woman , no longer heading towards a career, I wondered what I'd replace these traditional markers of success with. The answer turned out to be nothing. I stopped trying to hustle toward something. No job, boss, passion, or person was going to truly reward me for committing to 70-hour weeks. Nothing was worth putting off a breakfast date with myself or an unplanned walk in the park, or that 15-minute phone call I told my friend I couldn't take. I decided to opt out of the competitive nature of the working world and instead focus on optimizing myself. 5 years later, my life looks different Five years later, I have a life my 26-year-old self would barely recognize. I work substantially less, have built a career around writing and research for companies with values I admire, and have spent the past several years living and traveling in different countries. The author said her life has much more balance now and includes time for her to travel, cook, and connect with friends. Courtesy of Catherine Work. I don't own a car or a home, and I'm not chasing a traditional career ladder. Instead of constantly asking what I should accomplish next, I have far more time for cooking, relationships, travel, and simply being alive. One thing I did keep from that previous era of my life was my deep conviction that I, and all women, need to be financially independent. I have stopped suggesting that my friends work through their lunch break; instead, we talk about ethical investing and the need to always have one's own bank account. Independence turned out to mean something else for me The surprising part is that opting out didn't ruin my career, and I didn't feel the need to replace work with anything else. I don't think chasing a job title, a salary, or a full calendar would have made me feel secure. I think I would have constantly felt the need to prove myself, which sounds exhausting to me now. Instead, I have the independence I sought when I was younger. It just took the form of letting go of the idea that I have to constantly prove my worth to myself. events.title: Banks expect to be hit with higher taxes in Budget
events.summary: Chancellor John Healey is planning to increase taxes on the bank sector, senior banking executives have told the BBC. Healey has described banks as part of "the crown jewels" of the UK economy, but leaders in the sector have said it will be "on the menu" at the Budget in two weeks' time. The biggest four banks collectively made about £15bn profit in the first six months of this year, and trade unions have called for them to face additional taxes. The trade body for the banking sector, UK Finance, warned "further increases in bank taxes would weaken competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government's ambition to deliver growth in every postcode". Barclays fell only slightly and HSBC actually rose as both have large international businesses and would be less affected by a hike in UK taxes. What is the Budget and what could be in it? There are a number of ways the chancellor could extract more money from the sector. One option is for Healey is to reverse a reduction in the surcharge that banks pay on corporation tax, from 8% to 3%, introduced in 2023, by Conservative chancellor Jeremy Hunt. Critics argue this would be unfair noting the cut coincided with a rise in corporation tax from 19% to 25%. Healey could also raise the bank levy - a small percentage charged on loans. The BBC understands that the Treasury is leaning towards changing the surcharge if they were to go ahead as it is easier to change an existing tax rather than impose a new windfall tax. Reversing the 2023 surcharge rate would raise around £2bn. However, the last government was persuaded that adding 8% on top of corporation tax of 25% would leave UK banks struggling to compete with European and US rivals - so it may be that it is raised, but not all the way back to the 8% level. Speaking to the press in Bangkok, Healey praised the role banks play in the British economy. Adding that he has "decisions to take in the Budget", he said: "My observation on the banks is that people too often see ​them as big, distant financial institutions, when they are hardwired into the economic fabric of this country and our future ⁠prospects." In the past banks have successfully argued that higher taxes would risk making the UK uncompetitive with other jurisdictions and would reduce their ability to lend, and therefore be anti-growth. Sir Philip Augar, an author and former banker in the City of London, told the BBC's Today programme there was "room for a moderate increase" in taxes on the sector that could raise up to £3bn a year. He said lenders were enjoying "booming conditions", benefiting from higher interest rates which boost their profits. Rising interest rates have expanded the margin between the rate at which banks lend to customers and the rate they pay savers. Sir Philip added that when the banking sector "hits really rocky times it expects the taxpayer to bail them out - when it hits boom times, it expects some kind of special treatment". He said banks cannot simultaneously be "too big to fail and too big to tax". Paul Nowak, general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, which represents trade unions, said Britain's four biggest banks are making a billion pounds a week, with bonuses at post-financial crash records. "These are bumper profits - driven by high interest rates and households' mortgage misery," he said. "Now it's time to make sure banks pay their fair share," he added. "But if the chancellor does ask the Banks to pay a fairer share of tax in the Budget, that's 100% the right call," he added. Burnham announces scheme to help first-time buyers onto housing ladder Published 27 September Healey says surprise UK growth is 'sign of resilience' ahead of Budget Published 1 day ago Faisal Islam: What surprise praise for UK economy tells us about the Budget Published 2 days ago Banks were pleased to have avoided being targeted at the last Budget, given the large profits they have made in recent years. There is another option that has been discussed with Treasury officials. Currently banks can use losses from the past to offset against profits - thereby reducing their tax bill in any given year. Lloyds in particular has been a beneficiary of this policy, as large losses from the financial crisis have been used to lower tax bills ever since. Some analysts and bank executives have pushed the idea of a moratorium on this practice for a few years, which would yield an estimated extra £1bn per year for the Treasury. That would provide a windfall while being "a lot more bearable", in the words of one bank executive. It would also spare foreign banks from an additional hit, including JP Morgan, whose chief executive Jamie Dimon has warned that the UK already has one of the highest tax burdens on banks in the world. He warned that adding further sector-specific taxes could discourage investment and damage competitiveness.

events.title: I've flown business class on dozens of airlines. My favorite premium cabin is on this lesser-known Asian carrier.
events.summary: I'm a frequent business-class flyer. This is why a boutique Asian airline is my favorite premium experience. Zach Benitez I flew on a "boutique" Taiwanese airline called Starlux, and it blew me away. The seat was like a private pod, and the food was some of the best I've ever had. The crew seemed rushed during boarding, but were impeccable inflight. I'm a regular business-class traveler, having flown on dozens of airlines and hundreds of thousands of miles over the years. I often get asked the same question: What's the best business-class seat you've ever flown in? It's not the usual fan favorites of Singapore Airlines or Emirates. It's Starlux Airlines, a Taiwanese carrier many Americans have never heard of. Starlux first flew in January 2020 and bills itself as a "boutique" international airline that operates nonstop flights from Taipei to several US cities, including Los Angeles, San Francisco, and Seattle. My flight was on an Airbus A350-900 from Taipei to San Francisco, a nearly 12-hour overnight flight. It was the second leg of a trip that started in Kuala Lumpur, and the entire itinerary cost 85,000 Alaska Airlines miles. The Starlux business class seat. Zach Benitez The cash fare on this route ranges from $2,600 to over $5,000, depending on the season, so the points redemption — Alaska is a Starlux partner — was a very good deal. And the experience blew me away. The whole idea from the beginning was to build a luxury airline from nothing with meticulous attention to detail and an emphasis on the small stuff. After flying Starlux , those minor details made all the difference. Here's what my flight was like and why I'd easily book again. The seat felt like a private suite Every seat in Starlux's business class opens straight into the aisle, and every one has a sliding door. The cabin is decorated with faux marble finishes and shiny black panels. It honestly looks more like a boutique hotel lobby than the inside a plane. One of the cubbies stored a remote and headphones. Zach Benitez This extreme attention to detail is what sold me most. My favorite example: there's a little gap under the storage cabinet door, so you can leave a charging cable running out of it with the door closed. Exploring the seat illuminated several thoughtful design choices. The pod felt deliberate in a way some brand-new airline seats just aren't. Some people call business class doors a gimmick, mostly because they don't go all the way up. I loved mine anyway. Once the seat was flat and the door was shut, it felt like my own little room, further emphasized by the warm mood lighting, pristine leather accents, and large seat walls. My little pod for 12 hours. Zach Benitez A flight attendant handed me pajamas before we'd even pushed back, so I changed right away. After dinner, the crew made up my bed with a thick mattress pad and one of the softest blankets I've ever been given on a plane. The lie-flat bed was comfortable despite the narrow footwell. Zach Benitez The footwell angles inward slightly, which makes it feel a bit tight when you're lying flat, but I slept well regardless. On an overnight flight this long, that's what matters most. The food was some of the best I've had in the air Dinner is where Starlux left every other business-class flight behind. It started with warm, fluffy garlic bread, which felt out of place alongside the Asian meal, but I was thrilled to see it. When the flight attendant came to clear my appetizer, she asked if I'd like more bread, to which I obviously said yes. The food was the best part of the flight. Zach Benitez Then a creamy miso mushroom soup showed up, and I'm not exaggerating when I say it's one of the best things I've eaten on a plane. It was rich and savory, the kind of thing I can still taste if I think about it today. The main was beef with fried rice, which was flavorful and cooked to perfection. The beef dish on Starlux. Zach Benitez Dessert was Italian gelato that was actually soft enough to eat straight away, which basically never happens with ice cream at 38,000 feet. Breakfast before landing: waffles with figs were also notable. One of the few airline breakfasts I'd happily order again. The waffle and fig dish on Starlux. Zach Benitez All of the food served looked as good as it tasted. Every course was properly plated, the flight attendant talked me through each dish, and she reset my table between courses without me noticing. The crew truly elevated the experience Starlux isn't perfect, and the first 20 minutes of my flight proved it. Pre-flight service felt as if the crew was simply going through the motions rather than trying to create a good experience. But when the meal service started, it was like a switch flipped. One flight attendant greeted me by name and knelt down next to my seat to take my order. At one point, my seatbelt locked up while I was reaching for my amenity kit; she saw it happen and handed me the kit before I'd said a word. The amenity kit bag is reusable. Zach Benitez My main course came out a few minutes late, and she apologized profusely for it, which she really didn't need to do, but it tells you what standard this crew holds itself to. By the time dinner was over, even the crew members who'd seemed checked out at first were warm and attentive. When I woke up and asked for tea, it was there almost immediately, with lemon and sugar on the side. I love how fun Starlux is The other thing I love about Starlux is that it doesn't take itself too seriously. There's a space theme running through the whole airline, from the Galactic Lounge in Taipei to the COSMILE loyalty program. Since 2024, it's been working with Peanuts, so Snoopy turns up on themed flights and merch. The Starlux lounge. Zach Benitez On my flight, the entertainment screen displayed a Snoopy welcome for me, and I still carry my things in a Starlux Snoopy tote bag. Even the toilet paper is custom printed with a runway design. All of these things make the airline feel like it's enjoying itself. The bathroom as a whole was clean and stocked with care products. Zach Benitez Starlux got the three things that actually matter right: the seat, the food, and the crew . And it did it with a sense of fun that a lot of the big-name carriers have somehow lost along the way. I've flown business class on dozens of airlines, including some of the world's most famous seats. If you're flying between the West Coast and Asia, I'd book Starlux. Starlux did not respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: The scariest thing about Elizabeth Holmes' new documentary is how much I wanted to believe her
events.summary: Elizabeth Holmes in "You Can See Everything." A24 A24's new documentary about Elizabeth Holmes, "You Can See Everything," is in theaters now. Directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, it's more character study than straightforward doc. The story about the downfall of Theranos has been told — but this one hasn't yet. Elizabeth Holmes famously does not blink, whether she's pitching investors or, by her own admission, flirting with a guy. Is her moony gaze haunting or hypnotic? A calculated act or proof of her naivete? At various points in A24's new documentary, "You Can See Everything," I vacillated between each of the above. A good portion of Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim's movie could be classified as a provocative staring contest, as Fielder probes Holmes about her life and the demise of her company, Theranos , in the weeks before she reported to prison to serve an 11-year sentence in May 2023. The answers he gets from Holmes are rarely satisfactory. (At one point, she insists she's never told a lie in her entire adult life; despite being convicted of fraud, she maintains her innocence throughout the film.) But with the camera zoomed in tight on Holmes' every micro-expression and clump of mascara, the movie's power is in the questions it raises in the space between her words. In these profoundly uncanny scenes, I found myself fluctuating between being freaked out by the lack of emotion in Holmes' vacuous gaze and, to my surprise, pitying her. Then I'd quickly shift back to being freaked out, because what if pity was exactly the reaction that Holmes — a talented, convicted fraudster — was angling for? If she could manipulate her voice to sound more authoritative in the workplace, she could certainly adapt her face to appear more sympathetic onscreen. It turns out that just because you can see everything, that doesn't mean you know anything. At least not for sure. 'You Can See Everything' is not the movie it appears to be Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes in "You Can See Everything." A24 Much like its subject, "You Can See Everything" is a slippery mind-trick of a film — part character study, part psychological thriller, part surrealist thought experiment. What it is not, despite its subject, is a movie about a tech company. The story of how Holmes went from being named the youngest self-made female billionaire by Forbes to being convicted of defrauding investors as the founder and CEO of the blood-testing startup Theranos is well documented. Holmes has already been the subject of a more traditional documentary, Alex Gibney's "The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley," which exhaustively maps the discrepancies within Theranos, and a scripted Hulu miniseries, "The Dropout," which dramatizes Holmes' origin story and attempts to illustrate how her ambitions outpaced her abilities. Both of those works lean into the prevailing narrative about Holmes, who was often pitched as " the next Steve Jobs " and proved especially skilled at wooing powerful men to her cause. "You want it to be true so badly," Tyler Shultz, a former Theranos employee-turned-whistleblower, says of Holmes' vision in Gibney's doc. "I was working with these devices every single day, and she could still kind of convince me. When I think back on those conversations, I just think, 'How did she do that?'" Elizabeth Holmes in "You Can See Everything." A24 The Holmes we see in "You Can See Everything" is tamer, gentler, and, at times, far more submissive than many headlines would have us believe. Yet even Fielder isn't immune to her strange charisma. Early in the film, Fielder admits to Holmes that he did a lot of research about her tenure at Theranos. He challenges her answers to questions, at one point telling Holmes, "I don't think anyone will ever believe you ever again." Yet, as time goes on, Fielder seems alternately bemused and unnerved by the onetime wunderkind — though never to the point of aversion. On the contrary, Holmes seems to draw Fielder ever closer, like a close-up magician with a deck of cards in her hands and a trick up her sleeve. Toward the end of the film, Fielder's memory is called into question. A friend asks if Fielder is retroactively polishing his interactions with Holmes, perhaps unconsciously, because he's grown to care about her. Maybe he wants to protect her. Seemingly taken aback, Fielder replies, "I'm not putting my feelings into this. I'm just trying to be accurate." It's one thing to be told someone is a master manipulator, as "The Inventor" and "The Dropout" plainly do. It's quite another to experience the manipulation firsthand. "You Can See Everything" offers audiences the latter. During a Q&A after an early screening of "You Can See Everything" in New York, Oppenheim described how he, Fielder, and the crew would swap interpretations of what they'd just seen and heard after the cameras were switched off. "The disagreements were so dynamic," Oppenheim recalled. It's been over three years since their close encounter of the Holmesian kind, and Fielder said he's still trying to process what he felt in her presence. "I'm really curious to hear what everyone else thinks, and what they make of certain things," Fielder said. "I think it will actually help me understand." "You Can See Everything" is in theaters now. events.title: India’s mass voter purge is hollowing out democracy
events.summary: The SIR is disenfranchising marginalised communities and advancing the Hindu nationalist project. Over the weekend, thousands of protesters demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, faced mass detentions and a heavy police crackdown in New Delhi. The demonstrations, which have brought together youth activists and opposition parties, centre on the removal of more than 130 million names from India’s electoral rolls, raising profound questions about the state of Indian democracy. The deletions are the result of the controversial Special Intensive Revision (SIR) undertaken by the Election Commission of India (ECI). The ECI periodically revises electoral rolls to add new voters and remove the names of those who have died or permanently moved away. The last intensive revision was completed in 2003-2004. What makes the current SIR unprecedented, however, is its scale, the arbitrariness and overreach of its procedures, and the mass disenfranchisement that has followed. The exercise has disproportionately affected Muslims, women, migrants and other marginalised communities while also raising questions about the legitimacy of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party’s (BJP’s) electoral victories in Bihar and West Bengal. Both the ECI and the ruling party have defended the exercise by using the language of “purification”. In a caste society, that rhetoric is deeply troubling but also revealing. The bureaucratic procedures and technological infrastructure underpinning the exercise barely mask its intention to create two classes of citizenship in India, one endowed with political voice through the right to vote and the other reduced to what the philosopher Giorgio Agamben calls “bare life”. The SIR’s intent, procedures and outcomes reveal a sinister design: to maximise voter exclusions rather than enhance voter participation. This subverts the promise of universal adult suffrage, a cornerstone of India’s constitutional democracy. The ECI initially excluded the government-issued Aadhaar card from the list of documents accepted for voter verification during the SIR, supposedly because it was considered “overinclusive”. If that did not expose the exercise’s exclusionary intent, the ECI’s invention of the category “logical discrepancy” during the West Bengal SIR certainly did. This pseudo-legal innovation accounted for 2.7 million of the nearly 9 million names removed from electoral rolls in Bengal. The demand for educational certificates, land records, legacy documents and family trees as evidence also places a heavy burden on poor and marginalised voters, especially in regions still reeling under mass poverty, landlessness and rampant illiteracy. With the “burden of proof” shifted to ordinary voters, the SIR aims to achieve precisely what it set out to do: mass deletions and consequent disenfranchisement. Customised apps and online forms, digitised electoral rolls and the requirement to upload scanned documents in prescribed formats are all presented as evidence of the SIR’s efficiency and objectivity. But this approach ignores the digital divide in a deeply unequal society. Technology does not operate outside relations of power. In fact, it often serves as a mechanism of control. The category of “logical discrepancy” relies on an AI-enabled application, ERONET (Electoral Roll Officers’ Network), which compares voters’ details with older electoral rolls and flags discrepancies in names and family relationships. The use of such centralised systems has also raised questions about who controls electoral data and how these discrepancies are assessed. Women are particularly vulnerable to these procedures. Many change their names or addresses after marriage and may lack the documents needed to establish links with older electoral records. The excessive exclusion of women demonstrates how ostensibly neutral technological procedures can reinforce existing inequalities and weaken people’s political voice. The SIR’s purported neutrality is at odds with its effects, which fall heavily on the weak and the marginalised. Among religious minorities, Muslims across the country bear a particularly heavy burden of deletions. In Bengal, Muslims reportedly accounted for about 65 percent of the 2.7 million people removed from electoral rolls on grounds of “logical discrepancy”. With only 19 specially constituted tribunals to handle more than 3.8 million appeals, the corrective process in effect has remained inaccessible to many excluded voters. In Hyderabad, 1.94 million names were marked for deletion under the “absent, shifted, dead and duplicate” (ASDD) category. An estimated 40.7 percent of those entries appeared to belong to Muslim voters, compared with Muslims’ 30 percent share of the city’s population. In some constituencies in Hyderabad’s Old City, Muslims accounted for as much as 80 percent of the names marked for deletion.

events.title: The case for CEOs who can laugh at themselves
events.summary: In today’s CEO Daily: An onstage incident turns into a leadership lesson. The big leadership story: Supermicro finally gets a new CFO. The markets: Stocks recover from a shaky week. Plus: All the news and watercooler chat from Fortune . Good morning. A few minutes into talking with Flex CEO Revathi Advaithi on stage this week at the Fortune Most Powerful Women Summit, I felt blood in my mouth. I knew what was coming as an injury to my lip had bled a few days earlier, unleashing a flood that reminded me of an old Saturday Night Live episode in which Julia Child (played by Dan Aykroyd) cuts herself while preparing a chicken. I tried to act nonchalant as a fistful of tissues turned red, and Advaithi paused a few times to ask if I was okay. My colleague Ellie Austin and members of the audience sprang into action, handing me fresh tissues and lip balm. Advaithi’s eyes conveyed concern as she answered my questions about data centers and geopolitics. I cracked a few jokes, called it our Halloween special, and gave Fidelity a shout-out for having the foresight to give away branded lip balm to participants. If you can’t hide it, ride it! (My colleague Emma Burleigh covered the interview here .) The incident was unfortunate, and a bit embarrassing, but it also gave Advaithi and me an opportunity to talk about being vulnerable and her decision to speak publicly about battling breast cancer as a CEO. The mood in the room was warm and supportive, and our interview had more moments of levity than I’d anticipated when we first sat down.  Rebecca Greenfield—Fortune I thought about that when watching Mark Zuckerberg wince on John Collison’s Cheeky Pint podcast while awkwardly sipping a pint of Guinness. It’s genuinely funny, and I’ve had a similar reaction when trying the beer in Ireland. (“That’s just my face,” Zuckerberg replied on X after the clip went viral.)  I think one of the underappreciated traits of leadership these days is a sense of humor. Richard Branson has long had it, as has Warren Buffett. Apple Executive Chairman Tim Cook often pokes fun at himself, replacing his last name with an Apple logo after President Trump called him “Tim Apple” during a White House meeting and mocking himself for posting a blurry iPhone photo a decade ago. Humor is a useful tool in any public role. ADP CEO Maria Black and I laughed onstage during the summit about what our Gen Z kids said during the recent Fortune CEO Initiative “generations” dinner. Lumen’s Kate Johnson and EY’s Janet Truncale joked about their first meeting at the Business Roundtable. And Marissa Mayer, the former Yahoo CEO who just launched Dazzle AI, has a wry take on some of the men now spouting doomsday rhetoric in Silicon Valley. (Check out Amanda Gerut’s Fortune coverage of my conversations with Black and Mayer .)  As a student at the University of Nairobi, I had an opportunity to write speeches for Mostafa Tolba, the then-executive director of the United Nations Environment Program (UNEP). His only instruction when writing my first speech about desertification at a conference for the homeless was to “make it funny.” I worked through the night, trying to come up with jokes about climate change and the homeless. Really. Dr. Tolba laughed because they were so bad and I’d clearly misconstrued his instructions. “No, Diane. Don’t joke about serious subjects,” he told me. “Joke about me.” Before we can connect to solve tough problems, he explained, we have to connect as human beings. Good advice that’s stuck with me ever since. Contact CEO Daily via Diane Brady at diane.brady@fortune.com This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

events.title: Trump says he won't use nuclear weapons or send ground troops to Iran
events.summary: President Donald Trump said he would not use nuclear weapons against Iran, telling Newsmax that the U.S. “doesn't have to.” Trump also said he did not foresee sending U.S. ground troops into Iran. His comments came after CNN reported that new U.S. strike options include possible use of the non-nuclear GBU-43/B MOAB against Iranian targets. U.S. President Donald Trump has said he does not intend to use nuclear weapons against Iran or foresee deploying ground troops in the country. Speaking in an interview with Newsmax, broadcast Thursday evening, he said: "I wouldn't use nuclear. We don't have to. We're the greatest nuclear power in the world." The right-wing cable outlet asked Trump about reports that Washington was considering using the GBU-43/B Massive Ordnance Air Blast, or MOAB, widely known as the "Mother of All Bombs." "The mother of all bombs is not nuclear. It's not nuclear at all. This is just an extremely large bomb. It's like a tiny nuclear bomb. But the mother of all bombs is one big bomb, but it's not nuclear," he said, without specifically confirming or denying the reports. When asked if he would put "troops on the ground," Trump said: "No, I don't see that, I don't see it." The MOAB is the largest non-nuclear bomb in the U.S. arsenal. It was used in combat in 2017 against ISIS militants in Afghanistan . Earlier on Thursday , CNN reported that the U.S. military has developed new strike plans to target Iranian energy infrastructure and nuclear sites. The strikes could take place if Trump orders combat operations to resume, either before or after the midterm elections, the outlet reported. The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment. Trump said on Oct. 8 that he would not order a resumption of military strikes before the Nov. 3 midterm elections. events.title: IBM talent exec says it's better to be a specialist, not a generalist, in the AI era
events.summary: Aparna Nair said that "the world of generalists is long gone." : Lindsey Nicholson/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images "The world of generalists is long gone," said IBM's chief talent, leadership, and culture officer. Aparna Nair said IBM's clients aren't expecting general advice; they're looking for deep expertise. She said even if workers wear many hats, they still need extensive knowledge about their specialty. It's a hotly debated question: Is it better to be an expert or a generalist in the AI era? For Aparna Nair, IBM's chief talent, leadership, and culture officer, there's no debate. She said she doesn't think generalists alone "will cut it" in the workforce in the AI era. "The world of generalists is long gone," Nair said. Aparna Nair is IBM's chief talent, leadership, and culture officer. IBM Nair said that generalists may be able to rely on AI to learn a lot, but at IBM, for example, the company's clients aren't expecting general advice from its workforce. IBM is hired for its deep technological expertise, she said. Nair said the same is true for entry-level hires. IBM, which has committed to doubling down on junior talent , expects new workers to arrive with the skills — and domain expertise — to take on more complex work earlier in their careers, Nair said. She said workers should identify an area that aligns with their employer's needs, become an expert in it, and "go deep." That expectation remains even as engineering roles are starting to blur with AI. In the past, a software engineer might have spent 20% of their time coding and another 20% testing, Nair said. Now, AI can handle much of the coding work , and engineers need the critical-thinking and judgment skills to evaluate what the technology produces, Nair said. They also have more opportunities to work across the business , such as speaking with clients and marketing teams and bringing what they learn back into the products they're building. While today's engineers may wear many hats and work closely with different teams, they still need deep expertise in their field — and an understanding of how their work shapes the experience of clients and colleagues. Without that added knowledge, Nair said, it would be difficult for them "to do anything meaningful." While domain expertise may be valuable, workers should also remain flexible. Nair said that there's "nothing more powerful" than when workers combine deep expertise with the right behaviors, and also use AI to their advantage. "That's a lethal combination," Nair said. events.title: Oil prices ease but head for another weekly gain on Middle East supply concerns
events.summary: Oil prices eased on Friday but were still headed for another weekly increase on lingering Middle East supply concerns and as global efforts to boost crude stockpiles continue. Brent, the benchmark for two thirds of the world's oil, declined 0.77 per cent to $105.10 a barrel at 12.59pm UAE time. WTI, the gauge that tracks US crude, retreated nearly 1 per cent to $97.04. For the week, Brent is set to add 0.32 per cent, while WTI is on track to jump by more than 5.6 per cent. Global energy prices remain volatile and elevated as the war in Iran, now in its eighth month, continues to choke energy supplies. That has prompted moves to ensure ample supplies globally. On Thursday, the International Energy Agency said its March pledge to release crude oil stocks will exceed its target. It will accelerate the release of the remaining supplies as global efforts to tame soaring energy prices continue. The Paris-based agency also pointed out that exports out of the Middle East have recovered to pre-crisis levels and that oil storage globally is not tight. Gulf oil producers, meanwhile, have pushed tanker transfers as far as India’s coast and slashed prices to keep crude flowing to Asia, as the makeshift export network around the Strait of Hormuz buckles under congestion and persistent attacks . There were 82 Ship-to-ship transfers in India's Gulf of Kutch last month, equivalent to about 680,000 barrels per day, shipping analytics company Vortexa said. Refined products accounted for about 65 per cent of the volume, with crude making up the remainder. Current oil market levels “still seem to be somewhat lofty compared to market realities … [but] we are not running out of oil, as flows out of the Middle East have largely recovered. Instead of tilting the oil market into a deficit, the Iran war has mainly erased the surplus that had been built in 2025", said Norbert Rucker, head of economics and next-generation research at Swiss lender Julius Baer. G7 leaders pledged this month to accelerate the IEA's co-ordinated emergency stock release by releasing 100 million barrels of diesel and other reserves to help stabilise markets. And in a surprise move last week, US President Donald Trump's administration lifted sanctions to enable Russia to supply millions of barrels of diesel to global markets. The IEA on Wednesday warned that the global diesel shortage triggered by the Iran war is set to persist well into next year, with depleted inventories not expected to recover until the second half of 2027. Meanwhile, questions have been raised over the validity of Mr Trump's declaration of an “ energy ceasefire ” between Russia and Ukraine, after Moscow offered no confirmation of such a truce and Russian strikes hit Ukrainian power plants within hours of the announcement.

events.title: Geothermal finds rare political sweet spot amid AI boom
events.summary: Geothermal — power drawn from the Earth's natural heat — is pulling off something remarkable in today's hyperpolarized America: Winning fans across the political spectrum. Why it matters: The bipartisan appeal, combined with surging electricity demand from AI , is helping fuel investment in a niche energy source yet to prove it can compete at scale. Driving the news: Geothermal received unusually extensive attention in a bipartisan Senate bill introduced late last month to expedite infrastructure permitting . The House this summer passed a package containing several of the same geothermal provisions, including measures sponsored by lawmakers as ideologically distant as Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Mike Kennedy (R-Utah) . The rising cachet of geothermal is the product of three trends converging: Technologies adapted from the oil and gas industry, including fracking, are making it possible to tap heat in more places than just far-flung hot springs and volcanoes. Tech companies, on the hunt for reliable electricity, are willing to pay a premium for next-generation geothermal to power data centers. Investment is surging as companies race to scale a renewable energy source that can generate power around the clock. Catch up quick: The geothermal-specific provisions in the Senate bill go further than the broader permitting reforms offered to other renewable energy sources, including wind and solar. The bill would make it easier for geothermal developers to explore and lease federal land, speed up drilling permits and exempt certain activities from environmental reviews. Geothermal retained federal clean-energy tax credits in Republicans' sweeping tax law last year, even as wind and solar faced an accelerated phaseout. State of play: Fervo Energy, an advanced geothermal company that went public earlier this year, is at the leading edge of this convergence. It was founded nearly a decade ago by Tim Latimer, a former drilling engineer in the oil and gas industry. "I don't think any of us saw in 2017 that a few years later we would be in the biggest demand power boom for electricity that we had ever experienced," said Latimer during a recent on-stage interview with Axios in an event aptly titled "The energy source nobody argues about." The AI boom has "accelerated our business tremendously." Chart: Amy Harder/Axios; Note: Other includes project finance and debt. Fervo's IPO proceeds reflect capital raised at the time of its listing, not its current market value; Data: Currence The intrigue: Geothermal's appeal crosses traditional political divisions precisely because it doesn't fit neatly into Washington's usual energy-policy boxes. Its renewable characteristics appeal to Democrats. Its reliance on drilling expertise and overlap with the oil and gas industry appeals to Republicans. Its ability to provide stable, carbon-free electricity makes it attractive to utilities and tech companies. By the numbers: The average winning bid for federal geothermal leases has surged, reflecting growing commercial interest. The average winning bid in 2023 was $10 an acre, and so far this year, the average is $182, according to Guy Cohen, a geothermal analyst at the market intelligence firm Currence. A record $1,207-an-acre bid was placed for a single parcel in Utah this summer . Reality check: Geothermal's political popularity and investment boom are running ahead of its commercial reality. The technology remains expensive, and questions persist about whether it can reliably generate electricity over decades. Geothermal currently generates less than 1% of U.S. electricity, and those eye-popping leases are for the right to explore for geothermal, not for active geothermal wells. Fervo's stock has fallen nearly 70% from its first-day closing price following its IPO earlier this year, amid what Axios Pro calls a broader slowdown among energy startups. Tom Erb, Fervo's government affairs and policy manager, says the construction costs at its flagship project in Utah are about half those of new nuclear plants. He acknowledged that underground heat can diminish over time, requiring additional drilling, but said those costs are factored into company projections. What they're saying: Jigar Shah, a former Energy Department official under President Biden, says geothermal's current momentum still depends on state policies encouraging clean electricity and tech companies willing to pay a premium. "I don't think this moment would work without above-market mandates from states or the data centers," Shah said. Friction point: Geothermal has also encountered local opposition, particularly over water. Traditional geothermal projects can disrupt hot springs and wetlands critical to wildlife, said Patrick Donnelly of the Center for Biological Diversity. Newer technologies like Fervo's avoid some of those risks, he said, but questions remain about their water consumption. What we're watching: Geothermal has found something rare in Washington: Political consensus. The test now is whether that consensus survives the industry's growth.

events.title: EU promotes sovereign, trusted AI as it struggles to catch US and China
events.summary: EU pushes homegrown AI agenda as US, China retain lead At an international AI summit in Dublin, EU leaders promoted trusted and independent artificial intelligence. Critics question whether the bloc can close the gap with the US and China while maintaining strict regulation. If supremacy in artificial intelligence was an Olympic discipline, there would only be two serious contenders for gold on current trajectories: the US and China . The European Union, as has been the case in many areas of cutting-edge technology in recent times, is barely in the AI conversation. Former European Central Bank President Mario Draghi, whose 2024 report highlighted the EU's desperate need to be more innovative to become more competitive, said recently that AI is "perhaps the most promising" route the EU has to raise growth today. However, he decried the fact that the European Union controls little of the value chain. "Being cut off from AI, once the economy runs on it, would be more like being cut off from the US financial system," he wrote in an opinion piece for the Financial Times. "The effects would be catastrophic." Draghi's spirit was on full display in Dublin on Wednesday at an international AI summit the Irish government convened as part of its six-month stint hosting the rotating EU presidency. The summit's motto, "Harnessing AI to Revolutionize Europe's Competitiveness," might as well have been dreamed up by the Italian former prime minister. AI safety concerns shadow growth agenda Harnessing AI has become a lot more complicated. A slew of controversies around AI agents going rogue, from the Hugging Face attack in June when 1,200 agents hacked an online platform, to an Anthropic-designed agent sending a fake tip to US police over an unsolved murder, have caused alarm. Many from within the tech industry, including Microsoft founder Bill Gates and the leading AI frontier labs themselves, have called for a development pause in order for safety measures to catch up. Trump announces creation of new 'AI Force' Yet positivity was largely the name of the game at the summit, with tech and AI industry leaders joining Irish and EU politicians to declare AI's transformative economic and societal potential — while also emphasizing the need for strong regulation and safety standards. Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin made it clear that Ireland was all in on AI. He echoed European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen 's recent assertion that the technology represented a "tipping point." He also repeatedly highlighted what he sees as the bloc's commitment to safety. "We are determined to capture the dividend by mitigating the risks," Martin told the event. "In Europe, we have charted our path ... balancing innovation and opportunity with a trustworthy, human-centered approach to AI." AI critics say key concerns overlooked Meanwhile, Henna Virkkunen, the European Commission executive vice-president for tech sovereignty, security and democracy, revealed at the event that the EU had begun its first enforcement actions under its new AI Act , requesting information around security and safety from advanced AI model providers. However, other topics that concern AI's many critics, from those fearing the massive environmental impact of data centers to others warning about possible AI-related job losses, were largely absent from the discussions. Outside the venue, a group of protesters led by People Before Profit, a left-wing Irish political party, criticized the summit for not focusing on these issues. "There is a deliberate blurring of the line here with the type of AI that is being promoted," Alexandra Day, one of the protest organizers, told DW. "It is really being pushed on workers with very little consent. There's no right for workers to opt out of using AI now that it's coming into the workplace." A sense of urgency was palpable from the speakers inside the summit. Executives from some of the world's biggest AI and tech firms talked up Europe's potential. Yet the EU evidently has plenty of ground to catch up on in terms of AI development. Despite ramping up its data center capacity, it still lags far behind the US and China. It hosts 5% of the world's AI computing capacity compared to around 75% for the US. Trump proclaims US 'golden age' of science The EU is conspicuously absent from lists of the leading AI frontier labs, with only French company Mistral coming close to rivaling the top labs. Its production of leading-edge chips is also nowhere near that of the top US or Taiwanese producers. As part of its plan to make ground on the US and China, the Irish government, in its role as EU presidency host, presented a policy document at the event. The so-called "Dublin Declaration" outlines political commitments to strengthen Europe's AI capabilities, including infrastructure investment and financial backing for European AI companies.

events.title: Photos show how Prince Harry and Prince William's relationship has changed through the years
events.summary: Prince Harry and Prince William sharing an embrace back in 2014. Chris Jackson/Getty Images Prince William and Prince Harry's relationship has been fraught in recent years. The brothers haven't been photographed in the same room since King Charles' coronation in 2023. Photos of the pair show the evolution of their relationship over the years. It's no secret that Prince William and Prince Harry have a complicated relationship. Harry, 42, first confirmed a rift in his relationship with William, 44, in 2019, and their bond only grew more strained in the years that followed as Harry stepped back as a senior royal and began speaking publicly about his and Meghan Markle's issues with the royal family. Still, the brothers didn't always have such a complex relationship, sticking close to each other during their childhoods. Take a look at some photos that show the evolution of William and Harry's relationship. Prince William was publicly photographed with his younger brother for the first time in October 1984. Princess Diana holds a newborn Prince Harry in her arms while Prince William looks on in October 1984. AP Harry was born on September 15, 1984, and though he was photographed for the first time just a day later, he wasn't pictured with his brother, then 2 years old, until the following month. William sat on the floor in front of Princess Diana, who held an infant Harry in her arms. The brothers were photographed with their extended family at Harry's christening in December 1984. PA Images via Getty Images William posed for a few photos at Harry's christening, including a shot with his parents, Queen Elizabeth, and the Queen Mother. In the photo, baby Harry reaches out to touch his big brother. A 1985 photo of the brothers hinted at their bond. Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images The brothers seemed to have a close relationship from a young age, as the pair were often side by side in pictures. In this shot, they play the piano together with Diana at Kensington Palace. As the boys got older, they were photographed playing together, as in this 1986 shot. Princess Diana, Prince Harry, and Prince William at Highgrove House in July 1986. Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images Cameras captured the brothers playing at Highgrove House , where they lived with Diana and Charles when they were young. William waited at the bottom of a slide as Harry made his way down. The family appeared close-knit in shots shared before Charles and Diana split, such as this 1989 photo. The Prince and Princess of Wales with their children during a family holiday in Tresco on the Isles of Scilly in 1989 AP Harry and William were typically photographed with one or both of their parents when they were children. For instance, the palace shared a photo of the pair on bicycles with their parents in 1989 on the Isles of Scilly. The duo continued to smile during public appearances after their parents split, including a 1993 trip to Thorpe Park. Diana, Princess Of Wales, Prince William, and Prince Harry at the 'Thorpe Park' Amusement Park in April 1993. Julian Parker/UK Press via Getty Images Charles and Diana officially separated in December 1992 after years of turmoil. Harry and William continued to appear separately with their parents, and they seemed cheerful despite the change in their home life. In April 1993, they grinned widely during a visit to Thorpe Park with Diana, not caring that a ride got them wet. The brothers supported each other at various milestones, such as William's first day at Eton College in 1995. Anwar Hussein/WireImage/Getty Images The brothers attended the same boarding school, Eton College . Prince George attends the prestigious school as of 2026. When William enrolled in 1995, Harry accompanied their parents to drop him off, giving him a familial send-off. Harry later joined William at Eton in 1998, though he said in his memoir "Spare" that William asked him "to pretend [he] didn't know him" at the school. The brothers were photographed on the grounds of Balmoral Castle together weeks before their mother died in 1997. Prince Charles, Prince Harry, and Prince William at Balmoral Castle in August 1997. Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images The brothers were vacationing at Balmoral Castle in Scotland with their father when their mother died on August 31, 1997. Harry said in his memoir "Spare" that Charles personally told him his mother had died, though he didn't hug him when delivering the news. On August 16, two weeks before Diana's death, photographers captured William and Harry exploring the grounds of the royal retreat with their father. They famously walked behind Diana's casket at her funeral a few weeks later, with their father, uncle, and grandfather. Prince William and Prince Harry processed behind Princess Diana's coffin at her funeral in September 1997. Tim Graham Photo Library via Getty Images During Diana's funeral, William and Harry, who were 15 and 12 at the time, walked behind her coffin as it processed from Buckingham Palace to Westminster Abbey. Charles and Diana's brother, Charles Spencer, accompanied the boys, as did their grandfather, Prince Philip. The brothers were often photographed side by side in the years after their mother died, like in this shot from March 2001. Sion Touhig / Getty Harry and William spent much of their teens in school, but when they appeared with the royal family, they were typically together, such as at the Queen Mother's birthday celebration in August 2001. Prince William later said that they were "uniquely bonded because of what we've been through" when speaking of Diana's death in a 2015 video shared by Time . While William and Harry pursued different paths after graduating from high school, they reunited in 2009 to undertake military helicopter training. Kirsty Wigglesworth/ AP Images. William attended the University of St Andrews, where he met Kate Middleton , while Harry took a gap year after graduating from Eton. However, in 2009, they were both in training to fly helicopters as part of their service in the Royal Air Force, and they shared a cottage during the experience. They jokingly told the BBC it would be their "first and last time living together," with William saying Harry snored and that he often tidied up after him. Harry wrote in "Spare" that he didn't snore and cleaned up after himself, so he found his brother's comments puzzling. Harry served as best man at William and Kate's wedding on April 29, 2011. Andrew Milligan - WPA Pool/Getty Images William and Kate tied the knot at Westminster Abbey. Harry was by William's side for the occasion, serving as his best man. They were photographed chatting before Kate walked down the aisle. Harry later wrote in "Spare" that although he was excited that Kate was joining their family, he felt, to some extent, like he was losing his brother as he got married. Kate Middleton started attending events with William and Harry after the wedding. Kat

events.title: I left my 13-year career at Google to work in sustainability. It wasn't an easy choice, but my values had changed.
events.summary: Bruno Bianchini. Bruno Bianchini Bruno Bianchini quit his job at Google to focus on sustainability in Cambodia and green finance. While still at Google, he pursued a degree at Harvard in sustainable studies. He says leaving Google was a hard decision, but his career shift aligns with his values. This as-told-to essay is based on an interview with Bruno Bianchini, the 40-year-old former Head of Global Partnerships for the Middle East, Africa, and Turkey for Google, who is based in the Netherlands. It has been edited for length and clarity. Growing up in the Italian countryside, sustainability was simply part of everyday life. At 18, I left my small village near Milan to study at Bocconi University in Milan. In 2005, I started my degree in accounting, corporate finance, and law. Then I did a master's in business administration. When I was about to graduate, a friend at the university said a group of professors had opened a boutique consulting firm. I interviewed for the role and landed it. That path led me first to consulting and then to Google, where I spent more than 13 years before leaving to pursue work in sustainability. I started work as a business analyst at the consulting firm in January 2011 At 25, I was working on three projects — a hotel, a food company, and a company that made pressure gauges. My experience was very much about seeing problems through an analytical lens. In 2012, I was invited to a friend's birthday dinner, where I was seated opposite a guy working at Google. Although Google was already a huge company, I had little sense of its scale. I thought of it mainly as a search engine. We stayed in touch, and they eventually asked if I'd be interested in an interview I remember wearing a jacket and tie, and I thought, I can't show up at Google like this; they're never going to hire me. I roughed up my hair, removed my jacket and my tie, and went to the interview. I had three interviews at Google on the same day. One interviewer asked me about role-related knowledge, the next about more general knowledge, and the third was Googleyness — whether I was a culture fit. I remember thinking in the interview that I wanted to work with these people. About a week later, I had a fourth interview. The process moved quickly because it was for a temp job. In July 2012, I joined Google . The Google office in Milan was colorful and playful I remember there was a game area. In consulting, I'd start work at 8:30 a.m. and leave at 10:30 p.m. every day. At Google, people were coming and going whenever they wanted. The culture was a huge change for me. It was fantastic. A year later, I applied for a full-time role working with DoubleClick for Publishers, now part of Google Ad Manager. I did lots of prep for the interview, and I got the job. In 2016, my boss asked me to give a presentation at the Google office in Dubai After the presentation, a guy who became my new boss asked if I'd consider moving to Dubai because they were expanding the team. Two months later, they opened the role; I applied, got the job, and moved to Dubai. That same year, I got to see the San Francisco campus for the first time. When I saw the scale of the buildings, the number of meeting rooms, micro kitchens, and the bicycles employees rode around campus, I was mesmerized. Working for one of the most innovative companies on the planet, I felt like I was always at the forefront of tech innovation. I definitely got a kick out of that. By 2024, I had become the Head of Global Partnerships for the Middle East, Africa, and Turkey at Google As I was managing a large region, there was a lot of travel. On office days, I generally worked 9-to-5, depending on projects and deadlines. I might have calls with people in the US, but travel was more hectic. From the moment I arrived, I was having breakfast with colleagues, attending an event, or meeting with clients. Throughout my time at Google, my value system changed I'd been thinking about sustainability for some time. When I was in Milan, I met someone from LA who told me they were vegan. They told me about the damage the dairy and meat industries are causing to the planet. I started reading more, and I went down the rabbit hole. I remember feeling that I wanted to be part of the movement for the solution. While still at Google, I looked into which universities offered degrees in sustainability and came across a program at Harvard. In December 2025, I resigned from Google I pursued my master's degree in sustainable studies at Harvard online while working at Google. The last part of my studies involved a thesis. I took a sabbatical from Google and traveled to Cambodia to work on an ambitious project that plans to reforest 100,000 hectares of flooded forest. I worked on the feasibility study. Google was kind enough to say, "Go pursue your dreams, and if something doesn't work, you're welcome to come back." Eventually, I decided it was time. After four months in Cambodia, I felt the umbilical cord was stretched enough. When I returned from my sabbatical, I handed in my notice. I feel now that I have a big purpose in my heart, confidence in the abilities Harvard gave me, and, at the same time, I feel financially secure. I could leave a high-paying role where I was making more than $300,000 in annual total compensation for the unknown. I'm now working as an independent consultant for this project in Cambodia. Leaving Google was not an easy choice Google nurtured me in so many ways, but as I was learning more about sustainability, my value system was changing. I was encouraging people to sell more stuff, and on my dark days, I remember thinking that staying at home on the couch was better for the environment. I want to capitalize on my background in business and finance. I'm currently working on publishing a research paper about the project in Cambodia. I'm doing this long-distance while we're securing funds for the pilot. This month, I moved to the Netherlands, as it is one of the best places for green finance. events.title: Banks are pulling back as AI's massive debt pile disconnects from economic reality
events.summary: Wall Street appears to be hitting its limit on AI, and financiers are starting to say the quiet part out loud: All of this AI spending doesn't look like it can pay off, at least not for everyone. Why it matters: The gap between what it costs to build AI infrastructure and what companies are actually paying to use it is widening. Wall Street's anxiety is surging as the debt piling up to fund data centers and chips looks increasingly disconnected from economic reality. Driving the news: A massive gap is opening up between AI infrastructure spending and expected returns. While AI providers are projected to spend $7 trillion on infrastructure through 2030, research from Gartner forecasts they will generate no more than $3.6 trillion in related revenue over that same period. More than $4 trillion in AI infrastructure spending could be at risk of write-downs by the end of 2032 if companies maintain their current investment pace. Gartner also predicts that more than 80% of specialized AI cloud providers, known as neoclouds, will cease operating independently by 2030. Case in point: CoreWeave, one of the largest neoclouds with among the closest ties to Nvidia — the AI boom's financial and spiritual foundation — has faced a multi-day selloff of its stock and debt. Yields pushed above 15% and its stock tumbled 15.5% before rebounding after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang spoke up on the company's behalf. Follow the money: Sources on Wall Street used to tell Axios that as long as the AI buildout was paid for in cash, there was nothing to worry about. But today, a third of the capex being spent on AI is coming from debt, and capital markets are showing signs of severe fatigue. It's getting harder to secure financing. Global AI-related debt issuance plunged to $23 billion in September 2026, down sharply from $113 billion in June, per the Financial Times . Banks are actively pulling back to avoid concentration risk, with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon confirming his bank is tightening up on credit. Infrastructure projects and providers are struggling: approximately $18 billion in bank loans for an Oracle data center campus recently slid into stressed territory, while Nvidia-backed AI cloud provider Firmus shelved an IPO that sought a valuation north of $30 billion. Zoom in: The constant spending relies on the belief that compute demand will never falter — a belief that has structural cracks. Reflection AI co-founder Ioannis Antonoglou told Semafor that businesses may need "a decade or two decades" to fundamentally redesign their operations around AI. That's 10 to 20 years of companies slowly adopting the technology that's being built (expensively) today. Between the lines: This creates a mismatch: Data centers and chips require enormous investment today, but the returns that could justify that spend will take years to materialize. Put bluntly, there is a massive gap between AI spending and AI revenue, one that won't close for many, many years. At the same time, companies that are adopting AI quickly are getting smarter about using tools more efficiently, turning to open-weight models that are less compute-intensive to cut costs. Reality check: Look at Anthropic's latest financials for a counterpoint to the bears. The company is raking in cash, turning free cash flow positive in the third quarter and growing revenue nearly 50% compared to the April-to-June period. But even Anthropic's staggering growth has slowed, albeit expectedly because trees can't grow to the sky. The bottom line: The debt-fueled AI buildout is not an isolated problem for tech investors alone to worry about. The stock market and economy have become increasingly tied up with the AI boom. If the AI bet doesn't work, markets and the economy could falter as well.

events.title: Trump's MAGA allies openly discuss martial law
events.summary: MAGA activists are pushing for President Trump to resort to extraordinary measures — including martial law — if they believe the midterm elections are "rigged." Why it matters: Some of the proposals go far beyond Trump's legal authority — and there's no evidence that the elections will be rigged. But people in this orbit have close access to the president. Prominent MAGA election activist Tina Peters met with Trump this month. Convicted in 2024 of crimes tied to a breach of election equipment, Peters was released this year after Colorado Gov. Jared Polis (D) commuted her sentence. Peters and her attorney, Peter Ticktin, also visited Trump at the White House in late June . Peters did not respond to attempts to contact her for comment. Zoom in: On a September 30 video call for MAGA election activists streamed on Rumble, speakers warned of widespread election security breaches they believe will occur in November — and urgently pushed for remedies. Ticktin, Trump's childhood friend, said on the call "there would have to be martial law in the event... [of] another rigged election." "They'll probably need to be commandeering of ballots and election equipment to make sure that we can get to the bottom of it before anything further occurs," he later told Axios. Gregory Stenstrom, who testified about alleged voting irregularities in Pennsylvania in 2020, said he most wanted the election paused over security concerns. Alternatively, he proposed Trump invoke the National Emergencies Act to force states to change how they run elections. Stenstrom could not be reached for comment. Peters was also on the call. She's been promoting her own plan online since August, which calls for switching to hand-marked paper ballots and a manual recount of all votes where feasible. "Her plan is secure the paper ballots and recount by hand," Ticktin said. In an interview with Colorado Public Radio, he further explained this "would eliminate whatever effect the machines have." State of play: The streamed call is a regular feature in this activist community, drawing voices from across the country. Steve Stern, the host, directs his viewers to sign up through the Republican Party to become poll workers and observers for November. Stern declined an interview request. Reality check: "Emergency powers are not just a blank check for the president to go do whatever they want. The president still has to act within the Constitution and within statutes set by Congress," said Derek Tisler, counsel for the Brennan Center's elections and government program. He said those legal limits include : Election timing: Congress sets the date of federal elections. Trump cannot unilaterally delay the midterms. Counting and voting systems: States choose their voting systems and determine how votes are counted, subject to federal law. Trump cannot mandate a nationwide hand recount or order machines replaced. Emergency and martial law authority: Emergency powers do not allow Trump to override state election laws or constitutional restrictions. Martial law would not give Trump authority to seize control of election materials or override federal and state election laws. The big picture: Skepticism about the 2020 election extends into Trump's administration, including officials now involved in election integrity. Heather Honey, most known for denying the results of the 2020 election in Pennsylvania and Arizona, is now the Homeland Security Department's deputy assistant secretary for election integrity and senior advisor to the ICE Director. White House adviser Peter Navarro continues to promote his own report of mass election fraud and irregularities around the 2020 election. Between the lines: "This election did not sneak up on the administration. They've been in office for 21 months. We're 20 days away from this election, and they haven't done any of this stuff," said David Becker, executive director of the Center for Election Innovation & Research. White House spokesperson Lauren Bis told Axios in a statement: "Americans deserves elections that are safe, secure, and transparent to ensure full confidence in the results. President Trump believes every legal vote must count, every election must be protected, and Americans must have complete confidence in the integrity of our elections."

events.title: Middle-income Americans are feeling the squeeze
events.summary: A Pew Research Center survey found 71% of middle-income earners have cut back on spending on extras, such as eating out. andresr/Getty Images A Pew Research survey found only 47% of middle-income earners could save money in the past year. Lower-income earners are also having a hard time saving and affording necessities. Inflation moving in the wrong direction doesn't help the affordability situation. America's middle earners are feeling the squeeze. A new analysis from the Pew Research Center examines how Americans' finances are faring, an especially salient topic in a midterm season where affordability is very much on the ballot. America's middle earners — those who make between $50,700 and $152,000 after adjusting for their family sizes and the cost of living in their areas — increasingly don't have enough saved for an emergency. Just over half of middle-income Americans say they don't have rainy-day funds that would cover expenses for three months in the event of an emergency. Meanwhile, 47% of middle-income earners — and a measly 24% of lower-income earners — reported being able to save money in the past year. Across all income tiers, the majority of respondents said they had cut back spending on extras like eating out or streaming services . Those dwindling emergency funds and sacrifices might be due to rising costs, which often take a particularly large bite out of lower-earners' wallets. It could be getting worse; inflation is moving in the wrong direction. In September, the consumer price index inflation rate rose from 3.4% to 3.7%, just above the 3.6% forecast. Plus, inflation-adjusted wages have been falling for six months. Today's economy is still more difficult for those at the bottom of the earnings ladder. Fifty-one percent of lower-income respondents said they can pay all of their bills in full in the 2026 survey, down from 56% in 2020. For middle-income respondents, the share dropped from 81% in 2020 to 78% in 2026, while the share of upper-income respondents held steady at 93%. Pew also found 71% of lower-income US adults struggled with at least one kind of basic necessity, like affording medical care or paying their rent or mortgage, in the past year, compared with 39% of middle-income and 13% of upper-income Americans. But the latest survey marks another sign that middle-income earners are increasingly aligning with their lower-earning peers, a dour sign for the health of the middle class. A separate report from the Urban Institute found that, even as lower-income renters were the most likely to report issues paying the rent, middle-income renters were increasingly likely to report struggling to pay. Similarly, middle-income earners' consumer sentiment has switched from mirroring their higher-earning peers to more closely aligning with lower earners — another sign that the middle class is falling on harder economic times. "Working people are living on the edge, working longer and harder than ever for less money," said AFL-CIO President Liz Shuler. "They're angry every time they fill the tank . They're terrified of what their heating bills will look like this winter." Read the original article on Business Insider

events.title: If you've gotten a raise in the past two years, it's now been nearly all eaten away by inflation
events.summary: Getting a job is the important part, as these job seekers might attest. But getting a raise is also a big deal: For many workers, the raises they've gotten over the past couple of years have now been wiped out by inflation. Allison Joyce/Bloomberg via Getty Images Have you gotten a raise over the past couple of years? Inflation has likely eaten it away. Inflation-adjusted hourly earnings, which had risen after Donald Trump first took office, are now declining. And there are ominous signs that inflation could get worse. If you've gotten a raise over the last two years, almost all of those gains have now been eaten by inflation. That is, if you're the average wage-earner, considering the latest statistics released this week showing that prices were rising at a faster clip than expected. It's more evidence that affordability challenges in the US economy aren't going away. It also means that average hourly pay, which had risen after Donald Trump took office in January 2025, is now right back to where it started, when taking inflation into account. The average hourly wage was $35.84 in January 2025, according to federal statistics, or $37.79 in today's dollars, adjusted for inflation. The average hourly wage last month was $37.81 — basically unchanged over the past 20 months. Wednesday's consumer price index inflation report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics came in hotter than expected, with prices up 3.7% over the year in September. Economists had expected a 3.6% increase, and the rate was well above August's 3.4%. "We read the September CPI report as another piece of evidence that the US is facing a persistent inflation problem," economists at BNP Paribas said in a note to clients. That problem means high prices — including gasoline that was up 9.1% in September compared to the previous month — are gobbling up pay increases you might get at work. Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, underlined that consumer price growth since 2025 has eroded nearly all wage gains, citing the impact of the war in Iran, which began at the end of February, on Americans' wallets. "This is a very different picture from President Trump's first term when wages were up over 15%, well above about 8% inflation," Long said. "It helps explain the frustration many households feel right now with the economy." Higher prices are adding to a general sense of malaise about the economy. The University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index dipped to 46.3 in October, down from 71.7 in January 2025. Joanne Hsu, the director of the survey, said higher gas prices driven by the Middle East conflict have added to the ongoing cost-of-living pressures over the past several years. Higher prices and inflation outpacing wage growth can be especially tough for Americans who are on tight budgets or living paycheck to paycheck. "When we look at the majority of the US workforce, people who are middle- and lower-income households, higher costs in things like gas and groceries take up a larger share of their income," said ZipRecruiter economist Nicole Bachaud. Have you made any changes to your budget or savings? Has your paycheck kept up with rising prices? We want to hear about how people are doing in today's economy. Reach out to this reporter to share at mhoff@businessinsider.com . It's important to note, there is more than one way to read the wage numbers as they relate to inflation — and in some ways, workers have actually come out ahead. For example, average weekly earnings have grown faster over the last year than average hourly earnings, as the number of hours the typical worker works has edged up. The Trump administration, when asked for comment, highlighted annual earnings. "Under President Trump, private sector workers have seen their wages continue to outpace inflation, with average annual earnings growing by more than $600," said White House spokesperson Matthew Middleton. Inflation will play a role in the midterms The midterm elections are in just a few weeks, and affordability will likely be a key concern. An Economic Innovation Group and Echelon Insights survey in September asked people what elected officials should prioritize most to make life better for workers. The survey said that 45% of American workers wanted officials to prioritize reducing the cost of everyday essentials, and 23% wanted them to focus on making housing more affordable. Long, at Navy Federal, said the "modest increase" in grocery prices is a silver lining in the latest consumer price index report. Food at home, which includes groceries, rose at a slower pace than April's 2.9%, with prices increasing 1.8% year over year in September. "But it's inevitable food prices will likely rise in the months ahead as higher diesel and transport costs are passed along to consumers," Long said. There are other ominous signs that inflation could worsen. Thursday's producer price index report showed that final demand prices rose 1.3% in September, the highest since 2022.
