events.title: Chip Industry Week In Review
events.summary: Manufacturing and process technology GlobalFoundries will operate two new fabs in Malta, New York , under a U.S.-Japan initiative involving up to $21B in investment. The first fab is expected to come online in 2029. GF also unveiled an FD-SOI roadmap for physical AI. Applied Materials unveiled its $5B EPIC Center , a 600,000-s.f. semiconductor process and equipment R&D facility in Silicon Valley. Infineon and Wolfspeed inked a new multi-year supply agreement for 200mm SiC wafers. Nikon introduced a new lithography system for advanced packaging, offering 1.5 µm line-and-space resolution and 40% higher throughput than its predecessor, at 72 panels per hour. The maskless system supports large substrates and RDL patterning, with availability planned for April 2027. Packaging and test FormFactor and Teradyne will co-develop semiconductor test technologies for HBM, advanced packaging, silicon photonics, and HPC. Teradyne also agreed to invest $300M in FormFactor. Teradyne also introduced a semiconductor test platform for edge-AI chips. ASE expanded its PowerSiP platform with a vertically integrated 3D packaging solution that places voltage regulation closer to AI processors, reducing parasitic routing losses by 50% or more to improve power efficiency in data centers and HPC systems. China narrows the gap CXMT reportedly plans to introduce a DDR5 server RDIMM using 4F² DRAM cells by year-end, potentially improving density and manufacturing costs. The development could help narrow China’s memory gap, although CXMT has not disclosed production yields, manufacturing volumes or evidence of cost competitiveness. China-based Langdao Silex unveiled a prototype EUV light source with 90% localized components, reports SCMP. TrendForce says the source exceeds 15W output but remains far below commercial EUV power levels, with mass production still estimated to be three to five years away. Nvidia ’s AI-accelerator shipments in China fell 44% year over year in the first half of 2026, leaving it with 34% of the data-center AI-accelerator market by units shipped, compared with Huawei’s 28%, according to IDC data reported by Reuters. Around the Valley This week’s SEMICON West conference: Synopsys CEO Sassine Ghazi said in a keynote address that autonomous chip design can already take some customer specifications to verified RTL, while physical implementation, verification and final sign-off still require human involvement. Nvidia expanded its AI tools for semiconductor manufacturing , including the new cuPotential CUDA-X library for atomic-scale simulation. Lam Research plans to integrate Nvidia NanoVDB into SEMulator3D, which is expected to speed select wafer-etch modeling by up to 30x. Siemens and Nvidia integrated cuLitho with Calibre to speed computational lithography , saying it’s up to 12x faster for full-chip OPC workloads. It supports High-NA EUV and curvilinear inverse lithography. Fig. 1: Synopsys President/CEO Sassine Ghazi and Semiconductor Engineering’s Ed Sperling at SEMICON West this week. Source: G. Haley/Semiconductor Engineering The OCP Global Summit was also held this week in San Jose. Find all the highlights in our New Technologies section below. Earnings season heating up TSMC reported Q3 revenue of roughly US$46.7B , up 41.2% year over year in U.S. dollar terms, with 2nm accounting for 8% of wafer revenue. CEO C.C. Wei said the company has seen “no sign of slowdown” in AI demand. But rising prices and macroeconomic uncertainty are weighing on consumer and other price-sensitive markets, prompting more cautious planning for 2027. TSMC also said it has discussed participating in Musk’s Terafab, but any fab collaboration would need to be operated by TSMC. ASML reported record Q3 sales of €11.7B, up about 55% from a year earlier, and said planned supply for the next two years will not fully meet customer demand. The company is evaluating additional capacity beyond its previously planned expansion. Market and investment More than $8.5B in Q3 chip industry startup funding was tracked across 80 companies, with AI inference, memory alternatives, photonics, networking, and other data-movement technologies drawing some of the quarter’s biggest rounds. SEMI projects global 300mm front-end fab equipment spending will rise 31% to $149B in 2026 and reach $227B by 2029, driven by AI, HPC, and leading-edge semiconductor demand. Equipment investment in the Americas is expected to more than double from $18.1B in 2026 to $40.6B in 2029. Fig. 2: SEMI 300mm Fab Outlook, Q326 update. Big hauls Salience Labs raised $125M to accelerate deployment of its optical circuit switching technology for AI infrastructure. Mueon raised $65M to scale up its stackable, modular 3D platform that integrates compute, memory, interconnect, power delivery, and thermal management. events.title: Revealed: VW, Ford and Tesla batteries linked to destructive deforestation of indigenous lands
events.summary: Mines in supply chains of western carmakers linked to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by Tolaki people in Indonesia Volkswagen, Ford and Tesla are among the electric carmakers whose batteries may contain nickel mined in indigenous woodlands plagued by deforestation, an analysis has found, highlighting the struggle to make vehicles that are free from environmental destruction. Corporate disclosures and trade flows from the last two years show mines in the battery supply chains of automotive giants are linked to the loss of trees in Sulawesi, a wildlife hotspot in Indonesia that houses the world’s largest nickel deposits. The metal is widely used in cathodes in car batteries because it boosts energy density and increases range. Ore from the Cahaya and Hengjaya mines was traced through regional smelters and Chinese processing plants run by Zhejiang Huayou Cobalt, a cathode manufacturer that supplies CATL, the world’s largest battery maker. Huayou’s corporate reports list US and European carmakers as end-users, while additional corporate files and trade data show a separate route from Huayou to LG, a South Korean group that also supplies battery products to leading carmakers, via Poland. Satellite analysis shows the mines have led to widespread deforestation of primary rainforest in nickel-rich lands inhabited by the indigenous Tolaki people. “We used to ask the forest for protection in return for our offerings,” said Wadimula, a Tolaki elder whose home sits on the edge of the 21,000-hectare Cahaya mining concession. “Destroying it means destroying our own life.” Electric vehicles are less environmentally harmful than fossil fuel-burning engines, which spew gases that foul the air and heat the planet, but western carmakers have struggled to clean up supply chains for batteries built with critical minerals from Africa, Asia and South America. Environmental groups warn that a failure to curb the boom of material-hungry SUVs is exacerbating the destruction by increasing the quantity mined. Ore from the two mining concessions is sent to a nickel smelter in an industrial complex in Morowali, on Indonesia’s eastern coast, operated by Huayou’s local subsidiary, where limonite is refined into mixed hydroxide precipitate, the primary raw material used to make battery cathodes. In 2024, $606m worth of mixed hydroxide precipitate was shipped from the Morowali plant to ports in China, followed by further shipments worth $470m in 2025. The processed ore was transported overland to Huayou cathode manufacturing sites in Quzhou, near Shanghai, and Yulin, near the border with Vietnam. Public filings do not disclose specific volumes or timings of sales from Huayou to CATL, which would be needed to directly connect specific ore shipments to car batteries, but Huayou confirmed group-level supplies to CATL in response to a regulatory inquiry by the Shanghai Stock Exchange in 2024. Chengdu B&M, a downstream subsidiary of Huayou, has also confirmed the supply of “large quantities” to CATL. The investigation, published in partnership with Voxeurop and other European media partners, traced shipments from mines and refineries in Sulawesi to China, and then again from Huayou cathode and CATL battery factories to the assembly lines of carmakers in the US and Europe. Volkswagen’s facility in Braunschweig, for instance, received a shipment in October 2024 of 24 tonnes of cell modules worth about $390,000, according to data from Volza, a trade platform. The shift to a carbon-free economy is pushing up demand for critical minerals in countries with weak environmental safeguards, though experts have argued the mining boom can be tempered without slowing the shift away from dirty fuels. In 2023, a report found lithium demand in the US transport sector could be reduced by 18% to 66% compared with a business-as-usual scenario, by improving public transport, walking and cycling more, and buying smaller cars. Better recycling could bring demand reductions as high as 92%, the report found. Global demand for nickel is set to double to 5.5m tonnes by 2040, according to the International Energy Agency, much of it mined in Indonesia and then refined in China. The loss of trees in mining concessions means the carbon footprint of nickel from the worst mines may be up to 500 times greater than previously reported, a study in Nature Communications found last year. The Cahaya and Hengjaya mines are located in woodlands designated as “production forest”, which are intended for forestry rather than industrial activities. However, successive Indonesian governments have weakened safeguards and carved out exemptions for miners as demand for nickel has soared. Nickel mining may be responsible for two-thirds of the forest loss recorded since 2001 within the area encompassed by the Cahaya concession, and over half of the loss in the Hengjaya concession, spatial analysis conducted by geospatial firm The TreeMap suggests.

events.title: From Dallaglio’s medals to Cantona’s shorts, sporting memorabilia is big business | Emma John
events.summary: From Dallaglio’s medals to Cantona’s shorts, sporting memorabilia is big business Like transfer fees and ticket prices, mementoes are one more marker of sport’s rampant self-inflation T he auctioneer cradled his gavel in his palm like a pipe, the handle pointing towards him. It gave his patter the air of a Victorian gentleman holding forth by the mantelpiece in a period drama. “Are you bidding, Wilf? You’re waving at me.” Under the hammer was a Barclays Manager of the Month trophy, complete with travel case, but no indication of which Premier League luminary once owned it. It outstripped its estimate and sold for £700. An hour and a half into what Budds auction house dubbed its “Octoberfest” of sporting memorabilia, David Convery at the podium showed no sign of fatigue, save the occasional swig from a water bottle. There were 332 lots in total; Convery regularly manages sales with twice as many. In his three decades as an auctioneer he’s even secured some world-record prices, from the oldest surviving FA Cup to Pelé’s 1970 World Cup final shirt. But sporting collectibles have never been bigger business than now. This week a jersey worn by Michael Jordan in the second game of the 1998 NBA finals – his “Last Dance” season for the Chicago Bulls – sold for over £10m , the kind of sum that might otherwise buy you a Mayfair townhouse. It was unprecedented in basketball but only just – two weeks previously, the jersey Jordan wore in game three had gone for £9.3m. And that had broken the record set by – you better believe it – Jordan’s game one jersey, which Sotheby’s sold in 2022. Last week’s Budds catalogue was never going to reach those heights but it still contained some star items. Almost all were the property of Lawrence Dallaglio, the former England rugby union captain, declared bankrupt a year ago and now treading the well-worn path of sportspeople forced to sell their mementoes of the glory days. Seven years ago Boris Becker raised nearly £700,000 by selling trophies he had amassed, including a replica of the US Open trophy he won against Ivan Lendl in 1989. Unfortunately in his case it wasn’t enough to prevent further trouble with the taxman. Running an auction is like writing a set list – you can’t just start with your biggest numbers, you have to warm up the audience, build to the good stuff. Diane Modahl’s leotard from the 1998 Commonwealth Games proved, somewhat ironically, a false start; no takers, even at £50 and with the 800m runner’s spikes and signature thrown in. A £5 note autographed by Jack Nicklaus did considerably better, and gradually the ephemera – signed prints, photos and programmes – gave way to more substantial stuff, like cricket caps and blazers from the days when England still wore the MCC’s colours and crest overseas. Admittedly, those postwar names are out of vogue now: still, it was a surprise to discover you could pick up one of Trevor Bailey’s touring blazers for less than you’d pay for a decent new one at John Lewis. Or that Paul Stirling’s Ireland T20 shirt is worth more than a pair of Godfrey Evans’s wicketkeeping gloves. A new fortnightly newsletter covering the intersection of sport and the climate crisis Dallaglio’s collection, when it arrived, was one for the bigger spenders. A set of tankards sold for £1,600 – perhaps to a rugby fan who knows he can never emulate the former England captain on the pitch but likes the idea of matching him at the bar. His 2003 World Cup winner’s medal was the prize item. It went for £54,000, near the bottom of its estimate, yet even more poignant was the rapacious flurry of bids on his England and Lions caps, with their old-fashioned gold braid and tassel, and individual numbers stitched on the peak. As Convery himself said, it’s rare for such items to make it to market. Still, no time for sentiment at an auction. The lots marched on, relentlessly, from the sublime to the ridiculous: Harry Kane shirts, Eric Cantona’s shorts, and the coffee table Des Lynam presided over in the BBC television studio at the 1998 Fifa World Cup. Whether Robbie Williams, its previous owner, was a careful one was not disclosed, but the added stardust fuelled a transatlantic contest between the UK and the US, with Blighty ultimately triumphing for £800. The US has always valued both on- and off-field artefacts – witness its trading card tradition, or the brawls in the bleachers when a baseball is hit straight into the stands. The jersey that Babe Ruth wore when he hit his “called shot” against the Chicago Cubs in the 1932 World Series – arguably the most legendary moment in his storied career – remains the most expensive item of sports memorabilia ever, having sold for over £18m in 2024 . But globalisation – and, needless to say, the internet – has transformed the market in the past two decades.

events.title: ‘Europtimism’ clashes with 1 in 3 founders wanting out. We need the EU to finally become a true single market
events.summary: As winter draws in, Europeans could be forgiven for feeling the summer glow fade as headlines warn of yet higher energy bills and renewed inflation. Yet Europe’s founders and investors see good reason to be optimistic – as long as EU leaders take further action, fast. New data from Norrsken’s European Impact Index 2026 (EII) finds that founders and funders are doubling down on building the clean electro-economy Europe needs to break its dependence on fossil fuels, and their confidence in Europe’s ability to deliver is growing.  The EII is an annual survey of 750 entrepreneurs and investors behind the companies working to solve Europe’s hardest problems. Of the investors surveyed, one in two said Europe has become a more attractive place to invest over the past 12 months, against one in four who said it has become less attractive. Founders are also gearing up for growth, with 85% expecting revenues to rise over the next 12 months and three in four planning to increase headcount. That is a marked shift in mood at a time when the wider economic picture would suggest the opposite. However, the same data came with a clear warning attached for Brussels. It revealed that a significant share of European founders are keeping one foot out of the door, and showed investors remain only cautiously optimistic about the political backdrop in which they operate.  A stark one in three founders said they had considered relocating their company outside Europe in the past twelve months, including 15% who considered it seriously.  Many said they were driven by high energy costs and other factors making it difficult to compete globally. Others cited recruitment challenges – almost four in ten said attracting top talent is harder in Europe than in the US.  Meanwhile, around 36% of investors surveyed in the EII rated the EU’s approach to innovation and entrepreneurship poorly or very poorly. Just 6% said the EU prioritises it very well.  Over half (52%) of founders also said regulatory differences between EU countries have hindered their ability to scale across borders, up from 47.5% last year. That is not a resounding endorsement. Energy is where the tension between optimism and caution remains sharpest. Investors now see access to cheap and reliable power as a precondition for European companies to compete long-term. 84% said they consider a company’s access to affordable, clean energy when assessing its long-term competitiveness, with almost six in ten calling it very important. Europe is now home to some of the most promising companies building clean power, while remaining an expensive place to buy it. Investors’ money is following that conviction. Nearly 37% of investors surveyed named energy and electrification as their top sector for impact capital allocation, more than three times the next closest sector. The Norrsken/100 2026 – the annual list of the world’s most promising impact companies, as selected by 80 top early-stage investment funds – published today, saw clean energy and electrification startups make up the single largest sector with 26 companies – a figure up 44% on 2025.   Companies appearing on the Norrsken/100 included those working on overhauling and strengthening grid capacity and transforming renewables storage. Swiss company Metafuels is working to convert clean electricity into jet fuel, while RIFT and Enerin, based in the Netherlands and Norway respectively, are delivering high-temperature industrial heat from electrons instead of gas.  These companies are opening up the markets that stand between Europe and an electrified economy. They are also exactly the kind of capital-intensive businesses that will go where power is cheap, permits are quick and markets are open. The IEA projects $2.2 trillion will flow into clean energy and electrification this year, against $1.2 trillion into fossil fuels. So for every dollar going into oil, gas and coal, close to two now go into clean power. As my colleague Fabian Erici, Partner at Norrsken VC, put it: “Europe’s hardest problems are becoming its biggest markets.” In responding to the EII, both founders and investors were clear that, in order to seize this momentum, their renewed Europtimism and commitment to decarbonisation, policymakers must now give investors and founders a better framework in which to grow and become global category leaders. The continent’s political leaders must seize the moment to act, and not let this moment of Europtimism slide.   Founders and investors were clear on what would keep them here. Their top ask is to make the EU a genuinely single market, named by 45% of founders and almost six in ten investors as the key priority for European policymakers. Companies delivering Europe’s electro-economy need easier access to Europe’s 450 million-strong market, and regulatory differences between EU countries continue to make it harder to scale. Brussels appears to be getting the message. During her State of the Union address on 16th September, President von der Leyen committed to overhauling single market rules by the end of next year and advancing EU Inc to streamline cross-border expansion. Alongside the Capital Markets Union, the Savings and Investments Union and reforms like EuVECA, the Commission’s focus on grid connections, energy costs and permitting backlogs points in the right direction. None of these commitments are new, however, and founders have heard versions of them before. The rising share reporting fragmentation as a barrier suggests the gap between announcement and delivery is now what they are measuring their decision to stay by. The same applies to electrification. At Norrsken, we have called for Europe to become the world’s first “electro-continent”, underpinned by a binding target of 50% clean electrification. The Commission’s proposed 46% target falls short of that ambition, and of its own analysis, which identifies 50% as the economically optimal pathway to 2040. A strong target in the post-2030 Energy Union Package, backed by a strong ETS review and national implementation measures, would give investors the certainty they are asking for. The founders who told us they had considered leaving Europe are still building here, still hiring and still expecting to grow.  Europtimism is real, but it is conditional. It rests on founders and investors believing Europe will follow through, and the clearest measure of that belief will be whether fewer of them are thinking about the exit when we run the index again next year. events.title: Warsh boosts market expectations of Fed rate hold in October
events.summary: At the IMF’s annual meetings in Bangkok, US Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh reiterated that the Fed will deliver price stability. Warsh did not signal any policy change, which lifted bets that the Fed will hold rates at its Oct 27-28 meeting. Market odds of a hike fell from about 27% to below 15%. He repeated that the Fed will deliver “price stability” and said he does not “prejudge meetings”. Stocks rose and the US dollar slipped after his remarks, said Derek Tang of Monetary Policy Analytics. Warsh also backed artificial intelligence as a major innovation, but warned it is boosting demand now and could overheat the economy. His AI task force will hold a field hearing in San Francisco Bay Area on Nov 16. US Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh did nothing to dispel market expectations that the US central bank will hold interest rates steady when it meets at the end of October . In a moderated discussion on Oct 16 morning in Bangkok at the International Monetary Fund’s annual meetings, he made no remarks on monetary policy or his outlook for the US economy, apart from reiterating that the Fed will deliver price stability. “We made very clear that we would deliver price stability, and we removed a dose of accommodation about a month ago,” Warsh said. “I don’t prejudge meetings. I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year.” Investors pared their bets for a rate hike at the US central bank’s Oct 27-28 policy gathering. The odds, which were hovering around 27% before Warsh spoke, dropped below 15% following his remarks. Stocks extended gains and the US dollar edged lower, with futures for the S&P 500 Index erasing losses of as much as 0.6% to climb 0.2%. “It was clear that he wasn’t going to deliver anything that the market could latch on to as hawkish,” Derek Tang, an economist at Monetary Policy Analytics, wrote in a note to clients. The Fed raised interest rates by a quarter percentage point in September , the first hike since 2023. It was backed by all 19 policymakers, and a majority also saw another increase as likely in 2026 . A few key officials in recent weeks reiterated that additional rate hikes may be needed, but emphasised they have time to gather economic data before acting again. Warsh repeated his bullish views on artificial intelligence, calling it the most important innovation in the global economy during his lifetime. But he also warned that it may be driving demand in the near term. The Fed chief said that as a central banker, he is taking the new technology seriously but also “soberly, responsibly”. “It’s obviously hitting the demand side of the economy before it’s going to hit the supply side of the economy,” Warsh said. “If you’re a central banker, you’re in the business of trying to ensure stable prices and full employment, you’ve got to recognise this as a shock.” While it is a positive supply shock in the medium term, Warsh argued, it is driving increases in aggregate demand now and the impact on employment is uncertain. Some of Warsh’s colleagues have expressed similar concerns, even questioning whether the surge in investment that is buoying the AI build-out could lead to an overheating of the economy. Warsh also announced that his task force on productivity and jobs – which is grappling with the implications of AI – will hold a field hearing in the San Francisco Bay Area on Nov 16. It is one of five task forces he convened that will present recommendations to the Federal Open Market Committee in late 2026 or early in 2027. BLOOMBERG

events.title: UBS exploring options abroad in case Swiss rules prove intolerable, sources say
events.summary: Switzerland is crafting new regulation for banks in response to the 2023 collapse of Credit Suisse. UBS is weighing overseas options, including moving its headquarters or merging, if Swiss banking rules become too strict after the Credit Suisse collapse. The bank is studying possible US bank purchases and even a takeover of UBS, but sources say there are no active talks. Swiss plans could force UBS to hold up to 100% CET1 capital for foreign units, which UBS says would trap more than US$20 billion and hurt competitiveness. ZURICH – UBS is working on possible scenarios including shifting its headquarters, or a merger with another bank , if Switzerland introduces new banking rules it deems excessively strict, according to three sources familiar with the matter. Switzerland is crafting new regulation for banks in response to the 2023 collapse of Credit Suisse , and a Lower House committee will later in October begin debating rules passed in September by the Upper House that UBS hinted were intolerable. A group inside the bank is considering the various options, which include drawing up a list of smaller banks in the United States that UBS could potentially buy, and the prospect of the bank being taken over itself, according to the sources. There are no active talks under way, the sources said. UBS, which is closely following how events play out in Parliament, said: “We don’t comment on speculation or views expressed on such matters.” The British government and UBS discussed in 2026 the possibility of a move to London if the bank were to redomicile, the Financial Times said on Oct 16. The city emerged as one of the best options in the bank’s 2025 contingency planning, a source told Reuters at the time. In March, UBS obtained a US banking licence and is eager to expand its business in the United States. But the rules drafted by the Swiss government are partly designed to reduce the risk taxpayers could face if the bank suffered losses in the United States. Sources familiar with the bank’s thinking say US investment bank Morgan Stanley would be the best theoretical match for UBS. The Swiss bank has repeatedly stated that it is not planning to move and sees great value in its Swiss base. There are notable ties between the leadership of the two banks, as UBS chairman Colm Kelleher spent many years at Morgan Stanley, eventually rising to one of the top jobs there. Kelleher said in September that UBS might need to consider its future in Switzerland if the incoming rules were too harsh. Under its overhaul, the Swiss government wants ⁠UBS to back its foreign units with 100% Common Equity Tier 1 (CET1) capital, which could tie up in excess of US$20 billion (S$25.6 billion). UBS views this as excessive and harmful to its international competitiveness. The Upper House in September trimmed that requirement to 90% CET1 capital, but UBS also regards that as excessively high. At present, the bank needs to 60% capitalise its foreign units, but that can be partly met with cheaper capital. Since 2025, speculation has swirled around the possibility that UBS could move its base abroad to avoid the tougher regulation, and sources familiar with the bank’s thinking say it has a duty to shareholders to consider all options. Swiss Finance Minister Karin Keller-Sutter, who has led the charge to introduce tougher banking rules, said in September she felt it was unlikely that UBS would leave its homeland, arguing this would be costly and legally complicated. events.title: Stocks, futures rise as Fed bets ease after Warsh: Markets wrap
events.summary: Stock markets were already rising on Oct 16 before US Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh’s comments as a selloff in chip stocks eased. Stocks rose after Fed chairman Kevin Warsh gave no signal of urgency for more rate hikes, and traders cut October hike bets to 15%. Asian shares gained as chip stocks recovered, with Samsung and SK Hynix up more than 4%, while South Korea’s Kospi rebounded 4%. Indonesia’s stocks fell sharply after MSCI removed its emerging-market status, and investors warned the rally may stay fragile if gains remain focused on AI shares. Stocks extended gains as traders pared bets on an interest-rate hike after United States Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh refrained from signalling greater urgency to tighten policy despite this week’s hotter-than-expected inflation data. The dollar edged lower. MSCI’s Asia Pacific equities gauge climbed 1.4% , while US equity-index futures climbed 0.2%. European shares were set to gain 0.8% at the open. The modest uptick in sentiment – stocks were already higher as a rout in chip stocks eased – came after Warsh’s comments about the benefits of artificial intelligence (AI) to the US economy. He made no remarks on monetary policy or his outlook for the US economy, save for reiterating that the Fed will deliver price stability. “Warsh’s refusal to commit to another rate hike is resulting in some Fed-rate-hike bets being unwound,” said Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo Markets. “His comment that ‘I don’t prejudge meetings’ after strong inflation prints is not helping the dollar.” Traders reduced bets on a Fed rate hike in October to 15% after Warsh’s speech, from more than 25% on Oct 15. A Bloomberg gauge of the dollar fell 0.1%, after dropping 0.3% the prior session, which was the biggest decline in more than a month. Gold was little changed at US$4,172 an ounce . Treasuries stayed lower on the day as Warsh spoke, after rallying across the curve in US trading. Global crude oil benchmark Brent dropped 0.7% to US$105.20 a barrel. Investors looked to Warsh’s speech in Bangkok for clearer signals on the policy path after the fastest US inflation in five months boosted expectations for further Fed tightening . US inflation has remained stubborn, fuelled by elevated oil prices since the Middle East war broke out. “We made very clear that we would deliver price stability, and we removed a dose of accommodation about a month ago,” Warsh said in Bangkok. “I don’t prejudge meetings. I don’t believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year.” The Fed raised rates by a quarter percentage point in September, the first hike since 2023. It was backed by all 19 policymakers, and a majority also saw another increase as likely in 2026. A few key officials in recent weeks reiterated that additional rate hikes may be needed, but emphasised they have time to gather economic data before acting again. “Markets are reassured to hear Warsh reiterating his belief that AI will uplift productivity in the medium term, which could help moderate inflation expectations and temper fears of back-to-back Fed rate hikes,” said Chang Wei Liang, a macro strategist at DBS Bank. Stock markets were already rising on Oct 16 before Warsh’s comments as a selloff in chip stocks eased. In Asia, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix both advanced more than 4%. That helped South Korea’s Kospi Index rise 4% rebounding from the slump on Oct 15 that sent the gauge to its lowest close since April. Indonesian stocks slumped as much as 11%, the most since January 1998, after MSCI said the country no longer merits emerging-market status. The rupiah also edged lower. The durability of the equity rebound may depend on whether gains spread beyond the technology heavyweights that have driven much of the advance in 2026. Broader participation across sectors would help reduce the market’s reliance on AI-linked stocks after this week’s volatility exposed the risks of that concentration. “It seems like we are seeing a technical rebound, with the overall market settling down somewhat,” said Ryuta Otsuka, a strategist at Toyo Securities. Volatility could remain relatively high next week as traders monitor earnings “while searching for a bottom”, he said.

events.title: Keeping the haze out: Malls shut automated doors, suspend outdoor activities
events.summary: A sign at VivoCity on Oct 16 stating that an automated door is closed to keep the haze out. Singapore malls are closing automated doors and outdoor areas to protect shoppers and staff as haze stays unhealthy for a 12th day. Lendlease, Far East Organization and CapitaLand Investment are cleaning filters, checking air systems and giving N95 masks to workers with outdoor exposure. Malls are following NEA advice and may change access or suspend events; past haze cost Singapore $1.83 billion in 2015, according to NTU researchers. SINGAPORE – As Singapore entered the 12th consecutive day of unhealthy air on Oct 16, major retail landlords told The Straits Times they were taking steps to reduce haze exposure for shoppers, tenants and staff. Lendlease, Far East Organization and CapitaLand Investment have stepped up air filter cleaning and monitoring for their air-conditioning and mechanical ventilation (ACMV) systems. To protect people indoors, they are keeping automated mall entrances shut, with landlords such as Lendlease and CapitaLand Investments distributing N95 masks to employees and contractors facing prolonged outdoor exposure. At noon on Oct 16, the hourly PM2.5 readings across the island hit the “high” range, which is above 150, while the 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) in the western, central and eastern Singapore remained in the “very unhealthy” range above 200. Singapore’s PSI has five bands – good (0-50), moderate (51-100), unhealthy (101-200), very unhealthy (201-300) and hazardous (more than 300). A CapitaLand Investment spokesman said management may reduce outdoor airflow at its malls – including Ion Orchard, Plaza Singapura, Tampines Mall, Junction 8, Funan and Kallang Wave Wall – by closing windows and automatic sliding doors where possible and directing shoppers to alternative entrances. Outdoor facilities at the malls may also be closed when air quality reaches unhealthy levels, the spokesperson added. A sign on the sliding entrance doors at Junction 8 stated they were disabled to maintain indoor air quality as pollutant levels hit the unhealthy range , directing shoppers to use the side entrances instead. Deborah Tan, director for operations and marketing at Far East Organization’s commercial group, said mall tenants with exterior exits have also been advised to keep their entrances closed. Far East Organization’s portfolio of malls include Orchard Central, Clarke Quay Central, Square 2 and One Holland Village. Tenants at One Holland Village, which has a more open layout, have been advised to keep their shop doors closed where suitable, while outdoor events have been rescheduled to November. Tan added that they are monitoring updates from the National Environment Agency (NEA) closely and will adjust their safety approach as conditions develop. Jenny Khoo, head of retail and workspace management at Lendlease, said staff are encouraged to prioritise their well-being and discuss any concerns with their supervisors, and that flexible work arrangements “may be considered where appropriate”. She added that under normal conditions, the malls’ ACMV air filters are cleaned and replaced on a stringent maintenance schedule. When haze conditions worsen, management steps up active monitoring of indoor air quality and filter performance, and carries out additional replacements. Khoo added that management has also enhanced the malls’ air quality with bi-polar ionisation systems, which release positive and negative ions to eliminate dust, odours and pathogens such as bacteria and viruses. Retail malls in Lendlease’s portfolio include Parkway Parade, 313@somerset, Jem and PLQ Mall. Khoo said outdoor play areas at Lendlease malls, such as Jem, may close temporarily when the 24-hour PSI reading exceeds 200. “Lendlease takes precautionary measures guided by prevailing NEA advisories, including suspending outdoor facilities and activities,” she added. Mapletree Pan Asia Commercial Trust, which manages VivoCity, declined to comment, although one of its entrances featured a sign stating it was closed to keep the haze out. VivoCity’s level-three rooftop features an open, shallow wading pool, while level two has free-to-access outdoor playgrounds alongside children’s ride operator ZooMoov. A spokesperson for City Square Mall said its outdoor playgrounds have been temporarily closed, while mall personnel’s non-essential outdoor duties have been reduced. “Non-essential” auto-doors have also been closed to limit outdoor pollutants from entering the mall. The mall will also give away 100 complimentary honey lemon drinks, while stocks last, at the mall’s customer service counter at B2 from Oct 19 to Nov 1, from 10am to 10pm daily. The Singapore Institute of International Affairs had in June issued a rare “red” warning in its Haze Outlook 2026 report, and said there was a high risk of severe transboundary haze affecting Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia and Singapore.

events.title: Drone strikes in the Black Sea raise fears of Russian escalation to test NATO
events.summary: Drone attacks on cargo ships in the Black Sea this month have raised concerns among NATO members SOFIA, Bulgaria -- A string of drone attacks on at least seven cargo vessels in the Black Sea this month, off the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria, has some members of the alliance wondering if Russian President Vladimir Putin is seeking escalation to test their support for Ukraine in its war against Moscow's full-scale invasion. The attacks in the two countries' exclusive economic zones threaten a global shipping route and have left two people dead, with at least 25 still missing. They also run the risk of drawing other countries directly into the war for Ukraine. Throughout the war, Russia has repeatedly bombarded Ukraine’s Black Sea and Danube river ports, leaving Kyiv increasingly reliant on alternative routes to get its grain exports to markets in Africa and the Middle East. Russian drones have repeatedly violated Romanian airspace near some of Ukraine's Danube ports. In the latest incidents, fires broke out on two ships struck by drones Wednesday and Thursday, one in Romania's territorial waters. Romanian President Nicusor Dan said Thursday in Brussels that “two drones” had hit the vessels but did not say whose drones they were. “There will be a reaction from the Romanian state,” he warned. Increasingly, the suspicion falls on Russia. “There is no logic in Ukraine attacking its own ships and crews, given that the outcome of all these attacks favors Russia — and indeed, the logic points in that direction,” Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told his country’s Parliament. “The problem is that we cannot prove it.” The San Marino-flagged Wine Trader , a chemical tanker traveling from Tunisia to Romania, was struck by a drone Thursday and caught fire. Five crew members were rescued but another seven are missing. On Wednesday, a drone strike and fire were reported on the Comoros-flagged Yara J, a chemical and oil tanker traveling from Turkey to Romania. Romania’s acting Defense Minister Radu Miruta said an investigation was underway. On Tuesday, two ships were struck by drones off Bulgaria's coast. Rescuers evacuated all 15 crew members from the Ukraine-operated Chelsea 3, sailing under a Maltese flag, but 11 crew from the Guinea-Bissau-flagged HS Dignity are still missing . The crew of the Chelsea 3 reported the ship’s deck and hull were hit by three aerial drones. Earlier this month, sea and aerial drones attacked two other commercial vessels in Bulgaria’s exclusive economic zone. A Togo-flagged ship sank with no sign of the 12 sailors reported on board, while a Bulgarian ferry evacuated 18 crew members from a Palau-flagged vessel that was damaged. A day earlier, a Turkish-owned cargo ship carrying corn caught fire following a drone attack and later sank off the coast of Romania. Two people died and 11 crew members were rescued. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described the attack as “a horrific strike by two Russian drones on a civilian vessel” in neutral waters. Russia's ambassador in Sofia, Bulgaria, said she didn't have any information from the Russian defense ministry. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said on X on Thursday that he met Radev and Dan to discuss security in the Black Sea and “the latest attacks on commercial shipping.” “NATO has strengthened our posture along the eastern flank including with increasing counter-drone capabilities,” he said. “NATO will continue to work closely with our Allies in the Black Sea, adjusting our deterrence and defense posture as needed.” Article 5 of the NATO charter has a mutual defense guarantee — an attack on one is an attack on all — but Romanian defense analyst Radu Tudor said it was uncertain as to whether it covers many of the Black Sea drone strikes because they occurred in the alliance members’ exclusive economic zones. Teen shooter kills 3 children, 1 teacher at elementary school in Bend, Oregon: Police Woman accused of stabbing husband and son to death at Great Wolf Lodge: Complaint Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded “It’s a matter of discussion whether the exclusive economic zone is included in the Article 5-type reaction or not,” he said. “And it seems that until now, it isn’t — which raised a lot of questions.” NATO has been too slow to respond in the Black Sea, he argued. “Tens of incidents are happening and Russia is getting closer to NATO borders. … Words are not enough,” Tudor said. The Black Sea drone incidents in October are just the latest in a long string of drone airspace incursions to rock Romania and other NATO members since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. While most have come from Russia, Ukrainian drones have also crossed borders.

events.title: What to know about Starshield, SpaceX's military-focused Starlink service
events.summary: Starshield is SpaceX's government-focused satellite network, and new restrictions reported by Ukraine have renewed scrutiny of how it differs from the company's commercial Starlink service. It is a secure satellite network for government and national security users, built using Starlink technology and SpaceX launch capabilities. The service adds government-focused security, dedicated user equipment, and missions such as Earth observation and hosted payloads. Uncertainty over who controls SpaceX's military satellite system, Starshield, has drawn renewed attention, as restrictions on the technology hinder Ukraine's defenses. Ukraine has accused SpaceX -owned Starlink of restricting its military-grade services , known as Starshield, as Russia intensified attacks on Kyiv. Officials in Kyiv said SpaceX had imposed restrictions on Starshield without advance notice, disrupting military operations and hampering efforts to protect civilians amid intense Russian attacks this week. In response, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk appeared to shift responsibility for any changes to Starshield's use in Ukraine to the U.S. government and President Donald Trump . He said that Starshield systems are owned and controlled by Washington, with the U.S. military and ultimately the president determining any limits on their use. The White House and the Pentagon didn't immediately reply to CNBC's request for comment. Here's what to know about Starshield, and how it differs from Starlink. What is Starshield and how does it work? Starshield is SpaceX's satellite network designed for government and national security use, building on the technology developed for Starlink. On Tuesday, Ukrainian officials reported that their Starlink communication systems were no longer working for terminals moving at speeds above 100 miles per hour, or about 160 kilometers per hour. Ukraine relies on this connectivity to track and intercept incoming threats. Ukraine's military also uses the commercial Starlink technology, according to media reports, but it is not clear which of its terminals operate under the commercial arm versus those provided through Starshield. Speaking to Piers Morgan on Wednesday, Zelenskyy lamented that "Starlink was switched off." He said connectivity in the middle of the night, disrupting Ukrainian drones used to intercept Russian attacks, and that restrictions had prevented Ukraine from intercepting some Russian drones, contributing to civilian deaths. He also criticized the lack of advance warnings about incoming Russian ballistic missiles. "Often when we destroy jet shaheeds, we use drones with Starlinks," he said. "It's not about attack. It's also about defending the lives… People were killed because not enough destroying, not enough interceptors, including interceptors with Starlink, which didn't work." "They knew what they did," Zelenskyy said, referring to SpaceX and the U.S. and describing the Starlink restrictions as particularly troubling given Ukraine's reliance on the U.S. as a strategic partner. Mykhailo Fedorov, who was until recently Ukraine's defense minister, said Wednesday that Starlink connectivity at speeds of up to 160 km/h was being restored, and that "removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense." According to SpaceX, Starshield currently focuses on Earth observation, secure global communications for government users, and so-called "hosted payloads," which refers to hosting specialized equipment aboard satellites for customers. Unlike Starlink, which serves consumers and businesses, Starshield offers enhanced security features, including high-assurance cryptographic capability designed to handle classified information. It says its satellites can handle a range of equipment and connect with other satellites through laser communications technology. SpaceX was awarded over $6 billion in multi-year U.S. government contracts for Starshield, primarily from two major Space Force contracts for low Earth orbit-based communications and sensing constellations, SpaceX said in its latest earnings report . Musk on Wednesday distinguished Starshield from SpaceX's commercial Starlink service, which he said was restricted to civilian and defensive purposes and could not be used for offensive military operations. How does Starshield differ from Starlink? Although Starshield serves a different purpose from Starlink's commercial internet service, which provides high-speed connectivity to regular people, the two are closely connected. Starlink is SpaceX's general satellite internet service, sold for consumer, civilian, and defense purposes, and offers internet access in remote areas where it has traditionally been limited. Starshield uses stronger encryption and specialized terminals for secure communications, but relies on Starlink's extensive satellite network to operate.

events.title: World Bank sets fivefold minerals goal as Fed chairman Warsh flags financial stability risks
events.summary: The World Bank aims to increase its critical minerals business fivefold over the next five years, while US Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh expressed surprise at the resilience of major economies amid geopolitical shocks and tighter monetary policy. "In critical minerals, we ⁠plan to quintuple our business in five years … this ​week, ⁠we launched our ‌first country compacts with MDB partners, to build local industries and keep ​more jobs and value at home," World Bank president Ajay Banga said at the 2026 IMF -World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok on Friday, as the multilateral lender seeks to support mining, processing and local industries. He also outlined plans to expand partnerships with countries developing critical minerals industries. The World Bank's new metals and minerals implementation plan is aimed at securing $19 billion in critical minerals financing over the 2026-2030 fiscal period, up from $3.6 billion in the 2021-2025 fiscal period. The lender has identified 20 countries with which it could partner on critical minerals development projects. It also launched its first country compacts with its partners this week, aiming to build local industries and retain more jobs and economic value in producing countries. Mr Banga also laid out a vision on Friday for how the World Bank should operate, focusing primarily on creating jobs, expanding economic opportunity and connecting private capital to developing nations that need investment. Addressing the plenary session at the annual meetings, Mr Banga said the current economic climate of tightening fiscal space, rising debt and global conflicts had made the work challenging – but not impossible. “Those are the twin challenges we have been working to address: making scarce resources go further, while helping countries create jobs at scale. They must be addressed together,” he said in prepared remarks. “The future of development will depend on bringing public finance , private investment, philanthropy and technology together around what each country needs. The partnership – and mix – should evolve as countries do.” He also spoke of the World Bank’s new initiative to focus on “small AI” – bespoke artificial intelligence-enabled applications that do not rely on the most advanced and expensive version of the technology, but can provide solutions for people in the developing world. “Practical, or ‘small’, AI can help a farmer improve yields, a teacher tailor instruction, a health worker make better-informed decisions, or an entrepreneur reach new customers,” Mr Banga added. Separately, Mr Warsh said the Fed needed to consider financial stability risks as it assesses the outlook for the US economy , while declining to offer indications about its next interest-rate decision. ⁠Speaking at the annual meetings, heh said he did not “prejudge” policy decisions before the Fed’s meetings from October 27 to 28, when markets expect interest rates to remain unchanged. The Fed raised rates in September and made it clear that it intended to deliver price stability and withdraw some monetary policy accommodation, he said. “I don't prejudge meetings. I don't believe in saying now what I might do at the meetings that we have in the balance of this year,” Mr Warsh said. He said ⁠the Fed must ​continually bolster its credibility to get ⁠monetary policy right, adding that that includes the supervision and operations side ⁠of the central bank. He also expressed optimism about AI and its potential to transform the real economy, although he said the technology’s near-term impact on employment remained uncertain. Mr Warsh also said he was surprised by the global resilience and how many G20 member ⁠states are “hanging in there” amid the geopolitical shocks of recent months, ​as ⁠most ‌central banks tightened monetary ​policy to deal with inflation. “We're seeing common things and we're taking action and I view that as a positive development,” Mr Warsh said. “I believe, optimistically, ​you ‌might think ⁠naively, at least ​in the US, we're ​going ‌to come out of ⁠this stronger with a ⁠more durable economy, more capable of leading the world on economic growth.” With reporting from Reuters and AFP

events.title: Russia returns to G20 table in Bangkok on U.S. invitation that angers Europe
events.summary: Russia's Anton Siluanov was listed at a G20 finance chiefs' meeting on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok. That marks Siluanov's second in-person participation in the meeting since the invasion, after his exclusion from the group photo in Asheville, N.C. German finance minister Lars Klingbeil, who protested Siluanov's previous presence, was also listed as being at the Bangkok meeting. G20 finance chiefs ended the meeting without a joint communique amid splits over Iran, trade imbalances, and Ukraine war. Russia's finance minister attended a Group of 20 meeting in Bangkok on Thursday, his second in-person appearance at the event since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, testing how far Washington's rapprochement with Moscow will strain ties with Europe. Anton Siluanov and Bank of Russia Deputy Governor Elizaveta Danilova were listed as Russia's delegates at the finance ministers and central bank governors' meetings on the sidelines of the IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, according to a seating plan seen by CNBC. Siluanov was in the meeting, according to a person familiar with the matter. According to the layout document, Russian delegates were seated between attendees from South Korea and the United Arab Emirates. German Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil was also listed as an attendee. At the August G20 finance meeting in Asheville, North Carolina, he told Siluanov that Moscow must end the war and declined to pose in a group photo with him. The traditional group photo was ultimately taken without the Russian delegation after European officials protested. Klingbeil has pushed back on the U.S. efforts to bring Russia back on to the international stage, reportedly saying after the Thursday meeting that "there will be no pretending that Russia is now returning as a normal member of the G20 and simply taking its seat at the table again — not with me, and not with the other Europeans." Russia's seat at the table tests how far Washington can ease pressure on Moscow without breaking with its European allies. The U.S., which took over the G20 presidency this year, welcomed Russia's finance minister back to the finance talks after years of isolation over the invasion of Ukraine. The Trump administration also introduced a deal to temporarily lift sanctions on Russian diesel imports until April, drawing criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and European allies. Dombrovskis told CNBC on Wednesday that "now it's not a time to ease sanctions on Russia." In a statement issued after the Thursday meetings, Australian Treasurer Jim Chalmers said Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on commercial vessels "must end." Those impacts "are exacerbated by Russia's unprovoked and unjustifiable war in Ukraine," he said, adding that Australia calls for Russia to end the war and respect Ukraine's sovereignty. The finance chiefs ended the meeting without a joint communique, underscoring persistent divisions among members over the Middle East conflict, trade imbalances, and Russia's war with Ukraine. U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who would normally chair the talks, skipped the meetings to stay in Washington. The Asheville meeting also ended without a communique, after China objected to language on several issues , including efforts to rectify excessive global trade surpluses. The U.S. instead issued a chair's statement backed by every member present except China, with Bessent calling China "the dissenter." Delegates started the day with a plated breakfast of baked goat cheese, spinach and egg soufflé with chutney made from locally grown Bijin tomatoes, according to a menu card at the venue. The bread basket came with "Nam Dok Mai" mango jam. Every card carried the U.S. presidency's stars-and-stripes G20 logo and its "Freedom 250" tagline, marking America's 250th anniversary . The finance ministers' meeting Thursday could have helped lay the groundwork for improved coordination on a raft of global challenges, including energy problems stemming from the Middle East conflict and concerns about record public debt in advanced economies. Leaders are expected to convene at the next G20 summit in Miami in December.

events.title: Commercial goods are no longer entering Gaza, raising fears
events.summary: No commercial goods are entering the Gaza Strip, Israeli authorities said, attributing the suspension to local vendors they said are fed up with Hamas raising taxes on them JERUSALEM -- No commercial goods have entered the Gaza Strip for two days, Israeli authorities said Thursday, blaming the suspension on merchants angered by taxes imposed by Hamas — a claim that Palestinian importers deny. The halt to commercial shipments, including fruit and winter clothing, cuts off a key source of food and other critical supplies as fears grow about procuring supplies needed to get through winter in the territory. The move stands to immediately reduce Gaza's supplies, because the closed-off territory is completely reliant on whatever goods Israel allows in through border crossings. Aid groups generally bring in staples such as flour, while merchants import more perishable foods like fruits and meat, according to data released earlier this year by COGAT, the Israeli military body that oversees humanitarian affairs in Gaza. The suspension is raising fears about affordability, with humanitarian workers saying a combination of aid and a robust commercial market is needed to keep prices under control. “The humanitarian sector on its own cannot meet the needs of all the people,” said Shaina Low, a spokesperson for the Norwegian Refugee Council, an aid group. “The markets need to be functioning.” COGAT announced the suspension of commercial shipments Wednesday. Its deputy spokesperson, Lt. Daniel Kantorovich, said the agency was acting on a decision made by Palestinian merchants a day earlier and could reverse it at their behest. “We were prepared to coordinate the entry of their trucks as usual, but the vendors informed us that they were cancelling the coordination due to Hamas’s taxation mechanism and threats against them,” Kantorovich said. “The merchants don’t want to bring goods into Gaza.” The world’s leading authority on food insecurity reported earlier this year that conditions in Gaza had improved since famine was declared in the territory in August 2025, but were still at crisis levels. Most families in the war-battered enclave weren’t getting nearly enough to eat, said the report, adding that “even small disruptions to humanitarian access could rapidly reverse recent gains.” Merchants in Gaza coordinate directly with vendors outside the territory, whose shipments are examined by Israel's military before entering Gaza. In announcing the measure, COGAT claimed to be communicating a decision made by local merchants in Gaza who had grown tired of Hamas taxing their trucks and threatening them. Israel has long accused the militant group of levying fees on imports to fund its operations. COGAT said no private-sector vendors had attempted to import goods to Gaza since the merchants alerted Israel on Tuesday. Teen shooter kills 3 children, 1 teacher at elementary school in Bend, Oregon: Police Woman accused of stabbing husband and son to death at Great Wolf Lodge: Complaint Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded But the head of Gaza’s private truckers union, Nahed Sheheiber, disputed Israel's account, saying they were the ones who had made the decision. “The merchants are not the ones who stopped the shipments,” he said. “The Israeli coordinator is claiming that Gaza’s merchants are responsible, but the truth is that the Israelis are the ones who imposed the restrictions.” Following COGAT's announcement, Sheheiber's union met with Gaza's Ministry of Economy to express concern and say Israel was citing fees levied by the ministry as a pretext to cut off commercial goods. The ministry had been asking merchants to pay 10,000 shekels (about $3,226) per truck entering Gaza, Sheheiber said. At the meeting, ministry Undersecretary Khaled Al-Raqab told the union that the amount was not a tax, but rather a donation sought by the ministry to help pay civil servants in the strip. It was not clear from the COGAT announcement if aid agencies would be allowed to increase shipments into Gaza to compensate for the loss in commercial goods. The agency claimed that Gaza's population — of roughly 2 million people — required approximately 250 truckloads of goods each day. That's far below the minimum of 600 trucks a day stipulated by a ceasefire brokered by the U.S. a year ago. The war started when Hamas-led militants killed some 1,200 people on Oct. 7, 2023, and took 251 hostages . Israel responded with a massive bombardment and a ground invasion that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to the Gaza Health Ministry. That includes over 1,400 Palestinians killed since the ceasefire took effect, the ministry says. Sporadic attacks have killed five Israeli soldiers in Gaza in the same period. The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, maintains detailed records and is seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts.

events.title: Yields on S’pore Government Securities climb higher: Should investors buy in or stick to stocks?
events.summary: The interest rate on the one-year T-bill rose to its 2026 high of 1.92% on Oct 15. T-bill yields in Singapore have risen to about 1.9%, and experts expect more gains as US Federal Reserve hikes push up short-term rates. Nov's Singapore Savings Bonds hit a 2026 peak of 2.45%, though early redemption cuts year-one yields to 1.67% Some investors still prefer dividend stocks, as their yields can beat T-bills and SSBs, while keeping more cash ready for market opportunities. SINGAPORE – The returns that retail investors are getting for Treasury bills (T-bills), a type of short-term Singapore Government Securities, are climbing after dipping to around 1.3% to 1.4% in 2025 and the first half of 2026. With yields now hovering near 1.9%, fixed-income experts believe there is more upside in the coming months. Another form of Singapore Government Securities, Singapore Savings Bonds (SSBs), will pay the highest rates so far in 2026 for its November issue. If investors hold the SSBs for the full duration of 10 years, they will earn an average return of 2.45% a year. T-bills are short-term securities with maturities of either six months or a year. Investors buy the bills at a discount upfront and receive the full face value at maturity, earning the difference as interest. In contrast, SSBs are longer-term instruments that can be held for up to 10 years, though investors have the flexibility to exit their investment in any given month without penalty. Both T-bills and SSBs are deemed risk-free investments backed by Singapore’s triple-A credit rating. The appeal of T-bills grew in 2022 as yields climbed steadily from sub-1% levels. The six-month T-bill subsequently hit a peak of 4.4% on Dec 8, 2022, and the one-year T-bill went as high as 3.87% on Jan 26, 2023. Drawn by their safe nature and rising yields, investors from all walks of life piled in. Senior lab technician Dallas Goh was one of them. He accumulated as much as $100,000 in T-bills at one point. Interest in these short-term government securities waned in 2024 as equity markets became more attractive. Investors – including Goh, who stopped buying T-bills in the middle of 2024 – looked elsewhere for higher returns. However, the yields on T-bills are climbing again. The interest rate on the one-year T-bill rose to its 2026 high of 1.92% on Oct 15, from 1.68% on July 23. There will be no more one-year T-bill auctions in 2026. Meanwhile, the cut-off yield for the six-month T-bill dipped slightly to 1.9% on Oct 8, remaining just shy of its Sept 24 peak of 1.92%. There are five more six-month T-bill auctions – on Oct 22, Nov 4, Nov 19, Dec 3 and Dec 17. Goh said the yields are “still too low” and that he will wait until they cross 2.5% before he considers investing in T-bills again. His wish may just come true. Market watchers anticipate higher yields in the upcoming auctions as the US Federal Reserve is expected to raise interest rates at least once by December 2026 and a total of twice within the next six months. Eugene Leow, head of fixed-income research at DBS Bank, said: “As long as Fed hike bets are in play, we would reasonably expect six-month T-bill rates to continue climbing.” He noted that the interest rates on a six-month T-bill reflect where investors expect the Fed to move rates over the next half a year. “We think the six-month and one-year T-Bill rates would still grind higher in the coming months as Fed hikes get delivered,” he added. Wesley Hoon, research analyst with the global fixed-income team at digital wealth platform FSM Global, noted that the Monetary Authority of Singapore manages the economy through the exchange rate rather than by setting interest rates. As a result, Singapore’s short-term rates largely take their cue from US interest rates. To illustrate his point, Hoon noted that following the Federal Reserve’s rate hike on Sept 16, the cut-off yield for the six-month T-bill auction on Sept 24 climbed from 1.7% to 1.92%. “If the Fed pauses in October and hikes in December, as markets expect, that adds upward pressure into year-end, though some of it is already reflected in today’s yields,” he said. Hoon expects six-month yields to keep climbing over the remaining auctions in 2026. FSM Global is also positive on the one-year T-bills. However, since there are no more one-year bills in 2026, investors must wait until January 2027 to participate. To avoid sitting on idle cash, Hoon suggested that investors consider building a T-bill ladder with staggered maturity dates by spreading their cash across multiple upcoming auctions. Because six-month bills are auctioned every two weeks, investors can allocate a portion into each of the next few issues, making January 2027’s one-year T-bill just another rung in their ladder rather than the final destination, he added. “With a ladder, you don’t have to call the peak to earn a decent yield,” Hoon said. “Part of your money matures every couple of weeks.

events.title: Fuel costs squeezing margins for some businesses
events.summary: Diesel prices in Jersey have reached more than £2 per litre in recent weeks Some businesses in Jersey have expressed concern about the impact of rising global fuel prices. Locally, and in the UK, diesel prices recently topped £2 a litre , and global leaders have since made efforts to ease the strain on supply. The Government of Jersey has proposed to freeze fuel duty in 2027 in a bid to "help ease cost-of-living pressures". A&A Scaffolding Solutions said it welcomed that move, but said it would provide "limited relief if global prices continue to rise". Listen to the latest news for Jersey Fuel duty was frozen in Jersey from 2023-2025, before rising in line with inflation in 2026. In the proposed budget for 2027 , external , the government has suggested freezing it once again. It said "maintaining fuel duty at its current rate will help avoid additional costs for households and businesses that rely on transport, providing continued support at a time when many islanders remain under financial pressure". However, some businesses on the island worry that it will not be enough to offset global prices. Which war is having the biggest impact on diesel prices - Iran or Ukraine? Published 3 days ago Kelly Keating, from A&A Scaffolding Solutions, said "rising diesel prices are a real concern for us, particularly when they come on top of so many other costs that seem to be increasing across Jersey". "Construction is taking a hard hit. We rely on diesel for machinery, vehicles and deliveries, so increases put direct pressure on the cost of carrying out work. "Alongside rising material, freight and operating costs, this is squeezing margins and making it harder to price projects with confidence". "A freeze in fuel duty would be welcome, but our concern is that it would offer limited relief if global fuel prices continue to rise. "The wider issue is the cumulative impact. Businesses can only absorb so many increases before they affect investment, project viability and ultimately the prices customers pay". Businesses said it was becoming more difficult to absorb price rises Fuel costs are also having a "noticeable impact" for tree surgeons, Jonathan Le Maistre Ltd. Darren Hopkins, from the firm, said "we depend on our vans, trucks, chippers, stump grinders, and other machinery that consume significant amounts of fuel". "Increased diesel prices will raise our operating costs, reducing margins on jobs and making it more difficult to absorb costs without passing some of them on to our customers". Hopkins said continued increases would be a "concern for their business, and the wider industry". However, some businesses are managing through the disruption. Jeremy Phillips, from Barette Plant Hire, said it "hasn't been too much of an issue so far, but that fuel surcharges are being added to hourly rates". However, he said that "if the prices keep going up, customers aren't going to be carrying on with their projects". Treasury Minister Alan Maclean said support was being targeted directly at consumers rather than expecting businesses to absorb costs In the run-up to the unveiling of the 2027 budget, Deputy Lucy Stephenson called for a reduction in fuel duty , but those plans were withdrawn following assurances from ministers that support was coming. Speaking at the time, Treasury Minister Alan Maclean said the government "didn't like the idea of reducing fuel duty because it wasn't targeted". Instead, ministers opted for a freeze on duty for 2027, prioritising targeted support for families and those "struggling the most". Responding to the fresh concerns from businesses, Maclean said: "Rather than expecting businesses to absorb increased costs such as higher fuel prices, the budget provides support directly to consumers to help them manage those pressures and spend in the local economy". "Fuel prices are largely driven by global markets and geopolitical events outside Jersey's control. "What the government can do is avoid adding further pressure where it can. "The proposed freeze in fuel duty will help mitigate the impact of prices rises by reducing the level of duty in real terms". events.title: Even Benchmark thinks AI is eroding the venture pact against backing rivals
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. For decades, the unwritten rule of venture capital was that a firm doesn’t back two companies that compete head-on. But speaking at TechCrunch Disrupt earlier this week, the partners of Benchmark readily acknowledged that the AI boom is straining that rule. It’s been on the verge of snapping for some time. The towering AI labs OpenAI and Anthropic share dozens of the same investors at this point. Then, at the end of September, Factory, a startup that builds an AI agent to write software, said it was firing board observer and adviser Chris Degnan for “unethical conduct involving Cognition,” its direct rival and the maker of the Devin coding agent. Factory’s CEO alleged Degnan had discussed a job at Cognition while privy to Factory’s board-level discussions. Degnan said he had already resigned and denied sharing anything confidential. Soon after, he announced he was joining Cognition as chief revenue officer. Powerhouse investor Vinod Khosla sided with Degnan on X, blasting Factory’s CEO and calling the company “a struggling second tier competitor.” Khosla Ventures backs both companies. Even Benchmark, a firm whose reputation rests on 10- to 15-year partnerships with founders at the earliest stage, said the old rule can no longer be counted on. Asked at Disrupt whether the pact against backing rivals still holds as portfolio companies expand into each other’s territory, its partners described the conflicts as a matter of necessity, not preference. “The harsh reality of this world is every company is evolving very quickly,” said Eric Vishria. Companies pivot and change, he said, and “you are going to get conflicts, and that’s just the reality of the current dynamic.” Vishria said Benchmark stays committed to each founder and keeps what it learns confidential, and he downplayed how much a VC could pass along anyway: “We are not product or technology experts.” Seemingly referring to the Factory-Cognition dispute, he said Benchmark has been fortunate not to land in “that type of insane direct conflict.” Exclusivity, he said, remains “really important” at the very early stage Benchmark favors. “But things are evolving. There’s no doubt about that.” Chetan Puttagunta said AI is accelerating the problem. As the cost of building software “effectively goes to zero,” he said, founders are “incredibly ambitious.” Because they now see a “surface area” and want to claim all of it, he continued, “[i]t’s probably going to happen more, where you start to run into each other.” He drew a line between a direct competitor at the outset, which he called “an easy answer,” and a portfolio company that expands into another’s turf over time. “That happens,” he said. Peter Fenton called the issue “kryptonite” and the firm’s toughest problem. He described a spectrum of how investors relate to their companies. At one end is the co-founder, who would never work on a competing company. At the other is the public-market stock picker, who can own several rivals because he is merely allocating capital, not shaping any of them. Benchmark sits nearer the co-founder end, Fenton said, and treats transparency as a golden rule. “There shouldn’t be the surprise after the fact.” If a conflict does emerge, a founder should never feel shortchanged, he added. Benchmark isn’t declaring the pact dead. At the same time, when a firm that built its name on loyalty says conflicts are coming, founders might rightly wonder who else will be this candid. events.title: 'TV and cheap booze' blamed for landlord quitting
events.summary: Landlord Patrick Hughes says fewer people are going to the pub Former pub landlord Patrick Hughes is blunt when explaining why he has called time on his tenure behind the bar. "I thought there was a gap in the market but there was no market for the gap", he said. The 66-year-old took over The Royal Mail Cart pub in Spalding, in August 2025, hoping to attract customers with live music nights and "a sense of community". Just over a year on he is packing boxes and looking around the empty rooms after he quit his tenancy with the pub's owner, Stonegate Group. The government said it was supporting pubs with business rates discounts. Patrick has given up his tenancy of The Royal Mail Cart in Spalding Patrick told BBC Politics North that he blames a perfect storm of rising utility and wage prices, people's changing habits and major roadworks directly outside the pub, which began in the summer. "These days people are used to staying at home, watching TV, having cheap drink from the supermarket or off licence and getting food deliveries," he said. "To make a pub like this work you need to turn over £12,000 a week, some weeks we were doing quite well, around £8,000, but once the road works began outside that went down quite dramatically." Figures from the Office for National Statistics , external show that 27% of pubs and bars in Lincolnshire closed between 2009 and 2025. That is a drop from 710 to 515. In South Holland, of which Spalding is a part, the rate is almost double that, at 53%, a drop from 75 to 35. That is also way above the England average of 19%. "The government needs to look at the low cost of alcohol in supermarkets primarily," said Patrick. "Certainly the taxation in supermarkets needs to be looked at to bring about some kind of equilibrium." Duty paid on draught alcohol in pubs and bars is up to 11 pence cheaper than that sold in supermarkets. But other costs associated with running a business still makes supermarket alcohol cheaper overall. Prime Minister Andy Burnham has announced a 20% cut in business rates for qualifying pubs, social clubs and live music venues in England, effective from April 2027. Emma McClarkin OBE, chief executive of the British Beer and Pub Association, says they want that to be made permanent at the Budget this month, "alongside a freeze in beer duty and a widening of the draft discount". "We're set to lose one pub a day by the end of the year and 295 have closed already," she said. "When a pub does close, it's not just the front door that's closing, it's the heritage, the culture, the economic contribution to society and the social value." Mark Newlands believes that people still want to visit their local pub Just outside Spalding, The Ship Inn pub stands by the River Welland in the small hamlet of Surfleet Seas End. "There used to be tables and chairs with people eating food and drinking by the river," said Mark Newlands, who lives a few doors down. The pub closed last year but now some locals, led by Mark, have formed The Shipmates group to try to raise £600,000 to buy and run it. So far they have managed to get the pub listed as An Asset of Community Value under the Localism Act 2011. That gives them the right to bid for the property, if it goes up for sale. "People have become fed up of the Covid way of living and they want to see their pub open," said Mark. "The indications from smaller and larger investors is that it's worth doing and we've proven to our own satisfaction that it is a viable business." An HM Treasury spokesperson said: "The Chancellor prioritised support for the hospitality industry in his first week in the job when he cut business rates by 20% for pubs, social clubs and live music venues - saving thousands of locals over £1,000 a year." Stonegate has been approached by the BBC for comment. Listen to highlights from Lincolnshire on BBC Sounds , watch the latest episode of Look North .
