events.title: The right’s scrounger rhetoric dominates the benefits debate. Labour must fight back – and win | Frances Ryan
events.summary: The right’s scrounger rhetoric dominates the benefits debate. Labour must fight back – and win The prime minister has a once-in-a-generation chance to reintroduce fairness to the system. He has to seize the moment B ack in 2009, months before the coalition government unleashed sweeping austerity, the then Conservative backbencher Iain Duncan Smith produced a study that would go on to lay the foundations for the rollout of universal credit. Now, nearly two decades later, Duncan Smith and his thinktank, the Centre for Social Justice (CSJ), has published State of Dependency: a landmark report promising to expose “the full scale of Britain’s worklessness crisis”. The study paints a picture of mass benefits reliance: it identifies 3,400 local areas where more than half the working-age population are on out-of-work benefits, or “economic opiates”, as the authors call them. They’ve even provided an interactive map (in the yellow and black colours of a road hazard sign, no less) so members of the public can type in their postcode to see if their neighbourhood is “a welfare hotspot”. This is not just another ugly social policy report from a politically sidelined former minister – it is a gauntlet being thrown down ahead of Britain’s big benefits debate. Next month, the government is expected to release two major reports into the social safety net: the Timms review on personal independence payments (Pip), which pays for some of the extra costs of disability in England and Wales, and the Milburn review into young people who are out of work. It wouldn’t be overstating the importance of Westminster reviews to say their recommendations could shape the future of our welfare state for decades to come. With almost 1 million young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) and the disability benefits bill rising in cash terms, Andy Burnham will face immense pressure to use the proposals to launch a once-in-a-generation overhaul of the social security system. An overhaul in itself is no bad thing. Disabled people applying for benefits face a debilitating mess of bureaucracy and barriers, while too many young people have been abandoned, facing greater obstacles and fewer services. The question is, will the overhaul actually improve conditions for the people who rely on it, or buckle to the anti-benefit sentiment that’s been bubbling up for months? That the right is not currently in power won’t stop it from wielding significant influence on what’s to come, in large part thanks to its dominance of Britain’s media ecosystem. Legacy media are not even hiding their attempts to shape November’s reforms before they are announced, with the Times this week launching a “ welfare inquiry ” to investigate the impact of the benefits “crisis” on public finances. Some of this is made up of concrete policy proposals, such as the Daily Mail’s pitch to radically means-test Pip . But increasingly much of it is just vibes, a vague sense that this disability problem is getting out of control (or having one is becoming “cool” , as the Telegraph recently put it), and that disabled people – particularly the young – are somehow grifting “perks” while everyone else struggles with rising bills. The changes in how people consume media since the last major benefits reforms in the early 2010s mean the risks of misinformation and outright bigotry are even greater. Last week, Nigel Farage announced plans for a new video studio in Westminster for the launch of Reform TV on YouTube , with the party’s proposed £50bn benefits cuts presumably being lined up as viral content. Keep an eye out too for a revival of the striver v scrounger rhetoric as energy and housing costs are set to lead to the worst living standards in modern times by 2029-30. There are few easier ways to convince workers that the unemployed should go hungry than when they’re cutting back on their own food shop. It is telling that the CSJ study includes a section directly comparing “economically inactive claimants” with workers: someone on minimum wage would have to work six days a week to match “the security, cash and ease” a disabled person gets from a package of state benefits, it proclaims. About 1.4 million foreign nationals receive working-age benefits, it ominously adds. Divide and conquer never gets old. A Labour government is no guarantee these divisions – worker v claimants, old v young, migrant v citizen – won’t be espoused from the cabinet table. No recommendations by Timms or Milburn have been confirmed yet, but Whitehall sources say there are potential plans to scrap a key part of universal credit for under-25s and replace it with a multi-billion pound package to get people back into work. Sure, it’s depressing if ministers are tempted to bow to the prevailing political winds by pulling cash from young people, but it’s not exactly surprising.

events.title: Repairing Brexit economic damage should be Burnham’s top priority, business chief says
events.summary: Shevaun Haviland argues PM is right to revisit Labour’s EU red lines as current trading relationship is bad for business Repairing the economic damage of Brexit should be the top priority for Andy Burnham as he reconsiders Labour’s red lines on EU membership, the head of one of Britain’s leading business groups has said. Shevaun Haviland, the director general of the British Chambers of Commerce (BCC), said she welcomed the prime minister reopening the Brexit battle lines despite the uncertainty it could create, arguing that the UK’s current trading relationship with the EU was bad for business. “We do think it’s right, because of what we know from the evidence of how businesses feel it’s not working,” she said. Highlighting the continuing economic hit from Brexit , Haviland said more than half of bosses surveyed by the business lobby group believed the deal negotiated by Boris Johnson’s government and enacted in 2021 was not helping them. “We expected it to be very difficult at the beginning, when [companies] were getting used to the new rules, and then it would sort of get easier as it went to along. But actually, that has not happened,” she said. Economists estimate the cost to the UK economy has been up to £240bn so far , with national income per head between 6% and 8% lower than it would have been had the UK not left the EU. The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates a long-term hit of about 4% of gross domestic product. At Labour’s conference in Liverpool last month, Burnham said Brexit had done “more harm than good” as he pledged to reassess Britain’s relationship with the EU. He opened the door to options including fully rejoining the bloc, and this week he said failing to pursue a better deal with the EU would be a “major dereliction of duty” . In an interview with the Guardian in Norwich alongside the head of the Norfolk Chambers of Commerce (NCC) chief executive, Nova Fairbanks, Haviland said the government had to take into account business frustrations with Brexit . She said the BCC would also consult its 50,000 members, who collectively employ more than 6 million people across the UK, on a range of options for Britain’s relationship, including rejoining the EU. “We are 10 years since the referendum,” Haviland said. “We would say the language of Brexit needs to move on. That’s gone. What businesses understand is what we had before and what we’ve got now. “We’re apolitical, it’s not a political question. It is an economic question. So we are going to set out the options, from the where we are to the most extreme. And in consultation with our chambers, and our partners, we will see where people are.” Fairbanks said it was clear that some Brexit-backing bosses recognised the economic damage. “It would be very interesting to see how many businesses that were very much pro-Brexit are still pro-Brexit, because I’ve certainly not heard any change of heart from those that were against Brexit. I think they are still very much: ‘We need to be closer to Europe.’” Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Speaking on the sidelines of an NCC trade fair at the Norfolk Showground, the business leaders said companies were coming under growing pressure from rising energy prices and other effects of the war in the Middle East. Haviland called on the chancellor, John Healey, to take bold action at this month’s budget to support firms despite concerns at the heart of government about the pressure on the public finances amid jitters in the bond market . “This rumour about a sort of ‘steady as she goes’ budget, and ‘let’s not upset the apple cart’. Business don’t really want just a ‘steady as she goes’. They want to see some action that will relieve some of those costs that will drive that fly wheel [of the British economy],” she said. “You can’t just trot along in a crouch position effectively. And surely the markets will be happy to see some spending cuts by the government, and some investment in private-sector growth?” Haviland called for action on energy bills, business rates and taxes on employment to help companies recruit more young people. “In your energy bill, about 40% of your energy is actually energy. The other 60% is about tax. So the government can get some of that out,” she said. “The big test for the chancellor is to put his money where his mouth is for business at the budget. Just showing that he genuinely believes that the wealth creators are the job creators – which is business.”

events.title: Commercial kitchen staff exposed to high levels of air pollution, study finds
events.summary: US research says nitrogen dioxide in restaurants that cook with gas can exceed WHO limits, which also affects diners E ach time we enjoy a meal out or order a takeaway, someone cooks for us in a commercial kitchen. In the UK, 3.6 million people work in catering and hospitality. In the US it is estimated at close to 16 million . A first-of-its-kind study in the US has found catering staff can experience high air pollution at work – and that this can affect diners too. Dr Drew Michanowicz, senior author of the study at non-profit research institute PSE Healthy Energy , said: “I was motivated by what we have learned over the years about what just 30 minutes of gas cooking can do to air quality in homes with the realisation that millions of people cook for a living for hours on end.” The researchers measured air pollution in 27 kitchens including fine-dining and casual full-service restaurants, those serving pizza and Chinese cuisine, catering facilities and kitchens in senior-living communities, universities and schools. Although the kitchens met US legal limits for air pollution in workplaces, nitrogen dioxide in 17 kitchens was greater than the World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines for indoor air . All of these kitchens cooked with fossil-gas or propane. Nitrogen dioxide is a pollutant in diesel exhaust, which has led to many UK and European cities introducing clean air and low-emission zones . Three all-electric kitchens, a full-service restaurant, a school cafeteria, and a conference centre kitchen were part of the study. These had the lowest air pollution, indicating benefits from decarbonisation in catering and ending fossil-gas combustion. The electric kitchens also had the lowest temperatures, an obvious benefit for staff welfare. This summer’s European heatwave forced some restaurants in the UK to cut hours or close due sweltering conditions. Christopher Galarza , a chef who worked with the researchers, said: “I’ve worked in kitchens where the heat was so intense that you would finish a shift drenched in sweat, dehydrated and physically spent.” The study also found air pollution did not stay in the kitchen. Median concentrations in dining areas were greater than WHO guidelines for outdoor air pollution . Dr Yannai Kashtan, first author of the study from PSE Heathy Energy, said: “It is difficult to contextualise the relative risk to diners, but as a diner in a restaurant with gas-fired appliances you may be exposed to elevated levels of nitrogen dioxide.” One result surprised the research team. Kashtan said: “In two-thirds of the gas kitchens, we measured higher levels of pollution overnight and in the early morning, when all the appliances were off. The culprit? Pilot lights that burn 24/7, whether or not ventilation is on.” In the UK many commercial kitchens have automatic systems that cut off gas when ventilation is not operating. Michanowicz said commercial-grade cooking appliances were not included in US energy efficiency regulations that led to pilot lights being phased out in the residential sector. “In most full-service kitchens with multiple appliances like ranges, griddles, fryers, ovens, steamers, and broilers, upwards of 20-30 small flames may be constantly burning,” said Michanowicz. In the study, air pollution from pilot lights spread into dining areas, increasing exposure for cleaners and other workers and the health risk for other people in multi-use buildings.

events.title: Ship attack reports near Hormuz reach record high as oil exports slow
events.summary: The number of ships that have reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz has hit a record high, BBC Verify analysis of data from a UK maritime agency shows. Twelve vessels were attacked between 5 and 11 October - the largest number of weekly strikes reported to the UK's Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency since the US-Israeli war with Iran began. The previous week saw 10 ships reporting attacks. Six of the vessels were struck last Sunday, according to the UKMTO - a one-day high. So far this week, there have been four reported attacks. As the number of strikes has risen, the recovery in oil shipments through the strait seen last month has slowed, industry data suggests. BBC Verify collated incident reports published by the UKMTO on its website and created a timeline based on the first date cited in each report. This is approximate because some incidents use the date of the attack and some the date on which it was reported. Experts say Tehran has been attacking ships in an effort to assert greater control over the waterway as the US military has increased the number of tankers it is shepherding through the south of the strait to evade Iranian strikes. Iran is also carrying out more attacks on vessels further away from the Strait of Hormuz, according to experts. The US military's Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, posted on social media that despite the attacks "commercial traffic continues to flow through the Strait of Hormuz with co-ordinated protection from US forces and regional partners". Two crew missing after one of Sunday's attacks The aftermath of one of Sunday's six reported attacks was captured in verified footage showing the Nicaragua-flagged tanker Petro Dolphin on fire, as filmed by the crew on a smaller boat nearby. The vessel was struck by a drone close to the Sohar Anchorage, Oman, more than 250km (150 miles) from the strait, according to the maritime intelligence firm Vanguard. Eleven Indian seafarers were rescued but two are still missing, the Forward Seamen's Union of India said. Attacks have continued this week with the container ship GFS Pride sinking after a strike by an unknown projectile in the strait on Tuesday. Twenty-one crew were safely evacuated. Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) published footage of what appeared to be the same ship sinking. It said the vessel was carrying "2,500 containers of contraband" and had taken an "unauthorised route". Middle East oil exports have slowed as the number of ship strikes has risen. About 12.6 million barrels per day went through the strait on 13 October, below the 15 million reported at the end of September, data from trade intelligence firm Kpler shows. This compares with a pre-war baseline of some 17 million barrels per day. The recent increase in attacks comes as US Navy data indicates the number of vessels given assistance to navigate the Strait of Hormuz during the first 10 days of October was up 85% compared with the same period in August. Most of the oil being shipped from Gulf Arab states recently has been carried using a "shuttle" system where a fleet of tankers load up and sail through the strait before transferring their cargo to larger tankers in the Gulf of Oman. These shuttle ships use a route close to Oman's coastline. Iran says this is "unauthorised" and insist vessels take an alternative route closer to its own shore. So-called assisted transits were a key factor in helping drive oil flows from the Middle East back towards pre-war levels in September. This does not include Iranian exports which have completely stalled as a result of the US blockade of Iranian ports and ships. Martin Kelly, CEO of Orbital Risk Intelligence, said Iran has "evolved its strategy" in response to this loosening of its control over the strait and has been carrying out "near daily or multiple attacks every single day". "The aim here is to stop the ships going through and to deter others," he added. The IRGC's navy has said strikes would not be "limited to the Strait of Hormuz" and later announced a "new deployment formation" across the region, according to state media. Martin Kelly told BBC Verify that Iran is widening its attacks and targeting ships near the coast of Gulf Arab states and in the Gulf of Oman. A tanker was struck by multiple projectiles north of Qatar on Thursday 8 October, more than 500km (310 miles) from the strait, resulting in multiple reported casualties, according to Vanguard. Another tanker was attacked close to the UAE town of Al-Jazirah al-Hamra on Friday 9 October, Vanguard said. Verified footage shows crew members running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rises over the ship. events.title: The IPO drought is driving private equity-owned companies to the debt market to pay investors
events.summary: Private equity firms are using more dividend recaps as IPOs and company sales remain subdued. Moody’s says EMEA PE-backed companies have about 41 billion euros ($46 billion) of additional debt capacity. More debt can return cash to investors but may reduce companies’ financial flexibility and complicate future exits. Private equity funds are increasingly pushing their portfolio companies to take on more debt to return cash to their investors, data suggests. It comes as the typical ways of monetizing private equity investments — selling company stakes via IPOs, or offloading them to other PE funds or buyers — have dried up in recent years. While investors get paid, the practice of private equity sponsors adding more debt to companies — known as dividend recapitalizations — risks weakening their ability to invest or weather future downturns in trading. "Dividend recap" activity has surged since 2022, and Moody's Ratings expects it to remain high in Europe, the Middle East and Africa as private equity firms look for ways to return money to investors while company sales and IPOs remain subdued. The ratings agency estimates that private equity-owned companies in the EMEA region could take on a further 41 billion euros ($46 billion) in debt before reaching leverage levels that typically prompt a downgrade. New Moody's analysis indicates the practice remains limited to the strongest-performing companies with the greatest capacity to take on new debt, indicating this "significant releveraging capacity" could support a further ramp-up in dividend recaps. Still, it does not address the exit backlog weighing over private equity, where funds are now having to hold onto companies for much longer than the typical period of around five to six years. "The fundamental problem is that exits are few and far between – the European IPO markets have been muted, and the capital that would generally fund strategic purchases by large corporates has become a lot more expensive after the last rate hike cycle," said Moody's analyst Mayank Mallik. "Generally, we are more focused on the impact that the general PE ecosystem has on corporate credit quality — and this is one of the key transmission mechanisms currently." Moody's said PE sponsors have remained "disciplined" in choosing dividend recap candidates, with services, consumer products and manufacturing the most active sectors. Mallik noted most dividend recaps have involved companies that outperformed their original business plans, with the new debt generally returning leverage to its initial level without "materially" affecting exit opportunities. "It is true, however, that companies preparing for IPOs like to show a track record of solid deleveraging for a couple of years before approaching the market," he told CNBC via email. "There is indeed a risk that, if an IPO window unexpectedly opens, issuers that have recently done a div recap may not be able to jump on the opportunity. Any company doing a div-recap is likely taking a forward-looking view that the IPO market will be closed in the short run." Distributions to investors have fallen sharply in recent years. Moody's, citing PitchBook data, said private equity distributions dropped from more than 30% of starting net asset value in 2022 to about 12% today. "The risk is that if PE exit backlog is prolonged, sponsors may start looking at relatively weaker credits to monetize, which may lead to credit deterioration across the portfolio," Mallik added. He said that those risks are greater than a decade ago, partly because documentation has become "quite permissive" for issuers looking to raise additional debt. Tighter credit markets support recaps — for now Portfolio companies' recaps are typically funded through the broadly syndicated loan market, where several investment banks will club together to lend money to a borrower, thereby spreading the risk. Alternatively, funding is raised by high-yield corporate bond issuance or private credit borrowing. Sunaina Sinha Haldea, global head of private capital advisory at Raymond James, said there is still "meaningful capacity" to fund recaps, highlighting how tight spreads and scarce new loan supply are helping support appetite. "Weaker earnings, wider spreads or investor withdrawals could tighten availability, while a recovery in acquisition financing would give lenders more alternatives to funding shareholder payouts," she said. Haldea noted that dividend recaps provide liquidity, relieving the pressure to sell without ultimately resolving the valuation gap. "Investors get some cash back, but the asset remains in the fund and still needs an eventual buyer," Haldea told CNBC via email. "A dividend recap need not derail an exit if earnings growth has created genuine borrowing capacity, but borrowing against hoped-for growth is a different proposition.

events.title: ASEAN companies keen on AI for business benefits, despite its energy costs
events.summary: Firms should assess not just the token prices before building an AI application, but also its carbon footprint, says an expert. SINGAPORE – Almost four in five South-east Asian businesses expect the benefits from artificial intelligence to outweigh its energy burden – even as they brace themselves for rising costs and infrastructure pressure. Out of 514 regional business leaders polled by The Business Times and market research firm Kantar, 78% see AI’s benefits outweighing its energy requirements. Released on Oct 12, The Business Times Insights: Powering ASEAN’s Future 2026 – the second regional survey by BT and Kantar – showed Singapore, Vietnam and Thailand as having the highest levels of optimism. This comes as AI adoption is accelerating across South-east Asia – 62% of respondents have increased their investments in AI or data-driven technologies over the past 12 months. Growth is particularly pronounced in Indonesia, where 85% of businesses reported moderate-to-significant increases in AI investment over the last year. The regional optimism around AI is “no surprise” to Sunil Veetil, whose Singapore advisory Perdura helps companies with green finance and the energy transition. He noted that AI returns materialise quickly when applied to the right use cases. For instance, it can enable multilingual customer service, providing distinct advantages in a region as diverse as ASEAN. In addition, said Manik Bhandari, ASEAN data and AI leader at EY, energy costs are currently “a very small fraction” of the overall AI token pricing, and thus “quite minimal” when building AI applications in an enterprise setting. Bracing for costs, infrastructure pressure That said, there is awareness of energy pressures – 41% of ASEAN businesses expect a moderate increase in energy demand as AI adoption scales, while another 40% are bracing themselves for a significant increase. Businesses expect energy demand to manifest in operational challenges: Rising electricity or operating costs, as cited by 46% of respondents; Pressure to upgrade existing infrastructure (39%); and Increased competition for energy resources (37%). While businesses may not currently be bearing the energy costs of AI, Veetil noted that this “changes when AI becomes captive or domestic, when companies run their own models or countries build sovereign (models) on local power”. “Then, the energy bill lands on the business.” Some markets are less optimistic about AI. In the Philippines, just 64% of respondents see AI’s benefits outweighing energy requirements, below the regional average. One explanation could be that “the trade-off looks different in markets where electricity costs, grid reliability and energy security are already significant business concerns”, said Zayana Zaikariah from the Institute of Strategic and International Studies in Malaysia. Climate exposure may be another reason. “In countries facing frequent typhoons, flooding and other disruptions, businesses may place a higher premium on the resilience of electricity and digital infrastructure before adding new sources of demand,” she said. It is thus critical for businesses to use AI judiciously. Lawrence Loh from the National University of Singapore said FOMO – the “fear of missing out” – is leading many businesses to step up AI adoption, and that their staff and management “may be experiencing severe AI fatigue now”. “The wrong metric for business is how much AI is being used,” said Loh, who is director of the university’s Centre for Governance and Sustainability. “The right one should be how much measurable economic and other benefits are being derived.” EY’s Bhandari said that before building an AI application, companies should assess not only the token prices, but also the application’s carbon footprint. Businesses can use smaller, task-specific models that reduce memory usage and can be run on standard hardware or edge devices, with a vastly reduced carbon footprint. “Not only is it cheaper for me as an enterprise, it’s also better for the environment,” he said. Zayana echoed that businesses should “match the level of compute to the value of the task”. A compute-intensive AI system “should not be the default if a smaller, task-specific model can achieve the same business outcome”, she said. AI-driven hunger for energy has implications not just for businesses, but also for countries’ energy resilience and decarbonisation goals. If not managed well, greater energy demand from AI could translate to more dependence on fossil fuels, said Dinita Setyawati, external affairs and strategic impact lead for Asia at energy think-tank Ember. Conversely, AI facilities “can actually become part of the solution if they help mobilise investment in renewable energy, storage and the grid infrastructure needed to support that demand”, she noted.

events.title: Proposed Dalby data centre to harvest rainwater from roof
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Proposed Dalby data centre to 'air-cool' operations and harvest rainwater from roof The concept model of a large-scale data centre project that has been proposed for the Western Downs. ( Supplied: Urbis ) The proposed Western Downs Digital Park says it will air-cool operations and not draw from bores or town water. Its developer says artificial intelligence customers would be responsible for paying for the power supply. The development application remains in its early stages and public consultation is ongoing. The international developer that has proposed Australia's largest data centre says it would be able to operate during even the worst droughts. The proposed $32 billion Western Downs Digital Park in regional Queensland would consist of four data centres, the first of which has been leased by Anthropic for use as early as 2027. Zerra DC is holding community consultation session in Dalby on the Western Downs. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) Planning documents by Singapore-based developer Zerra DC said each of the four buildings planned for the Western Downs Digital Park would require 21,000 litres of water a day, equivalent to the water usage of a small shopping centre. The company's chief data centre officer Matt Ward said modelling showed that even in 2019, when Dalby received less than 200 millimetres of rain, it would catch enough rainwater to operate. Matt Ward says the developer is committed to being a "good neighbour". ( Supplied: Zerra DC ) Mr Ward said the buildings housing the data centres were "large sheds" with "35,000-odd square metres of roof space" and the facility would be entirely air-cooled and would not draw from bores or town water. Mr Ward said supplying new power to the grid would be the responsibility of its artificial intelligence customers such as Anthropic, which the company has signed an agreement with. He said Zerra DC would act like the "landlord of any commercial building", where the tenant, Anthropic, would be responsible for paying for power supply. The data centre is proposed on the site of a feedlot outside of Dalby. ( ABC News: Nathan Morris ) It comes as the federal government works to establish a framework that would require data centres to bring as much power into the electricity grid as they take. Australia's largest proposed data centre could draw a quarter of Queensland's energy use The proposed $30 billion data centre in Queensland has a peak capacity comparable to the average power requirements of 1.5 million households. But who pays for that power production was a dilemma, according to Climate Energy Finance director Tim Buckley. He said both sides needed to be "collectively held to account" to commit to new renewable energy generation. "If they aren't held to account in substance over the life of the project, we will inevitably see higher power prices for everyone across Queensland as a result," Mr Buckley said. Some in the Western Downs have questioned how the region would benefit from the multi-billion-dollar investment. Zerra DC began community consultation sessions during the day last week, but recently announced the "drop-in" sessions would run in the afternoons from midday to 8pm. Robyn Sheehan attended an information session in Dalby about the proposed data centre. ( ABC Southern Qld: Grace Nakamura ) Dalby resident Robyn Sheehan said she took part in a session because she felt tired of big industries making "empty promises" in the area. Zerra DC has committed to 1,500 jobs per year during construction and 1,400 ongoing operational jobs at full capacity, which would transform the local economy. "To keep this thing running, we'll need a team of skilled people across mechanical, electrical, security, engineering at a 24-7 basis," Mr Ward said.

RBA workers are demanding an 11 per cent pay increase over three years, but the RBA is offering 9.5 per cent. The latest data show Australia's unemployment rate is 4.7 per cent, but economists say the RBA may not have finished lifting rates. The Reserve Bank's senior officials are among the highest paid people in Australia. RBA governor Michele Bullock received total remuneration of $1.22 million in 2025-26, with a base salary of $1.01 million. Deputy governor Andrew Hauser received total remuneration of $955,033, with a base salary of $903,217. Half of young adults living with parents Half of all young Australians are still living with their parents, up from 39 per cent in 2001, a survey reveals. The RBA's four assistant governors received total remuneration between $743,000 and $868,000 each, and its chief operating officer received total remuneration of $905,543. The figures can be found in the RBA's 2026 annual report , which was released on Thursday afternoon. The median annual earnings for all employees in Australia is $74,672 . In March this year, Ms Bullock received unwanted media attention when she and her husband bought a $2 million home in Yamba, in northern NSW, on the same day that the RBA lifted interest rates on February 3. It was her third investment property. Her property purchase was recorded in her declaration of material personal interests on the RBA's website. Michele Bullock says she sympathises with the plight of Australian workers. ( ABC News: John Gunn ) The RBA governor's pay is slightly above most federal departmental or agency heads, which are mostly clustered around $900,000-$1,000,000. However, the chief executives of some publicly owned corporations are paid far more. Ellie Sweeney, the NBN Co chief executive, received $3.4 million in total remuneration in 2025-26, up from $1.9 million a year earlier, making her Australia's highest-paid public servant . Paul Graham, the chief executive of Australia Post, received $3.3 million in 2024-25. Dennis Barns, the chief executive of Snowy Hydro Limited, received $2.1 million in 2024-25. RBA workers don't want a real wage cut The RBA is currently arguing with junior RBA staff about pay and conditions. Lower-ranked RBA staff have been asking for a pay increase of 11 per cent over three years and an inflation-protection mechanism that triggers additional pay rises if inflation outpaces wages, to avoid real wage cuts in coming years. Workers' pay not keeping pace with productivity growth Workers' pay not keeping pace with productivity growth, research suggests But last month, hours after the RBA lifted rates for the fourth time this year, Ms Bullock emailed RBA staff and asked them to vote for a pay offer of 9.5 per cent over three years. A majority of RBA staff had rejected a similar proposal in July. The Finance Sector Union says enterprise agreement negotiations have been dragging on since late last year and the RBA has refused to move on its original pay offer. The latest round of voting for the RBA's proposed enterprise agreement will close on Monday at 5pm . After lifting interest rates last month, Ms Bullock said she sympathised with the plight of Australian workers. But she said the only way workers could keep receiving sustainable increases in real wages was from productivity growth, and Australia's economy was struggling to deliver it. "People are feeling, quite rightly, very annoyed and very upset about the fact that the costs of everything are rising, that their wages are not keeping pace with that, they’re seeing real wage cuts," she said . "If we don't get productivity growth, there's not going to be real wage rises coming down the pipeline." According to the RBA's annual report, the bank has 2,201 employees, equating to 2,082 full-time equivalent employees. It has 76 senior executives, and another 222 highly paid staff. The RBA's workforce has increased by 8 per cent over the past 12 months. The RBA says that reflects the additional resources it needs to implement its transformation and change agendas. The additional staff are concentrated in technology and corporate support functions. RBA staff numbers increased by 8 per cent in the past year. ( Source: RBA annual report 2026 ) Higher unemployment will help to control inflation Australia's unemployment rate is 4.7 per cent, in seasonally adjusted terms.

events.title: Malaysia’s growth tops forecasts as AI boom drives export surge
events.summary: The government expects Malaysia’s economy to grow at 4.2% to 5.2% in 2027, supported by sustained domestic demand investment activity. Malaysia’s GDP rose 5.3% in the third quarter, beating the 5.1% forecast, but growth slowed from 6% as mining fell and most sectors still stayed positive. AI demand lifted exports, especially electronics, while strong domestic spending and household support kept the trade-dependent economy resilient. The government expects about 5% growth in 2026 and 4.2% to 5.2% in 2027, with full third-quarter GDP details due on Nov 18. KUALA LUMPUR – Malaysia’s economic growth slowed but still exceeded expectations as the artificial intelligence boom continued to bolster exports and domestic demand remained resilient. Gross domestic product (GDP) rose 5.3% in the three months through September from a year earlier, according to advance estimates from the Department of Statistics Malaysia on Oct 16, beating the 5.1% median prediction in a Bloomberg survey. Third-quarter growth, however, slowed from the 6% expansion in the previous three-month period. Third-quarter growth was underpinned by positive performance across most economic sectors, the department said in a statement. Only the mining and quarrying sector contracted, it added. The better-than-expected reading underscores the resilience of Malaysia’s economy, even as growth moderates from a strong first half. Robust domestic consumption and demand for electronics used in AI have helped cushion the trade-dependent economy from disruptions caused by the US war against Iran . “The out-turn is broadly in line with our forecast and suggests the growth momentum remains robust, albeit moderating from strong growth in the first half of 2026,” said Lavanya Venkateswaran, economist at OCBC Bank. “This very much leaves the door open for Bank Negara Malaysia to normalise its policy rate by 25 basis points. Our baseline for the adjustment is in January but it is a close call for the November meeting.” The ringgit was steady at 4.08 to the US dollar after the GDP print, while local stocks held losses. The services sector rose 5.4%, bolstered by wholesale and retail trade, information and communication as well as finance, the statistics department said. Manufacturing strengthened by 7.5%, backed in part by export-oriented industries, particularly electrical and electronic products. Bank Negara Malaysia governor Abdul Rasheed Ghaffour said in an interview this week that the economy is likely to grow about 5% in 2026, with the nation’s diverse sources of growth helping to cushion it against any slowdown in the AI boom. Malaysia’s economy grew 5.5% during the first three quarters of 2026, the department said, above the government’s revised growth forecast of 4.8% to 5.3% for the year. The government in October raised the forecast from 4% to 5%. Household spending remains firm as fuel subsidies helped shield consumers from elevated energy costs. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim earlier in October also announced more cash aid and a higher minimum wage for 2027 to ease cost-of-living pressures. The Malaysian government expects the economy to grow at 4.2% to 5.2% in 2027, supported by sustained domestic demand investment activity. Preliminary GDP data, which will provide a detailed analysis of the third quarter, will be released on Nov 18. BLOOMBERG

events.title: Number of cloned number plates on UK roads at record high, data shows
events.summary: More than 11,400 drivers last year were fined for offences they did not recognise as RAC says system needs reform The number of reported “cloned” vehicles involved in offences on UK roads has reached a record high, official data shows. More than 11,400 drivers contacted the DVLA last year after being issued with fines for offences they said they did not recognise or accept responsibility for – most of which are believed to be down to cloning, where a number plate is copied fraudulently on similar vehicles to avoid enforcement cameras. The number of complaints about misattribution was 9% higher than in 2024 and almost double the figure recorded in 2018, according to the RAC motoring organisation, which analysed data obtained under freedom of information requests. The rising figures underscore concerns about the number of illegal number plates in use, allowing criminals to evade detection and dangerous drivers to avoid being caught. Although drivers should provide number plate suppliers with the V5C vehicle logbook and proof of identity, an investigation last year uncovered more than 130 official suppliers in the UK willing to sell cloned versions, which allow drivers to dodge police and congestion charges. Cloning vehicles has left many innocent car owners having to struggle to prove they were not responsible when enforcement camera images apparently caught their vehicle committing offences . A parallel concern is the use of “ghost” plates which are designed to be unreadable by the UK’s 18,000 automatic number plate recognition (ANPR) cameras, which enforce safety measures such as speed limits or lane closures on smart motorways. The RAC said the UK needed to overhaul an outdated and poorly regulated number plate system. Its head of policy, Simon Williams, said: “If number plate suppliers were carrying out all the checks they’re supposed to, it would be much harder for dodgy drivers to buy cloned plates in the first place. It’s only when a fine arrives at a vehicle keeper’s home address that they realise someone else is driving around using their vehicle’s number plate illegally.” He said that more also needed to be done to catch drivers with ghost plates, “whether that’s more police officers being equipped with handheld devices that can detect if plates are unreadable, updating ANPR cameras and introducing higher security standards for number plates and for those who produce them”. The government last month said there would be a new nationwide crackdown on illegal number plates, with funding from the Department for Transport for a new roads policing team. A new National Roads Policing Coordination Centre would share intelligence as well as trialling new technology such as specialised goggles to detect number plates that have been designed to be unreadable by cameras. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Drivers using an incorrectly displayed number plate can be fined up to £1,000. A Department for Transport spokesperson said: “We’re cracking down on illegal number plates with significant investment in a new roads policing team and innovative tech to stamp out the scourge of cloned numberplates. “Illegal number plates help facilitate crime, and we are supporting the police to work with the DVLA to make it easier to report these crimes and support victims through a new digital tool.”

events.title: ‘People’s dignity, and democracy, is at stake’: meet the economist ditching ideology for reality
events.summary: Exclusive: Isabella Weber prescribes a common-sense solution to poverty, inequality and fascism – making life’s essentials affordable for all T he trouble with economists, Isabella Weber believes, is they do not behave like dentists. They obsess over ideological purity and are inflexible when searching for solutions, regardless of society’s symptoms. Dentists have no such pretensions – patients have little patience for dogma when in insufferable pain. John Maynard Keynes, Weber clarifies in the canteen of the Wissenschaftskolleg zu Berlin (Berlin’s Institute for Advanced Study), was the first to draw this dental comparison – and she is running with it. As she sees it, the symptoms could not be more severe. “The status quo for the majority is entirely unbearable,” while extreme inequality and corporate concentration has reached levels “simply incompatible with democracy” worldwide. This is exacerbated by a climate crisis that “generates massive windfall profits” for big business as the “ecological foundations of our lives disintegrate”. All the while the far right is making hay. This analysis echoes much mainstream liberal and left-leaning thinking. But Weber is concerned that her peers in the economic establishment act as if they are oblivious. “What’s common sense to most people is not to economists,” she says, and as such our economic system has “promised but not delivered”. She reels off disturbing statistics that highlight the growing disparities between haves and have nots. “As economists, we should do better. People’s dignity, and democracy, is at stake.” In progressive circles, Weber, 38, is quickly becoming one of the most sought-after economists of her generation. An associate professor at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and an associate at Harvard’s Fairbank Center, she advises policymakers in the US, Europe and Latin America. She popularised the term “ greedflation ” to describe profiteering during recent cost of living crises. Her new book, Anti-Fascist Economics , is the culmination of years of research into inequality and inflation, and a lifelong commitment to fighting fascism. As she writes: “If we understand economics as the study of the material foundations of society, then economics is key to averting the catastrophes in front of us.” Weber is calling on fellow economists to “abandon ideology” and develop a “big tent economic policy” that can counter an ascendant far right . Their gains, she argues, are not the result of a particularly compelling offer, but a direct consequence of traditional political parties refusing to acknowledge the endemic hardship facing their constituents, and the absence of a coherent economic vision from progressives, liberals and the centre right. “Currently, only the extreme right is willing to say yes, something is broken, and a different present and future is possible,” Weber says. “We can’t leave an alternative to this dystopia to them.” In Anti-Fascist Economics , she pitches a solution: make life’s necessities affordable. That is housing, transport, food, water, energy, healthcare: the stuff humanity depends on. “Fascism is rising from frustration, born out of a crisis of livelihoods,” says Weber. “So, we need to reclaim these essentials now.” Progressive politicians are already heeding her instructions. At a meeting of city mayors last month, the New York mayor, Zohran Mamdani, outlined how Weber’s work, which he had followed for years, had informed his affordability agenda in the city: free buses, universal childcare, rent caps, public groceries. Weber has consulted with other US politicians – Elizabeth Warren, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Bernie Sanders – and UK ministers including Ed Miliband. The speech of the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, to Labour conference last month was Weberesque in its messaging. “Homes. Water. Energy. Transport. Care. Broken up and sold off,” he declared from the lectern . “Economic control diminished by selling off essentials.” While it is a simple slogan, making the essentials affordable is a complex policy challenge. Each sector has unique properties, and functions differently from place to place. Weber argues that any and all levers should be pulled in pursuit of putting this floor under livelihoods, from novel approaches to centuries-old thinking. “The goal isn’t more state intervention,” she clarifies, “it’s just a tool, as are profits and markets to ensure affordability. In economics, we tend to have these overarching models and an inclination for silver bullets. I’m arguing not for universal solutions but nitty gritty detail.” Take food, for example. At every stage of the value chain from source to table, she is urging governments to identify and implement interventions to keep prices down. At one end, four multinationals control between 70% and 90% of global grain trading (with profits that “thrive on volatility”). This does not optimise affordability. Her proposal?

events.title: Palm oil stocks slide after Singapore begins looking into which firms responsible for haze
events.summary: Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said that where warranted, Singapore will take action under its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act. Singapore is investigating which firms may be behind haze-causing fires, and may act under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, PM Lawrence Wong said. Palm oil shares fell after a report named First Resources and Bumitama Agri in areas with haze source points; First Resources blamed outside fires and a severe El Nino drought. Singapore’s air quality worsened sharply, with the central PSI at 227 and “very unhealthy”; Indonesia blamed peatland damage and said it will restore its peat ecosystem. SINGAPORE – Shares of palm oil producers fell on Oct 16, a day after Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said that Singapore is looking into which companies may be responsible for haze-causing fires. Where warranted, Singapore will take action under its Transboundary Haze Pollution Act, and also explore joint action with other countries, said PM Wong in a Facebook post on Oct 15 . Bumitama Agri retreated 7.5% to an intraday low of $1.73, then rebounded somewhat to close 4.8% lower at $1.78. Golden Agri-Resources shares dropped one cent to 28 cents. A report by The Straits Times on Oct 15 cited a recent Greenpeace investigation which named First Resources and Bumitama Agri among entities with concession areas registering haze source points. First Resources on Oct 15 defended itself, stating that fires detected within its Indonesian palm oil concessions were largely caused by external blazes spreading across its boundaries. The company attributed the elevated fire risk in West Kalimantan to a “severe” El Nino-induced drought. Indonesia on Oct 15 blamed peatland degradation by past food estates for its worst wildfire season in 11 years, and said it will work to restore its peat ecosystem. Air quality deteriorated across all areas of Singapore overnight. The 24-hour PSI reading for the central region hit the “very unhealthy” level at midnight on Oct 16 and stood at 227 at 9am – a new high for 2026. Readings for the rest of the country were at the “unhealthy” level. On whether Singapore will take action against errant companies under the Act, Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu said on Oct 14 that the country was “keeping its options open”. That followed a National Environment Agency spokesperson stating that the agency “has been closely monitoring the haze situation, gathering information on fire hot spots, their sources and impact on Singapore’s air quality”. events.title: Nationals say Liberals oppose EU trade deal, Liberals beg to differ
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Liberals insist EU free trade position not settled, despite Canavan's assertion Some Liberals are frustrated by Matt Canavan's suggestion that both Liberals and Nationals oppose the free trade deal with the EU. ( ABC News: Callum Flinn ) Liberals insist they have not agreed to oppose the proposed Australia-EU trade deal, despite Nationals leader Matt Canavan claiming both parties are against it. Some Liberals believe Trade Minister Don Farrell could renegotiate aspects of the deal, an idea strongly rebuffed by those on both sides of the negotiations. A joint parliamentary committee is expected to scrutinise the deal early next year. Nationals leader Matt Canavan's claim that both Nationals and Liberals are against a slated European Union trade deal has angered some Liberals who privately insist the issue has not been settled. In an opinion piece published in The Australian today, Senator Canavan said the deal landed by Trade Minister Don Farrell would "weaken Australia's sovereignty on climate change policy" and was bad for the steel industry and some farmers. He said the deal, which parliament must approve, was opposed by both Coalition parties. That assertion was backed by his colleague, Bridget McKenzie. "Don Farrell can try all he likes to find a Coalition senator willing to vote for it. He won't because we are absolutely united," she told ABC Radio National today. But two Liberal senators subsequently told the ABC the proposed deal was better than the status quo and should be adopted. One cited the diplomatic importance of the deal at a time when the US was waging trade wars. "As long as it's not a really bad free trade agreement, and I don't think it is, we should support it," the senator said. "It goes to what the Liberal Party stands for. "There is a lot of internal disquiet about this." 'Opposed … subject to proper process' Multiple senior Liberals told the ABC the matter had not been considered by shadow cabinet or discussed in the Coalition party room, and that could only happen after scrutiny by the parliament's joint standing committee on trade. Farmers rubbish 'worst ever' EU free trade agreement The National Farmers' Federation says the deal will leave farmers without meaningful access to the EU market. "You can't short-circuit that by [writing] an op-ed," one said, framing Senator Canavan's intervention as a clear attempt to strongarm Liberals, reigniting tensions between the parties that plagued the leadership of Angus Taylor's predecessor, Sussan Ley. The joint standing committee process is still some time away. While the deal's text was agreed between leaders this year, it will not be signed until Australia and each EU member country complete the requisite legal checks, most likely early next year. Some Liberals believe this leaves time to renegotiate aspects of the deal. Two Liberals seeking to downplay any disagreement said the agreed position was "opposed to the deal as it stands, subject to the proper parliamentary and Coalition process". Senator Canavan used more cautious language in a press conference today, saying the opposition was "opposed to the deal in its current form". Farrell says veto would be 'vandalism' The government has rubbished the idea that renegotiation would be possible. "There is no room … the deal is done," Senator Farrell said today. The minister has projected confidence that the Senate, where the government does not have the numbers in its own right, will not stand in the way of the deal, telling the ABC on Wednesday he believed "enough senators … understand how important this is". One interpretation of that comment is that Senator Farrell believes enough Liberals might cross the floor to vote for the deal, although none of those who spoke to the ABC suggested they would. Don Farrell (right) led negotiations with the European Union and says the deal is no longer up for negotiation. One diplomat from an EU nation told the ABC it would be "very damaging" if Australia did not ratify the deal and echoed Senator Farrell's comments: "There is no appetite [in Europe] to revisit this … the deal is done." events.title: Indonesia gets a ‘wake-up call’ as MSCI prepares to remove it from global indexes
events.summary: MSCI said on Oct 16 it would put Indonesia on a path to “standalone” status. MSCI said Indonesia is no longer fit for ‘emerging market’ status and plans to move it to ‘standalone’ status, which could force major fund outflows and cut it from global indexes. The announcement shocked investors, sent Jakarta shares down 11.57% in their worst fall since 1998, and pushed the rupiah to its weakest since late July. Indonesia rejected the move, said it has improved transparency, and the regulator fined market participants over alleged manipulation in three listed firms; MSCI will consult until April 2027. JAKARTA – Indonesia’s stock market is no longer worthy of “emerging market” status, MSCI said on Oct 16 , laying out a plan to expel it from a suite of indexes tracked by funds, a shock move that sparked the steepest one-day drop in Jakarta shares since 1998. Coming a month ahead of a scheduled review, MSCI’s change of tack stunned investors and irked Jakarta officials, with the Indonesian regulator unveiling sanctions against those linked to alleged trading manipulation in shares of three firms. The benchmark stock index, already the world’s worst performers in 2026, closed down 11.57%, in its biggest single-day drop since January 1998 . The rupiah currency slid as much as 0.8% to 18,070 per US dollar, its weakest since late July, but recovered some ground . Equities in South-east Asia’s biggest economy have struggled since January, when MSCI froze Indonesia in its indexes and threatened a downgrade to “frontier” status because of opacity in ownership and trading behaviour. The market has lost more than US$350 billion (S$447.77 billion) in capitalisation since, with about US$60 billion wiped out on Oct 16 alone. MSCI cited insufficient reforms to tackle the problems and said even a downgrade to “frontier” status would not reflect the severity of the issues, but proposed instead to move further beyond that, to “standalone” status. “Significant concerns remain around market dysfunction,” MSCI said in a statement on Oct 16. “Accordingly, MSCI considers Indonesia’s continued classification as an emerging market no longer appropriate.” The lower “standalone” status it proposed would exclude Indonesian stocks from global indexes tracked by billions of dollars in passive investment, forcing funds that follow, or are ranked against, the indexes, to sell. UBS estimated a removal by MSCI could trigger about US$4 billion of passive outflows from Indonesia, with active investors potentially adding a further US$15 billion in outflow. Foreign investors have already net sold US$4.7 billion worth of Indonesian stocks in 2026. Indonesia’s senior economic minister Airlangga Hartarto said there was “a big question mark” over why MSCI did not discuss downgrading the country to “standalone” status during a meeting this week in Bangkok. He made the comment ahead of a meeting of the country’s top officials, including the finance minister, the governor of the central bank and other related officials to discuss MSCI’s announcement. The Indonesia Stock Exchange said it has taken concrete steps to enhance transparency and integrity in the country’s capital market, and chief executive Jeffrey Hendrik said in a statement he would request further clarification on the basis for the announcement. Angus Mackintosh, an ASEAN specialist at Aletheia Capital in Singapore, said the move does not reflect the health of the vast majority of listed companies or indeed the Indonesian economy, and “grouping Indonesia with Lebanon, Palestine and Argentina does not make sense”. “This is a wake-up call for Indonesia,” he said. Indonesia would be the largest economy in the group if it was downgraded to “standalone” status. MSCI scrutiny raises more questions MSCI’s announcement piles pressure on the government under President Prabowo Subianto. It is the latest of a series of setbacks in 2026, with Moody’s and Fitch cutting their sovereign rating outlooks to negative, citing reduced policymaking credibility. “The proposal highlights MSCI’s dissatisfaction with the pace of reforms and raises further questions about the investability of the market,” said Tan Altundag, investment manager for emerging equities at Pictet Asset Management. “ The investment implications could be significant,” said Altundag, who has no holdings in Indonesia. The office of Finance Minister Suahasil Nazara, who chairs the country’s financial stability board, did not reply to a request for comment. In a sign of investor anxiety over the index provider’s move, there was a rush for the exits when the market opened, triggering a 30-minute trading halt on the Jakarta exchange. “It’s the first time this has ever happened in my 20 years in the stock market,” said Liza Camelia Suryanata, head of research at stockbroker Kiwoom Sekuritas Indonesia.

events.title: 3M lays out 'attack' on Commonwealth's $2 billion PFAS lawsuit
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts 3M sheds light on defence to Commonwealth lawsuit over PFAS contamination 3M is being sued by the Australian government for PFAS contamination. ( ABC News: Simon Amery ) The Australian government is suing 3M, the manufacturer of a firefighting foam it claims contaminated 28 Defence Force bases across the nation. The US chemical giant has detailed its planned defence to the $2 billion lawsuit. 3M must file its defence by December 11. US chemical giant 3M has shed light on its planned "attack" on the federal government's $2 billion lawsuit, which alleges the company withheld evidence that its firefighting products were toxic to humans and the environment. The Commonwealth is seeking damages arising from per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) contamination at 28 Defence Force bases across Australia and the areas surrounding them. The largest-ever court claim brought by the Australian government alleges the company continued to make and sell aqueous film-forming foam (AFFF) until 2003, despite knowing the dangers of its chemical make-up since 1979. The 1,600-page statement of claim says the use of 3M's AFFF "resulted in significant contamination" of land and water, including drinking water, that posed risks to human and animal health and the environment. Citing 310 internal company documents, the federal government's lawyers allege 3M falsely made assurances the product was safe despite having studies that proved variants of PFAS were toxic to animals, could cause birth defects and harmed the environment. During a case management hearing in the Federal Court today, King's Counsel for 3M Phillip Solomon outlined what the defence's case would entail when it was filed to the court on December 11. Mr Solomon KC said a "large team is working hard" and that it would "attack" the case. He told the court that there were three courses of action it would plead to; public nuisance, a Victorian Environment Protection Authority claim, and a misleading and deceptive conduct claim. Mr Solomon said the latter would need to be "delineated" between the overseas manufacturer and the local distributor of 3M products. In its statement of claim, the Commonwealth alleges the company caused a public nuisance by interfering with the use and enjoyment of the environment and by hindering access to contaminant-free water. Justice Catherine Button was told by the defence that the issue of public nuisance was not available in the matter. "We will plead and ultimately contend that it doesn't contend a nuisance claim," Mr Solomon said. "The allegation [is] that we had the means to abate the nuisance, that we caused the nuisance, that we were responsible for the special loss associated with the nuisance … and broadly had the ability to control the nuisance." Williamtown residents in NSW have been exposed to PFAS chemicals from firefighting foam used at the RAAF base. ( Four Corners ) The 28 bases have been split into three categories, including steady state, expanding, and in exceedence of Australian Drinking Water Guidelines and Australian Recreational Guidelines. The Commonwealth has proposed that 3M plead to six "representative bases" that have features across those categories, including Wagga (NSW), Tindal (NT), Townsville (Qld), Oakey (Qld), Edinburgh (SA) and East Sale (Vic). Mr Solomon told Justice Button the defence would be seeking to focus on one of the 28 bases in question, rather than six. In reply, counsel for the Commonwealth Fiona McLeod AO SC said the Crown was "seeking representative bases" that covered issues such as cross-contamination, topography and soil type. Questions over liability and toxicity 3M's AFFF firefighting foam was used by the Australian Defence Force for training and operational activities. ( Supplied: CRC CARE, file ) The Commonwealth is seeking $2 billion to cover "substantial costs" incurred from contaminated land and water. That includes $214 million for investigations, remediation and ongoing monitoring, and $367 million in settlements from five class actions brought against the government. Mr Solomon told the court the case raised questions about allegations of toxicity and whether there was subsequent liability, particularly in instances where remediation had been carried out. The court also heard discussion about the definition of the term "potentially toxic". "[The phrase] "potentially toxic" isn't a legal concept," Mr Solomon told the court. "If [the Crown] mean to tell us that their reliance isn't really on a collection of words but a particular concentration [or] type, they can tell us.

events.title: Prime Minister Mark Carney says US is trying to break Canada as Alberta votes on separation path
events.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has campaigned for national unity as advance voting is underway in oil-rich Alberta in a referendum that could set the province on a path toward a future vote on separation from Canada CALGARY, Alberta -- Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney warned Thursday that the United States is trying to break Canada so it can “own us” as he urged oil-rich Alberta not to begin a process toward separation in Monday’s referendum. The vote is not a direct referendum on independence. Alberta, which has the world’s fourth-largest proven oil reserves, will decide whether to remain a province or instruct the government to begin the legal process toward a future referendum on separation. “This referendum comes at the worst possible time,” Carney told a large pro-Canada rally in Calgary. “The world has become more dangerous and divided. Some outside our borders are working to break us so they can own us.” He did not directly mention the U.S. or its President Donald Trump in that passage, but has done so in similar past speeches. Carney’s warning came as U.S. President Donald Trump wages a trade war with Canada and after his repeated threats to make Canada the 51st U.S. state. Carney has argued that Canada needs to become more economically resilient and less dependent on the United States. Carney urged Albertans not to use the vote simply to send Ottawa a message, saying a decisive result could settle the separation question. “Don’t be fooled by the idea you can ‘send a message’ with your vote,” Carney said. “This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep division and great uncertainty.” Carney, who grew up in Alberta, spent Thursday campaigning in Calgary before addressing the Forever Canadian rally at the BMO Centre. His office estimated about 5,000 people attended, with some waiting more than two hours to get through security. Organizers were also holding a second rally with Carney in Edmonton on Friday. Earlier Thursday, he pointed to the many Albertans who were born or educated elsewhere in Canada and to firefighters who come from across the country to help Alberta during wildfires as examples of the ties binding the province to the rest of Canada. At the rally, Carney also acknowledged the grievances that have fueled alienation in Alberta. “The frustrations that many Albertans have felt are real,” he said. Carney said that while growing up, Ottawa made Albertans feel “like our resources weren’t our own” and that more recently the province was made to feel its energy contributions were “against the tides of history.” The setting is striking for a Liberal prime minister. Alberta has spent decades feuding with Liberal governments in Ottawa, particularly over energy and federal power. But Carney has broken with some of the policies associated with his predecessor, Justin Trudeau, fast-tracked a proposed new oil pipeline to the Pacific and called Canada an energy superpower. Carney pointed to the Pacific Link pipeline as evidence of a changed relationship, saying it would create more than 140,000 jobs and generate revenue for social programs. His biggest cheer came when he said the pipeline would reduce Canada’s dependence on the United States. “Careful, they might think that’s election interference. A little touchy,” Carney joked, drawing laughter. He was referring to U.S. Ambassador Pete Hoekstra’s warning to Canadian politicians not to interfere in the U.S. midterm elections. Tanya Clemens, co-chair of the pro-independence group Let Alberta Decide, acknowledged Carney presents a challenge. “He’s formidable for sure,” Clemens told The Associated Press. Teen shooter kills 3 children, 1 teacher at elementary school in Bend, Oregon: Police Woman accused of stabbing husband and son to death at Great Wolf Lodge: Complaint Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded Clemens argued, however, that Carney’s agreements with Alberta Premier Danielle Smith amount to “pinky promises” that do not resolve long-standing grievances with Ottawa. Keith Wilson, another leader of Let Alberta Decide, rejected Carney’s argument that global instability made this the wrong time for the vote. “The worst timing for this, why? I don’t understand what’s the logic,” Wilson said. “Then it’s the best time for him to get back to Ottawa.” Wilson said Carney should ask Parliament to repeal federal measures that separatists say have hurt Alberta, including authority he says could be used to tax oil exports in retaliation against the United States. He predicted Carney would eventually impose such a tax despite Carney saying he sees no value in using Canadian energy exports as leverage against the U.S. “It’s one cabinet meeting away,” Wilson said. “He’s gonna do it. He has to do it.” Smith, who called the vote but supports remaining in Canada, cast her ballot Wednesday and said she voted for Alberta to remain in Canada.

events.title: Fund managers quit to trade their own money in Taiwan stock boom
events.summary: Limits on trading on personal accounts are more onerous in Taiwan, and stringent checks at work for fund managers have overwhelmed the benefits of those jobs for some. Taiwan’s stock boom is luring fund managers and analysts away from traditional firms. They want to trade their own money and keep more of their gains. Strict personal-trading rules, low pay and heavy checks at asset managers are pushing talent to private investment shops and offshore hedge funds. This is making hiring harder. Regulators may review the rules, but they want to protect investors and stop conflicts of interest. The talent drain is reshaping Taiwan’s asset-management industry. TAIPEI – The world’s biggest equity rally is creating an unusual bout of FOMO (fear of missing out) among Taiwan’s professional stock pickers. Barred by local regulations from owning individual stocks in their personal accounts, fund managers and equity analysts are ditching prestigious finance jobs so they can bet their own money on shares they have spent years analysing. Fewer than half of the 20 largest local equity mutual funds have retained the same portfolio manager for more than three years, according to fund-data website MoneyDJ. The temptation is clear: Taiwan’s benchmark stock index soared 62% in 2026 to become the world’s best-performing major equity gauge, adding about US$1.8 trillion (S$2.31 trillion) in market capitalisation. Some stocks buoyed by the artificial intelligence trade such as memory and circuit makers Nanya Technology and Macronix International have more than doubled in 2026. While personal trading restrictions are common across global finance, they bite harder for Taiwan’s money managers. Limits on trading on personal accounts are also more onerous in Taiwan, and stringent checks at work for fund managers have overwhelmed the benefits of those jobs for some. As seasoned professionals leave traditional money managers, they are often ending up at less-regulated trading firms that allow more freedom for employees to trade their personal accounts. That is coinciding with the allure of faster career progression where junior staffers spend less time early on doing more mundane work and, crucially, a chance to earn large bonuses in a profit-sharing model. “The trend is impossible to ignore,” said Huang Wen-ching, chief strategy officer at Taishin Securities Investment Advisory. “Private investment firms are springing up everywhere, and the pools of capital they command are getting bigger and bigger.” Institutional money managers, for years the destination of choice for the island’s top finance talent, face an increasingly difficult hunt for personnel, according to people familiar with the recruitment process. That is forcing them to accept less skilled hires due to the dwindling pool of potential recruits, they said, asking not to be identified discussing private information. Mutual fund managers in Taiwan typically start out earning about half what their Hong Kong counterparts make, and the gap persists as pay rises with experience in subsequent years, according to industry veterans and headhunters who spoke with Bloomberg and data from recruitment firm Robert Walters. Taiwan’s portfolio managers receive the equivalent of around US$124,354 to US$310,884 annually, depending on performance and seniority, compared with base salaries in the range of US$229,372 to US$637,144 in Hong Kong. The concerns over missing out are becoming more acute due to the breadth of Taiwan’s stock-market surge. Around 10% of Taiex shares have more than doubled in 2026, compared with just 2% of South Korea’s main index and around 5% of Japan’s Nikkei 225 index. Even as global stocks sold off recently, the island’s equity benchmark outperformed all major peers, extending the resilience it has shown throughout 2026. For Ken Tsai, one winning bet still stings. In 2024, while at one of Taiwan’s biggest asset managers, the 40-year-old fund manager made a Taiwanese supplier of components that transfer data between AI servers his fund’s biggest holding. The stock surged more than fivefold the following year – then another sixfold in 2026. Bound by rules, Tsai did not own a single share in his personal accounts. Tired of seeing his calls enrich the fund – but not himself – he departed in July for a Taipei-based private investment firm that provides a more attractive revenue sharing model and grants bigger room for personal investments. Tsai declined to name the firm. “It left me with a strong sense of relative deprivation.” he said, “People who were free to buy the stock ended up making more money than I did.” Cases like Tsai’s are creating fresh challenges for asset managers trying to retain senior talent and recruit younger ones.
