events.title: Leaving portfolio decisions to the professionals
events.summary: Investors have more information at their fingertips than ever, but deciding what to do with it can still take time and judgement. HSBC Portfolio+ gives retail banking customers access to professionally managed portfolios, an approach traditionally more closely associated with wealthier investors, through its mobile app. [The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.] For anyone with a smartphone, market information is rarely far away. Market prices, company news, economic data and analysis can all be pulled up in just seconds. But access to information does not necessarily make the next investment decision any easier. It is a dilemma many investors will recognise. Research may be readily available, but deciding how much to invest, where to allocate it, when to make changes and whether market movements warrant action still requires judgement. The challenge does not end once investments have been selected. Portfolios need to be monitored over time. A strong run in one market can leave an investor more exposed to that market than originally intended, while changes in interest rates, valuations or economic conditions may also affect how different assets are allocated. For a keen investor, following those movements may be part of the appeal. But for someone juggling work, family and other commitments, managing a portfolio can start to feel like another item on an already crowded to-do list. Recently launched in Hong Kong, the digital discretionary portfolio management service allows retail banking customers to have a portfolio managed by HSBC investment professionals according to their investment objectives and risk tolerance. HSBC is also the first retail bank in Hong Kong to offer a discretionary portfolio management service to retail banking customers. Under discretionary portfolio management, the investor sets parameters such as objectives and risk appetite, while investment professionals make ongoing portfolio decisions within those parameters. With Portfolio+, HSBC portfolio managers construct the portfolios, monitor them and rebalance allocations when required, including executing transactions where necessary to keep the portfolio broadly aligned with its intended strategy and risk profile. This means investors do not have to decide for themselves whether every market movement calls for a change. Starting with what the money is for Investors may have very different reasons for putting their money to work. Some may be investing mainly for longer-term capital growth. Others may be seeking income, while sustainability considerations may influence how some investors want their money allocated. HSBC Portfolio+ offers three core strategies: Growth, Enhanced Income and Sustainable. Investors can also select Future Trends as an optional add-on for exposure to opportunities in innovation-led sectors. Different strategies can be combined into separate portfolios according to an investor’s preferences and objectives, while personalised names can be assigned to make individual portfolios easier to distinguish. Delegating decisions without losing visibility Handing over day-to-day portfolio management can make visibility just as important as professional oversight. HSCB Portfolio+ provides a look-through of holdings within individual portfolios as well as across all of an investor’s portfolios, with allocations available by region, sector and company. Market commentary from HSBC portfolio managers and shorter market insights can also be accessed through the app. That distinction is important for investors who want professional management but still want to understand where their money has been allocated. The service therefore separates two activities that are often treated as the same thing: keeping informed and making every investment decision personally. An investor can still follow markets, read commentary and see what is held in the portfolio without having to decide whether each development calls for a trade or a change in asset allocation. Professional management through an app Discretionary portfolio management has traditionally been more closely associated with wealthier investors receiving personalised investment services, partly because the cost and complexity of ongoing portfolio management made it difficult to offer at retail scale. Digital wealth infrastructure is making that model accessible to retail investors. Capabilities such as digital onboarding, data-driven investor profiling, automatic portfolio rebalancing and fractional ETF investing can make professionally managed portfolios available to a larger group of customers. HSBC Portfolio+ applies those capabilities through HSBC’s mobile app, enabling retail banking customers to access professionally managed portfolios. HSBC is currently offering a HK$0 platform fee for Portfolio+ until 1 January 2027.

events.title: Capital World’s ability to keep operating depends on completing Mustafa mall deal, auditor says
events.summary: Singapore retailer Mustafa is planning an outlet at Capital World’s Capital City Mall in Johor Bahru. Capital World’s future depends on finishing the Mustafa mall sale, as auditor Moore Stephens warned of a “material uncertainty” over its ability to keep operating. Mustafa agreed to buy 591 unsold units for RM368 million, but completion is still pending. Capital World has received RM143.7 million in deposits and says the rest is administrative. The group is also asking creditors to delay about RM29 million in payments, has unfrozen bank accounts, and is facing legal cases, restructuring plans and a share consolidation proposal. SINGAPORE – Capital World’s ability to continue operating depends on the real estate developer completing a long-running property sale to Mustafa, the Singapore retailer planning an outlet at its Capital City Mall in Johor Bahru. In an Oct 14 exchange filing, the company disclosed that its auditor, Moore Stephens, had flagged a material uncertainty that could cast significant doubt on the group’s ability to continue as a going concern. The auditor said this depended on completing the property sale. Mustafa had agreed in January 2023 to buy 591 unsold retail units and other assets at Capital City Mall, which has 11 storeys, for RM368 million (S$115 million). The other assets included accessory parcels and carpark spaces. However, completion remains outstanding, with government approvals obtained for only 55 of the 591 units, Capital World said in a July 9 update. The Straits Times reported in February that Mustafa was in negotiations with the individual owners of the retail units at Capital City Mall, which is a strata-titled mall. Mustafa had planned to open its store in JB in the second half of 2023. Capital World later clarified that it was not aware of the details of Mustafa’s negotiations with other unit owners at the mall. It announced in April 2026 that fit-out and renovation works had begun at the mall for Mustafa’s JB outlet, and that the retailer would initially occupy about 240,000 sq ft on the mall’s ground floor. An opening date was targeted “before the first quarter of 2027”. In its Oct 14 filing, Capital World said it had received RM98.2 million in deposits from Mustafa by June 30 and another RM45.5 million after the end of its financial year. Capital World’s board added that it viewed the remaining completion process as administrative, with nothing being brought to its attention suggesting that the sale would not be completed within the next 12 months. Meanwhile, the company also revealed that it has asked two creditors to defer payments totalling about RM10 million, and is negotiating with a third creditor to extend repayment of approximately RM19 million. The board expects the first two requests to be granted, as those creditors had previously agreed to instalment plans. The company added that all six bank accounts of its subsidiary Capital City Property, which were previously frozen in connection with a Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission investigation, had been unfrozen and were available for normal operations. Taking these factors into account, the board said its cash flow forecast indicated sufficient working capital to meet its obligations falling due over the next 12 months. While the group’s short-term assets exceeded its short-term liabilities by RM135 million, substantial sums were tied up in properties rather than readily available cash. The auditor highlighted inventory properties valued at RM110.7 million and non-current assets held for sale worth RM200.6 million, saying the group’s ability to continue operating hinges on closing the Mustafa deal. Despite the auditor’s warning, the board said it considered the group able to continue operating, citing the expected completion of the Mustafa sale, deposits received and efforts to defer payments to creditors. Meanwhile, the group continues to face several legal proceedings involving property purchasers. Capital City Mall is the retail component of Capital World’s flagship mixed-use development in Jalan Tampoi. In April, the developer said it was seeking additional tenants across food and beverage, fashion, lifestyle, entertainment and essential services. In an Oct 1 update, it revealed that a Federal Court matter involving 99 purchasers had been scheduled for a physical hearing of a motion on Nov 2. A separate case involving 20 other purchasers had concluded its trial, with a decision scheduled for Dec 8. Other proceedings remain ongoing, including an appeal by purchasers scheduled to be heard in July 2027. In its financial disclosures, management said it did not consider an outflow of resources from the third-party claims probable, citing legal advice. Separately, the Catalist-listed developer is proposing a capital restructuring to write off RM938.7 million in accumulated losses. An extraordinary general meeting has been scheduled for Oct 29.

events.title: El-Sayed pushes back at Republicans who judge him because he ‘might pray differently’
events.summary: The News MARQUETTE, Mich. — Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed on Thursday night accused President Donald Trump and Republican rival Mike Rogers of using his Muslim faith as a political cudgel. “Judge me by my actions and my work, but please do not assume that because I might pray differently than anybody who’s ever held this office, that somehow I am not deeply committed to this Constitution,” El-Sayed said in response to a question from Semafor. Republicans have recently amplified claims that El-Sayed and his family have ties to the Muslim Brotherhood. Trump posted a video Thursday night that directly called El-Sayed a member of the group, which was founded in Egypt; his administration has designated chapters as terrorist organizations. El-Sayed, an American of Egyptian descent who would be the first Muslim senator if elected, has rankled at the GOP accusations, including in a recent TV interview . His comments on Thursday are as close as he has come on the campaign trail to alleging Islamophobia by his opponents. “They don’t want to talk about any of the other issues that people are actually experiencing in their lives. They want to talk about me or point to my mom or my sister,” El-Sayed said. “My mom and my sister are not running for office. I’m running for office.” El-Sayed called it “an insane thing to assume” that members of his family were part of the Muslim Brotherhood, saying he didn’t “know what my mother was doing in Egypt in the 1970s.” Republicans have cited social media posts from his half-sister that appear to refer to his mother’s engagement with the group. “My parents got divorced when I was very young — 3,” El-Sayed said. “I didn’t see my mom for years after I was raised by my dad and my stepmom, and when I asked, [to] the best of my knowledge, nobody in my family’s been a member of this organization.” Know More El-Sayed said insinuating he might not be loyal to the Constitution because of his faith was “the same thing that was done to JFK when they tried to say that, ‘Oh, well, he’s going to answer to the Pope because he’s Catholic.’ Same thing they tried to do to President Obama.” John F. Kennedy, the first Roman Catholic president, faced some false accusations of “dual loyalties” because of his faith. And the hard right pushed conspiracy theories about the religious practices of Obama, who is a Christian and was the first Black president. El-Sayed was campaigning in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula this week as part of a swing with progressive Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. El-Sayed and Democrats are hoping they can grow the electorate in what has traditionally been redder territory in the state. Notable A Washington Post analysis found that rhetoric about El-Sayed from right-wing social media users has increasingly focused on his faith since his Michigan primary win this summer.

events.title: Tesla reveals SpaceX-powered Roadster that flies and falls with style
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Tesla just revealed its redesigned second-generation Roadster with SpaceX thrusters, a vehicle CEO Elon Musk has called “the best of the last of the human-driven cars.” Musk showed off the car at an event outside Waco, Texas, with a demonstration that saw the car use a mixture of high-powered fans and thrusters to drive up an inverted ramp, spin around, and ease itself to a landing on the pavement below. The car also used the thrusters to lift itself over a Cybercab, Cybertruck, Tesla Semi, Model Y, and Model 3 while in motion. “This will be the actual car that’s on the roads,” Musk said of the car, which Tesla showed accelerating 0 to 60 miles per hour in one second. “It literally is just going to puff itself up, and uh, and be able to do this, these maneuvers whenever you’d like.” Musk said Tesla will finally build the long-delayed vehicle in 2028, but didn’t name a price. Tesla will offer it in three trims. The first is “Performance,” which Tesla describes as “road ready.” It seats two, has active aerodynamics, and features a “multi-mode suction system for next-level performance on and off the track.” The second trim is “Thrust,” which is “race ready” and seats two, and has rear-mounted cold-gas thrusters that enable sub-one-second 0-to-60 mph acceleration. The third is “Rocket,” which is “air ready” and seats one, and has 10 cold-gas thrusters positioned around the car. All three trims will have 300 miles of range and be capable of speeds exceeding 230 miles per hour. Tesla’s website showed Thursday the company is taking reservations for the car, charging $50,000 just to reserve the Performance, and $250,000 for Thrust. The Rocket trim is billed as “invite only.” Engineering VP Lars Moravy said at the event that the Roadster uses 10 thrusters connected to 600 liters of compressed air to lift and spin the car in midair. The air tank can be recharged, he said. “Every usable void in the car is packed with Carbon Fiber Overwrapped Pressure Vessels (COPVs),” Tesla wrote in a post on X, referring to the type of pressure vessel that has been at the root of multiple SpaceX rocket explosions. The company said “every usable void” in the car is filled with these vessels. Musk also said at the event that Tesla may try to jump the Snake River Canyon — the site of Evel Knievel’s famous attempt to cross the gorge in a steam-powered rocket. Musk has positioned the Roadster as a true halo car for Tesla, saying at one point that he’s “not sure it moves the needle massively from a revenue standpoint.” But he has previously said that “safety is not the main goal” with the new Roadster. “If you buy a Ferrari, safety is not the number one goal. I say, if safety is your number one goal, do not buy the Roadster,” he said on a podcast earlier this year . Tesla would “aspire not to kill anyone in this car,” he said. “This is the culmination of incredible work by Tesla and SpaceX Engineers working closely together to make something you haven’t seen in any movie, better than any James Bond car,” Musk said at the event. “I’ve never seen anything like this. You know when I suggested this to the team, I thought, ‘Am I crazy?’” Musk had previously claimed that the car “will be very different from what was shown previously” and promised the demo would be the “most exciting, whether it works or not, demo ever of any product.” The design changes were notable. The car, shown in stark white, now has a more angular design reminiscent of a Lamborghini or the famous Lotus Esprit used by the James Bond character in “The Spy Who Loved Me” — a car Musk owns , which was on display at the event. In another post, Tesla said the design was inspired by the SR-71 reconnaissance aircraft and the F-35 fighter jet. “Our design language has evolved since the last reveal: from S3XY to Cybertruck, Cybercab & Optimus,” the company wrote. Tesla held the event almost nine years to the day after the company first revealed the second-generation Roadster, a modernized take on its first-ever car. Unveiled as a surprise at the end of the Tesla Semi reveal in 2017, the revamped Roadster was supposed to be delivered in just a few years. Tesla allowed customers to place $50,000 deposits to reserve the car. Some even paid $250,000 to reserve one of 1,000 “Founders Series” versions. Musk first talked about adding thrusters to the car in 2018. “SpaceX option package for new Tesla Roadster will include ~10 small rocket thrusters arranged seamlessly around car,” he wrote on Twitter that year. “These rocket engines dramatically improve acceleration, top speed, braking & cornering. Maybe they will even allow a Tesla to fly …” But the Roadster project took a back seat. In 2018, Tesla suffered through what Musk eventually dubbed “production hell” with the Model 3 sedan.

events.title: White House’s AI task force gets to work
events.summary: The White House’s AI task force has formally adopted its charter, kicking off the short 120-day window it’s been given to answer some extremely thorny questions about how the government should handle the rapid development of AI technology. According to an announcement shared first with Semafor, the task force agreed after its first official meeting Thursday to commission a report from the President’s Council of Advisers on Science and Technology to evaluate AI risk in three areas: cybersecurity and critical infrastructure protection, biosecurity and dual-use applications, and model control and accountability. “Throughout its work, the [task force] will engage with frontier model developers and other SI companies, consumer protection groups, and civil liberties advocates, industry stakeholders, and federal and state law enforcement agencies to inform and implement its efforts,” a White House official said in a statement. “The [Super Intelligence Force] stands ready to ensure implementation of the Accord and continued U.S. leadership on SI for the benefit of the American people.” It also agreed to make a working group tasked with implementing the White House Accord on Super Intelligence that major AI CEOs signed this month, a process led by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, the task force’s chair, along with National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross. Defense Undersecretary Emil Michael, a task force vice chair, will lead an effort to develop protocols for labs to tell the government about breaches, hacks and other cyber issues. Michael is also in charge of interfacing with frontier AI labs and figuring out long-term coordination on AI across the government. The task force also agreed to create a “law enforcement and consumer protection coordination committee” including the Justice Department and Federal Trade Commission, led by FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson, also a vice chair. The last vice chair, Office of Personnel Management Director Scott Kupor, will work with the public and private sector on critical infrastructure protection, and will work with the Department of Labor on studying the impact of AI on the American workforce and economy. Members of the task force beyond the chairs include: Vice President JD Vance, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Office of Science and Technology Policy Director Michael Kratsios, plus Cairncross, Chris Klomp, the nominee to be the No. 2 at the Department of Health and Human Services, Social Security Administration Commissioner Frank Bisignano, and National Security Agency Director Joshua Rudd, along with White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and her deputy, Richard Walters. It’s not yet entirely clear how compliance with the task force will be enforced or how current law may apply to companies who don’t adhere to the new protocols. A White House official told Semafor one stick could be export controls, which the Commerce Department at one point temporarily imposed on Anthropic after the company refused to grant the government unfettered access to its models.

events.title: Singapore’s key exports soar beyond expectations in September on AI and non-electronics boom
events.summary: Non-oil domestic exports expanded 68.4% from a year ago, from August’s rise of 46.1%, driven by non-electronics. SINGAPORE – Singapore’s non-oil domestic exports (NODX) rose in September, extending from August’s expansion, led by non-electronics shipments, while electronics continued to rise amid strong AI-driven demand. This marked the seventh consecutive month of double-digit expansion for the country’s NODX and far exceeded economists’ forecast of 32.2% in a Bloomberg poll. Economists said that NODX will continue to be supported by the AI boom in the near term, but they do not expect the exceptional performance from non-electronics to repeat in October . Non-oil domestic exports (NODX) expanded 68.4% from a year ago, from August’s rise of 46.1%, driven by non-electronics, data from Enterprise Singapore (EnterpriseSG) on Oct 16 showed. Non-electronics shipments expanded 54.2% year on year in September, following the previous month’s 11.9% increase. The growth was led by a 124.3% jump in non-monetary gold exports and a 50.4% rise for specialised machinery. The year-on-year growth for “lumpy exports” of structures of ships and boats was not cited, as the exceptionally high percentage growth reflects a low base effect in the same period in 2025. Surging 107.6% in September following a 131.6% rise the previous month, electronic product shipments continued to climb on the back of robust AI demand. Growth was driven by a 149.5% jump in personal computer exports. Shipments grew 312.4% for disk media products and 74.7% for integrated circuits, or chips. Standard Chartered economists Edward Lee and Jonathan Koh said that the outlook for electronics NODX remains sanguine over the next few quarters. However, they warned that growth is likely to moderate beyond the near term as base effects become less supportive and the AI cycle matures. “ The Monetary Authority of Singapore expects the exceptional pace of AI-related activity to ease in the second half of 2027. A sharper or more sustained correction in AI-related assets could pose an additional downside risk if tighter financing conditions cause technology firms to reassess AI capex, weighing on electronics demand and NODX,” said Lee and Koh. Meanwhile, DBS senior economist Chua Han Teng said that uneven dynamics persisted in non-electronics exports. “While lumpy exports of structures of ships and boats as well as specialised machinery performed well, petrochemicals and pharmaceuticals shipments stayed in contraction,” he noted. Trading platform eToro’s analyst Zavier Wong said he does not expect September’s exceptional growth to repeat in October , given that ship and boat structures contributed $3.7 billion on their own, in a category EnterpriseSG calls “lumpy” . This means that those exports can fluctuate sharply from month to month because of a few large transactions. Chua added that the global economic landscape remained complex, with rising energy and input costs, ongoing supply chain disruptions, existing tariffs amid evolving geopolitical developments, and tighter financial conditions posing challenges to certain non-technology-related manufacturers and exporters. NODX to the US, Taiwan and Hong Kong expanded in September, while NODX to India declined. NODX to Taiwan expanded 96.9%, extending August’s 58.5% rise, driven by an 85.2% jump in non-electronic NODX. NODX to Hong Kong surged 112.1% in September, following a 62.6% increase in August, propelled by a 183.4% jump in non-electronic shipments. Key exports to the US , Singapore’s single-largest export market, expanded 73.2%, while those to India dipped 5.6%. Wong said he expects the NODX growth forecast to be lifted, given that EnterpriseSG upgraded its full-year forecast to a range of 14% to 16% in August, and NODX has already grown by 27.6% in the first nine months of 2026. “Fourth quarter would have to fall by roughly a fifth for the year to finish inside the range, and electronics is still more than doubling. I expect the range to be raised, though how far depends on whether the ship deliveries keep coming,” he added.

( Reuters: Brendan McDermid ) The cost of insuring against a debt default by Wall Street's tech titans has hit record levels. Neocloud company CoreWeave is among the most expensive to insure against. Analysts view the firm as the "canary in the coalmine" for the artificial intelligence boom more broadly. The cost of insuring against a big technology firm defaulting on its debt has soared to record highs. These contracts are known as credit default swaps. Heavily indebted data centre operator CoreWeave has been among the hardest hit. Investors who lent the company money are now paying a lot to buy these credit default swaps to insure against losing their investments if the company defaults. The so-called neocloud company has taken on more than $US50 billion ($72 billion) in debt. The yield on CoreWeave bonds maturing in 2031 has hit 15.78 per cent. This week, the spread on its five-year credit default swaps soared 16 per cent to a record 1.14 per cent, before easing slightly to 1.03 per cent. Floodlines Research founder Anna Wu said the record highs in tech credit default swaps were an extension of CoreWeave's spreads blowing past 1 per cent. "[It] has revived worries about how the AI build-out is being financed," Ms Wu said. Wall Street's big tech firms are increasingly turning to debt and private credit financing, having exhausted options to raise money in the share market. But elevated global inflation is putting upward pressure on interest rates, which is increasing the cost of this debt. Competition for debt from governments and other big tech firms is also increasing interest rates, and the cost of servicing this debt. Investors are increasingly concerned that debt costs are rising too much for big tech firms to service, and they are buying insurance to prevent harmful financial losses. Ms Wu conceded financial markets were growing more anxious about these mammoth companies' financial health. "Nvidia's Jensen Huang defended CoreWeave in Stockholm yesterday, saying its cost of capital is falling and it needs no Nvidia backstop, but I think investor sentiment on tech is fragile after the chip sell-off, so this is more sentiment than fundamentals for now," she said. Elsewhere in the market cloud ⁠computing giant Oracle has seen its credit default swaps rise 0.3 per cent this week, while costs to insure against debt defaults for Nvidia, STMicroelectronics and SpaceX also rose sharply. Credit default swap ⁠spreads for Amazon, Alphabet and Meta also traded at record highs, data from LSEG and S&P Global Market Intelligence showed, though they have risen far more slowly than Oracle, or CoreWeave. Jensen Huang has defended CoreWeave's debt levels, saying its cost of capital is falling. ( Reuters: Evan Vucci ) "This is not the first time we've had a sizeable market wobble on the back of AI fears, ⁠but as we move to a capex cycle funded out of debt rather than simply free cash flow, we have to increasingly respect the credit price action," Deutsche Bank strategist Jim Reid said. "AI financing costs aren't dramatic overall, but there are worrying themes at the edges." The US is experiencing a 'boomcession'. Is Australia, too? Australia's 'quirky' obsession with housing is fuelled by necessity How Australian mortgages compare to the US, Japan and South Korea Former RBA member explains what happens inside interest rate meetings Marcus Today senior markets analyst Henry Jennings described CoreWeave as the "canary in the coalmine" for excessive big-tech debt on Wall Street. Wall Street risk signal flashing red Credit default swaps for US big tech companies are soaring to record highs. It means investors are fearful of a major Wall Street company collapse. "[CoreWeave's credit default swaps show there is a] 60 per cent chance of default within five years," Mr Jennings said. "Jensen Huang was quick to defend CoreWeave but then again, he is an investor and supplier to the company. "Investors are freaking out on the cost of debt for wannabes," he said. XTB research director Kathleen Brooks agreed. "Its bonds have sold off sharply … this is a sign that investors might be going off the AI investment narrative, which has included massive debt issuance to fund AI ambitions.

events.title: Safety concern in remote community with police station unstaffed
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts FNQ community concerned about lack of support as remote police station left unstaffed Locals are concerned about a lack of police support in Laura, which covers part of the tourist-travelled Peninsula Development Road. ( ABC News: Brendan Mounter ) A remote police station in Far North Queensland has been left unstaffed after its only officer took unplanned leave. Residents near Laura, in southern Cape York Peninsula, say the understaffing of their police station has led to safety concerns, including for those at risk of domestic violence. The Queensland Police Service says recruitment for a relieving officer is underway. A remote Far North Queensland community fears it is being left without police support while authorities try to fill vacancies at its empty police station. Earlier this week, Queensland Police Service (QPS) confirmed the Laura police station was sitting empty while recruitment was underway to replace the solo officer, who had taken unplanned leave. The remote Cape York township posting, 310 kilometres north-west of Cairns, covers a vast remote area incorporating the tourist gateway Peninsula Development Road (PDR). QPS said patrols and call-outs in the meantime were covered by officers from Cooktown and Hope Vale, more than 140km away. The Laura police district covers a large area in southern Cape York Peninsula. ( ABC News: Peter Mullins ) The Indigenous Family Violence Legal Service said any gap in remote police staffing was deeply concerning for domestic violence victim-survivors. Acting chief executive Thelma Schwartz said she was not surprised by the vacancy, describing remote understaffing as a long-standing problem. "It doesn't matter if you're a victim-survivor of domestic, family and sexual violence living in metropolitan Queensland, regional Queensland, rural and remote Queensland," she said. Thelma Schwartz is concerned an empty Laura police station puts women's safety at risk. ( ABC News ) Ms Schwartz said she had frequently raised slow response times, including to the commission of inquiry into police domestic violence responses . She said calls from towns without a local officer were diverted elsewhere, which could mean delays of several hours. That risk grows as the wet season arrives and flooding threatens to cut roads across the tropical north. Ms Schwartz said the risk of opportunistic violence from perpetrators due to lack of police presence was also well known. Locals said the Laura division was already stretched even before the vacancy, with its two-officer posting long staffed by just one. Palmerville Station resident Archie Levers said his community often had incidents where they struggled to get police support. "We have a lot of illegal campers and illegal prospectors and people lighting fires, arsonists," he said. Laura is a remote centre in southern Cape York Peninsula. ( Richard Dinnen ) Laura Quinkan Dance Festival organiser Debbie Symonds said she was concerned the community was not informed of the unstaffed police station, particularly given the amount of tourists passing through the area. "It is the last bit of bitumen till they finish between the PDR before you hit dirt, and that's where a lot of issues can start and end in that town," she said. While she welcomed news police were in the process of recruiting, she hoped QPS would ensure any new officers brought to the region were equipped to understand and work with the community. "[We need] someone that is very balanced between cultural significance and events as well as being able to uphold law and be respected for that," she said. Queensland Police Union president Shane Prior said QPS could have sent a relief officer to Laura straight away while it recruited. Laura is home to the famous Laura Quinkan Dance Festival. ( ABC Far North: Christopher Testa ) "That position could have been filled, it simply wasn't because it was going to cost too much money," Mr Prior said. Mr Prior said Laura was not an isolated case, with 745 positions vacant across the service. Shane Prior has accused the police service of cost-cutting. ( ABC News: Luke Bowden ) He said the union met with QPS on Thursday morning and understood the station would be staffed as soon as possible. A QPS spokesperson said recruitment for a relieving officer was underway, with the aim of having them start as soon as possible. QPS said it could not detail how long Laura was unstaffed due to operational security. "Far North police remain focused on the safety of local communities, their officers, and ensuring the highest levels of service delivery are always maintained," the QPS spokesperson said.

events.title: "Oh, shut up": Maine Senate debate gets testy
events.summary: Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins and her Democratic challenger Troy Jackson were sparring in a testy debate Thursday night when a protester loudly interrupted them. "So this is obviously one of Troy's supporters," Collins said. "Oh, shut up," Jackson shot back. "I don't even know that kid." Why it matters: Collins and Jackson are competing in one of a handful of races that will determine the Senate majority. The two have traded barbs in a series of tense debates, but this was the first time they sounded like children arguing on a playground. Zoom in : At another point in the debate, Collins, who's been accused of not standing up to President Trump enough, was asked by a moderator to name a time when she opposed him and it changed the outcome. "At one point, I had organized people to vote against Secretary Hegseth," she responded, referring to the Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's confirmation. "As you undoubtedly have read, at the very last minute one of our Republicans changed his mind. Otherwise he would've been defeated for that job." Collins was talking about Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), who went on to call his eventual decision to vote for Hegseth the "biggest regret of my career." "So that didn't change the outcome," the moderator said.

events.title: Trump names scapegoats as Republicans sweat in Texas
events.summary: President Trump is preemptively blaming Sen. John Cornyn and Karl Rove for "doing everything possible to make it hard for Ken Paxton" to win the Texas Senate race. Why it matters: The president is publicly spinning what would be a disaster for Republicans on election night. Texas hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988. "If Ken Paxton loses , it will be because of WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks like John Cornyn and Karl Rove," Trump posted on Truth Social. Trump won Texas by 14 points just two years ago. What to watch: Trump's post comes the same day FEC campaign finance reports confirmed Elon Musk's efforts to help Paxton across the finish line. Musk gave $158 million to the Senate GOP's main super PAC in September over two transactions, as Axios reported Thursday morning . The day after each Musk donation , SLF made an equal-sized transfer to a Texas PAC— a pop-up super PAC dedicated to electing Paxton. The big picture: A new poll this week in Texas showed Democrat James Talarico with a narrow lead over Paxton, 50% to 47%. Republican leaders warned Trump for months that if Paxton won the primary against Cornyn it would be cost the party far more to keep the seat. Those predictions are proving true, with more than $500 million in ad spending already flowing into the Texas Senate race, according to AdImpact. "Got to be more careful when you run with the big dogs," Cornyn told Semafor earlier in October after audio leaked from a Paxton event in D.C. The other side: Talarico is getting pummeled with some of that money, but he's far from defenseless. He was already on the air in August, when Paxton and Republicans were still figuring out their game plan — and who would foot the bill. Talarico raised $64 million in the third quarter off an army of small donors. His campaign said 97% of contributions were under $100. Talarico's fundraising prowess allowed him to raise hard dollars, which command lower ad rates. "Oh my god, holy crap, I saw Talarico," Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) said on Thursday. "I don't even know how you raised $64 million in a quarter. I mean, that's a number that's mind-blowing." Paxton brought in $18 million.

events.title: China’s plan to make renminbi a global currency enters faster phase
events.summary: China’s challenge is no longer simply to persuade its trading partners to settle transactions in renminbi. China is speeding up efforts to make the renminbi a global currency by building a wider financial system, not just using it for trade settlement. Beijing is adding offshore investment products, derivatives, hedging tools and easier bond issuance to support liquidity, financing and reserve use. Cross-border renminbi payments are growing fast, with annual transaction value reaching 180.2 trillion yuan in 2025, and CIPS and QR payments may expand further. BEIJING – China’s campaign to promote the global use of the renminbi appears to be accelerating as the authorities seek to build a more comprehensive financial ecosystem for the currency beyond just trade settlement. Beijing is focused on developing the infrastructure needed to expand the renminbi’s use in global financing and investment, and to strengthen its role as a reserve currency. This includes broadening the range of available investment products and financial instruments, such as derivatives and hedging tools, while making it easier for borrowers to issue so-called dim sum and panda bonds. It must also ensure that the currency has sufficient liquidity, financing channels, investment products and reserve assets to play a larger role in global portfolios and capital flows. Here are four areas where Beijing is making progress towards the renminbi’s internationalisation: 1. Creating more offshore renminbi investment products Measures to broaden offshore renminbi-denominated investment products include plans to increase the scale and frequency of government bond issuance in Hong Kong, where policymakers are seeking to develop a yield curve for the currency. The Hong Kong authorities are also studying the introduction of short-term renminbi debt instruments and plan to launch a redesigned renminbi-denominated gold futures contract. “The next policy focus will likely be on speeding up the development of renminbi asset markets,” said Tommy Wu, a senior economist for Greater China and North Asia at Standard Chartered in Hong Kong. “One of the key challenges is how to capitalise on global investors’ increasing needs for diversification and attract them to increase their investment in renminbi assets.” 2. Adding renminbi derivatives and hedging tools Many overseas investors will be reluctant to increase their renminbi holdings unless they have ways to manage volatility, interest rate and currency risks. The Chinese authorities are seeking to address these concerns in several ways, including by expanding a major derivatives trading link with Hong Kong to give foreign investors access to more onshore interest rate products. In August, they also introduced a new set of government bond futures in Hong Kong, giving global investors another hedging tool. “Institutions will not hold substantial renminbi balances without instruments offering suitable duration, liquidity and risk management,” said Tommy Xie, head of Asia macro research at Oversea-Chinese Banking Corporation in Singapore. “The missing piece is therefore not just ‘more renminbi assets’ but a full asset liability and hedging chain.” 3. Deepening renminbi’s role in financing Mainland China and Hong Kong are both seeking to make the currency a more widely used financing vehicle by expanding onshore and offshore funding channels. China plans to make panda bond issuance and trading more accessible to overseas borrowers. Panda bonds are renminbi-denominated debt issued in mainland China by foreign entities. Hong Kong is seeking to encourage further issuance of renminbi-denominated debt in the city and aims to develop an “enhanced tenor structure” for dim sum bond issuance. Dim sum bonds are securities denominated in the renminbi and issued outside mainland China. The city is also seeking to increase renminbi liquidity, making it easier for governments and companies to raise funds in the currency. 4. Expanding cross-border renminbi clearing and settlement China’s cross-border renminbi payment and settlement system is gaining traction. The annual transaction value in 2025 had almost quadrupled in 10 years to 180.2 trillion yuan (S$34.5 trillion), based on data compiled by Bloomberg. The expanding Cross-Border Interbank Payment System (CIPS) allows companies and financial institutions to transact more easily in renminbi outside China, Standard Chartered’s Wu said. “We could see efforts to further expand CIPS’ usage for cross-border clearing and settlement, as well as the promotion of cross-border QR code payments, especially with ASEAN countries,” he said. events.title: Basel Committee finalises measures to address window-dressing in the G-SIB framework and consults on G-SIB methodology review
events.summary: The BIS supports central banks' pursuit of monetary and financial stability through international cooperation. Cyber Resilience Coordination Centre BIS research focuses on policy issues of core interest to the central bank and financial supervisory community. Our authors publish economic analysis and research on monetary and financial stability issues. The BIS hosts committees engaged in standard setting & the pursuit of financial stability through the Basel Process. Basel Committee on Banking Supervision Committee on the Global Financial System Committee on Payments and Market Infrastructures The BIS publishes select speeches delivered by its senior management, focusing on topics that align with the organisation's mission. Access our statistics in the BIS Data Portal Ethics & conduct, risk management & internal audit Consultative Council for the Americas Historical monetary & financial statistics Regulatory Consistency Assessment Programme (RCAP) Countercyclical capital buffer (CCyB) Global systemically important banks (G-SIB) The Basel Committee has published amendments to address window-dressing behaviour in the framework for global systemically important banks (G-SIBs). Banks will be required to report and disclose indicators used to calculate G-SIB scores based on average values over the reporting year, rather than year-end values, by January 2030. The Committee consults on whether to incorporate its previously agreed treatment of cross-border exposures within the European Banking Union (EBU) into the methodology. The Basel Committee on Banking Supervision today published final amendments to address window dressing in the G-SIB framework and a consultation on the G-SIB methodology review. "Window dressing" seeks to temporarily reduce banks' perceived systemic footprint around the reference dates used for the reporting and public disclosure of G-SIB scores . As noted previously by the Committee, window-dressing by banks is unacceptable. Such behaviour undermines the intended policy objectives of the Committee's standards and risks disrupting the operations of financial markets. The amendments aim at constraining banks' ability to lower their G-SIB scores through window-dressing. This will be achieved by requiring banks participating in the G-SIB assessment exercise to report and disclose all stock G-SIB indicators based on an average of values over the reporting year, rather than year-end values. To provide sufficient time for banks to develop a robust and comprehensive reporting process, the revised standard will be implemented by 1 January 2030. In addition, the Committee has agreed to increase the G-SIB reporting and disclosure threshold from EUR 200 billion to EUR 350 billion in leverage ratio exposure measure, to be implemented from 2027. Separately, as part of the Committee's periodic review of the G-SIB assessment methodology , the Committee is consulting on whether to incorporate the treatment of cross-border exposures within the EBU in the G-SIB framework. The Committee welcomes comments on all aspects of the consultation from stakeholders. Comments should be submitted here by 14 January 2027 .

events.title: GOP senator: Cancel Thanksgiving recess if we lose
events.summary: Sen. Bernie Moreno wants his fellow Republicans to cancel their holiday plans and jam through "everything that we could possibly get" if they lose the majorities in November's midterms. Why it matters: Republicans couldn't muster the votes for a megabill this summer, and leadership is not confident they can now. But Moreno (R-Ohio) is calling for the GOP to make a bigger push in the event of losing power. "We will do a reconciliation bill, one way or the other," Moreno — who said it is "more likely" the GOP holds the Senate — told reporters outside the Capitol on Thursday. But if Republicans lose: "It'll be the 'Last Supper.' So it'll be a giant reconciliation bill where we take all the Republican priorities that we can get done." "If we lose the House and the Senate, we should be here from Nov. 9 until Dec. 31 with no break at all," he said. "Like, we'll have turkeys here for Thanksgiving." Zoom in: Conversations have been ongoing in congressional offices about what a reconciliation package might look like in the lame-duck session between the election and the new Congress next year, a source familiar with the matter tells Axios. "We are working with the House and White House to develop what all is included to be able to sell to the public and our Republican colleagues when we return," Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wis.), chair of the Budget Committee, told Axios. Election outcomes won't substantively change much for frequent holdouts like Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas), Thom Tillis (R-N.C.), Bill Cassidy (R-La.) and Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) who are on their way out. That's not to mention Sens. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) and Susan Collins (R-Maine), who are appropriators and known to break from the party. What to watch: Republicans face a long to-do list in the lame-duck, including funding the government past Dec. 11, passing emergency defense spending and raising the debt ceiling. Those could all be considered part of a massive reconciliation package that requires just a majority vote to pass. But not everything qualifies for the reconciliation process — and big bills can cause big headaches. Other to-do items include: Passing the National Defense Authorization Act Reauthorizing FISA Section 702, the warrantless wiretap authority Passing the farm bill Passing permitting reform Confirming nominations Between the lines : Some of the administration's top priorities are banking on the partisan-led funding maneuver of reconciliation, including Trump's sprawling Golden Dome missile defense system, autonomous weapon advancement efforts and upgrades to the F-35 fighter jet. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told attendees at an Army conference on Wednesday the Pentagon needs "a minimum" of $350 billion to "rebuild the military." The intrigue: If Republicans lose their Senate majority, it will almost certainly be Moreno's job to try to win it back. He is running for National Republican Senatorial Committee chair — so far, unopposed. Axios Defense reporter Thomas Novelly contributed to this story.

events.title: When it came to Cal AI’s viral success, a small army of influencers paid off
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Zach Yadegari has enjoyed an immense amount of success for someone who only recently graduated from high school. Founder of the AI-fueled calorie tracking app Cal AI, Yadegari is only 19 but his company has rocketed to viral fame over the past two years. At TechCrunch Disrupt on Thursday, Yadegari shared details of that surprising rise to prominence. Cal AI, which was founded in 2024, exploded onto the internet thanks largely to Yadegari’s strategy of deploying a small army of influencers to promote the brand. The company generated over $30 million in revenue in two years and was acquired by MyFitnessPal for an undisclosed amount of money in March. Discussing his social strategy onstage, Yadegari noted that an early sign of success came when an influencer’s post about them led to approximately a thousand new users over the course of two days. “From there, we figured out, okay, this can actually work for us, and so we started recruiting influencers as fast as we could — paying as many people as possible to start posting for us,” he said. “What we saw was that it was a clear formula. It was pretty linear, but it was extremely fast. I guess linear in the sense that every post they did would get a certain number of viewers that would convert.” The Forbes 30 Under 30 alumnus told the audience that part of his company’s strategy was to negotiate rates with influencers, promising them certain payouts for a certain scale of reach. A lot of influencers are “broke college kids” who “just want cash,” Yadegari added. “You just ask them, okay, we’ll pay you this, but we need to get us at least this amount of use and keep posting until you get there.” Another important component of success was finding the right influencers whose reach can be quantified. “The biggest thing for us was finding influencers that had very tight communities,” the founder said. Yadegari, whose father was in the audience, also credited his family with giving him the freedom to go after his ambitions. Does he also credit higher education for his success? Not so much. “I think the only real reason to go to college is if you want to have a fun social time as a kid and be with other people,” he said, to audience laughter. Earlier this month, Yadegari also launched Persona, a new AI agent startup that has already raised $10 million . Yadegari said the “overarching mission” with Persona is to “make computing seamless with human life.” The company’s personal AI assistant will “live anyplace with internet connection,” he said, including “iMessage, app, email, phone call.” He added that part of what distinguishes the company’s plans for this AI assistant is to build a “hardware ecosystem around” the app. When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . For three days this week in San Francisco, 20 eager startups participated in the Startup Battlefield at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026. The top 20 were chosen to represent the best of the Startup Battlefield 200, and they competed for a chance to take home the Startup Battlefield Cup and $100,000. With that intense pitching now complete, we have a winner. These startups were handpicked to compete in Startup Battlefield , and all of them presented a live demo in front of VCs and tech leaders who served as judges. After hours of deliberation, TechCrunch editors pored over the judges’ notes and narrowed the list down to five finalists: Apate, Flox Intelligence, Intero Biosystems, Industrial Next, and Satlyt. The final five made their way to the finale to demo in front of our final panel of judges: Alexa von Tobel of Inspired Capital, Chi-Hua Chien of Goodwater Capital, Dayna Grayson of Construct Capital, Karl Alomar of M13, and Stacy Brown-Philpot of Cherryrock Capital. We’re now ready to announce that the winner of TechCrunch Startup Battlefield 2026 is: Intero Biosystems is a Denver-based startup founded by Charlie Childs and Madeline Eiken that spun out of the University of Michigan. It’s developing 1mm human intestinal “organoids,” lab-grown tissue that mimics the gut, offering another way to study how drugs and other compounds might affect the human body before they are tested in people. The startup sells its flagship product, GastroScreen, to pharmaceutical, biotech, food, and chemical companies for testing drugs and other compounds. It deploys thousands of AI agents that masquerade as innocent victims, answering scam calls, responding to shady messages and emails, following phishing links, and joining social media groups to bait fraudsters. In addition to access to Apate’s fleet of agents, customers get an insights portal that offers intelligence and analytics on scams targeting their end users or employees, brands, products, and more. events.title: Mayor says flood-prone airstrip may need to move despite $27m upgrade
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Mayor says flood-prone Burketown airstrip may need to move despite $27m upgrade Topic: Rural and Remote Communities A Gulf of Carpentaria mayor says the new Burketown airstrip is an improvement, but still wants it relocated. ( ABC News: Abbey Halter ) Massive floods in 2023 that tore through the Gulf of Carpentaria severely damaged infrastructure in Burketown. The federal and Queensland governments gave $27 million for works to repair and improve the community's airstrip. The Burke Shire mayor wants to see the airstrip relocated further from the Burketown centre, despite the upgrade. A flood-prone airstrip in the Gulf of Carpentaria may need to be relocated to avoid future disasters, despite a recent multi-million-dollar upgrade, the local mayor says. The community of Burketown, 420 kilometres north of Mount Isa, had been without a commercially functioning airstrip after a "biblical-style flood" engulfed the region in 2023. For the past nine months while construction was underway, the only way in or out of the region has been by bus on unreliable dirt roads. The Burketown airstrip upgrades after major flooding in 2023 cost $27 million. ( Supplied: Durack Civil, Jake Rich ) The $27 million Queensland and federal government-funded upgrade raised the airstrip by 400 millimetres, and commercial flights are expected to resume in mid-November. Burke Shire Mayor Ernie Camp said he while was "incredibly excited" to see the upgraded airstrip, owned and operated by the council, back up and running, it should be moved to a more flood-resistant location. "This essential asset supports the RFDS, Rex Airlines, local charter operators, general aviation and the glider pilots who visit each year," he said. "[Regular Public Transport] services are the lifeblood for small communities, aircraft aren't getting any smaller, and the number of people travelling on them aren't either." Although use of larger aircraft on Gulf routes could take years — meaning there is no immediate need for relocation — planning for future aviation trends in the next "10 or 15 years" was important, Cr Camp said. Ernie Camp has been campaigning for regions in the Gulf of Carpentaria to be more flood-resilient. ( ABC News: Abbey Halter ) He said he was a "little bit worried" the new airstrip would not survive another weather event such as the one in 2023, but it was a "more resilient". "It certainly has been an eye-opener in the amount of human resources and heavy equipment to come here because we had to totally rebuild that airstrip," he said. "The tarmac had been compromised from not only the 2023 flood, [but also] the previous flood; the clay has certainly degraded." Cr Camp said he had raised concerns with some politicians, but their suggestion was to "work with what we've got". 'Longevity' needed for Gulf investment Western Queensland Alliance of Councils (WQAC) Executive Director Greg Hoffman said while he was pleased to see the airstrip improved and reopened, the challenge in the Gulf was to ensure assets have longevity and were not severely impacted by further weather events. "The biggest challenge we have these days is to build sufficient resilience to get ahead of the game, so we don't find ourselves in five, 10 years having to do it again," Mr Hoffman said. "[WQAC] has been very … in our advocacy to the governments to say that there needs to be long-term plans that take into consideration these potential adverse impacts into the future." Mr Hoffman said investing to improve asset resilience was essential. "Particularly in the case of Burketown and Gulf communities, the importance of air services and airports," he said. "In the context of the importance of aerodromes in flood-prone areas, [Cr Camp's] argument has got a lot of merit [but] sadly, it will probably require a disaster to prove the point that what's been done at the moment hasn't achieved the objective of being flood-proof." The RFDS and emergency services are crucial in Burketown, especially during the summer wet season. ( ABC News: Abbey Halter ) The government launched a joint $119 million flood recovery package across northern and central Queensland after the 2023 monsoonal event. A spokesperson for Queensland Emergency Management Minister Ann Leahy said the Burketown Airstrip was a crucial public asset for residents, and it was unclear whether the federal government's proposed disaster funding cuts would have delivered this project. The spokesperson did not respond to questions about relocating the airstrip.

events.title: Netflix names former Disney executive Rice as new content chief as Bajaria departs
events.summary: Rice will oversee Netflix’s content strategy from Oct 26, including series, films and live events across regions. Netflix named former Disney executive Peter Rice as chief content officer from October 26, replacing Bela Bajaria, who is leaving after nearly a decade. Rice will lead content strategy for series, films and live events worldwide. Bajaria helped deliver hits like Bridgerton and Squid Game, and deals with WWE and the NFL. The move comes after Netflix said it would cut 6% of staff, about 1,000 jobs. The company faces pressure as YouTube and TikTok draw viewers with free content. Netflix said on Oct 15 that it has appointed former Disney executive Peter Rice as chief content officer, succeeding Bela Bajaria, who is leaving after nearly a decade at the streaming platform. Previously, he served as chairman of Walt Disney Television and chairman of general entertainment at The Walt Disney Company. Meanwhile, Bajaria joined Netflix in 2016 and was named chief content officer in January 2023. During her tenure, Netflix released pop-culture hits such as Bridgerton and Squid Game and expanded live programming through multi-year partnerships with World Wrestling Entertainment and the National Football League. The announcement comes a day after Netflix told staff in an internal memo that it was laying off 6% of its workforce, roughly 1,000 employees, marking its biggest job cuts since 2022. The streaming giant has faced doubts over its ability to sustain growth as engagement becomes a key concern for investors, with platforms such as YouTube and TikTok attracting viewers through free, user-generated content that gives them a cost advantage over Netflix. events.title: Living with a stink? Technology might help
events.summary: The operators of Newby Island landfill have been ordered to take action over odours Published 16 October 2026, 00:18 BST Milpitas, an affluent city in California's Silicon Valley tech hub, has an odour problem. For decades, residents have had to endure rank smells wafting from industrial sites, among them a 342-acre landfill. "When I first moved here, I could not open my window for over 10 years," says Chia-Ling Kong, an engineer for a tech firm who lives around half a mile from the dump. While things have got better in recent years, Kong says she and her neighbours must still contend with around "two or three hours of bad smells a day". Perhaps befitting Silicon Valley, the community is putting its hopes in technology. The operators of Newby Island landfill have been ordered by local authorities to use drones and install monitors to systematically track and measure the chemicals responsible for bad odours. They have also been told to automate the collection of landfill gases responsible for smells. Kong is optimistic a data-driven approach will make a difference. "Hopefully with this continuous monitoring, it makes it easier to pinpoint problems at the moment it starts." The operators of the landfill say they are committed to operating it safely and protecting air quality. Just like in Milpitas, where Kong is part of a citizen's campaign against the odours, communities around the world are raising a stink about bad smells making day-to-day life miserable. Sometimes a rubbish dump is to blame, or it might be a sewage treatment works, or a reeking factory. When the complaints start stacking up, resolving them is not always simple. Many countries have no regulations in place dictating how to manage smells. In the US, for example, the Environmental Protection Agency does not regulate environmental odours as a pollutant. This leaves states and local governments to take charge of the issue. Urban sprawl is often part of the problem, bringing communities closer to stinky facilities that may historically have been kept at a distance. This is creating more demand for technologies to monitor and prevent smells. Odour consultant Micheal Bull says people are increasingly concerned about neighbourhood stinks. "You're getting developments being built nearer to odorous processes… as land has become more valuable, there is also infilling," Bull says. He is speaking about his experiences in the UK, but it's a similar story in many parts of the world. Bad smells from waste sites are among the most difficult to resolve The technologies used to tackle industrial pongs generally fall into three categories: they absorb odours; convert them into something less smelly through a chemical reaction; or burn them away. Experts on fixing industrial odours say that the best technologies, when used correctly, can remove 90% or more of the target compounds responsible for smells. But this can be expensive and some operators opt for simpler and cheaper solutions. These include masking odours from landfill or sewage processing by spraying giant quantities of deodorisers. Odour experts contacted for this article were dubious about the effectiveness of such industrial scale air fresheners. "In my view they're not likely to change the odours," says Bull, who likens them to fabric conditioner. Bad smells from waste sites – a common cause of complaints – are among the stinkiest and most difficult to resolve, according to Carlos Diaz, an environmental consultant based in Spain. "Landfill is difficult to treat because you have a very large surface," he says. In some places at least, technology is making a real difference. Residents in Des Moines, Iowa, have long complained of the so-called Eastside Funk, a putrid scent that residents report drifts over parts of the city. A study commissioned by city authorities showed that a trio of industrial meat companies were among culprits. "Within 10 miles, there's about half a million people," says Dalton Jacobus, who works in the Department of Neighborhood Services. "If the winds are out of the wrong direction, 100,000 people can be in the middle of that odour plume." The authorities are now paying around $240,000 (£182,000) a year on technology to track the stink, so they can take action. "What we wanted to do was build a ring of odour monitors around the facilities that we suspected of emitting odours," says Jacobus. The monitors, which measure levels of chemical compounds in the air, work in combination with a weather station to provide real-time data on the concentrations that are coming from each facility based off the wind patterns. This has put an end to finger pointing about who's to blame each time a smell sparks complaints, says Jacobus. "Now we can say with reasonable certainty that 'this odour event did originate from your facility, what was going on'?

events.title: I find it quite demoralising in store - why I do all my shopping online
events.summary: Jess says returning online purchases is less hassle than shopping in person Published 16 October 2026, 00:16 BST Jess Bacon does all her clothes shopping online. As a plus-size woman, she finds the size ranges available in stores unreliable. "The sizing in store is notoriously bad. I find it quite demoralising in store," she says. "The average size woman in the UK is a size 14 or a size 16. I think a lot of people just don't feel seen or represented," says the 29-year-old from Peterborough. Jess, a culture journalist and author, finds shopping online "much quicker than going into a store, paying for parking, trying things on". And she feels posting back items that don't fit is less hassle than returning in store, while frequent visits to her local post office give her "more of a community connection". Jess notes Primark is one of the few High Street retailers where plus-size people can shop. In her experience, Primark stores usually stock up to a size 22. But soon she'll have the option of staying home even for this - as, after years of holding out, Primark now plans to launch a home delivery service in Britain . Even throughout the Covid-19 pandemic, when shops were closed, Primark didn't offer the ability to shop online. In 2022 it launched a click-and-collect service, but shoppers still had to travel for their purchases. The retailer has not said when it expects to launch the service, but has bought a warehouse in Sheffield to enable it to ship products to homes. Analysts say the decision shows Primark is facing major challenges from ultra-fast-fashion brands such as Shein. Online shopping had been on the rise even before the surge seen during the pandemic. Online accounted for 27.3% of all retail sales in August this year, according to the Office for National Statistics, up from 18.1% in August 2019. Internet shopping has also been boosted by the decline of the High Street in many parts of the country, something which Jess has noticed in Peterborough. "We don't have John Lewis [anymore]. There's kind of not that much of a reason to go into town." 'I basically never go into clothes shops' Like Jess, Julia Mitchell, who lives near Chichester, doesn't enjoy in-person clothes shopping. She finds it overstimulating and thinks there are better bargains to be had online. "I basically never go into them [clothes shops]. It's not really something I enjoy," the 32-year-old says. "I guess some people might be able to see stuff and pick it up and look at it, but for me, being able to get the best price is more important." Julia does most of her shopping online, but likes going into book stores Julia, a content creator, tries to shop ethically and most of her purchases are second hand from Vinted. The one thing she never shops online for, though, is books. "The thing about bookshops is that they are cultural spaces and community spaces." Sandra Davies does all her shopping online. She has had three strokes and finds walking to and around stores too much physically. "I've tried it on two occasions but on both times, standing in a queue for over 10 minutes was too much for me and I collapsed." The 61-year-old from Sheffield says waiting for deliveries can be taxing as well, as she worries about missing the postie and having to reschedule. Julie Palmer, a retail analyst, is not surprised that Primark has finally moved into home deliveries as it has evidently recognised that "online sales bring scale". However, she says a shop's returns policy for online purchases can "make or break" it. Many brands offer hassle-free returns, which Palmer says Primark must match in order to compete. "Shoppers want them to be free, simple and quick. That means a generous window, lots of drop-off options and refunds that land within days, not weeks. "When a policy is clunky or slow, customers remember it and shop elsewhere next time." But returns are expensive for retailers. Some, like Asos, have started charging a fee if customers make frequent returns. This is a balancing act, Palmer says, "because a fee can easily push a customer to a competitor". "Most retailers that charge still offer free returns in store, which is a deliberate way to get people through the door and hopefully spending again." events.title: Sandalwood industry left in limbo as WA government mulls new rules
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Sandalwood producers say WA government has left industry in limbo ahead of major rule change Topic: Forestry, Logging and Timber Industry Australian sandalwood oil is a highly valuable commodity, prized in perfumes, cosmetics, and incense around the world. ( ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas ) Western Australia's government is renewing the 2015 Sandalwood Order that governs the state's $40 million native industry. The government has indicated it will reduce wild harvest by 500 tonnes and restructure the industry under the Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions. Existing regulations will continue until the end of the year, with a new Sandalwood order to take effect on January 1. Sandalwood producers in Western Australia say a lack of communication over looming changes to rules governing their lucrative industry has left them in limbo. The native wood, prized for its use in perfumes, cosmetics and incense around the world, can fetch as much as $25,000 a tonne on the open market. Sandalwood is one of the state's oldest export industries, dating back to 1844, and now a major cash crop in the Eastern Goldfields and Wheatbelt. ( Supplied: Battye Library ) Under the current Sandalwood order, in place since 2015, 2,500 tonnes of wild sandalwood can be harvested annually. But with that order due to expire at the end of this year, producers say the government has not been clear enough on what will replace it. Sandalwood harvesting is managed by the Forest Products Commission, but new plans will restructure it under the DBCA. Chief amongst their concerns is a proposed shift in oversight from the Forest Products Commission, the state's dedicated forestry body, to the larger Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions (DBCA), which governs WA's national parks and conservation estate. Michael Matthiessen says many are confused about how the transition to the DBCA is going to work. ( Supplied: Mike Mathieson ) Harvester Michael Matthiessen got into the industry after moving to Kalgoorlie-Boulder, 600km east of Perth, 20 years ago. While in favour of harvest reduction and a greater focus on regeneration, he said the shift to DBCA oversight had not been fully explained, and it was putting the industry in danger. "I definitely think there's a risk to the industry if the transition isn't managed properly," he said. "No one has been asking the questions to myself or other contractors that would give our perspective on the industry. "And what is and isn't important going forward." With sandalwood trees taking upwards of two decades to mature, Mr Matthiessen said harvesters needed to plan years in advance, making uncertainty challenging. "It takes a lot of time, effort, resources and experience to be a really efficient and effective harvesting contractor," he said. "Once it's gone, it's going to be quite difficult to recover." Native sandalwood chips thrive in tough, arid environments. ( ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas ) The ABC asked WA Premier Roger Cook about the industry's concerns and he said the government were stepping through the process carefully. "We're consulting widely and doing some work inside the FPC at the moment just to make sure we've got the best settings," he said. Exporters warn of international impact Exporters share the on-the-ground harvester's concerns. Wescorp Sandalwood executive chair Fleur Coakley said the industry was being left in the dark. "FPC contracts are coming up to finish at the end of December, and none of us knows what's happening beyond that," she said. "If it's not managed well and there isn't that cycle of investment going in … that's what my customers internationally are already concerned about." Sandalwood oil can sell for nearly $2,000 per 100ml. ( ABC Goldfields: Jarrod Lucas ) Ms Coakley recently joined a number of industry stakeholders, backed by the state opposition, to call for greater transparency from the government. "Everyone's not sure whether we invest or whether we start doing plan B," she said. "There's really no clarity at all and no formal announcement for any of us." Ms Coakley is worried that the lack of clarity is creating uncertainty among investors and is worried about the impacts on the international market. She wants the state to take a greater focus on illegal harvesting and regeneration. "We've had different views, different approaches, and there's no continuity of discussing how transitions will happen or how this might work," Ms Coakley said. "Having those different government departments, different ministers, it's really confused all of us.
