events.title: Supercars to return to Phillip Island, plugging hole left by MotoGP exit
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Supercars to return to Phillip Island next year, helping to plug hole left by MotoGP loss Supercars will return to Phillip Island for the first time since 2019 as part of a five-year deal struck by the Victorian government. ( AAP: Dave Hunt ) Supercars will return to Phillip Island for the first time since 2019 as part of a five-year deal with the Victorian government. The event will help offset the $80 million drop in revenue caused by the loss of the MotoGP to Adelaide from next year. The first Supercars event will be held on Phillip Island in 2027. Supercars will return to Phillip Island next year, helping plug an economic gap left by MotoGP's move to Adelaide. Victorian Major Events Minister Anthony Carbines today announced a five-year deal to host a Supercars Championship final series round. It will be the first time since 2019 that the island has hosted Supercars. "We know Supercars fans are wrapped with this news. We know our drivers are wrapped because they love Phillip Island, they love the circuit and they can't wait," Mr Carbines said. "It was critical that we got back out there and made sure we locked in something that was going to make a big difference to the community of Phillip Island and the vast coast, but also to bring Supercars back to the Island." Phillip Island will host its final MotoGP from October 23 to 25. The track has hosted the event since 1989, but lost it to South Australia after the Victorian government rejected a request to move it from Phillip Island to Melbourne's Albert Park. It later lost the Australian round of the FIM Superbike World Championships, which will be held on Phillip Island for the last time in 2027. The loss of the two events has created anxiety in the local business community , which relies heavily on event-driven tourism. Local tourism body Destination Phillip Island says racing is worth $80 million to the local economy. Phillip Island will host a Festival of Motoring in March next year, with Labor and the Coalition both promising to back the event. Opposition major events spokesperson David Southwick today said the Coalition would provide $100,000 to fund the event if it wins November's state election. Victorian opposition major events spokesperson David Southwick and Bass Liberal candidate Rochelle Halstead say the Coalition will back a motoring festival on Phillip Island. ( ABC Gippsland: Madeleine Stuchbery ) "We know the government has announced supercars today from Federation Square," Mr Southwick said on Phillip Island. "They don't care about Bass Coast, they don't care about the island. "We're here today because we care and we know it all starts with homegrown events." Motorsport central to Phillip Island President of the Association of Motoring Clubs Keith Mortimer said motoring culture connected many people to Phillip Island. He said the goal for the next 12 months was to ensure the first motoring festival's success and make sure the event "is here to stay". He said motorsport, whether it's bikes, classic cars, or Supercars, connected many visitors to the island. Keith Mortimer says motorsport connects many visitors to Phillip Island. ( ABC Gippsland: Madeleine Stuchbery ) "There are some wonderful things to see here, around Churchill Island, around the chocolate factories, around the local produce," Mr Mortimer said. "It really does have something for everyone." Destination Phillip Island chief executive Kim Storey said one in four jobs on the island were connected to the visitor economy. She said the five-year commitment will boost confidence in local accommodation, hospitality, retail and tourism. "Supercars represents meaningful progress towards rebuilding major event visitation," she said. "There is still important work ahead to replace lost demand across the year and support the broader economic transition facing Phillip Island and San Remo.

events.title: Rubio urges Lebanon to resist Hezbollah pressure over seized explosives
events.summary: Secretary of State Marco Rubio pressed Lebanon President Joseph Aoun not to return to Hezbollah a truck full of explosives it attempted to smuggle into Beirut several days ago, according to a State Department official and another source with knowledge of the call. Why it matters: The issue is a test case for the Lebanese government's resolve to stand up to Hezbollah and implement its policy of keeping weapons outside the control of state security forces. Driving the news: Lebanese security forces intercepted the truck last week at a checkpoint on the highway connecting the Bekaa Valley to Beirut. The truck was carrying approximately 780 kilograms of explosives, including TNT and C-4, Lebanese officials said. Two suspects were arrested for transporting the shipment. After the arrest , Hezbollah acknowledged that the explosives belonged to them but claimed they were intended for use against the Israeli military in southern Lebanon. Hezbollah's opponents in Lebanon seized on the incident as further proof of the danger of the Shia militia's weapons and its independent military activity. Hezbollah and its allies in Lebanon have since pressed the government to release its two members and return the explosives to the militia. Behind the scenes: The State Department official said Rubio urged Aoun to "hold accountable all those who ordered, financed, and directed the shipment, and underscored that returning explosives to Hezbollah should be out of the question." Aoun assured Rubio that the Lebanese army and security forces are fully implementing decisions to prevent armed displays, confiscate weapons and ammunition, and combat smuggling, the president's office said. Aoun also stressed that the judicial authorities will show no leniency toward those responsible and will enforce the laws without favoritism. "No one will be released unless he is innocent," Aoun told Rubio according to a Lebanese official. The big picture: Rubio also raised Lebanon's 1955 Boycott Law, which bans any contact with Israelis, during the call, the State Department official said. The topic stems from a complaint filed in a Lebanese court against Nada Hamadeh Moawad, Lebanon's ambassador to the United States, when she called her Israeli counterpart Yechiel Leiter after his son was wounded in a West Bank terror attack. Rubio told Aoun this Lebanese law "is routinely used for politicized prosecutions that deter steps towards peace with Israel." State of play: Israel has continued its strikes in southern Lebanon and claims it is targeting Hezbollah targets. Aoun asked Rubio to press Israel to stop these attacks and allow farmers to access their fields without being targeted, his office said. After his call with Aoun, Rubio spoke with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, though the State Department would not comment on the conversation. What to watch: Negotiations between Israel and Lebanon have slowed down ahead of the Israeli elections. The implementation of the U.S.-brokered agreement over the IDF withdrawal from pilot zones in southern Lebanon is also moving slowly. U.S., Lebanese and Israeli military officers are expected to meet at CENTCOM headquarters next week to discuss the implementation.

events.title: New Victorian laws reveal auction reserves, so buyers stop wasting weekends
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Victorian laws force house price transparency in national fight against underquoting Victoria has already had one of the weakest property markets in the country in recent years. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore ) Victoria has introduced new laws to target real estate agents underquoting house prices to try to bring more transparency to the market. Parts of the industry are supportive of the move but say the laws are confusing and inconsistent. Industry figures say the laws do not take into account changing market and auction dynamics, which can significantly move the reserve price. New laws will let prospective homebuyers know the price a seller is willing to say "yes" to. The Victorian laws that took effect at the start of the month are being watched closely nationwide and bring radical transparency before and after sales. Make the reserve price public at least a week before an auction. Publish the sale price for at least 18 months after the sale. Agents use underquoting to artificially increase turnout to auctions by attracting bidders unlikely to be able to afford the property. ( Supplied: Mount Isa City Council ) The laws aim to reduce underquoting, when agents market a property for a price for well below what it is expected to sell for to artificially generate interest in a property. "Victorians are sick of wasting their weekends chasing homes they were never going to get," said state Minister for Consumer Affairs Paul Edbrooke. Paul Edbrooke says Victorians are sick of wasting their time chasing homes they can not afford. ( ABC News ) But Real Estate Institute of Victoria (REIV) chief executive Toby Balazs, who represents agents, opposes the details of the new laws. "If you look at the problem that was trying to be solved, egregious underquoting, and the results — people wasting their time and money on getting things like building reports — that's a good thing," he said. The institute thinks potential buyers should have guidance on the likely range a property will sell, but not the precise figure. Why housing's the great Australian talking point Why are Australians obsessed with property? Because we have to be. And there are big reasons why it's always on our minds. Because most sales campaigns run for a month and the reserve price must be published 7 days before the auction, Mr Balazs argues there is little time to get feedback from potential buyers. "What you're probably going to get is overquoting … because if I [quote] over, it's easier to come down." He argues the seller (otherwise known as the vendor) "has a right to manage what is the sale of, most likely, their biggest asset". Laws with good intent but poor design, expert argues Independent property economist Cameron Kusher is all for crushing the scourge of underquoting, which is generally illegal in Australia . But he does not think these laws will do it. Cameron Kusher says real estate agents do not have a clear picture of the auction a week out, and it will be harder to set an accurate reserve price. ( ABC News: Adam Griffiths ) "Declaring [the reserve] on the morning of, or before the auction commences, is a much better solution than having to declare a week out," he said, because agents and the seller were still understanding who the bidders were likely to be and what they were willing to pay. Cate Bakos, a buyer's advocate in Victoria, agreed and added that, while underquoting was a big problem, the new laws could make things more difficult for both vendors and buyers. "Seven days is a long runway for vendors; I don't think it's enough, and it will make it really stressful for them." She said that, ultimately, real estate agents would still find a way around the rules. Ray White Group managing director Dan White said the new laws were inconsistent and confusing for buyers, vendors and agents. He said the government gave the company conflicting advice on whether the reserve could be changed after it was set. The government did not respond to ABC requests for clarification. "The minister said you can change it, and the cabinet said you can't," Mr White said. Dan White, Cate Bakos and Cameron Kusher all say that a lot can change in the week ahead of an auction from when a reserve price is published. ( ABC News: Michael Coggan ) But, he said, the reserve was only one piece of information and buyers should do their own research. While the new laws mean the property price statement now includes a swathe of facts about the property, Ms Bakos says this could make buyers feel more informed than they really are.

events.title: Reassembling John Travolta's jet down to nuts and 5,400 bolts stage
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts US team arrives on South Coast to reassemble John Travolta's old luxury jet John Travolta's old 707 has been slowly reassembled inside its new hangar in Shellharbour. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) A team of US aviation experts has arrived to reassemble John Travolta's old luxury jet in a NSW museum. The Boeing 707 was transported by ship in May after being donated nearly 10 years ago. Once the wings and tail are attached, local volunteers will restore the plane to the point where it can taxi with tourists on board. They took it apart piece by piece and shipped it across the Pacific Ocean, but John Travolta's Qantas-liveried jet is now in the final nuts-and-bolts stage of its journey at an Australian museum. An American team of aviation experts has arrived to put the old luxury aircraft back together. The movie star donated the famous Boeing 707 to the Historical Aircraft Restoration Society (HARS) in Shellharbour nearly 10 years ago, but mechanical issues prevented it from being flown to Australia. Earlier this year, a team from Worldwide Aircraft Recovery in the United States dismantled the wings and tail, allowing it to be shipped to Port Kembla. Bill Lemieux is part of the American team that has flown to Australia to work on the plane. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) "Both wings are 2,700 bolts per wing, so it's a lot of labour," Worldwide Aircraft Recovery vice president Bill Lemieux said. "You need a couple of cranes and lot of willpower and certain aeroplanes are better than others, but this one's a little tougher. "There's about four different overlaps on the whole wing, so it's got to line up pretty darn close before you get it, and once you start, it works like a zipper, and it zips itself right up." The five-man team will work exclusively on the plane for six weeks. They will also attach the plane's wheels and, if time permits, help with attaching the engines. The organisation is the only one in the US that dismantles, reassembles, and transports aircraft. Thousands of screws that came out of the plane to dismantle it have to be put back in. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) Mr Lemieux said taking the plane apart was more difficult than putting it back together, and the work done at HARS since the plane arrived in May has made his job easier. "That way our time is minimised to just do the big parts, and they did a great job getting everything ready because it's hard to coordinate from the States," he said. "It's been fun, and it's nice to be around people who are appreciative of the job. "Everyone here cares about it, which is nice." Jim Marshall first worked on this exact plane early in his aviation career. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) Despite the repairs and refurbishments, the plane will still not be airworthy. Instead, HARS staff will bring the aircraft back to a point where it can be driven around the tarmac under its own power. "We've spent a lot of time on the interior because it had a bad smell from being closed up on the ship," HARS 707 project engineer Jim Marshall said. "We've tidied it up and done a lot of corrosion work and the paint job is 90 per cent finished." Two cranes were used to hoist the wings of the plane into place before landing gear could be attached. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) Since 2015, HARS has housed a retired Qantas 747, but the jet once owned by the star of Saturday Night Fever and Pulp Fiction is expected to become an equally significant tourist drawcard. It offers a rare insight into the life of the rich and famous and has been fitted with two bedrooms, a shower, a spacious lounge room, and ample plush seating. John Travolta has pledged to return to Shellharbour for the official unveiling of his old aircraft. ( ABC Illawarra: Justin Huntsdale ) Before the movie star owned it, Frank Sinatra regularly hired it. For Mr Marshall, acquiring the plane was a full-circle moment. He worked on the aircraft from 1964 to 1968 as a maintenance engineer in the Qantas hangar in Australia, where it was kept. "It brings back a lot of old memories and all those seats in there, you wonder who's been sitting in them during its life — from Frank Sinatra to John Travolta, who's been on board we don't know, but they would be well-known people," he said. "It means a lot to me because it will probably be the last big job I do. "I look after the Connie [Super Constellation] and the Convair, but this one's going to eclipse them I think. It's a big job but we'll get there." A date for the official unveiling is yet to be announced.

events.title: The cost of insuring against AI company defaults spikes
events.summary: The News More investors are looking to hedge against a potential downturn in the AI boom, driving up the cost of credit default swaps tied to hyperscalers. Investors are piling into the insurance contracts as anxiety grows over the huge amount of capital it will take to scale up artificial intelligence and how quickly the revenue will materialize to support it. The cost of protection on hyperscalers that have taken on the most massive levels of debt is going up the most, including cloud provider CoreWeave, whose debt load has tripled over the past year, and Oracle, whose $160 billion of debt is teetering just above junk-rated status. The cost to insure $1 million of CoreWeave’s bonds against the risk of a default has risen from under $40,000 a year ago for five years to $100,000 today. This week, CoreWeave bond prices fell sharply, causing yields on the debt to top 15%. Its CEO sent a memo to employees saying the market was acting “irrationally.” The cost of hedging against an Oracle default has risen 12% in a week, with a $1 million policy now costing $28,000. Part of investors’ concern about the company is tied to a data-center project in New Mexico that Oracle is building that’s run into setbacks. The company last month informed one of the lenders, including Blue Owl, that it would defer lease payments and other financial obligations tied to the deal if the datacenter fails to come online as planned in 2028. It has already faced regulatory snags and opposition on the ground. Oracle still has to pay some interim costs, as well as the rent for the space. “There’s a derivative market. If you want to make a bet that Microsoft could default and not pay their lease, you can go in the derivative market and do that,” Blue Owl CEO Doug Ostro ver said o n a recent episode of Compound Interest . “We don’t. But it’s available to us.” New debt deals are struggling, too. This week a deal for Volta Infrastructure faltered as investors feeling full-up on data center debt demanded higher yields. Know More Credit default swaps are a financial engineering tool that allows investors to protect themselves against potential defaults, similar to paying a premium on an insurance policy. Should something go awry, the swap would compensate the buyer. Record amounts of debt have been issued over the last year as companies look to rapidly build the infrastructure and compute capacity needed to power the AI boom. That issuance has slowed in recent months, as interest rates are rising and as investors get more selective about who they’re willing to lend to.

events.title: Trump sues California to prevent counting 20,000 voters' ballots
events.summary: The Trump administration is suing California and two election officials over claims that there are suspected ineligible voters who received mail-in ballots for this November's election . Why it matters: The lawsuit is asking the court to prevent about 20,000 voters from having their ballots counted until their citizenship status is confirmed. What they're saying: "State-facilitated voter fraud is unacceptable in the United States of America," Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a press release statement. "If found responsible in a court of law, the State of California will have seriously undermined confidence in our electoral system and violated laws that protect our nation's representative system of government," Blanche said. Zoom in: The Justice Department alleges that California is knowingly allowing noncitizens to vote in the federal elections, according to the lawsuit. The lawsuit says U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services and ICE's investigative arm compiled the list of potentially ineligible voters using agency data and records from the Social Security Administration and State Department. But administration-created lists of potential noncitizens on the voter rolls have been found less than accurate before in Nevada , Pennsylvania and New Jersey . Zoom out: California's top election official and Los Angeles County's election chief received letters two days ago threatening "emergency action." The Justice Department gave Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder/County Clerk Dean Logan a password-protected thumb drive listing more than 20,000 voters and instructed him to verify their citizenship within 48 hours, according to the department's letter and statements. "Maintaining accurate voter registration records is a fundamental responsibility of our office. Our response will be grounded in compliance with federal and state voter registration laws and procedures," Logan said in a statement on social media after the initial letter. Friction point: Federal law restricts systematic voter roll maintenance within 90 days of a federal election — in part to prevent eligible voters from being removed shortly before voting. This litigation also follows legal attempts from the federal government to get California's voter rolls, beyond public lists, which have failed in court. The other side: "This is a sad, desperate attempt by Trump to use his politicized Justice Department to try to suppress California voters just three weeks before Election Day," Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) said in a statement. "The courts have made clear that the federal government has no role in how a state carries out its election process, and now, in the middle of Californians voting, they have asked local officials — who do a damn good job defending democracy — to violate federal law."

events.title: AI Hacks Leave a Mess That AI Companies Aren’t Paying For
events.summary: When Philadelphia police criticized Anthropic last week for submitting a false tip about an unsolved murder, I thought it might become one of the first cases where an AI company faced legal consequences for misconduct by their agents . The incident occurred on July 18, when Anthropic said it was testing its Claude Haiku 4.5 model’s ability to perform “example tasks on randomly selected webpages.” The model was instructed not to “submit anything destructive,” and yet, Claude filed a tip to police looking for information about an ongoing murder investigation. “I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area … during that time period,” Claude wrote. The submission, which didn’t include a name or contact information, landed in a spam folder, and officers didn’t review it until Anthropic discovered the gaffe on September 28 and notified the department October 7. Knowingly providing fictitious information about a crime to police is a misdemeanor in Pennsylvania, but so far, authorities have not pressed charges against Anthropic, and it's unclear if they ever will. Solomon Leach, a spokesperson for the Philadelphia district attorney, says the office “does not comment on whether something is being actively investigated.” Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Despite all the attention paid to OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face and many other examples of AI agent misbehavior that have come to light in recent months, only one major known lawsuit has been filed seeking to hold model makers liable. That case was brought by an advocacy group , rather than a direct hacking victim. AI agents have interfered with hobbyist forums, government websites, and various software tools. The victims have shouldered some costs, including for extra strain on their servers and the time they have expended plugging latent security vulnerabilities. Government regulators, including the European Union, the US Federal Trade Commission, and some US states, are reportedly still investigating OpenAI and Anthropic over the incidents. But a deference across continents toward promoting innovation could enable companies to escape any immediate penalties . When Rick Elrod, a software engineer living in Germany, noticed a URL shortener he helps maintain behaving oddly recently, he called up two security researchers he was friendly with to see if they could diagnose the issue. The researchers found agents from Anthropic and other providers using the service, known as da.gd , to get around rules the AI labs put in place to control their behavior, Elrod says. (For instance, Anthropic says it limits the length of website addresses Claude can visit to prevent it from taking malicious actions by stuffing data onto the end of the URLs.) Da.gd’s investigation and ongoing efforts to prevent further abuse of its tool have taken “a fair bit of time,” says Joe Needleman, one of the security researchers providing pro bono assistance. But he and the others supporting da.gd view the situation as a valuable learning opportunity. “This was eye-opening,” Needleman says, adding that da.gd has “no means and no plans” to seek compensation from Anthropic for the cleanup, since “we saw many agents doing similar activities, not all was attributable to autonomous agents,” and “not all of it was Anthropic alone.” Sellers of cybersecurity tools are eager to pass the buck to the victims. At an event this week hosted by the bug-hunting software developer Snyk, panelists from the startup, one of its investors, OpenAI, and Google all encouraged organizations to use AI agents to shore up their defenses against, well, other AI agents. “We've got to reinvent everything to match machine scale with machine scale,” said Ed Sim, a general partner at Boldstart Ventures. He and others expressed little interest in regulating AI labs. Manoj Nair, chief technology and innovation officer at Snyk, said large businesses patch an average of one bug for every eight they find because of limited human resources. But he said it was imperative for people to hand over some of the bug hunting, fixing, and monitoring to AI agents. “You got to get to a point where you can fix everything, because in the age of agentic hacking, “those 10 things are gonna become 100 things before you know it.” He later added that AI “is not an adversity if you flip it to a strength.” Some companies are responding to the call to arm up. Bank of America announced this week it had hired 1,000 contractors to remediate bugs discovered by AI. Nair said just last week he heard from major corporations who were willing to temporarily shut down their systems to prioritize plugging security holes. Anthropic and OpenAI have said they expect to continue reporting concerning incidents from their own testing. But the companies’ revenues continue to surge , whether it be from attackers or defenders, as consequences prove elusive. This is an edition of the Model Behavior newsletter .

events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Farmers relieved as global sugar prices rally amid key producer Brazil's presidential election The sugar price has risen to over 20 US cents a pound. ( Giulio Saggin, file photo: ABC News ) The raw sugar price hit a 19-month high of 21.10 US cents a pound (30 cents) on October 13. Brazil, the world's largest sugar producer, is in the midst of a presidential election that could further impact global prices. The rally brought relief to Australian farmers, who faced months of uncertainty as input costs rose. Global sugar prices have surged off the back of rising oil costs and political uncertainty in Brazil, bringing relief to struggling Australian farmers. Raw sugar has risen sharply in the past few weeks to reach a 19-month high of 21.10 US cents (30 cents) a pound on Tuesday, after slumping to 13.36 US cents (19 cents) a pound in June. The rally comes as Brazil, the largest producer of sugar in the world, deals with a poorly performing crop and a run-off presidential election that could have widespread implications for several commodities. Bryce MacDonald says the higher prices will relieve some pressure on farmers. ( ABC Rural: Sophie Johnson ) In North Queensland, Canegrowers Tully chairman Bryce Macdonald said the stronger-than-anticipated market had given farmers some breathing room. Bolsonaro defies expectations in Brazil presidential vote Brazilian senator Flávio Bolsonaro has finished ahead of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the country's election, which will go to a run-off. "It will give some comfort to some farmers for those expensive inputs, particularly fuel." But already speculators and future uncertainty were putting the much-needed gains under pressure. Chief executive of Green Pool Commodities, analyst Eder Vieto, said the recent rally was driven by a recent crop report out of Brazil that showed the volume of cane crushed was down, which was expected. The sucrose content refers to the yield of the crop based on how much sugar is recovered during crushing, while the sugar mix is the proportion of a mill's sugarcane processed into raw sugar for food versus ethanol for fuel. How Brazilian politics can hurt Aussie farmers Brazilian politics might be half a world away but that doesn't stop it putting pressure on Aussie farmers. Mr Vieto said heavy rain forecast for October suggested the lower sucrose levels and lower volumes were likely to continue. With low sucrose levels and high oil prices due to conflict in the Middle East, Mr Vieto said it was advantageous for Brazilian mills to make ethanol instead of sugar. "Even if they do manage to extend the crop and crush more cane, that will be done at lower sucrose and sugar mix levels than expected before," he said. With less sugar supplied to the global market, prices lifted, but he said that could change. The price increase has been driven largely by what has been hapenning with the Brazilian crop. ( Supplied by Queensland Sugar Limited ) The first round of the presidential election was narrowly won by right-wing senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who faces incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the run-off. Mr Vieto said government spending and fiscal policy had been a major focus of the presidential campaign. "The next question is, indeed there is a change in power in Brazil from 1st of January … are we going to see a different approach to fuel pricing?" Mr Vieto said. Sugarcane farmers are relieved to see the market rally after months of extremely low prices. ( ABC Far North: Sophie Johnson ) If oil and ethanol prices reached parity, mills would turn their attention back to making sugar, lifting global supply and dropping prices. The Brazilian real strengthened sharply after Bolsonaro's first-round result, while Brazilian shares also rallied. However, as it all plays out in the long term, Innisfail cane farmer Josh Oldarno was hopeful the market strength would hold. "It's got a bit of a way to go, but it's in the right direction, which is a huge positive, " he said.

events.title: The ‘intangible economy’ is making everyone miserable
events.summary: As the economy is increasingly built on intangibles, it may be hard to feel satisfied when so much of what we have is no longer in the physical realm. These are the best of times for Americans – at least economically and at least on paper (in the metaphorical sense of course, since no one uses paper any more). We have never been richer or more prosperous as a nation. Living standards and life expectancy are at all-time highs. Yet, it feels like the economy is broken. What explains this anomaly? Consider how few of the things we own are physical any more. Our economy is increasingly built on intangibles, and it may be hard to feel satisfied when so much of what we have is no longer in the physical realm. Take our wealth. I wrote a few months ago that more young people are investing in the stock market instead of housing. It has been a wise choice: The stock market has offered a higher return and less risk for the past decade. Stock investing does not require a down payment or tie the buyer to a single place in their prime skill-building years. Rising stock values are a big reason why Gen Z is the richest generation for their age. But owning stocks is an intangible form of wealth. You own a share of the US economy, but it is hard to look at Amazon.com Inc and feel as though part of it is yours. More of the American stock market, too, is made up of companies whose value is in their intellectual property, another intangible. Compare this to owning a home. You physically own property. You can put money or even your own labour into renovating your kitchen. You know your neighbours, feel like part of a community and have an interest in investing in both. I do not look at fellow S&P 500 index owners and feel a common sense of purpose, though theoretically I should. The sense of community and belonging has been replaced with social lives that are less tangible as well. More socialisation takes place in the virtual world. We spend less time with other people in person or even on the phone. We buy more online rather than see people and merchandise when we shop. This may leave us feeling more disconnected and lonely, even if we have more connections and can communicate with people all over the world. Our human capital has also become more intangible. More of us work in the services sector and build skills relevant to it, rather than making things. Service jobs often earn more and are less physically arduous, but there is no output from our labour. Even in my own profession, journalists rarely see their ideas on the printed page any more. The premium placed on knowledge work, meanwhile, has contributed to income and wealth inequality. Wages are lower in a physical economy but also less disperse. These shifts may help explain the backlash to data centres. Building factories tends to be popular and seen as a political triumph. Data centres also bring economic benefits to a community as they create construction jobs and are associated with growth. Yet, they have only been met with suspicion. Some of the distrust springs from the belief that they will cause pollution and drive up electricity bills, though there is not much evidence that is true. Another point of friction is their newness and the difficulty of understanding what they produce and to whose benefit, particularly when the fear of job loss to artificial intelligence looms large. Before we go full luddite, quit our jobs and live off the land in Alaska, it is important to remember that the intangible economy is why we are richer and live longer lives. Today’s technological innovations reward knowledge and expertise much more than the tangible world ever valued physical labour. We also do much less physical labour, which is one reason we live longer and healthier lives. So why are the benefits harder to feel good about? We are social creatures who evolved to compete for finite resources. This new world is less zero-sum, since knowledge is infinite, but it leaves us competing for status and attention instead, which can be less satisfying and more ephemeral than a big house or a chunk of gold. It creates new status games, for example on social media, that we cannot ever really win. We also just like stuff. A large, beautiful house may bring more satisfaction than a one-bedroom rental apartment and a US$2 million (S$2.6 million) brokerage account balance. Yet I am optimistic we are not doomed to a life of misery that is devoid of meaning. It just takes time for norms to change. Growing your own food once felt like the most honest work compared with having a boss and working in a factory. We may still have a romantic attachment to the idea of farming, but few people want to be subsistence farmers. What we consider valuable and meaningful is always evolving and sometimes the transition takes time as the economy moves faster than our norms and culture do. This process can be destabilising and isolating.

events.title: US extends sanctions waiver on Russia's Lukoil until 2027
events.summary: The US on Thursday extended a sanctions waiver on Russian oil giant Lukoil , allowing its service operations outside the country to continue until April 2027, the Treasury Department announced. Under the new general licence, Lukoil petrol stations will be able to serve customers until April 25, 2027. This includes petrol stations in the US, the department said. The waiver replaces a previous licence that was set to expire this month. The licence prohibits the “transfer of funds to any person or account located in the Russian Federation”, it reads. It also excludes transactions involving Russia 's central bank, its national wealth fund and the Ministry of Finance. In a separate licence, the Treasury Department also authorised certain transactions for Lukoil Bulgaria's firms in the same time period. The decision comes a week after US President Donald Trump said he had reached a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin that would allow Russia to supply diesel to the US and the global markets. The agreement deepened a rift between the US and its European partners, including Ukraine, and within Mr Trump's Republican Party. Mr Trump said Russia would immediately release 300,000 tonnes of diesel to the US and global markets, with another 500,000 tonnes released in November and a million tonnes “immediately thereafter”. He also said Russia would release three million tonnes of fuel “within a short period of time” depending on the condition of the country's diesel refineries. Oil prices remain high during the seven-month Iran war, as tanker traffic through the Strait of Hormuz is significantly well below its prewar levels and as Iranian attacks continue in the waterway. Futures for Brent global benchmark crude fell 0.27 per cent to settle at $105.8 a barrel on Thursday, with West Texas Intermediate futures gaining 2.76 per cent at $97.71 a barrel. Diesel prices also remained elevated at $6.31 a gallon, compared to the average of $3.65 a gallon at the same time last year. The International Energy Agency's governing board on Thursday said it would quicken the release of more than 20 million barrels of diesel and the remaining volumes of the 400 million barrels of emergency stocks of crude and other oil products previously agreed to in March. The IEA said on Wednesday it expects oil market balances to remain in a deficit well into 2027. “As the remaining buffers in the system continue to erode, in the absence of a resolution to the conflicts in the Middle East, oil markets may experience more turmoil in the months ahead before any eventual surplus emerges in 2027,” it said.

events.title: Amazon devices chief Panos Panay on the importance of failure and bouncing back from it
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Amazon executive Panos Panay has a message for startup founders: Failure is an inevitable, required part of building a successful product. Panay, Amazon SVP of Devices, Alexa, and Leo, shared that advice onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco, drawing on his own experience at Microsoft, where he spent more than 19 years and weathered one particularly expensive failure. “You have to be willing to fail, and actually, not just willing, you actually have to go fail,” Panay said. “If you haven’t failed, you probably haven’t pushed the boundary. It’s literally about harvesting the lessons learned when you fail. You have to be willing to face it, and as you face it, learn from it.” Panay said it’s possible to recover from all sorts of failures, even catastrophic ones, noting that he experienced one himself at Microsoft. He described the launch of the Surface RT, Microsoft’s first tablet computer, as a significant failure during his tenure at the company, one that ultimately led to a nearly $1 billion write-down. “I remember being on the front cover of a newspaper, and it just said failure,” Panay said. “But, here’s the thing, it was easy to admit failure. The trick was, and always is, did you harvest the learnings and understand what happened? All right. What did you learn? Because the failure wasn’t that moment. It was decisions that led up to it two years before that, whether the software wasn’t complete or the inventory was wrong or how we balanced into retail. There were all these steps along the way.” He said founders need to be willing to understand what went wrong, and avoid making excuses, and ultimately accept the failure. “Here’s the other side of it,” he said. “You want to succeed, yeah? You take that failure, but you don’t let go of your vision. That’s it. Surface has done pretty well. You don’t let go of your vision. You don’t break it.” Panay emphasized the importance of staying committed to a vision, learning from experience, and moving quickly. He believes that by embracing failure and learning from setbacks, founders can adapt and make progress faster, even as they encounter new obstacles. “It goes back to the same fundamental, like, have you learned?” he said. “Were you learning along the way? Because if you were learning, then you just change your vector. Usually, it’s not 180 degrees. Usually, it’s just 30 degrees. Take your lessons learned, change a little bit, adapt your vision where it needs to be, and then go. I believe there’s people that hang on too long, but it’s because they haven’t accepted the moment of failure at all.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Steelworkers down tools for last time amid first wave of redundancies
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Whyalla steelworkers down tools for last time amid first wave of redundancies Whyalla steelworker Barry Drage is among more than 250 who have this week lost their jobs. ( ABC News ) Whyalla has many faces, and one of them is Barry Drage's. The 58-year-old steelworker has been employed at the local plant for about two decades in "one fashion or another" — as an industrial cleaner, a labourer, a fitter and a lime kiln attendant. Most recently, he has been a furnace man. Whyalla steelworkers 'stubbornly determined' to keep plant going The closure of the blast furnace at the Whyalla steelworks has not come as a surprise to locals — who say it brings a mix of relief and uncertainty to the regional city's economy and residents. But that fire goes out — in a figurative sense — on Friday. Mr Drage is part of the first wave of workers who have accepted redundancies, following last month's announcement that hundreds of positions at the long-troubled site, on South Australia's upper Eyre Peninsula, would be lost . "Hopefully I can get a job here and stay in my home," the former One Nation candidate said of his immediate future. "If not, I'm moving to Adelaide on a semi-temporary basis, staying at a friend's place, and [will] work there. Whyalla is no stranger to storm and stress. Twice in little more than a decade, its steelworks have been plunged into administration, most recently in February 2025 . Whyalla's workforce has been whittled away by several hundred. ( ABC News: Lincoln Rothall ) In September this year, the state government revealed that the steelworks' blast furnace, which had been shut down for months, would not be restarted — an outcome that placed more than 600 jobs in jeopardy. More than 250 workers are finishing up this week , including Mr Drage, who initially considered redeployment before deciding against it. "By the time the new blast furnace was going to be operational, I was going to be near retirement age anyway," he said. "I didn't think [such a job] was going to suit my body too well, so I thought, 'Well, a good chance to get out'." The body-blow to Whyalla, however, is more difficult to calculate. Barry Drage on his final day of work at the Whyalla steelworks on Friday. ( ABC News ) "I've known a few [workers] who are facing the reality of having to leave, even go up to Roxby Downs for work or even over to WA," Mr Drage said. "If they keep their base here as a FIFO worker, then the town's still got a decent economy. For workers, however, it's not the future of the city that currently matters most — their own lives and livelihoods are the pressing priorities. At an employment event called Employer Connect, which was hosted by a Whyalla hotel, locals gathered on Thursday to explore possible options. "Today was very helpful — I think it's going to help a lot of people decide where their futures might head now," said Jill Allcock, who is an operator at the steelworks' power and services plant. Jill Allcock very much wants to stay in Whyalla. ( ABC News ) Ms Allcock still does not know whether she will keep her job at the steelworks — but her strong preference is to remain in Whyalla, where she has a house and family. "I still need to pay bills and mortgage, and [have] family to help and support." Jeffrey Duance's job as a mechanical engineer at the steelworks' pellet plant will end in a fortnight's time. "For the businesses who are here and the people who are here, they'll struggle — they really will struggle," he said. "One engineering company I know of used to get a lot of work but ever since this happened, their work has just stopped." The steelworks was forced into administration in February 2025. ( ABC News: Lincoln Rothall ) Mr Duance knows what it feels like to have been made redundant — he has been through it, he said, on two previous occasions. He had a message for those experiencing it for the first time. "There is work out there," he said. One option for some is mining — and among those at the Employer Connect event on Thursday was Peter White, who runs NSW-based Specialised Crusher Services. Peter White is the managing director of NSW-based Specialised Crusher Services. ( ABC News ) He said his company, which already has contracts at BHP's Carrapateena and Prominent Hill projects, was looking to further branch into SA. "The beauty of heavy industries is many of the skill sets are transferable," he said. "The safety culture and the principal processes around how work's conducted are readily transferable to the mining industry.

events.title: Targeted ads delivered 0-click exploits to install mercenary malware
events.summary: Researchers say that mercenary hackers laced ads with zero-click exploits that installed sophisticated malware on the devices of targeted individuals when they did nothing other than load a website or open an installed app. The finding, published Thursday by the University of Toronto’s Citizen Lab, said the incident is likely to be the first confirmation of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered through targeted ads. The attacks, which worked on iOS and Android devices, are particularly pernicious because they work without requiring any interaction from the target and are invisible unless users run special forensic hardware or software. Citizen Lab said it confirmed that AdFection, as it named the campaign, infected 45 devices at international media organization Al Jazeera in 2024 and 2025. A clear warning signal “This investigation should … serve as a clear warning signal to news organizations around the world that they may be being actively targeted via this new threat,” Citizen Lab researchers wrote. “This targeting may happen both in newsrooms and to individual journalists, editors, and other staff members.” Their report went on to say: “The distribution of spyware via targeted ads represents a security risk not only for potential victims but also for states and civil society at large.” Read full article Comments

events.title: They asked for 80 homes – she gave them 157! Council-housing miracle named Britain’s best new building
events.summary: Rising from bluebell woodlands and framed by rolling hills, this cluster of pink and brown brick towers in Croydon is a bittersweet winner of the prestigious RIBA Stirling prize If Andy Burnham is looking for inspiration for his great “ council housebuilding comeback ”, he would do well to visit Croydon. There, nestled into a steeply sloping site, sheltered by a canopy of mature trees, stands a cluster of crystalline pink and brown brick towers, where generous flats look on to a landscape of allotments, playgrounds and to the rolling hills of south London beyond. Designed by Mary Duggan Architects, with Ruff Architects, it is a model of council-led housebuilding – so much so that it has also been named this year’s best building in the UK, confounding the bookies’ outsider odds. Only once before has the RIBA Stirling prize ever been awarded to a council housing project, when Goldsmith Street in Norwich scooped the gong in 2019, for its rows of low-energy brick terraces, designed by Mikhail Riches Architects and Cathy Hawley. This year’s winner, Lion Green Road in Coulsdon, is an entirely different animal, and it puts a welcome spotlight back on housing design at a time when the government plans to pump £39bn into the sector. It is also a bittersweet vindication of Croydon council’s erstwhile housebuilding company, Brick by Brick, a bold and sadly brief experiment by the previous Labour administration, which was halted in 2020 when the council went bankrupt, seeing numerous projects cancelled. events.title: Car insurance premiums jump by almost 60 per cent in four years
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Car insurance premiums increase almost by almost 60 per cent in four years Car insurance premiums continue to hike, by nearly 60 per cent over four years in some cases. ( ABC News: Keana Naughton ) Comprehensive car insurance premiums have jumped another 10 per cent after similar hikes last year. It follows an ASIC review that called for more transparency behind insurer calculations. The federal government has called on insurers to step up with fairer pricing and greater transparency. Car insurance premiums continue to increase well beyond inflation as customers who have already endured exponential hikes since 2020 are slugged with another 10 per cent. Comprehensive car insurance for this journalist's station wagon, for example, has just gone up 10 per cent (after a similar increase last year), representing a 57 per cent hike since 2023 when it cost $703. Recently billed $1,110 to insure it for another year, the same car under the same conditions cost just $566 in 2020 — an astonishing 96 per cent increase since the start of the decade that would have been higher without a change of insurer. It follows an ASIC report released in August that found premiums had surged by more than 42 per cent from 2019 to 2024, and a further 8 per cent in the 12 months to July 2025. It also found insurers were not detailing how their premiums were being calculated, and 73 per cent were only giving generic reasons for rate increases. This comprehensive car insurance premium jumped 57 per cent in just four years despite a "platinum" safe driver rating. ( 891 ABC Adelaide: Malcolm Sutton ) Federal Assistant Treasurer and Minister for Financial Services Daniel Mulino said the government had committed $2.4 million to reforms to improve insurer transparency. "I have also called on the industry to step up with fairer pricing, greater transparency, and better value for Australians." An Insurance Council of Australia spokesperson blamed the insurance premiums on the cost of paying claims, which had risen "sharply". She said the average motor claim had increased 32 per cent to $6,266 over the four years to 2026 due to higher vehicle replacement, parts and labour costs, and longer repair times. She said this was "caused by national parts and skills shortages, and the specialised equipment and expertise modern vehicles require". "The Insurance Council has called on governments to regulate the credit hire industry, address repair workforce shortages and require manufacturers to make spare parts available in Australia." The government said it was strengthening skills and training for Australians, having legislated to make its Free TAFE program permanent and deliver at least 100,000 fee-free places annually from 2027. Free TAFE enrolments have already surpassed 850,000 people since the program was launched in 2023. But the Motor Trades Association of Australia last month said the vacancy fill rate for automotive workers was just 48 per cent, and average applicant numbers per job had fallen from 8.2 in 2024 to just three in 2026. It estimated there was a 38,000-person shortfall in automotive trade professionals and technicians. It called for automotive trades to be recognised alongside other "priority occupations" in the wake of Federal Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke's skilled migration changes announced last month . An ASIC spokesperson said "misleading pricing practices that affected the cost of living for Australians were an ASIC enforcement priority" this year. How to avoid paying a 'loyalty tax' for your car insurance Is your car insurance policy due for renewal soon? If you're a loyal customer, your insurer may not be giving you the deal you deserve. It said its 2026 review found that car insurance premiums had increased significantly and most consumers were being given only vague or incomplete information about why. "ASIC's aim through the review was to achieve compliance outcomes across the motor insurance industry by lifting the standard of disclosures and information provided to consumers," the spokesperson said. The ASIC review called on insurers to explain the key factors behind their premiums, why they had changed, and how factors like excess and payment methods affected price. An AAMI spokesperson said premiums were recalculated each year using the most "up-to-date information available at the time of renewal, rather than using or carrying forward the previous year's premium".

events.title: Fired FBI agents sue Kash Patel to get jobs back
events.summary: Nine former FBI agents and intelligence personnel sued the Trump administration Thursday, alleging they were unlawfully fired for working on the investigation into President Trump's handling of classified documents . Why it matters: The agents' bid to regain their jobs adds to a growing number of legal challenges accusing the Trump administration of retaliating against FBI personnel who investigated the president. Driving the news: "Plaintiffs were unlawfully terminated not for any cause or any legitimate reason, but only to satisfy the President's personal vendetta," the 70-page lawsuit says. "As a result of their unlawful and hasty firings, Plaintiffs' investigations were not properly transferred to other FBI Special Agents or Analysts. The impact of these heedless actions on America's national security is immeasurable." All nine plaintiffs are seeking their jobs back. FBI Director Kash Patel , Attorney General Todd Blanche and their agencies are named as defendants. The other side: Patel said in February termination letters that the employees had "exercised poor judgment and a lack of impartiality in carrying out duties, leading to the political weaponization of the government," according to the lawsuit. The FBI did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment on the lawsuit. Zoom in: The lawsuit disputes Patel's accusations, saying none of the plaintiffs had any history of "misconduct or poor behavior while employed with the FBI." None had been internally investigated for wrongdoing, nor were they given the opportunity to explain or appeal their terminations. The lawsuit alleges the firings bypassed FBI policy requiring an administrative inquiry before disciplinary action. The complaint also notes that "[i]n many instances, Plaintiffs' immediate supervisors expressed disbelief and regret that Plaintiffs' FBI careers had been ended." What they're saying: "With over a century of experience among them, these former FBI agents and analysts served our country with honor and distinction," Margaret Donovan of Koskoff, Koskoff & Bieder, a firm representing some of the plaintiffs, told Axios in an emailed statement. "[T]hey investigated leaks of national security and defense information, thwarted threats and attacks from our enemies, and responded to critical incidents like the Boston Marathon bombing, the interdiction of Iranian weaponry intended for the Houthis, and the assassination attempt against then-candidate Donald Trump." "In return for their service, they were fired because they did their jobs, as they always did, to follow the facts and law without bias or favor." Context: Multiple plaintiffs said they were involved in investigating Iranian intelligence threats when they lost their jobs. One, Jeremy Linton, was managing "several dozen" Iranian counterintelligence cases and was fired three days before the U.S. and Israel launched strikes against Iran, without an opportunity to transfer his work or convey intelligence he had received to colleagues. The suit alleges this process endangered American national security. Zoom out: Other fired FBI agents have also sued the administration, alleging they were punished for investigating alleged wrongdoing by the president. In February 2025, a group sued to prohibit the administration from obtaining a list of agents who investigated the Jan. 6 Capitol riot. Agents who investigated Trump's conduct during the 2020 election sued over their firings in March. Three former FBI officials filed a separate lawsuit in September 2025. Mike Rogers brought in $9.6 million, Sen. Susan Collins raised $5.2 million in Maine, Ohio Sen. Jon Husted took in $4.8 million, and Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton raised $18 million. Paxton and Husted in particular demonstrate the GOP disadvantage at the candidate level, although the Republican super PAC spending in Texas and Ohio is intended to counteract it. events.title: Americans open to data centers with guardrails, poll finds
events.summary: AI companies can soften support for statewide data center moratoriums like New York’s by committing to pay for related electricity costs and lessen local environmental impacts, according to a new poll from major firms in both parties. The research was conducted by Fabrizio Ward and Impact Research — run by Trump pollster Tony Fabrizio and Biden pollster John Anzalone, respectively — on behalf of the American Infrastructure Alliance, a coalition of AI companies, private equity firms, and labor unions advocating for “responsible” data center development. Fifty-eight percent of those polled nationwide said they oppose building data centers in their state, according to results shared first with Semafor. But 54% said they would actually support data center construction if companies pledged to cover electricity costs, protect consumers from higher utility bills, and safeguard surrounding environmental resources; 31% still opposed data center construction outright. The poll also found that seven in 10 voters worry that outright moratoriums on AI data centers could lead to China having more control over infrastructure that houses US information. Meanwhile, 64% said they’re concerned that bans will lead to jobs, investment, and economic growth going to other states instead.

events.title: Amazon devices chief Panos Panay sees a future where AI devices replace the need to use apps
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Amazon is placing its bets on ambient computing, not apps, as the future of personal AI. Alongside the launch of the company’s new AI wearables from Bee , Panos Panay, who serves as Amazon’s SVP of Devices, Alexa & Leo, took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt on Thursday to talk more in depth about where he sees personal computing headed. “A lot of times, what you’re doing right now — what we all do right now — is we have to remember what we’re asking our tool to do for us,” Panay began, explaining that this is how we engage with our modern smartphones. “It’s like point, shoot, return,” Panay continued. “I think where we’re headed is a world [that] starts with ambient devices.” By “ambient devices,” he means those that work quietly in the background, using sensors and AI to help you figure out what needs to be done, instead of the other way around, where you’re telling the device what you need to do. “As it works in the background, you’re able to stay more present. You’re able to get more done. You’re about to spend more time with people … you’re not afraid if you miss something. It’s incredibly powerful,” Panay said. Amazon’s biggest entry into this space is the set of new Bee devices it introduced on Thursday, which include a band you can wear on your wrist or detach to wear as a pendant, as well as a new credit-card-sized device that attaches magnetically to the back of your smartphone. These gadgets passively record audio and take notes about your day, finding the to-dos, reminders, and insights you may later need to refer back to. To balance the need to be useful with user privacy, Bee’s devices don’t actually store the raw audio from your conversations; they process the audio in real time and then delete it when done. Transcripts of conversations are encrypted using keys that your device creates and controls. That means no one else, including Amazon employees, can access those files unless you intentionally share them. Panay said that privacy was a key consideration for how these new ambient devices should work. “You have to give customers that control,” he said. “Every product is different, but for Bee specifically, as an example in the ambient space like that, you have to design with privacy in mind. And that’s what we do. That’s critical.” The executive, who came to Amazon after 19 years at Microsoft where he oversaw the development of Surface devices, has spent a lot of his life thinking about how personal computing will evolve. With Bee — and ambient computing more generally — Panay also envisioned a future where the idea of interacting with apps becomes less important, as more tasks are handled via AI. “Do I think we have a future where there’s a bit of a balance — a whole generation that doesn’t say ‘give me the app’ for that, but says it should just understand what I need? Yeah, I do. I think that transformation is coming. I think that is the next generation,” he said. That doesn’t necessarily mean the smartphone itself won’t continue to be an important personal computing device (as much as Amazon would like it to be an Alexa tablet or Echo smart speaker), Panay pointed out. Rather, he believes a new crop of devices will emerge that use sensors to understand users better, and to bring intelligence to the world around you. “I’m not a proponent that says one form factor is going to replace another. I don’t think that’s the case,” he clarified. “I think there’s an intelligence layer that connects it all … and it has to be useful.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission . events.title: Trump administration advances plan for peptide drugs favored by RFK Jr.
events.summary: Federal health officials are moving ahead with plans to broaden access to a class of unproven injectable drugs called peptides WASHINGTON -- U.S. health officials are moving ahead with a plan to allow specialty pharmacies to produce certain peptides , a class of largely unregulated injections that have become popular among followers of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and other wellness influencers. Kennedy's Department of Health and Human Services submitted a peptides “interim access policy” to the White House for review, according to a posting Thursday on a government website. The plan was sent to the Office of Management and Budget, which reviews federal rules and regulations with the potential for significant economic impact. HHS officials did not immediately respond to requests for comment Thursday afternoon. Peptides are the building blocks of more complex proteins, triggering hormones inside the body needed for growth, metabolism and healing. Drug companies have brought several to market as medications, including mainstay treatments for diabetes and weight loss . But the ones at issue here haven’t gone through that rigorous vetting process. Nevertheless, they have gained a foothold among Americans interested in bulking up, looking younger or boosting energy. Those uses are not approved by the Food and Drug Administration and most of the data on peptides comes from animal studies. Before joining the administration, Kennedy publicly declared that “FDA’s war” on peptides and other wellness products would soon end. After becoming health secretary, Kennedy said U.S. compounding pharmacies must be allowed to sell peptides because Americans were increasingly turning to “gray market” peptides made in China and other countries. Those products remain widely available for purchase via online platforms like TikTok. The White House filing doesn’t give specifics of the new policy, but two people familiar with the plan say it is intended to allow pharmacies to temporarily compound some of the most popular peptides, including BPC-157, a chemical promoted to build muscle and heal injuries. The people spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss confidential government deliberations. The update is the latest indication that Kennedy and other Trump administration officials are looking to ease access to unproven products that are popular within the Make America Healthy Again movement. Some of the biggest MAHA figures sell peptide injections and supplements. The FDA previously placed BPC-157 and more than a dozen other injectable peptides on its list of substances that are too risky to be compounded by pharmacies. Possible risks include contamination, allergic reactions and tumor growth, according to the FDA. But earlier this year, Kennedy directed the agency to reconsider a short list of chemicals that have been widely promoted by wellness influencers and fitness celebrities. Teen shooter kills 3 children, 1 teacher at elementary school in Bend, Oregon: Police Woman accused of stabbing husband and son to death at Great Wolf Lodge: Complaint Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded In July, a panel of external FDA advisers recommended the agency drop its restrictions on six of the seven peptides put before them. That recommendation went against the scientific conclusion of FDA’s staff scientists, who reiterated that none of the peptides had been studied enough to establish their safety and effectiveness. The new policy sent to the White House would essentially assure compounding pharmacies — specialty businesses that mix customized medications that aren’t available from traditional drugmakers — that they won't be targeted for producing certain peptides, according to the people familiar with the plan. That approach, known as enforcement discretion, allows the FDA to selectively choose to not enforce some of its own regulations. Formally adding the peptides to FDA's list of drugs that are safe for compounding would require federal rulemaking, a process that could take years and involves multiple rounds of public comment. It was not immediately clear if the administration still plans to pursue that process. The proposal was quickly praised online by some Kennedy allies who sell peptides. “This is huge,” Brigham Buhler, a wellness clinic operator who sells peptides through an online service, posted on X. “This isn’t about whether you’re for or against peptides. It’s about whether you’re for or against MEDICAL FREEDOM.” The panel of outside experts that met in July was selected by Kennedy's health department and included several doctors, pharmacists and consultants who work in the peptide field. The peptide business has caught the attention of major telehealth providers, including Hims & Hers and Noom. Both companies recently announced plans to offer peptides to their customers if the federal government eases access. Wall Street analysts estimate the market could be worth $2 billion to $3 billion.

events.title: Bluesky wants to make it easier to buy, sell, and fundraise on the network
events.summary: Last day to save up to $200 to TechCrunch Founder Summit on Oct. 16. Register now. Disrupt doors open Oct. 13. Get your pass and bring someone with you at 50% off. REGISTER NOW. Bluesky plans to introduce payments in the coming months, a first step in its strategy to make money without relying on advertising. CEO Toni Schneider and COO Rose Wang outlined the plans Thursday at TechCrunch Disrupt , explaining how the company hopes to build on the commerce and fundraising activity already happening on its decentralized social network. “People are actually selling things, fundraising very successfully, supporting each other on the network,” Schneider said. “We want to make that easier, and the way we’re going to do this is if you see something on the network that you like and support, you can support that monetarily, and we want to do it in a way that works for Bluesky and for all the other apps out there as well, so that it works across the entire network.” Schneider, the former CEO of Automattic, took the reins of the company in March after longtime CEO Jay Graber stepped down. He said, while onstage, that he was surprised by the reaction to his appointment, with some users joking that it marked the beginning of the end for the platform. Those comments reflected fears that a leadership change would bring unwanted changes to Bluesky. Schneider said he understands that users can leave Bluesky for another platform if the company introduces features or changes they dislike, a reality that he said keeps the leadership team accountable as it prepares to introduce monetization in the coming months. The executives argued that advertising isn’t the only viable business model for a social network. “I think there’s a story around monetization that feels like advertising is the inevitable thing we have to do that will ruin the network,” Wang said. “What was really promising about having Toni join us is he built at WordPress Automatic a $10 billion business where a billion of it goes back to the parent company and the rest of it goes to the ecosystem.” Wang also pointed to Bluesky’s status as a Public Benefit Corporation (PBC), which she said puts the company’s mission at the center of its business strategy. “Yes, we need to make money, but because of our infrastructure, we cannot lock people in,” Wang said. “And so the thing that really matters for us is the people who are creating value on the networks these days are the ones who are getting the value that is coming in or the money that’s coming in. And I kind of think of it as like feudal society where we’re working for a few landlords and they dictate everything, and then we have to pay up our dues as tariffs.” Bluesky aims to give users ownership of their digital identities and control over their networks while creating a more open internet where value and revenue can flow directly to the people who generate them. “First, we’ll start with payments, but I think it’s about disrupting the actual infrastructure layer, which is what we’re doing, and not just building another app,” Wang said. events.title: Amazon sold light months after being told of fire danger
events.summary: News Home Just In For You Analysis Rural Watch Live Health Indigenous Politics Science Deep Time Elections World Environment Investigations Business Local news Quizzes Sport AFL NRL Football Tennis Cricket Netball Lifestyle Wellbeing Relationships & Family Food & Recipes Personal Finance Home & Garden Entertainment TV & Movies Books Music Pop Culture Arts Amazon removes ceiling light after it catches fire and melts in safety test A ceiling light bought on Amazon Australia caught fire and melted during safety testing. It remained for sale after Amazon was warned, and was removed following ABC questions. The ACCC is backing stronger product-safety obligations for online marketplaces. This ceiling light, bought on Amazon Australia, catches fire during laboratory safety testing, begins to melt, and keeps burning even after the test is over. It was one of dozens of products Lighting Council Australia (LCA) warned Amazon Australia about in June. Yet months later, it was still for sale. The online retailer removed the listing for the $48 LED oyster ceiling light on Thursday, three hours after receiving questions from the ABC. Testing of more than 130 lighting products available through online marketplaces has alarmed the lighting industry. ( Supplied: Lighting Council of Australia ) The incident highlights a broader concern raised repeatedly by CHOICE, Australia's leading consumer advocacy group: shoppers may assume the law prevents unsafe products being sold on online marketplaces, when it does not. LCA chief executive Malcolm Richards commissioned the test after purchasing the LED oyster light from Amazon to determine whether it met Australian safety standards. During one test of its fire-retardant properties, a glow-wire was held to the product for 30 seconds and removed. Under Australian lighting safety standards, plastic subjected to a flame test must self-extinguish within 10 seconds, without flaming material dripping onto and igniting the tissue paper underneath. Mr Richards says he warned Amazon Australia repeatedly. ( ABC News: Tobi Loftus ) The light continued burning for more than 30 seconds after the flame was removed and molten drops burnt the tissue paper, prompting an automatic failure and raising concerns about fire safety. Further tests, conducted by Victorian firm Clevertronics, found live wires were accessible within the product, a safety breach Mr Richards described as "dramatic". "If you unscrew the cover, which a home owner can do, you can touch the 240V as they're not insulated and be killed instantly," he said. Have you been injured by a product sold on an online marketplace? Contact Amy Greenbank at greenbank.amy@protonmail.com or amygreenbank.01 on Signal. In June, LCA conducted wider testing on more than 130 lights bought through online retailers including Amazon, Temu, AliExpress, eBay and Kogan. The peak lighting body found seven in 10 failed to comply with Australian safety standards, and nine in 10 lights purchased from Amazon failed at least one compliance check. Amazon Australia told the LCA in October it had taken steps to remove the products identified as non-compliant. But Mr Richards said about half of the Amazon products were still available, and others had re-emerged under a different listing or seller. Amazon Australia removed the lights from sale on Thursday. ( AAP: Revere Agency ) The former electrician said Australian businesses could spend $20,000 to $50,000 per product line testing and registering lights to meet local requirements, while some overseas sellers on Amazon were flouting those rules and avoiding the compliance costs. In a statement, Amazon said it was in the process of removing the non-compliant items and it required all products sold on its platform to adhere to applicable laws. "We leverage robust seller verification processes, require third-party lab testing to confirm compliance for certain products before they are listed, and employ a variety of additional robust, proactive controls," a spokesperson said. The problem stretches well beyond lighting. CHOICE research found 6 per cent of people who purchased products online in the past two years reported an injury or property damage caused by an unsafe product. It found the sale of unsafe products was "systemic" across major online marketplaces. Amazon removed the non-compliant products identified by CHOICE in June, but the consumer group has already identified others. "We urgently need a general safety provision, to ensure dangerous products never reach shelves in the first place," CHOICE senior campaigns and policy adviser, Bea Sherwood said. The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) said existing product safety laws generally only applied to suppliers who sold their own goods, not online marketplaces. The ACCC is backing reforms including giving the regulator effective enforcement powers irrespective of the method of purchase, a spokesperson said.
