events.title: AMBA C2C: Moving Forward With A Converged AMBA Foundation For C2C Connectivity
events.summary: In this blog post, we introduce AMBA C2C, a new specification being developed with the AMBA ecosystem. It provides a unified and scalable approach to connecting AMBA protocols across chiplets, including AMBA AXI and AMBA CHI. The evolving C2C landscape Chiplet technology and AI are evolving rapidly, bringing new benefits and protocol requirements. AMBA CHI C2C has established strong momentum as a foundational protocol for chiplets and chip-to-chip (C2C) connectivity. It is particularly suited to fully coherent, advanced heterogeneous compute and superchips. However, chiplets span a much wider range of use cases. These include memory expansion, IO and accelerator attach, and advanced heterogeneous systems. Each use case comes with different requirements and trade-offs in functionality, performance, bandwidth efficiency, and implementation complexity. AMBA CHI C2C already supports scalability in implementation complexity through a property negotiation mechanism . Implementations can support only the capabilities they need while preserving interoperability across chiplet types, vendors, and generations. Our continued collaboration with the ecosystem has highlighted an important additional requirement. Many chiplets do not need the full feature set of advanced coherent systems and require an even simpler approach for C2C connectivity. This is particularly important for the vast installed base of AXI-based designs. These designs can benefit from the greater reuse and composability that chiplets enable. This has been an important focus area since we first introduced AMBA CHI C2C in 2023 . At that time, we discussed how C2C connectivity could extend to simpler, often AXI-based use cases. Partner feedback since then has reinforced the need for a unified and converged C2C approach for AMBA protocols. This approach includes both CHI and AXI, rather than separate, protocol-specific point solutions. Introducing AMBA C2C To address these evolving requirements, we are developing AMBA C2C. AMBA C2C builds on the success of AMBA CHI C2C. It provides a converged and scalable C2C foundation across AMBA protocols, including AXI and CHI. At the heart of AMBA C2C is protocol subsetting. Defined subsets enable the protocol feature set and complexity to scale across different use cases. For example, device or accelerator attach subsets can support the simpler requirements aligned with AXI-based IO and non-coherent traffic. More advanced subsets can support the richer functionality required by coherent and heterogeneous systems. AMBA C2C uses defined protocol subsets to scale functionality and implementation complexity across different use cases. These subsets can align with on-chip protocols such as AXI and CHI. AMBA C2C then defines how these protocols are packetized for chip-to-chip transport. The packetization is optimized for each subset while providing a common approach across AXI- and CHI-class traffic. Interoperability remains fundamental to the architecture. AMBA C2C builds on the property negotiation mechanism introduced with AMBA CHI C2C. This mechanism enables implementations with different capabilities to interoperate across chiplet types, vendors, and generations. This includes backwards and forwards compatibility. A layered architecture for an evolving industry An open chiplet ecosystem requires open standards and a clear, layered standardization approach. This includes a clear separation between the protocol and the underlying transport. This is a proven industry model that UCIe and the broader ecosystem have adopted. AMBA CHI C2C, for example, uses UCIe Streaming as discussed in the UCIe 1.1 specification announcement . Similarly, PCIe and CXL protocols can be transported over UCIe. More recently, UALink has adopted a similar layered architecture. It defines a packetization strategy alongside its protocol functionality while separating it from the underlying data-link and physical layers. AMBA C2C follows this same principle. AMBA defines the protocol and packetization mechanism, while transports such as UCIe provide the underlying die-to-die connectivity. This enables AMBA C2C to work with a variety of die-to-die and chip-to-chip transports. More importantly, it provides a clean architectural boundary that enables AMBA protocols and underlying transport technologies to continue evolving at pace. Fig. 1: Transporting AMBA protocols over UCIe with AMBA C2C. For AMBA AXI, this separation is particularly important. AXI is widely adopted across the industry and continues to evolve. However, unlike packet-based protocols, AXI defines interface behavior rather than a native packet format. AXI is also highly configurable, and capabilities vary between implementations. Transporting AXI over a C2C link therefore requires an architectural definition. This definition specifies which AXI semantics are carried and how they are packetized. That definition must evolve alongside AXI itself. Putting it all together AMBA C2C is the next evolution of AMBA’s C2C work. It builds on AMBA CHI C2C and extends the approach to a broader range of AMBA-based chiplet systems. AMBA C2C provides a common foundation that can scale from simple AXI-based designs to advanced, CHI-based fully coherent heterogeneous systems. Interoperability is built into the architecture. AMBA C2C follows the development and licensing model that has supported the AMBA ecosystem for decades. We are developing it in collaboration with industry partners. The specification will be freely available, royalty-free, and architecture-neutral. Over decades, this model has helped establish AMBA as a dependable and trusted industry foundation. It has supported widespread adoption, a thriving ecosystem, and a broad marketplace of compatible solutions. We look forward to continuing our collaboration with the industry to enable an open, interoperable chiplet ecosystem, with AMBA C2C evolving alongside complementary industry standards. The post AMBA C2C: Moving Forward With A Converged AMBA Foundation For C2C Connectivity appeared first on Semiconductor Engineering .

events.title: Why Open-Weight AI Matters
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Local inference and model routing can help manage cost and protect sensitive data, but chip architects must account for memory capacity, sustained performance, changing models, and deployment security. For EDA, model quality depends on clean, trusted design data and integration into workflows, not just on choosing a larger model or fine-tuning its weights. Open weights can reduce dependence on proprietary AI services, but they do not automatically provide open training data, source code, or unrestricted usage rights. Open-weight AI models are creating new challenges for chip architects as rapidly changing workloads strain memory, interconnects, and compute flexibility. The focus is no longer just peak TOPS. The checklist has grown to include the best way to feed memory-hungry models, sustain performance across long-context and multi-agent inference, support rapidly changing numeric formats and sparse computation, and isolate models, data, and tools as part of the security boundary. Model architectures can change in weeks while silicon takes years, so the winners will build adaptable hardware-software platforms, rather than accelerators optimized for a benchmark that may be obsolete before tape-out. Massive data centers are not a prerequisite for AI-driven scientific advances. Science has different infrastructure needs from consumer AI platforms serving millions of users. Open-weight AI models — whose trained parameters are publicly available — can be deployed locally, potentially widening access, improving compute efficiency, and supporting independent research. Open weights also raise questions about control, cost, and who can build on AI technology. Sharad Chole, chief scientist and co-founder at Expedera , said publishing weights can reduce vendor lock-in as it allows users to host a model themselves or choose a service provider. “If you want to use a service, or host it yourself, there is no vendor lock-in in terms of who is providing the next token for you or who is servicing your next request. But there are geopolitical and investment sides to it. There is also a push for open hardware, like what Meta and others do to enable different competing solution providers. As of September 2026, the larger open-weight models come primarily from outside the U.S., either Europe or Asia, and we are moving toward trillion-parameter models.” Open-weight models make trained parameters downloadable, letting users run and adapt them on their own hardware rather than relying on a provider’s API, according to Guillaume Boillet, vice president of strategic marketing at Arteris . “They are not necessarily open source: training data, code and usage rights may remain restricted.” While open-weight AI model releases publish trained parameters, open-source releases aim to publish the full recipe, and closed models publish neither, said Ashish Darbari, CEO of Axiomise . Representative open-weight releases include Meta Llama, Alibaba Qwen, DeepSeek, Mistral, Google Gemma, Microsoft Phi, and OpenAI’s gpt-oss family. OpenAI reports that gpt-oss-120b runs on a single 80 GB GPU and gpt-oss-20b can run on devices with 16 GB of memory; both use MXFP4 quantization, Darbari noted. “These specifications illustrate the widening range of deployment options, but memory fit alone does not establish useful performance.” Some U.S.-based AI companies use knowledge distillation to develop smaller models from larger teacher models, but approaches vary. Smaller models may also be pretrained independently or developed through a mix of techniques. Large-scale pretraining remains computationally intensive, while distillation and post-training are important parts of the model-development process. Chole said the largest models continue to push toward trillion-parameter scales, while models intended for devices or local AI are often distilled into smaller versions. “It’s not like suddenly we’re going to have 100-billion-parameter models breaking all the benchmark records,” he said. He cited an effort to distill a 400-billion-parameter DeepSeek-C model into an 8-billion-parameter Qwen model, while noting that model distillation itself is not new. The broader point is that users now have many choices across model size, capability, and deployment method, and the largest model is not necessarily the right choice for every task. On Hugging Face, the ‘GitHub for AI models’, there have been approximately 250 open-weight models released in the last two years by major companies, not including quantized variants or models from smaller companies, Chole noted. But abundance is not the same as readiness, and turning this expanding model catalog into useful design intelligence requires EDA teams to supply trusted domain data, workflow context and rigorous ground truth. From general-purpose models to EDA workflows Whether commercial or open-source, general-purpose LLMs aren’t built for chip design tasks, according to Thomas Andersen, vice president for AI and machine learning at Synopsys . “A lot of them are very good at common tasks. They’re very good at creating PowerPoints and summarizing things. They’re good at coding, obviously, because there’s a lot of code out there. Those have been optimized to death. They’re not necessarily well suited to hardware development, not even the RTL coding, because even the RTL that’s out there is just not nearly as much as software. Because of that, every party, including EDA vendors and customers, needs to add their data, and that data is obviously proprietary. This is the difference versus all these models that take public knowledge and put it into the training data. There are both pre- and post-training capabilities, even beyond the weights themselves, where you can add data, and that’s an important key point. Otherwise, it just doesn’t work. It’s like asking a chatbot a question. It doesn’t always give the right answer because it has conflicting data, searches the internet, and people say all kinds of things. What’s the ground truth?” Accurate results rely on both the query and the quality of the source data. “The source data itself needs to be very clear, very crisp,” Andersen said. “On the internet, it doesn’t exist. You go on Reddit, people will say five different things when you ask them a question. That becomes the problem of the LLM. In our case, we obviously need very crisp data. In a corporate environment, it’s different. You have much better documentation of processes, of tools, and so on, so it’s a little bit easier. Without that, it doesn’t work. Still, general training of run-of-the-mill models is absolutely required.” That said, open-weight models will have a place in chip design. “An open-weight model simply means you have an LLM model where you can train the weights of the model,” Andersen explained. “Agentic is a loop that sits around this LLM and then does certain tas

events.title: Agentic AI Alters The CPU-GPU Balance
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Agentic AI, reasoning models, mixture-of-expert architectures, and reservoir computing are changing how AI workloads use compute resources. Agentic AI is particularly popular, and because it requires more CPU, CPU supply is coming under pressure. Mixture-of-experts models are becoming very popular, enabling specialized queries that require fewer parameters to load. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and large language models (LLMs) have dominated commercial AI for some time. Proprietary recommender models for companies such as Meta have also had significant societal impact even though only one company employs each such model. GPUs perform the heavy lifting for many of those types of models. But agentic AI needs more orchestration, and that’s a job for CPUs. When AI’s only job is to run a model, it turns to GPUs or dedicated neural processing units (NPUs). Agents still use these models, but each is only part of the solution. Those agents must make decisions based on what the models return, and that requires if-then-else logic, and that’s what CPUs are good at. GPUs, not so much. According to some industry estimates, agentic workloads could alter the ratio of CPUs to GPUs from 1:4 to as low as 1:1. Newer model types are also emerging, most of which are still based on LLM fundamentals. Unlike agentic AI, reasoning models, mixture-of-expert (MoE) models, and reservoir computing still rely on GPUs. But they’re also ripe for use by agents. Pixels and parsing For several years, practical, commercial AI meant CNNs and recurrent neural networks, or RNNs. The former were good at analyzing camera input, while the latter were proficient at analyzing sound and language. The second “L” in LLM means “language,” but LLMs do much more than language today. The notion is that some piece of text is abstracted into a token, and now practically anything can be a token. The benefit of LLMs over RNNs is that they can maintain an arbitrarily long context, making them better at picking the right words when interpreting and generating text. In addition to requiring fewer resources, RNNs can analyze incoming frames of sound immediately without waiting to establish context, improving real-time response. The challenge with early LLMs was that they had one job — to predict a likely next word in a sequence. That word had to make sense syntactically, but not necessarily semantically, and it certainly didn’t check facts to ensure correctness, hence the frequent “hallucinations.” One way to improve that was through retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). Instead of just figuring out a word that could maybe work, models could access “embeddings” that contained real facts, helping generate text that was both syntactically, semantically, and factually correct. Secret agent man Today’s hot topic is, of course, agentic AI. An agent is a new entity, not one that replaces or modifies an LLM (or any other model). It effectively represents a higher level of abstraction, acting as an orchestrator of models. It’s not a model itself, although it must be trained. “There is some new research out there that says agentic inference is going to dwarf everything else put together before it,” said Ed Doe, CEO and co-founder of Delos Data. The whole point of an agent is that it does more than find an answer to a question. It does something with that answer. What it does will likely depend on the answers it’s received so far. In other words, it can send tokens to a model and, when it receives the result, decide what to do next, embarking on a sequence of decisions and actions. A well-trained agent is meant to handle a set of tasks without tight supervision. “If, as a leader, you have to tell your team every step to accomplish, you’re going to be more consumed with every step of the way,” explained Rob Knoth, product management director, digital and signoff group at Cadence . “But if you say, ‘I need you to go over there and get this work done,’ then you can go focus on another task, occasionally looking over to make sure that things are going well.” This is a new space. “Since last year, agentic AI took off,” noted Satadal Bhattacharjee, global head of cloud and AI infrastructure silicon at Arm . “Now you can say, ‘I want to go to Costa Rica for 10 days. I need hotels, car rental, and entry tickets for these parks. Here is my budget. Go and reserve all of that.’ You give it an outline, just like to a travel agent, then the agent calls APIs to take action on your behalf.” A new job for CPUs An agent’s decisions typically involve if-then-else branching, and that’s not what GPUs are good at. CPUs do far better at such decision-heavy code, so they’re becoming a more important part of the computing cluster. For typical LLMs, they mainly serve as hosts, setting things up and managing communication through PCI for things like scale-out. That’s a relatively light CPU load, allowing it to handle host duties for multiple GPUs at the same time. The ratio of CPUs to GPUs will vary by system, but it’s around 1:4 for typical LLMs. With agents, CPUs will be far busier doing actual work (rather than just enabling the GPUs to do work). So while the GPU has been the belle of the ball for a long time, CPUs are getting renewed respect as the CPU: GPU ratio moves closer to 1:1. That will also raise demand for CPUs, which can nudge prices upward. “The challenge used to be how many AI accelerators we can get per CPU,” said Ron Lowman, strategic marketing manager for IP at Synopsys . “With agentic AI, there’s more CPU load demand, and therefore the ratios have changed.” Bhattacharjee agreed. “Demand for CPU has risen a lot because everyone is looking for a lot more compute and in a power-efficient way to run these agents,” he said. “In the last 18 months, everyone is clamoring over agentic AI,” said Yong Meng Sua, CTO at QCI. “This is why CPUs are getting very expensive right now.” “The CPU is back, but is being used in a very different way than it was used in the rest of the data center,” Doe said. Agentic queries are also more compute-intensive because, instead of just one query, sending a request to an agent typically results in many queries as the agent completes its series of tasks. More advanced agents must also understand sequencing, and that can be programmed. “There is a programming part as well,” Arm’s Bhattacharjee said. “You can run JSON scripts to tune it and sequence it. There’s a lot more that can be done with agents.” Show your work The other challenge with early models is that humans can’t understand them. Models are a big cloud of numbers, and no single number can realistically be tied to anything physical or factual. The weights achieved during training aren’t sacrosanct. Training starts with random weights that get refined over many passes. Start with a different random assignment and the training will evolve to a different — and yet still correct — model. events.title: Riots erupt in Albania's capital as students join anti-government movement
events.summary: Riots have broken out during a student demonstration in Albania’s capital Tirana TIRANA, Albania -- Protesters in Albania attacked government buildings, banks, businesses and other sites during riots that lasted more than eight hours across the capital Tirana on Wednesday in a violent escalation of an anti-government movement that has staged rallies for months. Hundreds of youths smashed store fronts, set fires and caused damage to at least four government ministry buildings during running battles with riot police, who used tear gas and water cannon to try and hold back the crowds. Authorities said 23 police officers and six other people were being treated for injuries, while 35 people were detained. President Bajram Begaj condemned the violence and appealed for calm, adding: “The constitution and the law must remain the boundaries for everyone, without exception.” The latest demonstrations, continuing for a second day, were organized by student groups seeking education reforms. But the protesters have joined a broader anti-government campaign opposed to a development project linked to U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner. The so-called flamingo movement is calling for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama over allegations of widespread corruption. The movement earned the name after protesters used signs depicting the pink bird. Rallies staged for months against the proposed coastal project have fueled political tensions in Albania , which is aspiring to join the European Union. It has struggled with repeated bouts of instability since the collapse of a harsh communist regime in the early 1990s. Teen shooter kills 3 children, 1 teacher at elementary school in Bend, Oregon: Police Woman accused of stabbing husband and son to death at Great Wolf Lodge: Complaint Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded On Wednesday, officers in riot gear clashed with youths who dismantled police cordons and set up their own street barricades using burning trash bins. Police struggled to cope with the multiple outbreaks of violence. Health Minister Klodiana Spahiu, who visited the injured officers in hospital, called the violence “intolerable.” The EU delegation in Albania called for a proportionate response from authorities following protest organizers' “allegations of excessive violence by the police against protestors and journalists.” “We express concern on the violent escalation at the protest in Tirana,” the delegation said. “Freedom of assembly and expression are fundamental rights and core European values.” ___ Cimili reported from Pristina, Kosovo, and Gatopoulos reported from Athens, Greece. events.title: How Close Are We To Fully Autonomous Chip Design?
events.summary: Key Takeaways: Autonomous chip design is advancing, but human engineers remain essential — at least for now. Systems companies are pressuring EDA to shorten chip design cycles so they can keep pace with rapidly changing AI workloads. Advanced packaging, physical AI, and digital twins require broader co-analysis and co-design for multiphysics. Sassine Ghazi, president and CEO of Synopsys , sat down with Semiconductor Engineering to discuss how AI is transforming chip design and engineering. What follows are excerpts from a keynote interview at SEMICON West this week, which was conducted before a live audience. SE: The big change over the past year, and really the big story right now, is AI. We’re processing more AI data. Chips need to run faster. They need to run cooler. Do we really need to rethink how we’re developing these chips? Ghazi : Absolutely. Actually, we started talking about how to re-engineer engineering, because you need to co-design and optimize across multiple intersections, starting at the physics level, material, process technology, architecture, design, along with the software and the model itself, because the model itself is what’s defining the workload, and how do you optimize along that stack? SE: So where does AI actually fit into chip design? We’ve been dealing with computational software since what, the 1980s? Ghazi : Yes. Around the 2016 time frame, we introduced reinforcement learning in a number of our technologies and tools to take advantage of a large space of parameters that you need to optimize, and to use AI to assist the human engineer in optimizing that large space. Today, we’ve moved from an assistant to an actual orchestration of multiple task agents. We have more than 40 task agents. Those task agents are experts of the tools, where you feed them all the knowledge, the capabilities that the tools need in order to optimize for a certain outcome. So those are specific task agents. The magic that has happened over the last year or so is the advancement in intelligence and reasoning of these models. You have long-horizon orchestration, where these models can orchestrate multiple agents, and all you have to do is give it an outcome you’re trying to achieve. That’s where we are today. So it is truly amazing the progress that we’ve made. SE: Where do you see this going? We’ve gone from GenAI over the past four years to Agentic AI. What comes next? Ghazi : You can look at it this way. We started from an assistant copilot, to generative capability, to now what we’re describing as long-horizon autonomous agents, where instead of giving a prompt, you give an outcome, and you expect that model is able to reason and trigger actions for multiple agents to achieve that task. So it’s autonomous engineering. Now the question typically comes up then, ‘What happens to the human engineer? What is the role that they play, and is that a risk for the industry?’ Actually, I don’t see it that way at all. Today, there’s a massive demand for more companies to define and specialize silicon, to customize silicon. And if you think about the challenges that the industry is having, it’s the shortage of human engineers to be able to architect, take a spec, define the silicon, and drive toward an outcome. So the whole autonomous orchestration is a very positive thing for the industry, where you still need the human judgment to define the architecture, to guide, and to sign off the final check before you go into product manufacturing. SE: At the Converge conference earlier this year, some of the big chipmakers said that they will be able to develop chips with no human in the loop. Is that realistic? And if so, where does the human play? Is it a matter of, ‘Check this, make sure it’s accurate, it actually works as I expect?’ Ghazi : That’s the ambition. Today, we do have a number of engagements and technologies where you can start with a spec. The spec comes from a system company. The system company can be — think of any hyperscaler, any frontier AI lab, any EV automotive, drone. Think of a system company defining a spec. That spec is based on the end product. At some point, you need to translate it into the electronic spec. Today, we have engagements where the customer can provide a spec to Synopsys Autonomous Agent, and it moves it to a verified RTL, which is the starting point for the chip design. That process used to take many months for many human engineers, to go from the spec to writing the RTL, verifying the RTL, and ensuring that it can be physically implemented and manufactured. So today we have that step being done autonomously. We have it. We have a number of customers engaged in it now. With the intelligence and the reasoning, can it expand into the physical implementation, physical verification, into the sign-off of the chip? I have no doubt we’ll get there. Is this here today? No. Is there an ambition to have more autonomy in that workflow? Absolutely. SE: So do agents now become the new IP? Ghazi : Maybe a different way to ask the question is, ‘What will be the core IP for Synopsys? Is it the tool itself? Is it the agent who is the expert on the tool and needs the tool in order to perform a task?’ So today, the model is fantastic at reasoning and exploring. You still need the tool, i.e., the agent, in order to generate and to validate. Because you can generate an outcome, you can explore many design options and possibilities. But at the end, you have to decide on one implementation that provides the best performance, power, cost, etc. SE: The reason I ask that question is that when Synopsys was developing — and still is developing — IP, almost all of that ended up as custom IP because your customers demanded that it fit into something. events.title: Thermal Co-Simulation Testing Of Co-Packaged Optics
events.summary: By Vladimir Stojanovic and Igor Elkanovich The CPO revolution is at our doorstep. But transforming data center interconnects requires overcoming new challenges in architecture, power delivery, mechanical design, and thermal management. Of these, thermal management has emerged as one of the most critical areas for successfully deploying co-packaged optics (CPO) in hyperscale AI environments. Thermal instability has been a concern for CPO technology. Ayar Labs and Global Unichip Corp. (GUC) jointly conducted thermal co-simulation of the advanced package design and determined the thermal floor map for the package and subsequent chiplets, including air- and liquid-cooled environments. Since thermal stability has been raised as a concern for micro-ring-based CPO, we want to address it head-on. Our co-simulation data show that CPO can operate reliably within the thermal envelope of advanced multi-chip packages. We’re sharing these results to give hyperscalers the confidence to move forward with CPO deployments at scale. Novel design enables over 100 Tbps speeds Let’s start with the new multi-chip package (MCP) design that integrates Ayar Labs’ TeraPHY optical engines into GUC’s advanced packaging and ASIC workflow. The new XPU MCP design replaces traditional electrical interconnects with Ayar Labs’ optical engines, which are attached directly to the MCP organic substrate. This architecture enables a full-duplex optical interface of more than 100 Tbps from the XPU package, an improvement of more than an order of magnitude over current XPUs. UCIe-S provides bandwidth between the optical engines and the I/O chiplets over the MCP substrate. UCIe-A, on the other hand, is used for communication between the I/O chiplet and the main AI die over local silicon interconnect (LSI) bridges. The scale of this design creates thermal challenges we must address. The complete package measures 105mm x 140mm, housing: 2 XPUs (25.69mm x 32.40mm each) 8 HBM4 memory modules 4 I/O chiplets 8 TeraPHY optical engines (12.5mm x 13.0mm each) The +3 kW power envelope in a single package underscores the importance of thermal management and the need for optical engines to operate reliably alongside high-power AI processors. This complex multi-chip architecture requires sophisticated packaging. The design uses a 9-2-9 layer substrate structure to handle the complex routing requirements. The design also addresses signal and power integrity challenges associated with the large-scale package. We perform thermal optimization at the XPU MCP level, while a stiffener design incorporates optical engines’ requirements and enables detachable fiber connections that meet mechanical stress and warpage requirements. What is thermal co-simulation and why is it important? Thermal co-simulation is the combined simulation of electrical behavior and heat flow across a chip. It lets designers predict temperatures, hotspots, and reliability issues in integrated circuits (ICs) and packages under realistic operating conditions. The data ensures the entire system operates within required temperature specifications. This is critical for successful deployment. In GUC’s thermal integrity design flow, we consider every chip’s power maps and perform thermal crosstalk and dynamic thermal co-simulation to ensure the MCP’s thermal integrity from early-stage through sign-off. This allows us to identify local thermal hotspots and the impact of thermal crosstalk on the optical engine. Thermal co-simulation is crucial for GUC’s advanced ASIC workflows. In our joint analysis, the MCP includes multiple chiplets to analyze thermal crosstalk between adjacent chiplet dies. Any heat generated by the entire interposer complex may affect the optical engine’s performance. Thermal modeling is needed to optimize optical engine performance. This joint technical exercise deliberately probes thermal hotspots and thermal crosstalk to evaluate overall CPO thermal stability in a realistic customer package form factor. Rather than avoiding the hard questions, we designed the simulation to stress the system and raise any potential concerns. These findings are invaluable for assessing advanced packaging designs and collaborating with ecosystem partners to design optimal cooling solutions for AI server and switch applications at the most demanding Thermal Design Power levels. This testing allows us to do just that. Thermal co‑sim testing We performed three simulations: an analysis to determine thermal resistance targets for each chip component, plus testing of two different cooling solutions. One solution met spec, and one did not. 3D VC heatsink test We tested a standard air fin heatsink at airspeeds of 5 m/s and 6 m/s at 25ºC. Fig. 1: GUC + Ayar Labs CoWoS-L CPO simulation using heatsink. This did not meet spec, as the temperature significantly exceeded spec for all components except the I/O die. Thermal resistance analysis We analyzed the maximum junction temperature versus resistance curve to determine suitable resistance for the Chip-on-Wafer-on-Substrate with Local Silicon Interconnect (CoWoS-L) advanced packaging and optical engine to meet the temperature spec. Fig. 2: GUC + Ayar Labs CoWoS-L CPO Thermal Resistance (Rsa) analysis. The system-level thermal solution successfully meets the specification when RSA-ASIC is ≤ 0.008 K/W and RSA-OE is ≤ 0.15 K/W. The cold plate design achieves these targets with pressure drops of 11.2 kPa for the ASIC cold plate and 18.8 kPa for the optical engine cold plate. This ensures efficient coolant flow while maintaining thermal performance. Cold plate test Finally, we tested an impingement-type cold plate thermal solution at 4.5 LPM. Fig. 3: GUC + Ayar Labs CoWoS-L CPO simulation using cold plate. This solution did meet spec. All components were below the temperature specifications. Cold plate details We selected the impingement-type cold plate for this application because it enables higher heat flux removal than conventional parallel-channel designs. The design uses optimized fin dimensions (thickness: 0.15mm, height: 2.4mm for the ASIC and 3.0mm for the optical engine) with thermal interface materials (K=5.2 W/mK) to achieve the required thermal performance. This approach effectively dissipates the concentrated heat from multiple high-power chiplets while maintaining the optical engines within their operational temperature limits. Key Results Determined the thermal resistance design targets for each chiplet for thermal sign-off constraints: HBM4 < 95ºC SoC < 125ºC Optical Engine < 100ºC Mapped the location of thermal hotspots. Showed that a traditional air heatsink does not work for this solution. Demonstrated that a real-world liquid cooling device meets the specifications needed. These results point to a significant breakthrough in CPO deployment. events.title: Everyone has the same question in the midterms — where's the beef? (And how much does it cost?)
events.summary: In the midterm elections, meat has become a surprising political battleground In the midterm elections , meat is on the menu. As Democrats and Republicans argue over high prices and the Iran war , they're also having a food fight over who's the most red-blooded carnivore. The latest example came this week in Mississippi, where Democratic Senate candidate Scott Colom released a video with a snippet of Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith saying that if consumers are upset over high beef prices, “you know you have so many proteins to choose from.” The video cuts to a man grilling burgers who says, “Pick another protein? I'd rather pick another senator instead.” The Mississippi race is somewhat unusual because it's the Democrat hammering the Republican over beef. Elsewhere, Republicans have branded Democrats as vegans or otherwise opposed to meat, trying to show that they're culturally out of step with voters, hostile to local cattle industries or just not manly enough. In Texas, Republicans seized on an old interview in which Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico boasted that his campaign, then for the Texas statehouse, was going vegan. Talarico has since been publicly scarfing down barbecue to rebut allegations that his dietary choices mean he's not a real Texan. In Colorado, Republicans have gone after Democratic congressional candidate Manny Rutinel for his activism against meat production and factory farming. In college, he was photographed shirtless with a banner for the People for the Ethical Treatment of Animals around his chest. In 2021, Rutinel founded Climate Refarm, which advocated for cutting down on the use of meat and has signed onto letters advocating for raising taxes on meat and dairy. He also supported a 2024 ballot measure to ban a lamb slaughterhouse in Denver, which failed. Rutinel, 31, is now running against Republican Rep. Gabe Evans in Colorado's 8th district, which includes a vast swath of the northeastern part of the state dotted with ranches, dairy farms and meat processing facilities, including the headquarters of beef production titan JBS Swift. Republicans have hammered Rutinel over advocating veganism, to the point that the conservative media group Daily Wire this week released an undercover video of a campaign official saying Rutinel eats meat “as little as possible.” Rutinel, who's made a point of publicly eating steak tacos on the campaign trail, scoffed at such arguments. “I don't think Coloradans care about what's on my plate, I think they care more about what's on theirs,” Rutinel said in an interview after a recent campaign stop. Evans said the issue goes beyond Rutinel's meal preferences. “I don't care what he eats personally,” Evans said in an interview. “I care that he wants to use the power of the government to make everyone eat that way.” Republicans have gone after two other Democratic House candidates on meat — hammering Lindsay James in Iowa's 2nd district, an area filled with hog farms, for supporting “meatless May” in a 2020 Facebook post, and Amish Shah in Arizona's 1st district for his longstanding vegetarianism and animal rights activism. Teen shooter kills 3 children, 1 teacher at elementary school in Bend, Oregon: Police Woman accused of stabbing husband and son to death at Great Wolf Lodge: Complaint Atlanta school worker dies after falling from Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia Also in Iowa, Republican Senate candidate and current Rep. Ashley Hinson slammed her opponent, state lawmaker Josh Turek, for opposing a bill banning lab-grown meat from being sold in the state. “He’d rather have meat that comes from a lab than from our family farms,” she said at a campaign appearance. Democrats have hammered on meat as well, but mainly just as one of the staples that cost more under Trump, squeezing voters' pocketbooks. Trump has tried to lower prices by opening U.S. markets to beef imports, especially from Argentina, which is governed by a close Trump ally. However, those moves have angered U.S. producers as prices have remained stubbornly high, creating a potential weakness in Republican-leaning states where Democrats hope to gain ground this year. According to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, the average pound of ground beef cost $6.79 last month, up from $5.55 in January of 2025, when Trump returned to office. That was the dynamic that Hyde-Smith, a cattle rancher and former state agriculture commissioner, was addressing in her interview that was clipped in Colom's video. The prosecutor — who also delivers the “pick another senator” line in the spot — is running a longshot challenge in Mississippi. A spokesman for Hyde-Smith's campaign argued that the Democrats deserve blame for high prices. “It is Scott Colom who supports Biden-era policies that drove up inflation,” said Nathan Calvert. Associated Press writer Hannah Fingerhut in Des Moines, Iowa, contributed to this report.

events.title: Oil transfers off India's west coast surge as Gulf shipping congestion worsens
events.summary: Gulf oil producers are pushing tanker transfers as far as India’s coast and slashing prices to keep crude flowing to Asia, as the makeshift export network around Hormuz buckles under congestion and attack . Ship-to-ship transfers in India's Gulf of Kutch reached 82 cargoes in September, equivalent to about 680,000 barrels a day, according to shipping analytics company Vortexa. Refined products accounted for about 65 per cent of the volume, with crude making up the remainder. " Fujairah and Sohar STS zones were handling record volumes with some indications of delays relating to operational limitations, and thus the activity has spilled over to India,” said Varaleka Pant, senior market analyst at energy intelligence firm Vortexa The expansion shows how the workaround sustaining Gulf exports is coming under strain. Producers have shuttled oil through Hormuz before transferring it to supertankers outside the strait, but congestion and longer voyages are tying up vessels and driving up costs. Crude transfers onto very large crude carriers (VLCCs) have held at about 5 million to 7 million barrels a day since September, accounting for 60 to 70 per cent of total Hormuz flows, according to Rystad Energy. The full process, including waiting time, now takes more than a week, compared with five to six days earlier in the conflict. "The overflow has started to move into the Arabian Sea, but it is still small," said Rahul Choudhary, vice president for oil and gas at Rystad. Some supertankers previously used for Saudi transfers are now discharging directly off India's west coast, he said. A recent tanker strike off Fujairah, the first there in six months, has added pressure to disperse operations. Attacks on Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline have further exposed the vulnerability of alternative export routes. Transfers move east The shift towards India is growing, though analysts differ over its scale. South Korea, India, China and Japan took almost 70 per cent of the Kutch volume, according to Vortexa. In one such transfer, a 2 million-barrel cargo of Saudi Arab Medium loaded at Ras Tanura on September 9 was moved onto the Front Forth VLCC tanker off Kutch in late September. It was bound for S-Oil’s Onsan refinery in South Korea, according to Kpler data. Bimco, the shipping industry association, reported a much smaller figure of 12 STS operations in the area in September, based on Signal Ocean data that counts transfers differently from Vortexa’s cargo-based tally. "The Gulf of Oman remains the main area for this," said Niels Rasmussen, Bimco's chief shipping analyst. The increase is unlikely to have changed overall tanker demand significantly, he said, though longer voyages to transfer points mean more ships are needed. Yui Torikata of Kpler cautioned that some eastern transfer arrangements were in place before the recent shift, including Japanese refiners receiving Aramco and Adnoc cargoes off Malaysia. Kpler has yet to establish how much activity has shifted east. Reported tanker activity near Sri Lanka is largely unrelated. Vortexa said vessels there were primarily sanctioned Iranian tankers stranded after discharging pre-blockade cargoes, while Bimco recorded no STS operations off the island. Security versus cost Moving transfers farther from Hormuz reduces the exposure of receiving tankers but does not eliminate the danger of transporting oil out of the Gulf. "The STS transfer itself is relatively low risk. The real risk lies in getting the barrels out of the west of Hormuz to the STS zone” Ms Pant said. Kutch offers relatively calm waters and proximity to Indian refiners, but the cargoes must still pass through contested routes before reaching the transfer point. Buyers could retreat after a security incident on that route, if discounts fail to cover higher freight and STS costs, or if congestion spreads to India, she said. Egypt's Sidi Kerir terminal is the safest place to take delivery, according to Kpler, because receiving tankers can avoid both Hormuz and the Bab Al Mandeb strait. But the journey to Asia takes about 55 days, compared with just over 20 days from the Gulf of Oman, according to Mr Torikata. Disruptions to Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline have also left Japanese-chartered tankers waiting for cargoes there, he said. Japanese refiners, and to a lesser extent South Korean ones, rely on medium-sour crude for blending, limiting their ability to switch suppliers. A Japanese refiner paid a record high price of above $80 million to charter a tanker from the US Gulf Coast to Japan, Mr Torikata said. "If they paid such high [rates] to buy US crude, they would go to Sidi Kerir to buy Arab Light as it takes approximately the same time as sourcing from the US Gulf Coast," he added. Arab Light is also favoured by Japanese refiners over US light sweet oil. Discounts deepen The disruption is dividing Gulf producers between those cutting prices to compensate buyers for transit risks and those able to command premiums for more secure supply. Iraq, which has no export route around Hormuz, offered October-loading Basrah Medium at a discount of $34.50 a barrel and Basrah Heavy at $37, compared with discounts below $30 in August, according to Rystad. The reductions have helped restore Iraqi production to within 10 per cent of pre-war levels, Rystad said. Iraq now pumps almost 70 per cent as much crude as Saudi Arabia, compared with less than 40 per cent before the conflict. Saudi Aramco cut its November Arab Light price for Asian buyers by $3 to $5 a barrel below the Oman/Dubai average, the widest discount since 2020, defying market expectations of an increase. QatarEnergy also cut its November prices by $3, setting Qatar Marine at $8 a barrel below the Oman/Dubai average and Qatar Land at $7.50 below, according to a pricing document. “In the short term, deep discounting of crude is protecting market share more effectively by providing price incentive for buyers to lift crude from the Gulf, but it’s a situational move,” Ms Pant said. Adnoc has taken a different approach, benefiting from its ability to export Murban crude through Fujairah without passing through Hormuz. "Murban carries none of the transit risk the other cuts compensate for," Mr Choudhary said. "It reaches Fujairah by pipeline and loads outside Hormuz, so buyers pay a premium for it." The grade traded as much as $26 a barrel above Dubai swaps in late September before easing to about $15, according to Rystad. For its other grades, Adnoc has used spot tenders rather than resetting official prices, preserving flexibility while testing what buyers will pay, according to Vortexa. The divergence underscores how secure access to export infrastructure has become a competitive advantage, allowing some producers to protect margins while others sacrifice revenue to keep their oil flowing. In a report released on Thursday it said 3.9 per cent of office jobs were vulnerable to artificial intelligence-driven displacement in developed markets in the region, including Hong Kong, Singapore, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, Australia and New Zealand. events.title: What Gulf economies need to watch out for as potential bond crisis looms
events.summary: Much has been heard recently about the risk of a bond market crisis, with US government bond yields this month reaching their highest levels since 2002, and some warning of 6 per cent US Treasury benchmarks. Yields in several advanced economies globally have also hit multi-decade highs on the back on inflation fears amid soaring energy costs. However, a crisis related to investors losing confidence in governments’ ability to control inflation and debt levels is only part of the story. The next bond-market crisis could start with more technical factors, an increase in issuance, a wave of selling that pushes prices lower, sparking further losses and forcing more investors to sell. Investors demand higher returns when inflation threatens to persist, governments borrow heavily or interest rates are expected to remain elevated. But markets can also move for reasons that have little to do with a sudden deterioration in economic fundamentals. When bond prices fall, leveraged investors can face margin calls or tighter financing conditions. Funds may need to sell assets to raise cash, while institutions managing interest-rate exposure adjust their hedges. Those transactions can put further downward pressure on prices, pushing yields higher and generating new losses. In a sufficiently stressed market, even investors who believe government debt will ultimately be repaid may sell simply because they cannot afford to hold their positions. The US Treasury market is particularly important because its securities underpin global borrowing costs, provide collateral for financial transactions and serve as a benchmark for corporate debt. A disorderly sell-off can therefore spread well beyond Washington. The market has already demonstrated its vulnerabilities. During the disruption of March 2020, US Treasuries experienced severe dysfunction despite their status as one of the world's safest and most liquid assets. Meanwhile, the OECD's Global Debt Report 2026 estimates that governments and companies will borrow $29 trillion from markets this year. The growing role of price-sensitive investors, alongside the retreat of central banks from bond holdings, adds to concerns about the market's capacity to absorb shocks. The AI boom could also complicate that equation. Technology companies and infrastructure developers are competing for capital rapidly. Bloomberg reported this month that major AI-related borrowers had issued nearly half a trillion dollars of debt in 2026. The Dallas Federal Reserve estimates that AI-related investment-grade bond issuance could reach about $300 billion this year, adding significant long-term borrowing to US financial markets . If borrowing rises sharply to finance data centres and other AI infrastructure, investors may demand higher returns, particularly if future revenues appear insufficient to justify the investment. A deterioration in profitability expectations could also undermine the value of AI-related debt, reduce financing and force companies to postpone projects, with losses and tighter credit conditions spilling into other markets. The interaction with government borrowing matters. Heavy Treasury issuance, substantial corporate financing needs and a reassessment of AI investment returns could coincide, putting pressure on all borrowing costs. If that happened alongside leveraged positions being unwound, an initial repricing could become more disruptive. A sharp reversal in the yen carry trade could amplify this dynamic for example, while higher Japanese bond yields may encourage domestic investors to repatriate funds rather than buy US Treasuries. For Gulf economies, the implications extend beyond investment portfolios. US Treasury yields influence international borrowing costs, and a sustained increase can make it more expensive for regional governments and companies to issue debt, refinance obligations and finance infrastructure and economic diversification projects. The effect is direct for Gulf economies whose currencies are pegged to the US dollar, because their monetary conditions are closely influenced by US interest rates. Gulf governments and investors are committing resources to data centres, computing capacity and digital infrastructure. If markets begin to question the returns on AI investment, financing conditions could tighten just as regional projects require more capital. That would not necessarily derail these ambitions. Strong sovereign balance sheets and long investment horizons provide resilience. But higher funding costs and a more selective investor base could change the economics of specific projects. AI could also generate substantial productivity gains, while higher bond yields can attract buyers and eventually stabilise prices. Neither heavy borrowing nor market volatility alone signals a systemic crisis. But the real concern is the possibility that several pressures coincide: heavy government issuance, rising corporate borrowing, doubts about AI returns and leveraged investors forced to unwind positions. For policymakers and investors, the priority should be to monitor market functioning as well as headline yields. Are transactions becoming harder to execute? Are funding pressures rising? Are investors demanding larger premiums to hold assets that would ordinarily be considered liquid? The next bond-market crisis, if and when it comes, may not begin when investors decide governments are insolvent. It may begin when a crowded financing cycle meets a sudden reassessment of risk, and investors who believe in the underlying assets still find themselves forced to sell.

events.summary: Finance ministers gathering for the IMF annual meeting know the need for multilateral cooperation to deal with many crises. Businesses and consumers are feeling the effects of a serious energy shock. Rising inflation has made it a lot more expensive for governments to finance their debts. events.title: The Nordics and NVIDIA Show What’s Possible When a Region Commits to Advanced Computing
events.summary: The Nordic countries have become the European leader in unicorn startup density, producing the most emerging companies valued at $1 billion or more per capita on the continent. Now, a new chapter for the region is unfolding as countries race to build one of Europe’s most consequential technology ecosystems. The many computing advancements already underway in the Nordics, combined with the opportunity that lies ahead, signal a region moving from ambition to application. NVIDIA’s Investments in the Nordics Over the past year, NVIDIA has invested in the technology ecosystem in the Nordics, including Sweden’s leading startups Lovable and Legora. Lovable , a Stockholm-based startup, provides a software creation platform that enables anyone to build and run software using plain language. In collaboration with NVIDIA, Lovable is optimizing inference for open models and training its models using NVIDIA Dynamo software and Nemotron tools. Legora provides an agentic operating system for legal work, supporting lawyers in research, review and drafting across complex matters. Nordics Emerge as Infrastructure Hub The foundation for establishing the Nordics as a technology powerhouse is already being built and the region holds a structural advantage: abundant renewable energy, rigorous data governance and a research tradition that bridges academia and industry. The Nordics are one of Europe’s fastest growing hubs for infrastructure. AI clouds are expanding with a projected 1 gigawatts of capacity to be deployed across the region by the end of 2027. Among these cloud providers are Bitdeer, CoreWeave , Crusoe , Hyperstack, Nscale , Verda and Volta . In Sweden, a consortium anchored by Ericsson, AstraZeneca, Saab, SEB and Wallenberg Investments, with SKF as strategic partner, launched Sferical One — a shared supercomputer running on two NVIDIA DGX SuperPODs with 16 racks of NVIDIA DGX GB300 systems and 1,152 GPUs. The consortium will build services using NVIDIA Nemotron open models, which allow researchers to customize and deploy their models in a secure environment. Some of the Nordics’ leading technology companies are now building proprietary intelligence on NVIDIA infrastructure. Spotify , which personalizes music, podcasts and audiobooks for hundreds of millions of listeners, uses NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM inference software to run AI-powered podcast recommendations faster and cheaper at scale. The deployment is a case study in inference efficiency: delivering the same recommendations to a global audience at a lower cost per query. ABB Robotics developed RobotStudio HyperReality using NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to bridge the gap between robot simulations and real-world performance. By combining NVIDIA’s advanced simulation capabilities with ABB Robotics’ virtual controller, running the same firmware as its physical robots, the solution enables engineers to train, test and validate robots virtually, while using real-world data to continuously improve the digital model. According to ABB Robotics, the solution delivers up to 99% simulation accuracy and reduces commissioning time by up to 80%. Finnish telecom company Elisa is launching a beta of Moontalk AIRI, a real-time enterprise agentic assistant that retrieves information, captures insights and documents decisions during meetings and calls. Built on NVIDIA Nemotron open models and distributed infrastructure, it uses company data and low-latency networking to deliver fast, context-aware responses. Sweden’s startup ecosystem raised $2.8 billion in the first half of 2026 and is projected to reach $5 billion for the year. This next generation is building fast — and on open models. Stilta is reinventing how companies protect their inventions with intellectual property. The Stockholm-based startup is post-training NVIDIA Nemotron open models to scale patent analysis from a single patent to entire portfolios — work that was previously out of reach. Nemotron gives Stilta the language model accuracy for continuous portfolio monitoring at scale, across the thousands of patents that large industrial and technology companies hold. ConfidentialMind’s SampoTron , built on NVIDIA Nemotron-3-Embed, delivers more than 20% improvement in cross-lingual retrieval accuracy across English, Finnish and Swedish. Agaton , a platform that analyzes customer conversations in real time, is using NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning to speed up Revenue Mining solution on live sales calls. By routing knowledge retrieval to Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, Agaton can cut response latency to deliver fast responses that inform customers’ buying decisions. Klang , a Swedish speech lab, fine-tuned the NVIDIA Parakeet v3 model to create Pianissimo — a Swedish transcription model that reduces errors by 75% while being 64x faster than the most accurate alternative. Built on over 50,000 hours of Swedish speech using the open source NVIDIA NeMo framework, the model is freely available on Hugging Face. Embedl , founded in Gothenburg and a member of the NVIDIA Inception program for cutting-edge startups, and Space Cargo Unlimited unveiled an onboard prototype that monitors protein crystallization, flags anomalies and recommends actions on a single NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX module, without continuous ground connectivity. Sweden AI Factory — one of Europe’s 19 EuroHPC-funded AI factories — announced a collaboration with NVIDIA to open its infrastructure and expertise to Inception startups and small- and medium-sized enterprises across industries, including life and material sciences, autonomous systems and gaming. Autonomous Machines on Nordic Roads and Factory Floors In Sweden, advanced computing is also powering vehicles on the road and machines in factories. Volvo Cars is combining its industry-leading vehicle safety systems and engineering expertise with NVIDIA Hyperion , Halos OS and Alpamayo Stack to enable future Volvo cars to safely navigate complex real-world environments from door to door. Autonomous freight company Einride is building its next-generation Einride Driver on NVIDIA Hyperion for autonomous freight trucks, using the NVIDIA Halos safety system and NVIDIA Cosmos open world models. Meanwhile, Toyota Material Handling Europe — the world’s leading forklift manufacturer — is bringing autonomous machines to factory floors. In a collaboration with NVIDIA and SoftServe, Toyota Material Handling Europe is adopting a simulation-first approach to autonomous material handling, cutting autonomous solution deployment time by up to 50% across its global engineering, manufacturing and innovation teams. Norrsken Foundation and NVIDIA are opening the Stockholm AI Lab, a physical hub for AI-native founders working on global challenges, set to open in 2027. Quantum Meets Accelerated Computing Finally, Swedish companies are advancing quantum research using NVIDIA’s quantum computing platform.

events.title: Asian markets fall on tech stock rout as high US inflation weighs on Wall Street
events.summary: Asian markets fell on Thursday, as artificial intelligence-related stocks plunged after a drop on Wall Street, fuelled by concerns about rising competition and profit growth in the chips sector. South Korea's Kospi slumped more than 7 per cent, while Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 index was down 5.12 per cent at midday local time on Thursday. Hong Kong's Hang Seng index dropped by 1 per cent, while China's Shanghai Composite Index fell 1.75 per cent. Asian markets are dealing with "not just the deeper sell-off in AI-related stocks but also the tightening of financial conditions that comes from higher yields and a higher US dollar", said Kyle Rodda, senior financial market analyst at Capital.com. In its report on Thursday, the International Monetary Fund also warned of the Asia region's heavy reliance on the AI boom. Strong global demand for semiconductors, AI infrastructure and related technology products has boosted exports and investment, particularly in economies integrated into technology supply chains. "The AI-driven technology boom has provided an important offset for economies in East and South-East Asia, although the evolution of AI investment and its long-term economic effects are uncertain," the fund said in a report on the outlook for the Asia-Pacific region. "A correction in AI-related investment or asset valuations could weigh disproportionately on Asia given its central role in global technology supply chains," it added. The IMF also said uncertainty over US monetary policy could keep Asian financial markets volatile. Overnight, stocks on Wall Street dropped as consumer price inflation rose more than expected in September. "Wall Street tumbled on further evidence that inflation in the United States is sticky, while a pullback in chip stocks on fears about rising competition and peak profit growth added to the woes," Mr Rodda said. The inflation figures were the "critical driver of markets in US trade", he added. US inflation rose to 3.7 per cent annually in September, above both the 3.6 per cent forecast for the month and August’s 3.4 per cent. Core inflation also was higher than expected, at 2.6 per cent year-on-year. "US stocks sold off as higher-rate expectations returned to the fore, with the S&P 500 recording its weakest session since late July and the Nasdaq hit harder by pressure on chip names," said Daniel Richards, senior economist at Emirates NBD. "The risk-off move extended into Asia, where falls in Japan and Korea this morning were much sharper." The US inflation data now points to a higher chance of a rate hike by the US Federal Reserve, Mr Rodda said.

events.title: IMF official says Iran war price shock buffers are narrowing
events.summary: A senior International Monetary Fund official has said prewar buffers are helping countries in the Middle East to limit the economic impact of the Iran war, but the region's outlook remains highly uncertain as it faces threats of renewed disruption. The prolonged closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world's energy supplies was shipped before the war, has rattled markets, as have Iranian attacks on vessels in the waterway and key sites in neighbouring countries. “The impact was more contained than the scale initially suggested,” the fund's regional director, Jihad Azour, told reporters during the IMF and World Bank annual meetings in Thailand. While the price of Brent crude is 47 per cent higher than its prewar levels, it has yet to hit the $200-a-barrel mark that was previously feared. The IMF this week maintained its 2026 global growth projection at 3.1 per cent and slightly raised its 2027 forecast to 3.4 per cent. Higher oil prices were partially attributed to the fund lifting its 2026 inflation forecast to 4.7 per cent. The UAE and Saudi Arabia have been exploring alternatives to send their supplies to markets, while International Energy Agency members agreed in March to release up to 400 million barrels of reserve stocks. Output from non-Gulf producers and an adjustment in energy demand have also mitigated the war's impact, Mr Azour said. “These buffers bought time, but they are finite. Inventories are lower, spare capacity is tighter, and renewed disruption could generate much larger price adjustments,” he explained. Iranian attacks continued in the Strait of Hormuz this week. At least 12 tankers have been attacked in and around the waterway in the past week, according to the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency. On Wednesday, Iran-backed Houthi rebels attacked Saudi Aramco's headquarters . Authorities said no casualties were reported. Meanwhile, a cargo ship sank after hitting a naval mine in the Strait of Hormuz , Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy said in a statement. The IEA said crude oil exports from Gulf producers, led by Saudi Arabia, jumped by 4.4 million barrels a day in September to reach more than 75 per cent of prewar levels. Iran's escalatory attacks on Saudi Arabia and tanker traffic threaten to derail those gains, the agency said. Brent crude rose 0.36 per cent at $106.1 a barrel on Wednesday, while West Texas Intermediate, which tracks US crude, rose 1.08 per cent at $95.16 a barrel. The IMF said its 2026 forecasts show a sharp divergence for oil exporters and importers, with the latter being assisted by remittances, tourism and government support. Regional economies are forecast to see a sharp divergence in trends due to the war. The IMF projected economic contractions of 11.3 per cent for Bahrain, 16 per cent for Iraq, 16.7 per cent for Kuwait, 15.6 per cent for Qatar , 3.3 per cent for Saudi Arabia and 3.9 per cent for the UAE this year. Growth is expected to rebound in 2027, but the conflict has inflicted a "long-lasting scarring impact" on regional economies, Mr Azour told journalists on Thursday. The economic recovery will take time and will require additional spending on infrastructure to boost resilience. "If we compare to the [growth] trajectory before the war, in 2030, we will be below it," he said. A more prolonged conflict remains the most significant risk for the region's highly uncertain outlook, with further disruptions likely to weaken economic activity, inflame inflationary pressures and place extra strain on fiscal positions across the region, he said. Mr Azour also said tighter financial conditions could deepen vulnerabilities in economies with large sovereign financing needs. He urged the region's economies to prioritise price stability, rebuild their fiscal buffers and build capacity to withstand future shocks. The IMF will release its outlook for the Middle East next week in Dubai. On Wednesday, UAE central bank governor Khaled Balama noted the region's experiences have shown that resilience depends on how quickly economies adapt to changing circumstances while building their fiscal buffers, state news agency Wam reported. Mr Balama was addressing the region's central bankers and finance ministers during a meeting alongside the IMF and World Bank gathering in Bangkok. He also said the UAE economy has shown resilience, supported by its robust fiscal buffers, low levels of public debt and its vast sovereign assets, helping to reinforce investor and market confidence. He also emphasised the importance of strengthening international co-operation frameworks amid geopolitical tension. Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al Jadaan was due to hold a media conference with IMF managing director Kristalina Georgieva on Saturday. The International Monetary Finance Committee, which is the fund's policy advisory panel, announced this week it had extended Mr Al Jadaan's position as IMFC chair by another year after his term ends on January 3, 2027.

events.title: A perfect storm: how the super El Niño is devastating the fishing industry
events.summary: Peru’s anchoveta have made up about a 10th of the entire global commercial fishing catch since 1970, more than any other fish. A combination of warming seas and decades-long overfishing spells disaster On 10 June 2026, the government of Peru made a decision that it knew would hurt one of the world’s major fishing industries. It stopped all anchoveta fishing boats from going out to sea, suspending the fishing season. At first the order was temporary, but in mid-August, the suspension turned into a total closure . This was no easy call. For one thing, it was a brutal blow to the Peruvian economy. Peruvian anchovies – the scientific name is Engraulis ringens – are not the salty, punch-packing little fillets in a puttanesca sauce or caesar salad dressing. That is a different species – Engraulis encrasicolus – which is smaller, tastier and found mostly in the eastern Atlantic and the Mediterranean. Only a small part of Peru’s anchoveta catch is eaten in fish form. The rest – more than 90% – is immediately processed as fishmeal and fish oil, packed in sacks and barrels, and shipped to fish, shellfish and seaweed farms, factory farms and nutritional supplement producers around the world. events.title: Roller coaster rider's death puts spotlight on the safety of ever more thrilling rides
events.summary: A man's death on a Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia has raised questions about ride safety and regulation The horrific death of a man who was ejected from a Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia is drawing attention to the safety of amusement park rides that have become increasingly faster and steeper in their quest for the biggest thrill. Fatal roller coaster accidents are extremely rare, and Georgia officials have said little about why Hassan Jihad Ibn Kariem, a 42-year-old school employee from Atlanta, was thrown from his seat on Monday while riding the Goliath at Six Flags Over Georgia, striking other patrons before falling below the ride. Four other passengers, all minors, suffered injuries that were not life-threatening, Cobb County police said. Goliath sends riders plunging from 200 feet (61 meters) at speeds reaching 70 mph (112 kph). Rather than upside-down loops and corkscrews, the two-decade-old coaster focuses on velocity and downhill plunges. Six Flags temporarily closed nine similar coasters across North America as a precaution. The ride's manufacturer, Bolliger & Mabillard, said it was “actively investigating the incident and will not comment further until we have a better understanding of what happened.” To his family, Kariem was a beloved and intelligent man who died during an outing with people he loved. “He was just a great, smart guy,” said She Robinson, who identified herself as Kariem’s cousin. “He was a gentle giant that everybody loved.” He loved Atlanta and Six Flags Over Georgia, Robinson said, and was visiting the park Monday with his significant other, her daughter and her niece, Robinson said. Another cousin, Kelvin Johnson, described Kariem as kind and considerate. “He’s just a very helpful, positive kind of person," Johnson said. "He’s that person that would step up first to volunteer for anything.” The federal government does not regulate roller coasters at major amusement parks. Instead, oversight falls to states, creating what some call a patchwork of rules that range from strict regulations to minimal oversight. U.S. Sen. Ed Markey of Massachusetts has repeatedly sought to close what he calls a federal safety “loophole” that allows the Consumer Product Safety Commission to regulate traveling carnival rides but not stationary attractions at major parks. Georgia’s Office of Insurance and Safety Fire Commissioner, which oversees annual ride inspections, is “conducting an in‑depth and comprehensive review” of Monday's death, said Garrison Bennett, a spokesperson. Amusement parks worldwide generally adhere to what are known as ASTM standards set by industry experts, which cover everything from ride design and construction to how much acceleration and force each rider is allowed to experience. The industry has multiple layers of inspection, said Dennis Speigel, a theme park consultant and past president of the International Association of Amusement Parks and Attractions, a trade group. Park operators are under pressure from insurance carriers that could face a hefty payout if something goes wrong. “With the checks and balances that are put in place, theme parks are really one of the safest places to be on the planet,” he said Tuesday. Industry figures show 1.27 serious and reportable injuries per million roller coaster rides in 2024. Across all amusement park rides, the trade group said “guest behavior” contributed to 66% of the injuries that year, with 15% due to technical factors and 9% to operational factors. Teen shooter kills 3 children, 1 teacher at elementary school in Bend, Oregon: Police Woman accused of stabbing husband and son to death at Great Wolf Lodge: Complaint Atlanta school worker dies after falling from Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia The trade group's current president, Jakob Wahl, offered condolences to Kariem's family Wednesday. Martin Lewison, a roller coaster expert and a professor at Farmingdale State College, said it was difficult to imagine there being a mechanical malfunction on a roller coaster such as Goliath because of its design. The ride features a pull-down lap restraint called a “clamshell” that works with a ratchet mechanism that makes clicking sounds as you press it down over your hips. They have multiple disks to ensure redundancy if one fails, Lewison said. “They’re dependable. They’re not so technically advanced that theme parks have difficulty with operations,” Lewison said. The operator then has a safety system that displays a green “go” light for every seat on the train before it can be dispatched. The train should theoretically not be allowed to proceed unless all restraints are locked, Lewison said. In 2022, a 14-year-old Missouri boy fell to his death from an Orlando amusement park ride when the harness didn't lock properly due to his size. In 2013, a 52-year-old Dallas woman was killed when she slipped from her seat on the Texas Giant ride at Six Flags Over Texas.
