events.title: Netflix to shed 1,000 jobs in steepest cuts since 2022
events.summary: Netflix has said it will cut 1,000 jobs globally as the streaming giant faces competition from rivals. The cuts - the steepest since 2022 - will mainly affect its human resources, legal, product and technology teams and equates to around 6% of its total workforce. Last month, Netflix 's co-chief executive, Ted Sarandos, told the Bloomberg Screentime summit that the company was "not growing as fast as I want us to". The streaming industry is going through a period of consolidation following Paramount's $110bn (£83.6bn) merger with Warner Bros, the owner of HBO, while free platforms such as YouTube and TikTok continue to attract viewers. In an email to staff, Sarandos and co-chief executive Greg Peters said Netflix would "continue to invest aggressively in high-impact areas to improve our service and further drive growth and innovation". Netflix had come close to its own deal with Warner Bros but was outbid in the end by Paramount . Commenting on the "organisational changes", Sarandos and Peters said: "Our mission - to entertain the world - is ambitious, and delivering on it requires us to be disciplined about where we prioritise our people and resources." Managers will tell employees whether their job has been cut "soon". TV series Below, starring Josh Hartnett, is one of Netflix's most popular shows The email added that the firm was on track to meet its financial forecasts. The streaming service is due to report its latest results on 20 October. Investors have been weighing up user engagement - the amount of time customers spend on Netflix - as it competes with platforms such as YouTube and TikTok. The firm has continued to commission shows - its most popular at the moment is "Below", an underwater mystery series. It has also been attempting to expand its business, including gaming and allowing adverts to play before and during shows and films. However, "they haven't been able to find another line of major revenue," said Ross Benes, senior analyst at eMarketer. He added that the company remains reliant on a subscription business that could be approaching a plateau. "Eventually, because they're nearing a ceiling with that, they'll need another revenue stream to diversify, and that's where it's been more of a struggle," he said. The last major redundancy round at Netflix was in 2022, when it cut about 450 jobs after losing subscribers for the first time in more than a decade. Are you affected by issues covered in this story? events.title: Aldar to launch major Dubai villa and townhouse project by end of year
events.summary: Aldar plans to launch a major development of villas and townhouses in Dubai by the end of this year as part of the company’s expansion across the UAE. The new project, whose value is not disclosed, will be built near Dubai Silicon Oasis, Aldar Development's chief executive Jonathan Emery told The National in an interview in London. It will be the fourth project in Dubai for Aldar, Abu Dhabi’s biggest listed developer, following the launches of the Haven, Athlon and The Wilds. “It’s another partnership with Dubai Holding , and it's a very large villa community [with] townhouses and also sits above the Blue Line extension,” Mr Emery said. In February, Aldar and Dubai Holding expanded their joint venture announced in 2023 by adding two plots in Dubai to deliver almost 14,000 new homes with a combined gross development value of more than Dh38 billion. The first plot of four million square metres, is along Dubai’s eastern growth corridor opposite Nad Al Sheba. The second plot, on Palm Jebel Ali, will be an ultra-luxury waterfront development of branded and non-branded residences. The new developments are coming even as buyers become cautious due to regional uncertainty driven by the Iran war. Transaction volumes and values fell in the third quarter. Dubai recorded home sales worth a total of Dh72.6 billion ($19.7 billion) in the three months to the end of September, down 47 per cent compared to the same period last year, while the number of transactions dropped 38 per cent to 34,000, according to the latest report from Cavendish Maxwell. “The customers are still there for the right product. Now, clearly, the international side of the market is the one that's just slowed a little bit. There’s uncertainty and people are taking their time to have a look. But we still believe in the fundamentals … the products that we have brought to the market have all done really well,” Mr Emery said. Aldar, which recorded strong second-quarter financial results, will hand over more than 3,000 units this year, representing the largest volume since the company's launch. The deliveries will go up to 4,500 next year, he said. Among the projects that are expected to be delivered this year are the Sustainable City on Yas Island, and the Grove and Louvre Abu Dhabi residences on Saadiyat Island. The Abu Dhabi-listed company will also hand over its first homes in Dubai next year, at its Haven project near Dubailand. New partnerships In September, Aldar and Sharjah-based Arada announced a partnership to build housing projects on Yas Island and at Seih Sdeirah in Abu Dhabi, with a combined value of about Dh15 billion. The partnership involves a master plan joint venture to create a large-scale mixed-use community at Seih Sdeirah on the Abu Dhabi-Dubai border and Arada’s acquisition of three residential plots on Yas Island. Aldar will continue to look for new partnerships with established developers, Mr Emery said. “Partnerships is a way that we believe we can diversify the customer offer, because you know if we pick the right partner that has a great proposition, maybe they have a great following with their customers … then it’s good to be able to introduce that to our customers as well,” he said.

events.title: Americans are losing faith in their fellow voters
events.summary: Data: Gallup ; Chart: Axios Americans' trust in their fellow citizens' democratic judgment has fallen to its lowest recorded level in more than five decades, according to a new Gallup survey. The big picture: Americans' growing distrust of political leaders and institutions now extends to one another, with Democrats and Republicans showing similar levels of skepticism. By the numbers: 51% of U.S. adults have a great deal or fair amount of trust in Americans as a whole to make democratic judgments, per Gallup. That's the lowest reading since Gallup began tracking the measure in 1974. The distrust cuts across party lines: 53% of Democrats, 51% of Republicans and 49% of independents trust Americans' ability to make democratic decisions. Flashback: Trust stood at 86% in 1976 and 78% in both 2002 and 2005. Trust has stayed below 60% since 2018, according to Gallup. State of play: Americans have more trust in their local government (67%) and state government (55%) than in their fellow citizens' democratic judgment (51%). The survey also found that 42% of Americans trust politicians who hold or seek public office, while 33% trust the news media. Zoom out: Americans' confidence in major U.S. institutions, including Congress, the presidency and the banking system, has also fallen to historically low levels. Methodology: Gallup surveyed 1,000 U.S. adults by landline and cellphone Sept. 1–17, 2026; the weighting-adjusted margin of error was plus or minus 4 percentage points.

events.title: Trump returns to Ohio as Democrats try to claw back his advantage
events.summary: David’s view YOUNGSTOWN, Ohio — Toward the end of Monday night’s MAGA rally, after Jon Husted heard Donald Trump compliment his jawline and his “ass,” he thanked the president for making Ohio so much easier for Republicans to win. “The Youngstown area, for decades, used to vote Democrat,” the Republican senator said. “And then you ran for office in 2016, and flipped it red forever.” For a decade after that, Youngstown has become the first stop on what media critics derided as “Trump voter safaris,” journeys into the working-class counties that never voted Republican until he showed up. Husted’s claim of a permanently red state, however, isn’t adding up for Democrats: As soon as I arrived this week, they insisted that MAGA’s advance was over. This isn’t because Democrats have snapped back to the image and values they ran on in the 1970s, when they had a lock on this state. No, the party insists that Republicans are in charge, making voters angry with their handling of the economy and the Middle East, so the culture-war politicking that worked for a decade won’t be as potent in November. “People aren’t buying that again because they’ve realized you can’t deposit culture war into your bank account,” said Chris Anderson, the chairman of the Mahoning County Democrats, who’d spent years trying to limit their losses and defections. “You can’t fill your gas tank with it.” Campaigns have a queasy rhythm to them — hype followed by panic followed by hype. We’ve reached the time in the cycle where the party that built a post-Labor Day polling lead begins to question its own confidence. “They’re undersampling Republicans,” Speaker Mike Johnson told the faithful in South Texas on Tuesday, a part of that state that seemed to be following the same rightward march as northeast Ohio — and before that, Appalachia. Republicans around Youngstown expected the trend of underestimating their vote to hold this year, but not accelerate. They agreed that Democrats would at least be competitive. Rep. Michael Rulli, who represents the Mahoning Valley in Congress, said that the GOP got an opening when “Clinton came in and lied about NAFTA,” which made local Democrats thrash around in search of a populist alternative. “When Trump came around, the people just took to it, and so they’re giving us a shot,” Rulli added. “This area will not always stay Republican or Democrat.” This year’s Democrats are making hard plays for northeast Ohio, at least to trim the GOP margins. Former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who lost the five most Democratic counties east of Cleveland for the first time in 2024, has painted Husted as a “Big Tech” shill, captured by the next industry that’ll threaten working-class jobs. Amy Acton, the party’s gubernatorial nominee, takes every chance to talk about her Youngstown roots; her ads often portray Vivek Ramaswamy, the billionaire GOP nominee, playing tennis as he daydreams about cutting Medicare and Social Security. “I know what it’s like to not have the heat on, or live in a tent in the winter and experience a lot of neglect and abuse,” Acton told me on Tuesday, when I asked her to respond to the president rallying in Youngstown — specifically, about him telling voters they’d get rebate checks and energy bill relief only if Republicans won. “And I can also tell you that I wouldn’t be here today if it wasn’t for the institutions that gave me a chance.” A Democratic comeback in Ohio is unlikely to look like the winning maps of Barack Obama’s campaigns, much less Bill Clinton’s. While losing to Bernie Moreno two years ago, Brown ran stronger in the suburbs of Cleveland and Cincinnati than he had in elections he actually won. On Monday, the standard Trump rally scene of MAGA-hatted voters in line and liberals yelling at them from free speech zones showed how the coalitions had changed. The protesters skewed older; the younger they were, the more profanity they were comfortable putting on cardboard. A “progress pride” flag was hoisted on a pole, right under an American flag. Any Trump fan who objected got an earful about the “pedophile president” they were lined up for. Trump, at this point, was not the rebel candidate who first showed up in Youngstown 10 years ago, with rally speeches about the threat of mass Muslim immigration. He was the party leader every Republican wanted to borrow some aura from, by communing with his superfans. Ramaswamy posed for selfies a few steps away from MAGA activist Vince Fusca . Blake Marnell , who wears a brick-patterned suit to every Trump rally, got a seat near the main stage. Both men were at the 2024 Trump rally in Butler, Pa., where a failed assassin’s bullet clipped his ear; neither needed convincing that he was saving eastern Ohio, where they didn’t live, from neoliberalism. The Covelli Centre, where Trump had rallied before, was a bit more than half-full when the president got onstage. Like Democrats used to, he described all the investments he was bringing to the region. Submarine construction was coming to Cleveland; nearby Warren was getting a new ​​Kimberly-Clark plant ; he would figure out how to save the local heating utility company. The applause thinned out when he talked about how he’d rebranded artificial intelligence as “Super Intelligence.” Notable David Skolnick covered the rally for the Youngstown Vindicator. Richard Cowan went to Warren, Ohio, for Reuters, to take the temperature of its Obama-Trump voters: “We ⁠believe our Christian ​values are more than gas prices.”

events.title: NVIDIA and Semiconductor Leaders Advance AI Across Chip Design and Manufacturing for AI-Defined Fabs
events.summary: News Summary: NVIDIA introduces cuPotential, a new NVIDIA CUDA-X library developers can use to build AI agents that simulate how atoms and molecules interact, accelerating already GPU-optimized workflows by an additional 2-3x in early-access testing. NanoVDB, an open source library for working with 3D data, accelerates chipmaking simulation for AI-defined fabs, helping Lam Research achieve 30x faster simulation. NVIDIA NPP, a library for processing images on GPUs, accelerates chipmaking inspection for AI-defined fabs, helping KLA accelerate inspection. Applied Materials, Cadence, KLA, Lam Research, Siemens, Synopsys and other semiconductor leaders are using NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and AI stack across chip design, manufacturing and testing, helping drive faster development, better yield and greater production capacity. NVIDIA today announced semiconductor leaders are adopting NVIDIA CUDA-X ™ libraries — including the new NVIDIA cuPotential library, which developers can use to build AI agents that simulate how atoms and molecules interact — to advance AI-defined fabs. AI-defined fabs are semiconductor factories where AI helps engineers optimize processes, solve production issues and improve production efficiency. As demand for advanced chips rises, such fabs must expand production while managing increasingly complex manufacturing processes. Engineers need new ways to model materials, analyze inspection data and test process changes in digital twins before applying them in production. The expanded CUDA-X portfolio gives AI agents and engineering applications accelerated tools for semiconductor simulation, 3D data processing and image analysis, helping automate more engineering work across chip design and manufacturing so fabs can predict process behavior and improve yield. “The semiconductor industry made the AI revolution possible. Now, AI is transforming how chips are built,” said Tim Costa, vice president and general manager of industrial and computational engineering at NVIDIA. “As fabs race to meet demand for advanced chips, NVIDIA CUDA-X and Omniverse libraries give AI agents accelerated simulation and inspection tools to help engineers manage complexity, improve yield and advance AI-defined fabs.” NVIDIA cuPotential Accelerates How Researchers Model Atomic Interactions Understanding how atoms and molecules interact is critical to modeling semiconductor materials and manufacturing processes, but these calculations can take significant amounts of time, even in software already optimized for GPUs. NVIDIA cuPotential accelerates atomic-scale simulation with specialized GPU-accelerated functions developers can add to existing software. It helps researchers model electrical forces and other interactions across large numbers of atoms to test and refine simulations faster. Synopsys is among the early adopters using cuPotential to accelerate materials simulations. By making these modeling capabilities available to AI agents, cuPotential helps agents run, evaluate and iterate on advanced molecular simulations. In early-access testing, the library accelerated already GPU-optimized workflows by an additional 2-3x. Semiconductor Leaders Advance AI-Defined Fabs With NVIDIA CUDA-X AI-defined fabs require faster ways to model chip designs, materials behavior and manufacturing processes before changes reach production. NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries — including NVIDIA cuPotential for simulating atomic interactions, NVIDIA cuEST for modeling electronic behavior and NVIDIA cuDSS for solving complex engineering simulations — accelerate these workloads to help make fabs more autonomous. Synopsys is using cuPotential, cuEST and cuDSS to accelerate semiconductor simulations, with early QuantumATK results showing a potential 30x speedup using cuEST, and S-Device benchmarks showing a 12x speedup using cuDSS. The company’s AgentEngineer solutions interoperate with NVIDIA Nemotron ™ open models and NVIDIA NeMo ™ to support AI agents for chip design and verification. Cadence is using NVIDIA accelerated computing, NVIDIA Nemotron open models and CUDA-X libraries to bring agentic AI to the design and simulation of electromechanical systems — from semiconductors to advanced packaging and printed circuit boards. Examples include Cadence AuraStack AI Super Agent optimizing advanced packages for heat and stress 8x faster using cuDSS with Cadence Celsius, and Nemotron with ChipStack AI Super Agent for semiconductor design and verification. COMSOL is accelerating semiconductor multiphysics simulations with NVIDIA cuDSS, delivering up to 10x faster simulations to help engineers optimize equipment and processes. Its upcoming COMSOL MCP Server will use the NVIDIA Nemotron Ultra open model to enable AI-assisted modeling and design exploration. Voltai accelerates advanced chip packaging with Voltaire, its agentic multiphysics platform for 3D-IC design and simulation. Voltaire combines AI agents with GPU-accelerated solvers powered by NVIDIA cuDSS and CUDA-X libraries, compressing complex electro-thermal-mechanical simulation workflows from months to a day. ChipAgents uses NVIDIA AI infrastructure and NVIDIA model-training and optimization software to develop specialized AI models for chip design. The company is also working with NVIDIA to develop Build-A-Chip Bench , a new AI benchmark that evaluates agents across end-to-end workflows from specification to graphic data system. The benchmark gives the industry a comprehensive measure of progress toward fully autonomous semiconductor engineering. NVIDIA Open Libraries Help Prepare and Optimize Manufacturing Workflows Fabs depend on thousands of process steps that must be modeled, refined and validated before production. The NVIDIA cuLitho library accelerates calculations for printing chip patterns; NanoVDB — an open source library for working with 3D data — accelerates chipmaking simulations; and the open NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo ™ framework helps train physics AI models to predict how physical systems behave. Siemens is using cuLitho to speed up Calibre software for chip-pattern refinement and mask preparation. Its Solido team is also developing agent-driven characterization workflows with Nemotron open models and NVIDIA NeMo open libraries. Lam Research intends to integrate NanoVDB into its advanced semiconductor process modeling platform SEMulator3D , part of the company’s Semiverse Solutions family of virtual products. The addition of NanoVDB is expected to accelerate select wafer-etch modeling by up to 30x, while using NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo has been demonstrated to assist in reducing plasma-prediction simulation time to as little as milliseconds instead of days. events.title: New inflation warning sign
events.summary: America's inflation problem is becoming harder to contain, with new evidence Wednesday that price pressures are extending beyond the war-related energy shock rattling the global economy . Why it matters: Inflation is squeezing household budgets and dimming hopes for relief. It is also increasing the prospect that the Fed will have to raise interest rates further. What they're saying: "Higher energy costs are beginning to seep into broader services prices, increasing the risk that this inflation burst will persist," Fitch Ratings economist Olu Sonola wrote in a note. The Consumer Price Index report "stands out as the first of the year in which price pressure appeared to be showing up in most corners of the consumption basket at once," Glenmede's Jason Pride wrote. By the numbers: The CPI rose 0.6% in September from the prior month, accelerating from August's 0.4% increase. The index increased 3.7% in the 12 months through September, compared with 3.4% in the prior month. Gasoline prices surged 9% in September, accounting for more than half of the monthly jump in consumer prices. Core prices, which exclude food and energy, advanced 0.3% for the second consecutive month. The annual rate accelerated to 2.6% from 2.4%. The intrigue: Over the past three months, core CPI has risen at a 3.4% annualized rate, up notably from 2% in August — a sign that underlying inflation pressures are strengthening. Inflation was stubborn in parts of the services economy that are less directly exposed to the energy price surge. Shelter costs accelerated last month, rising 0.4%, while used car prices climbed 0.7%. Airfares jumped 1.2% as airlines grappled with soaring jet fuel costs. "Supercore" — a narrower measure of inflation that excludes housing and energy services — was hot again last month. Prices in that category have risen at a nearly 4.6% annualized rate over the past three months. The big picture: Top Fed officials in recent days have played down the urgency of another interest rate hike later this month. But Wednesday's inflation data swiftly revived bets that the central bank will have to act sooner than the following meeting, in December. The two-year Treasury yield — particularly sensitive to Fed policy expectations — jumped roughly 12 basis points after the report. Traders now see a 47% chance of a quarter-point rate hike at the Oct. 27–28 policy meeting, up from 22.1% yesterday (and 18% this time last week), according to CME FedWatch. What to watch: Fed governor Christopher Waller told Bloomberg Tuesday that rising Treasury yields could help cool the economy, potentially reducing the need for another rate hike. But the inflation report complicates that argument — showing that underlying price pressures remain stubbornly elevated. Instead, the report lends support to more hawkish policymakers like Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack, who warned Monday that inflation was "relatively broad-based rather than concentrated in one component." Hammack cited tariffs, the AI investment boom and rising services prices as additional sources of price pressures. The bottom line: For American consumers, the risk is that another bout of inflation proves harder to shake — prolonging the affordability squeeze while keeping borrowing costs elevated. The squeeze is already showing up in paychecks, with inflation outpacing wage growth for six consecutive months. Real average hourly earnings fell 0.5% in September and were down 0.7% from a year earlier.

events.title: Why one spoiler candidate is now trying to replicate his work nationwide
events.summary: The News Aaron Day’s third-party campaign cost Republican Kelly Ayotte her Senate reelection bid in 2016. Now he’s trying to take his spoiler project national. With several Senate races tight enough for an alternate candidate to make a real difference, whether they’re Libertarian or another third party, Day is looking to spend as much as $2.5 million — or perhaps less, if his effort works as designed — to cost the GOP the Senate. Day’s strategy is simple: Use his Stark Freedom PAC to spend relatively small amounts on online ads made with AI that boost name ID for spoiler candidates, figuring he can do just enough to hand those races to the Democrats. Republican leaders are highly skeptical of Day’s efforts, but he sees a real chance at disrupting races across the country. What’s more remarkable is how open he is about his goal of ending the Senate Republican majority. “You call it a spoiler campaign, I call it holding Republicans accountable,” Day told Semafor in an interview. His website is equally explicit: “We fund the margin. It costs the GOP the Senate.” Day is targeting eight states where he’s deduced that boosting third-party candidates would hurt the Republican nominee: Texas, Iowa, New Hampshire, Minnesota, South Carolina, Michigan, Ohio, and Kansas. It’s a “Moneyball” theory of modern politics, banking on a relatively small amount of cash to mess up the margins in close contests. Nudging a third candidate’s vote share up by a couple of percentage points higher, as he explained, takes a lot less money than the obscene amount needed to actually win a race. “People are going to be shocked after the fact at how effective this is,” Day said. “Most voters don’t know that the third-party option exists, and a lot of these candidates don’t actually have money, and they’re not allowed to participate in the debates.” In addition to Ayotte’s 2016 New Hampshire campaign , Libertarian candidates’ support boosted former Democratic Sen. Jon Tester in his 2006 and 2012 Montana races. The effect was clear in Nevada’s 2024 Senate race, which Democrats narrowly won as nearly 5 percent of voters picked a candidate outside the two major parties. And no one can forget Jill Stein’s Green Party spoiler effect on Hillary Clinton’s presidential chances in 2016. It’s hard to see how giving Democrats the Senate helps advance Day’s causes — which include concerns over centralized digital currencies and government surveillance via cryptocurrency legislation. But Day says he wants to check President Donald Trump through “gridlock” and that with Democrats in charge, the crypto market structure bill and other legislation he dislikes will continue to stall. Several Republican groups, including the National Republican Senatorial Committee and Senate Leadership Fund, declined comment. While third-party hopefuls appreciate his support, their goals are different. Ted Brown, the Libertarian candidate in Texas, said he’s running to win, not to cost Republicans Senate control. “I’m running to defeat the corrupt two-party system,” Brown told Semafor. “But I would say this, if the Republicans lose the Senate on November 3: The good news is, the Republicans lost control of the Senate. The bad news is, the Democrats won control of the Senate.” Day said his model would be replicable to punish a Democratic majority in the future as well, by boosting Green Party candidates to eat into their candidates’ margins: “I actually view this, if it works, as something that can be used to hold both major parties accountable.” Know More So, why do this? Day was originally planning to be a candidate himself this fall, even fighting to get ballot access in New Hampshire to take out former Sen. John Sununu, R-N.H. But he said he didn’t run, in part because he was in negotiations with Republicans and the Trump administration over a list of demands that weren’t fulfilled: “I was told something definitive was going to happen, and it did not.” He declined to go into further detail; the White House did not comment. After the schism, he threw his support behind Edmond Laplante, a Constitution Party candidate in New Hampshire. He then decided to “duplicate” his 2016 bid against Ayotte by boosting anti-war candidates to reach the small percentage of “disaffected voters in these swing states.” “People do not want to vote for the Republican, but a lot of people still don’t want to vote for the Democrat,” Day said. “Texas is in play, Kansas is in play, South Carolina is potentially in play. I mean, who would have ever thought? But it’s true, and this really could make the difference.” Day’s ads are unique to each race, but most have peppy AI music critiquing the GOP candidate. They knock Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., for her pro-war votes and boost Libertarian Kasie Whitener; in New Hampshire, they hit Sununu for supporting the Wall Street bailout; in Texas, they whack state attorney general Ken Paxton for being a “mouthpiece for DC” and dub Brown the “voice of Texas.” Republicans are more worried about Day’s machinations in New Hampshire and don’t believe he’ll be effective anywhere else. Burgess’s view I’m a skeptic, and so naturally lean a bit bearish on the idea of a national spoiler campaign funded by the political equivalent of spare change. I watched a bunch of Day’s ads, as well, and found them somewhat tedious but also relentlessly on-message in driving the name ID of these somewhat obscure candidates. (It’s possible that AI-generated music just isn’t for me.) But Day is onto something with the spoiler effect, whether it’s induced by him or not. It’s undeniable that disaffected Republicans who cast primary votes for, say, Sen. John Cornyn in Texas or Rep. Ralph Norman in South Carolina may struggle with voting for Paxton and Graham — but not want to support their Democratic counterparts either. It just won’t be clear until Election Day how big of a threat these candidates are. The percentages they are drawing in polls are small enough to be a rounding error; given how tight the polls are, a rounding error still could cost Republicans multiple Senate seats. Notable Brown is courting jilted Cornyn voters , Houston Public Media reported earlier this year.

events.title: Diesel shortage to persist into 2027 as Iran war disrupts supply, IEA warns
events.summary: The global diesel shortage triggered by the Iran war is set to persist well into next year, with depleted inventories unlikely to recover until the second half of 2027, the International Energy Agency warned on Wednesday. Supplies of gas oil, which contains diesel and heating oil, will fall short of demand in the fourth quarter, even as refineries increase output towards the yea's end, the Paris-based agency said in its monthly oil market report. Without a recovery in refined-product exports from the Middle East, further cuts in consumption and the “heavy economic costs these will entail” may be needed to balance the market, it warned. Wholesale diesel prices surged to record highs of about $220 a barrel in Europe and the US last month and exceeded $200 in Singapore. Prices have since eased but remain nearly double crude benchmarks and prewar levels. US diesel pump prices topped $6 a gallon for the first time in September, up about 70 per cent since the Iran war began, the IEA said. The shortage reflects a sharp decline in shipments from two major suppliers. Combined net gas oil exports from the Middle East and Russia plunged more than 60 per cent annually to 820,000 barrels per day last month, a loss of 1.3 million bpd. Gulf export routes remain constrained, while Ukrainian drone strikes have damaged Russian oil refineries. Higher shipments from the US and China have failed to offset the losses. Inventories offer little relief ahead of winter. US diesel stocks ended September at a 14-year seasonal low, while European commercial gas oil inventories fell to a 25-year low in July. On October 2, G7 leaders pledged to accelerate the IEA's co-ordinated emergency stock release , prioritising diesel supplies. About 96 million barrels of the 400 million pledged in March have yet to be released. The IEA expects higher refinery output to return the diesel market to a seasonal surplus by early next year but said the recovery would be insufficient to replenish inventories depleted during the conflict. Gulf rebound Gulf crude exports rebounded sharply last month, rising by 4.4 million bpd to 13.9 million bpd, more than three quarters of prewar levels. Oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz climbed to 10.9 million bpd, supported by increased ship-to-ship transfers in the Gulf of Oman. However, refined products and liquefied petroleum gas shipments have recovered much more slowly, remaining below half their prewar volumes. The IEA warned that the recovery remains fragile following the bombing of Saudi Arabia's East-West Pipeline on September 11 and an escalation in Houthi attacks on regional energy infrastructure and shipping throughout this month. North Sea Dated crude, a physical oil benchmark, was trading near $134 a barrel when the report was prepared, reflecting mounting supply risks and record freight costs. Global observed oil inventories stood 509 million barrels below prewar levels at the end of September, leaving markets increasingly exposed to more disruption. Demand outlook cut The IEA cut its 2027 oil demand forecast by 630,000 bpd and downgraded its global economic growth outlook by 0.4 percentage points to 3 per cent, as central banks raise interest rates to contain war-driven inflation. Global oil consumption is now expected to rebound by two million bpd next year, but remain 620,000 bpd below 2025 levels. For 2026, demand is forecast to fall by 2.6 million bpd to 102.4 million bpd, with diesel accounting for about a quarter of the decline. The agency also trimmed its global supply forecast for this year by 60,000 bpd to 100.7 million bpd, a decline of 5.8 million bpd from 2025. Output is projected to rebound by 7.7 million bpd in 2027, although recovery remains vulnerable to renewed disruption in the Gulf.

events.title: U.K. Sanctions Cryptomus for RU Money Laundering
events.summary: The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus , a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions. Heleket’s support agent on Telegram claims, despite all evidence to the contrary, that it is not affiliated with Cryptomus. Image: Richard Sanders. On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay , TokenSpot , and the Tsunami Payments service . As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “ How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks ,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “ Heleket ” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations. The blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis said the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy. “Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.” The Cryptomus support bot on Telegram, responding on Oct. 8 to an inquiry by saying the platform was suddenly unable to process transactions. In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations. TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted new “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing. Richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders said the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are important because Canada’s sanctions against the platform were ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible. “A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn . “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.” As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, launched Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders said. Sanders said the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, New Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction. Where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation. Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent company Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation , which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara . That entity’s website — crasadr.com — says it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara. The website crasadr dot com, the official website of the Central Reserve Authority of Western Sahara, which lists the entities awarded licenses for cryptocurrencies, gaming and foreign exchange services.

events.title: UAE-backed GlobalFoundries to run two chip plants under $21bn US-Japan deal
events.summary: Japan is set to invest up to $21 billion in two chip-production plants in New York state that will be operated jointly by GlobalFoundries and the US government, the semiconductor manufacturer said on Wednesday. In a separate agreement, the Commerce Department will take a 4 per cent equity stake in the company, bringing the US government's stake to 7 per cent, chief executive Tim Breen told Reuters. The company is majority owned by Abu Dhabi’s Mubadala Investment Company. The move is part of a deal struck last year, under which US tariffs on Japanese imports were lowered from 25 per cent to 15 per cent while Japan will invest $550 billion in the US economy . “This is a bold new initiative for semiconductor manufacturing, bringing together the United States and Japan with GF’s differentiated technology and decades of manufacturing expertise to accelerate trusted capacity in New York,” Mr Breen said. Shares in GlobalFoundries were trading 4.9 per cent higher at $48.99 each as of 10am ET. Under the agreement, Japan will provide all the capital while GlobalFoundries will input its technological and manufacturing expertise, and operational capacities. The company makes integrated circuits on silicon wafers designed to help support AI and high-performance computing, communications infrastructure, and applications for aerospace and defence. The deal comes with an initial investment of about $10 billion to boost the construction of a new 300mm semiconductor manufacturing plant – or “fab” – expected to come online in 2029, with an additional $10 billion to fund a second fab. The company said the first fab will add about 900,000 of the 300mm wafers to annual US manufacturing capacity when fully operational, with a second factory adding about the same. GlobalFoundries also agreed with the Commerce Department to amend its existing award under the Chips Act to reallocate $955 million and accelerate investments in silicon photonics, silicon-germanium and advanced packaging at its sites in the US states of New York and Vermont. The announcement comes about a week after GlobalFoundries announced a $2 billion manufacturing agreement with TSMC.

events.title: Trump's diesel deal with Russia is unlikely to significantly lower global fuel prices despite expectations of rapid relief
events.summary: Trump's diesel deal with Russia unlikely to bring down fuel prices As the world's largest diesel exporter, the US benefits from high prices. At home, however, consumers are feeling the strain of rising living costs. Why Donald Trump's deal with Russia is unlikely to change that. With or without a deal with Russia, diesel prices on global markets are unlikely to fall significantly anytime soon. That is the assessment of experts interviewed by DW regarding the latest fuel-supply agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin . "The main reason for high diesel prices is the war in Iran and the simultaneous disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait," said Samina Sultan, a foreign trade expert at the German Economic Institute (IW) in Cologne. The situation has led to production outages and made fuel shipments "more expensive, less secure and more difficult," she said. Trump's deal with Russia also has an additional geopolitical dimension, Sultan said: "It causes the wars in Ukraine and Iran to become completely intertwined." Things are looking up, though. Roughly 13.5 million barrels of crude oil are once again flowing through the Strait of Hormuz a day, according to shipping and commodities analytics firm Kpler. But for refined products such as diesel, volumes remain far lower at around 677,000 barrels per day, compared with 3.6 million barrels before the war. Carsten Fritsch, a commodities analyst at Commerzbank, also attributes the price increases to the wars. "If nothing changes in Ukraine and the Middle East, I see very few ways to resolve these supply bottlenecks," he said. Trump expects prices to fall at record speed In a social media post on October 9, Trump announced that he would temporarily suspend some sanctions on Russia and begin importing Russian diesel. He wrote "diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" in a mix of lowercase and all caps. Russia confirmed the arrangement. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency TASS on October 13 that supplying diesel fuel was "in the interests of Russia, the United States and global energy markets." Diesel prices in the US and many EU countries have risen sharply over the past 12 months. According to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), prices in the US have climbed by about 60% and now stand at $6.30 per gallon, equivalent to $1.66 (or €1.49) per liter of diesel. But even if Russia were able to flood global markets with cheap diesel, prices would not fall nearly as much as they recently rose, something all of the experts contacted by DW agree on. Many refineries around the Gulf region have suffered disruptions or damage, while transporting fuel via shadow fleets and securing insurance remains costly, cumbersome and risky. Another key shift is that Russia is no longer the world's largest diesel exporter. In fact, it is facing its own fuel shortages at home. The US is now the world's biggest diesel exporter. In 2025, it exported an average of 1.26 million barrels of diesel per day, accounting for roughly 15.4% of global diesel exports. At the same time, Russia fell to second place with a 9.5% share, and that was before major Ukrainian drone attacks on its refineries. Debates over export restrictions continue Besides the new US-Russia diesel agreement, Trump also recently floated the idea of US diesel export restrictions. But the idea was abandoned because it could lead to even higher diesel prices in the country, according to Samina Sultan. "There simply is not enough diesel storage capacity in the United States," Sultan said. "Production would have to be reduced, and then prices would rise again." Trump, Russia and Ukraine: Has the US changed sides again? If the US were to impose export restrictions on diesel, buyers in Latin America and the European Union would be hit particularly hard. Since Russia invaded Ukraine, EU countries have increasingly imported diesel from the US instead of Russia because of sanctions . "An export ban merely redistributes the shortage; it does not solve it," said ING chief economist Carsten Brzeski. "Global prices would continue to rise, while refineries would scale back production as margins shrink," he added. Export restrictions aside, few people consider that the US-Russia diesel deal will have any big impact. According to calculations by the platform The World Data , the promised shipment of 2.2 million barrels of diesel from Russia would not even cover a single day's US diesel demand of roughly 4 million barrels. Even if all of the diesel volumes announced by Trump were combined, totaling 35.8 million barrels, they would only cover about nine days of US domestic demand. "I CANNOT OVERSTATE HOW MUCH OF A NOTHING BURGER THIS IS," Canadian oil market analyst Rory Johnston wrote in an all-caps post on X shortly after the announcement.

events.title: Social Security recipients will see rise in monthly payments next year
events.summary: Data: Social Security Administration; Chart: Neil Irwin/Axios Social Security recipients will see the largest rise in their monthly payments in four years in January, with a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment. Driving the news: The Social Security Administration announced the 2027 COLA adjustment for 76 million recipients of retirement and disability benefits, which by law is calculated based on the Consumer Price Index for the July-through-September quarter. That will increase the average retiree's benefits by $900 a year, or $75 a month. The agency also said that the cutoff for Social Security taxes will rise to $192,300 in 2027, from $184,500 this year. Income above that threshold is not subject to payroll tax. How it works: The adjustment is, by statute, determined by the year-over-year change in CPI for the third quarter. Thus, the September data released this morning was the final input needed to calculate the adjustment. Between the lines: The adjustment will mean more nominal income for seniors and disability recipients, amounting to a mild fiscal stimulus come January. However, it also accelerates Social Security's looming fiscal problems, with its trust fund scheduled to expire in six years. The most recent projections issued by the program's trustees assumed a 0.9 percentage point lower COLA for 2027, the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget notes.

events.title: Turkish authorities raid TV channel as press freedom groups warn of a crackdown
events.summary: Authorities have raided Halk TV, one of Turkey's few independent broadcasters, and appointed a trustee manager as part of a corruption investigation ISTANBUL -- Authorities on Wednesday raided the headquarters of one of Turkey ’s few broadcasters not aligned with the government, and appointed a trustee manager to oversee the popular news channel as part of an investigation into alleged corruption. Press freedom groups and opposition parties, however, denounced the move against Halk TV, calling it yet another step by the government to silence opposition voices. Press freedoms in Turkey have steadily eroded during the more than two decades that President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has been in power and a majority of media outlets are either under government control or aligned with it. The country ranks 163rd out of 180 countries in the Reporters Without Borders’ world press freedom index. A statement from the Istanbul Chief Prosecutor’s Office said an investigation was launched into Halk TV chairman Cafer Mahiroglu over allegations of bid rigging, bribery and money laundering. Detention warrants were issued against 17 suspects and 11 of them were taken into custody, the statement said. Trustees were also appointed to run other companies owned by Mahiroglu. The channel’s broadcasts were temporarily halted. Police surrounded the station’s headquarters while financial crimes investigation teams conducted searches inside, media reports said. The raid on the channel came as Istanbul's imprisoned mayor, Ekrem Imamoglu , was due to appear in court to defend himself against allegations of widespread corruption in a case that critics also see as a politically motivated move against the opposition. Imamoglu, who has been behind bars for more than a year, was considered the main challenger to Erdogan. Halk TV has reported extensively on the trial and other cases against Imamoglu. In a video message posted on X, Mahiroglu condemned the appointment of a trustee for the channel, calling it a politically motivated move and a “dark day for Turkey.” Mahiroglu, who lives abroad, denied the allegations against him as “baseless” and said seven of his relatives were detained. The Ankara-based Contemporary Journalists Association decried the action against the channel. “The appointment of a trustee to Halk TV and the suspension of its broadcast constitute a grave intervention against press freedom and freedom of expression,” the group said. “This decision, which disregards constitutional rights and the public’s right to access information, is unacceptable.” Teen shooter kills 3 children, 1 teacher at elementary school in Bend, Oregon: Police Woman accused of stabbing husband and son to death at Great Wolf Lodge: Complaint Atlanta school worker dies after falling from Six Flags roller coaster in Georgia Ozgur Ozel, the leader of the main opposition New Party, said the raid amounted to an abuse of power by the government. “Raiding a television channel at dawn and appointing a trustee is an act only dictators would commit,” he wrote on X. “Unfortunately, this is the state to which they have reduced our country.” Amnesty International urged Turkish authorities to "immediately restore Halk TV’s independent operations and end their attacks on media freedom.” Other television stations, including HaberTurk and Tele1, have similarly been placed under trusteeship. Last week, two journalists were arrested and two others were placed under house arrest for alleged misleading reports on a recent Turkish investment fund scandal — which has implicated a senior figure from Erdogan’s ruling party. On Monday, international and Turkish human rights groups urged social media platforms, including X, to resist court orders blocking hundreds of accounts belonging to journalists and activists. They also called on the Turkish government to stop issuing orders to block the accounts. The government has cited public safety concerns to justify the restrictions. events.title: Qatar’s wealth fund keeps spending as war slashes government revenue
events.summary: The News Qatar’s sovereign wealth fund isn’t slowing its dealmaking, a senior executive said, even as the Iran war gutted the state’s revenue by 42% in the first half of the year. The war “hasn’t impacted our progress,” Mohsin Pirzada, head of funds at Qatar Investment Authority, told Semafor. “We continue to invest, we continue to deploy.” “We’re obviously very mindful that we manage the surplus wealth for the state of Qatar, and that is largely derived by LNG exports,” Pirzada said. The sovereign fund has remained an active investor, with its funds division deploying billions of dollars already this year. QIA announced a $20 billion investment partnership with JPMorgan last month, following a $25 billion agreement with Goldman Sachs just before the Iran war began. While no new fund deals are “on the radar” now, Pirzada said, QIA “will have a handful of strategic platform arrangements with managers or institutions like JPMorgan, or like Goldman Sachs,” focused on firms that the fund has had long-standing relationships with.” Know More Before the war, QIA said it planned to invest $500 billion in the US alone over the next decade. The fund had expected to nearly double in size, boosted by an 85% expansion of its liquefied natural gas (LNG) output by 2030. That gas expansion has now been delayed — an Iranian attack on the Ras Laffan complex knocked out about 17% of its existing capacity. Qatar’s economy is expected to contract 15.6% this year , and the government will likely post a deficit. QIA, with around $580 billion in assets, is a significant backer of Wall Street firms and US technology. Its appetite mirrors that of its Gulf peers: with the exception of Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, all are on track for one of their most active years of dealmaking ever, according to fund tracker GlobalSWF. Qatar has been one of the most impacted Gulf countries by the US-Iran war. Unlike some of its neighbors, it has no export routes that bypass the Strait of Hormuz, and has been reluctant to move LNG tankers — which are more flammable and expensive than crude carriers — through the strait. Despite the disruptions, there are signs of recovery. QatarEnergy Chief Executive Saad al-Kaabi said last month that the expansion project is expected to begin production in the first half of 2027. Meanwhile, an LNG export facility in Texas, majority owned by QatarEnergy in a joint venture with ExxonMobil, shipped its first cargoes in April. Notable Qatar cut government department budgets by around a third and funding for overseas aid by about 85% to cope with the financial strain of the war , the Financial Times reported. A “dinosaur” gas tanker is one part of an ambitious effort to revive Qatari energy shipments , Bloomberg reported.

events.title: Inflation heats up as gas prices surge
events.summary: Data: Bureau of Labor Statistics ; Chart: Courtenay Brown/Axios U.S. inflation picked up in September as soaring energy prices added to already stubborn price pressures, the Labor Department said on Wednesday. Why it matters: The latest Consumer Price Index shows that the inflation fight is far from over — and makes further Federal Reserve interest rate hikes more likely as Americans struggle with higher costs. By the numbers: CPI rose 0.6% in September from the prior month, with the annual inflation rate at 3.7%, the government said. That compares with a 0.4% monthly increase and a 3.4% annual rate in August. Core prices, which exclude volatile food and energy costs, gained 0.3% on the month, compared with a similar monthly gain in August. In the 12 months through September, core CPI rose 2.6%, up from 2.4% the prior month. Zoom in: The latest figures capture the toll of the Middle East war on American consumers as disruptions to global energy supplies push up fuel prices. Gasoline prices spiked 9.1% in September after climbing 3.9% in August, when they accounted for more than a third of the monthly increase in consumer prices. Prices for shelter, one of the largest components of the index, increased 0.4%, compared with a 0.3% gain in August. Food prices were flat, compared with a slight 0.1% increase the previous month. Zoom out: The surge in fuel prices has prompted extraordinary measures from the Trump administration, particularly as soaring diesel costs threaten to push up prices for goods transported across the country . President Trump temporarily eased restrictions on tax-exempt diesel and lifted some U.S. sanctions on Russian fuel to boost global diesel supplies. Airline fares surged 1.2% in September — bringing the annual increase to 22% — as higher jet fuel costs put pressure on ticket prices. What to watch: The Social Security Administration is set to announce the 2027 cost-of-living adjustment for millions of retirees, based on inflation figures released on Wednesday. The increase will take effect in January. The big picture: The report comes as Federal Reserve officials weigh how soon to raise interest rates again , with policymakers divided over the persistence of inflation. In a speech on Monday, Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack warned that inflation pressures extend well beyond energy — citing tariffs, AI investment and rising services prices. Fed governor Christopher Waller told Bloomberg on Tuesday that higher Treasury yields are already helping restrain economic activity, possibly reducing the urgency of another rate hike this month. New York Fed president John Williams said one more increase might be ahead this year, though he cautioned the central bank might not have to raise again in 2027. The bottom line: In the wake of the inflation report, financial markets are now betting that an interest rate increase is more likely when the Fed meets later this month. Odds of October rate hike jumped to 44% from 22% Tuesday, according to CME FedWatch data. The yield on the two-year Treasury note — the security most reactive to Fed policy expectations — jumped 12 basis points, while the 10-year Treasury yield rose 7 basis points. events.title: Malawi launches black market fuel crackdown as prices soar
events.summary: Malawi launched a nationwide crackdown on fuel hoarders and black market sellers as the nation struggles with shortages that have left truckers queuing for up to a week and bus fares doubling on some routes. Diesel and petrol have been scarce for weeks because the country lacks the hard currency to buy fuel supplies, sparking a scramble for dollars that has seen the central bank sell off gold to pay suppliers and the government return to the IMF for a bailout. Malawi, which has among the highest fuel pump prices in Africa at more than $3 a liter, highlights the impact of a $100-plus per barrel crude price on import-dependent economies with thin buffers. Unlicensed resellers face arrest , and stations caught hoarding can lose their license under the new measures. The IMF last week said it was making “ considerable progress ” in designing a “package of macroeconomic policies.” Its last program was a $175 million loan that expired in May last year, the latest in a string of support packages for one of the continent’s poorest countries, whose agriculture-based economy has been hit hard by extreme weather patterns. — Tiisetso Motsoeneng

events.title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
events.summary: AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet of Things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered. Still, the results raise concerns about the possibility of new forms of computer worms. Challenging to shut down Anthropic further warned not only about the new potential malware, but also that it could be difficult to stop. In its blog post, it wrote that “a replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off—though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days). Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own.” Read full article Comments

events.title: Former DR Congo president forms new rebel movement
events.summary: DR Congo’s former President Joseph Kabila has formed a new rebel movement incorporating Rwanda-backed forces, openly taking charge of the insurgency despite US sanctions against him. The move deepens the political and security threat to President Félix Tshisekedi’s government and challenges Washington’s efforts to end fighting and secure access to the country’s critical minerals. UN experts reported in June that Kabila’s growing prominence appeared intended to obscure Rwanda’s role by portraying the rebellion as a Congolese movement addressing a national problem. Rwanda has acknowledged defensive “security coordination” with the M23 insurgents, who have held large swaths of mineral-rich eastern DR Congo for more than a year. US sanctions against rebel leaders and Rwanda’s military, a Washington-brokered peace deal, and talks mediated by Qatar have so far failed to end the fighting. Insecurity has complicated DR Congo’s hopes of profiting from rising demand for copper, coltan, and cobalt used in digital infrastructure and the energy transition. Washington has paired its peace efforts with a bid to loosen China’s grip on mining in the world’s largest cobalt producer. — Ruben Nyanguila

events.title: IMF raises sub-Saharan Africa growth outlook
events.summary: The IMF raised its 2026 growth forecast for sub-Saharan Africa to 4.5%, cementing its position as one of the world’s fastest growing regions. The IMF said the new projection, marginally higher than July’s 4.3%, “ masks substantial divergence, ” with oil-importing economies the most exposed to higher energy and food prices driven by Iran-war-related supply chain shocks. The IMF expects the continent’s biggest economy, South Africa, to grow more than four times slower than the region this year and next, as the higher oil prices hit its already fragile prospects. On the flip side, the fund raised its projected growth rate for Nigeria, Africa’s top crude oil producer, to 4.2%, citing a “favorable terms of trade effect.” Looking globally, the IMF named rising national debt as a growing risk to financial stability, “especially with high borrowing costs.” Last week, the World Bank said that nearly four-fifths of African countries spend more on interest payments than on health or education. — Tiisetso Motsoeneng

events.title: Companies may be held liable when AI harms their clients and customers
events.summary: When AI messes up on a tax return or in a court filing, it's no laughing matter. DigitalVision Vectors/Getty Images Artificial intelligence has moved quickly from a novelty on the job to a common workplace tool. Gallup found that 52% of U.S. employees and 68% of professional services workers were using AI by February 2026. Thomson Reuters similarly found in spring 2026 that 74% of professionals use AI several times a week for work. This widespread use shouldn’t surprise anyone. For accountants, attorneys, consultants and other professionals, AI can accelerate research , summarize complex information and assist with writing and other forms of communication. But its rapid adoption has a big downside – AI can produce information that sounds authoritative and looks polished while being completely wrong . And when AI generates mistakes, responsibility for those errors belongs to the professional or business relying on the AI output – not companies that develop AI systems. AI errors have led to lawsuits, court fines, financial consequences and public embarrassment from fabricated citations, nonexistent sources and inaccurate AI-generated information. These cases raise an increasingly important question: How can professionals benefit from AI without outsourcing the judgment their work requires? Fake citations We are two certified public accountants who research tax accounting . In the September 2026 issue of Journal of Accountancy, we examined what happened in Clinco v. Commissioner , a case before the U.S. Tax Court where an attorney submitted a brief to the court with allegedly fake citations. The Tax Court is a specialized federal court that resolves disputes between taxpayers and the IRS. This case involved a restaurant owner accused of underreporting more than US$2 million in business receipts and claiming unsupported depreciation deductions on rental properties. The main issue concerned Clinco’s accounting records used to determined how much of their income to tax. The taxpayers’ attorney, Abraham Wagner, cited four cases to support his argument that an IRS notice assessing additional taxes was invalid. The court determined that three of the citations appeared to be AI-generated hallucinations that cited nonexistent Tax Court cases. The court rejected the taxpayer’s argument and warned Wagner that submitting fake citations could lead to sanctions from the court, including financial penalties or disciplinary action against Wagner. Ultimately, the court did not sanction Wagner in the case, but the decision stands to put attorneys and other professionals in Tax Court on notice that AI hallucinations will not be tolerated. Using AI for audits and other professional work may save time but also poses some legal hazards. iStock/Getty Images Plus When AI gets it wrong AI errors made on behalf of clients are not limited to briefs drafted by attorneys. Nor are these mishaps limited to the United States. When Deloitte produced a 237-page report in 2025 for the Australian government examining its automated system for penalizing welfare recipients who failed to meet job-seeking requirements, it contained nonexistent academic citations and a fabricated quotation it attributed to a federal court judgment. The global consulting firm later issued a revised version of the error-ridden report. Deloitte blamed generative AI for the errors in the original and agreed to partially refund its fees. Like most airlines, Air Canada has a chatbot on its website to respond to its customers’ questions. The chatbot told a customer in November 2022 that he could buy a plane ticket under a bereavement policy and be reimbursed later. This was not company policy, and Air Canada refused to honor what the chatbot had told the customer. The customer sued the airline and won 812 Canadian dollars in damages. The British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal ruled that Air Canada had failed to take reasonable care to ensure that its AI bot provided accurate information and agreed with the customer that the airline had negligently misrepresented the bereavement policy. AI lawsuits There have been other lawsuits filed against AI platforms and providers. In 2025, for example, a Georgia court dismissed a defamation lawsuit against OpenAI after its ChatGPT tool falsely accused Mark Walters, a radio host, of embezzlement. The court ruled in favor of summary judgment for OpenAI and found Walters had not established fault and damages. There is also an ongoing case, Keene v. Google LLC , that is similar to the Walters case. Keene, a TV producer, sued after Google’s AI summaries allegedly published false information about Keene’s criminal history. In September 2026 the court ruled that some of his defamation claims may proceed, without deciding yet whether Google was liable. Hallucinations and ‘confabulations’ Unfortunately, for anyone using AI to save time and use less labor, AI errors are often hard to spot. Unlike most obvious mistakes humans make, an AI-generated error may include supporting explanations, citations or references that make a passage appear complete and credible. The National Institute of Standards and Technology issued a report on AI risk management in July 2024 that calls AI mistakes and hallucinations “confabulations” – the confident presentation of erroneous or false information. Some researchers draw a more specific distinction between hallucinations, in which AI invents information outright, and confabulations, in which it fills gaps or distorts real information in a plausible way. Either kind of problem can be hard to detect without independent verification, but confabulations mimic actual research so closely they can trick AI users into believing the AI output is valid. AI errors in the workplace A 2024 Stanford University study of specialized AI tools for legal research found erroneous results in 17% to 33% of the responses tested. Yet those findings and other grounds for concern about accuracy have not stopped many law firms from embracing AI tools due to their potential to save time and improve efficiency. Recent surveys indicate law firms and other employers have not adopted enough workplace safeguards to spot and root out AI-generated mistakes. A 2026 survey by the Nationwide insurance company found that only 36% of surveyed businesses have written AI policies, and only 37% provide any training on responsible AI use. As AI becomes more and more common in the workplace, we believe it’s clear that telling employees simply to “check the AI” is not enough. Businesses and the people working for them need clear expectations about when it’s appropriate to use AI, which outputs require independent verification, and who is ultimately responsible for the final work. AI may change how professional work gets done, but it does not change where the buck stops. The University of Dayton is an academic partner of The Conversation. Kaitlin Newkirk is affiliated with the Ohio Society of CPAs.

events.title: The Download: faking blood and the future of batteries
events.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. The US military’s race to make fake blood In February 2007, a US military helicopter carrying blood to a field hospital was shot down in Iraq, killing all seven crew members. The mission was a reminder of the risks of transporting blood, which has a limited shelf life and is often in short supply. Now, a $73 million DARPA effort aims to create shelf-stable versions of plasma, platelets, and red blood cells. The idea is to develop dried blood products that can be stored for long periods and deployed quickly on the battlefield.  The project aims to have bags of dried blood products deployed in the field by 2029. But getting it all done will be tough, and researchers still have major questions about the safety and effectiveness of synthetic alternatives. Discover how the military hopes to make blood last longer . —Andrew Rosenblum This story is from the next issue of our print magazine. Subscribe now to get your hands on a copy as soon as it lands on Wednesday, October 21!   10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: WeLion New Energy and its semi-solid-state batteries WeLion New Energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026 , available exclusively to subscribers . WeLion New Energy is on a quest to make safer, better batteries. The Chinese company’s liquid-solid hybrid cells aim to pack more power into electric cars, boats and drones, potentially improving safety and offering greater energy density than lithium-ion batteries. In 2023, WeLion released a battery pack with EV-maker Nio that offered a range of over 1,000 kilometers. Now, the company is developing batteries with even higher energy density. But scaling up production and competing on cost remain major challenges. Explore WeLion’s push to make safer, higher-capacity batteries . —You Xiaoying Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch , spanning everything from geothermal power plants to carbon dioxide batteries .  MIT Technology Review Narrated: Weight-loss drugs show signs of slowing biological aging, say drugmakers Popular weight-loss drugs may do more than help people shed pounds. But how much can we read into these results? This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . events.summary: Tokenmaxxing may have been the shortest-lived corporate try-hard hustle in history, but many of Wall Street’s year-end bonuses still hinge on AI use. Applicants’ AI skills are nearly four times as important in hiring decisions as where they went to college, and a quarter of US financial firms have tied raises, promotions, and bonuses to AI proficiency , according to a survey of 500 companies by financial recruiting firm Selby Jennings. Breathe easy, bulge-bracketers: The practice is more common among fintech startups and smaller firms than brand-name banks and trading houses, Jacob Summers, Selby Jennings’ head of tech recruiting, told Semafor. Nearly a third of firms surveyed have created new roles or departments to track AI use, where total token burn is less important than wringing some actual value out of all the token use. But in many organizations, monitoring that work falls to managers, turning them into part-time AI accountants. — Jake Angelo

events.title: Saudi set to drop plans for five 2034 World Cup stadiums
events.summary: The Scoop Saudi Arabia’s sovereign wealth fund is preparing to inform organizers of the 2034 men’s soccer World Cup that it plans to drop five new stadiums it proposed to build to host the tournament, according to people familiar with the matter. Public Investment Fund will likely narrow its focus to three new stadiums as it cuts spending on some of its signature domestic investments, the people said. Dropping the five venues would leave the kingdom with 10 stadiums for World Cup matches. The changes are part of a revised plan the kingdom is preparing to submit to FIFA, the tournament’s organizers, the people said. PIF is looking to drop plans to develop stadiums in King Abdullah Economic City and Qiddiya Coast, both near Jeddah; Roshn and New Murabba in Riyadh; and NEOM, in the kingdom’s northwest. Several of the cancelled stadiums are attached to broader real estate projects that have been halted or where work has slowed. Saudi Arabian officials are still working on the updated proposals and the plans could change, the people said. PIF and the Saudi Ministry of Sport didn’t respond to requests for comment. Know More Reuters earlier reported on the cancellation of the NEOM stadium, which was envisaged as being on the roof of The Line, a 500-meter-tall skyscraper. Work on The Line has effectively ground to a halt , and NEOM has not allocated any funding for the project until after at least 2030, Semafor previously reported. Saudi Arabia had also proposed a 45,000-seat stadium at Qiddiya Coast, a planned entertainment and tourism destination north of Jeddah. That development has also been put on hold. Another 45,000-capacity stadium in Riyadh’s New Murabba district is also set to be dropped. Work on the wider development has slowed after the departure of Chief Executive Michael Dyke and the suspension of work on the project’s centerpiece, a 400-meter-tall, cube-shaped skyscraper with screens lining its interior, similar to The Sphere concert venue in Las Vegas. The kingdom is still proceeding with plans for other new stadiums including one in Dhahran being developed by Saudi Aramco, and the King Salman International Stadium and Prince Mohammed bin Salman Stadium in Riyadh. The cuts could leave Saudi Arabia developing just six new stadiums and refurbishing four existing ones for the World Cup. Four of the stadiums it plans to use in 2034 are also due to host matches for the 2027 Asian Cup, which starts in January. The outlook for that contest going ahead in Saudi Arabia has been thrown into doubt by the kingdom’s involvement in the war in Yemen against Houthi militias. The group has launched multiple attacks against Saudi cities in recent weeks, shutting down the capital’s airport and killing at least 18 and injuring hundreds. Qatar also previously dropped four of the stadiums it had planned to build for the 2022 World Cup as it got closer to the tournament.
