events.title: These Women Were Trying to Escape Domestic Abuse. ICE Detained Them Instead.
events.summary: They were victims, not abusers. That’s what they told police officers, attorneys, visitors and anyone else who would listen. It didn’t matter. The women were all taken to a sprawling immigration detention center in the woods of west Michigan and handed thin jumpsuits — red, to mark them as a high security risk. Inside the North Lake Processing Center, they talked about the men whose calls to police landed them there. The boyfriends or husbands who threatened to get them deported and cut them off from their children. The men, or sometimes women, who hit them, pulled their hair or choked them, bruising their throats. They didn’t know where to go for help before, but now, in the confines of a cold cellblock in a former prison, the women helped one another. If one spoke to somebody on the outside who could connect them with advice, legal aid or money for the commissary, she’d pass around a tablet used for calls so others could tell their stories. Migladys Bermudez, an immigration attorney in southeast Michigan, remembers a call in May from a Peruvian woman detained at North Lake. Her name was Pilar, and she’d heard about Bermudez from a fellow detainee who had been a client. Pilar told Bermudez about the boyfriend she tried to escape before her arrest, when she used makeup to cover the marks she said he left on her face. But he had accused her of being the abuser, resulting in her arrest. Pilar handed the tablet to a Cuban woman named Leya. Over the echoes of the other detainees’ chatter, she described how her boyfriend insulted her, isolated her and gave her a black eye. Then, after grabbing him by the arm during an argument, she was the one behind bars, separated from their nursing daughter. On video calls, the girl didn’t seem to recognize her mother anymore. She stopped calling her “Mamá.” Bermudez was taken aback. All three women in that chain — the former client, Pilar and Leya — said they were trying to get out of abusive relationships when they were arrested by local police on domestic violence allegations. In all three cases, the charges were dropped or never filed at all. The U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detained the first woman during a routine check-in a few months after her charges were dropped. The others were handed over to ICE by local officials.  It’s long been intimidating for immigrants who suffered abuse to call 911, regardless of who was in the White House. They knew — and their abusers knew — that their immigration status made them vulnerable. But previous administrations treated victims as just that, people who needed help, not as targets for deportation. Bipartisan coalitions in Congress have long supported the Violence Against Women Act, which creates a pathway toward legal status for immigrants who are victims of domestic violence or other serious crimes. Now, under President Donald Trump, all bets are off. On inauguration day, his administration rescinded guidelines that largely prevented immigration agents from making arrests at sensitive locations — including domestic violence shelters and hospitals. About a week later, the administration eliminated key protections granted to VAWA applicants and other crime victims. For the first time in decades, immigration authorities could disregard those protections and more freely arrest, detain and deport immigrant victims. Life became more harrowing in other ways for immigrants who were victims of domestic violence. Federal immigration agents made arrests outside specialized domestic violence courts. And the administration persuaded more and more local police and jails to carry out the president’s mass deportation campaign, sweeping still more immigrants into custody.  Even communities without these so-called 287(g) agreements are helping the government round people up. In west Michigan’s Kent County, where Pilar and Leya were arrested, the county jail turned over more immigrants to ICE in the first six months of 2026 than it did during the entire Biden administration. Advocates across the country say they’re seeing signs of an alarming increase in the numbers of domestic violence victims who are detained and deported. And many immigrants are staying in abusive relationships, fearful of calling for help or even stepping outside their homes. “It’s just probably the most dangerous time for immigrant women right now who are victims of domestic violence,” said Bermudez, who took on Leya’s immigration case. The arrest and detention of domestic violence victims is, in part, an unanticipated consequence of an effort meant to keep them safe. In much of the country, law enforcement officers are encouraged — or even required — to make an arrest when they have probable cause to believe that a domestic violence assault has taken place. Sometimes victims are mistaken as the abuser and taken into custody. Then, if they’re immigrants, they can be turned over to ICE — even if they were never criminally charged. There’s no comprehensive way to track how often this happens or how many domestic violence victims have been detained by ICE or deported. But ProPublica spoke with a half-dozen alleged victims who were locked up together in a single facility, North Lake, and reviewed police records about others who were there, too. Their stories offer a picture of why Congress created programs like VAWA in the first place, and what’s at stake when those guardrails are taken away.  A coalition of immigrant survivors and advocates have sued the Trump administration, saying changes to how immigrant victims are treated not only undermined public safety, but also broke promises enshrined in federal law and policy. “We were seeing our clients be more scared, be systematically targeted, be arrested, and deported very quickly,” said Kathleen Rivas, supervising attorney of the survivors team at Public Counsel, a law firm that’s involved in the litigation. In May, a federal judge ordered the government to restore protections while the case played out. The Trump administration has appealed the order.  White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement that ICE is targeting the “worst of the worst.” The real story, she added, is the “American women whose lives have been taken by illegal alien criminals.” A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that “we will never apologize for deporting illegal aliens, because that’s how we save lives.” But Leya, Pilar and other immigrants we interviewed have no criminal records. And advocates said communities are less safe now because immigrants are afraid to call police when their partners hurt them. events.title: Kenya clears path for Dangote refinery IPO investment
events.summary: The News Kenyan investors hoping to participate in the Dangote refinery initial public offering now have access through a financial instrument being used for cross-border African investment for the first time on Nairobi’s bourse. The use of global depositary receipts (GDRs), which allow backers to buy a stake in a foreign company without leaving their home market, bypasses regulatory barriers that have held up intra-African investment. The use of GDRs offers a template for exchanges across the continent to expand pan-African trade and broaden their investor bases. After an extension of the IPO period was announced on Monday, Kenyan individuals and institutional investors will have until Oct. 27 to buy into their country’s $300 million allocation of Africa’s largest public offering. The minimum entry price in Kenya was slashed from $824 to $4.12, matching what Nigerians were being offered. Announcing the extension, Dangote said he wanted greater African participation and highlighted the Kenyan arrangement that he hoped could be replicated. African policymakers are keen to deepen capital markets as a way to mobilize more of the continent’s domestic resources to fund infrastructure projects and reduce borrowing costs. Know More The refinery’s stock market debut was touted as a way for African investors to own a stake in the continent’s largest refining plant. But the prospectus for the $1.6 billion share shows it was not registered as a public offering outside Nigeria, Reuters reported. That has left investors relying on their own country’s regulations or finding workarounds using the few eligible online financial platforms. Reuters reported patchy take-up outside Nigeria , reflecting low levels of cross-border investment. The Nairobi Securities Exchange’s (NSE) approach is structured around Standard Bank’s Kenya subsidiary Stanbic, which will hold the shares and issue the GDRs. These will be traded on the NSE in Kenyan shillings, and Stanbic will manage the foreign exchange conversion and pay out dividends. Karimi Warui, vice president of investment banking at Renaissance Capital, which is overseeing the IPO in Kenya, told Semafor that the Dangote Group initially intended to pursue a conventional cross-listing approach to get on the NSE and other stock exchanges, but ultimately settled on GDRs for ease. Trying to deal with the rules and regulations of 10 different jurisdictions “became a bit onerous for them,” she added. She said this approach in Kenya could inspire others. “I wouldn’t be surprised if companies that are already listed like [Kenyan telecoms company] Safaricom pursue GDRs in the future to tap into markets like South Africa and Nigeria,” she said. “I actually think we will see more of this now,” saying the IPO would “show regulators the need to work with financiers and issuers” to accelerate growth and integration of Africa’s financial markets. Warui also emphasized the need for regulators to customize policies to fit African markets instead of copying Western regulators. The use of GDRs comes amid a significant push to enhance retail investing in the country. Safaricom this year rolled out NSE trading on the mobile money service M-Pesa, helping drive retail participation in the IPO of the state-run Kenya Pipeline Company (KPC) . Warui told Semafor that Renaissance Capital was copying the KPC blueprint for the Dangote IPO — with an online platform for share purchases during the offer period, and trading on the M-Pesa platform expected once it is listed on the NSE. Besides Kenya, Uganda’s markets regulator has approved a restricted offer limiting participation to high net-worth individuals and professional investors. Botswana has been selected to host the southern African portion of the public offering, Bloomberg reported. Step Back Some analysts have cautioned that the GDRs could leave Kenyan investors exposed to FX risks as the GDR tracks the Lagos share price, which is in naira, meaning currency devaluation could significantly affect investors. Acknowledging the concerns, Warui noted that Dangote Refinery’s revenues were dollarized and that dividends could also be paid in dollars, mitigating the potential impact of naira devaluation. Previous GDR listings by African companies have been outward, where issuers list the underlying shares on exchanges outside the continent — mostly on the London Stock Exchange (LSE) to attract Western capital. Room for Disagreement Sultan Mwangi, a Nairobi-based investor and financial researcher, predicted that participation in the Dangote IPO among Kenyan investors would be far lower than expected, especially among retail investors. He attributed this to the handling of the IPO which he said had left investors “disappointed” despite initial excitement. Among issues he cited were inadequate investor education and a need to address concerns regarding the use of GDRs, especially over whether this will leave people exposed to fluctuations in the value of the naira. According to Mwangi, the extension of the IPO offer as well as lowering the minimum investment were a response to low uptake among retail investors. “People were not convinced, and the amount of time available to explain it has not been enough,” he told Semafor. Dangote Industries has yet to respond to enquiries from Semafor on whether the lowering of the minimum investment was a response to underwhelming participation among Kenyan retail investors. Notable African nations should turn to an estimated $4 trillion in capital held by domestic institutions, such as pension funds, to develop infrastructure, the Africa Finance Corporation has said.

events.title: It’s a different oil crisis, but Saudi Arabia will still pay
events.summary: Wael’s view In June 2008, I sat in a Jeddah Hilton conference room packed with ministers from more than 100 countries waiting for King Abdullah to arrive. Oil was closing in on a record price. Saudi Arabia’s message that day: The world had enough oil. It offered a modest increase in output and told governments to cut taxes and rein in speculators. Less than three weeks later, on July 11, crude hit about $147 a barrel. This week in Riyadh, another ministerial gathering took place. The man now leading the kingdom’s response, Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman, was an assistant oil minister two decades ago. This time the crisis is different — and so is his answer. Then, the argument was about speculation. Saudi officials said investors had pushed prices well past what supply and demand justified, and that financial trading in oil had grown many times larger than the physical market. Washington thought OPEC should pump more. Riyadh replied that it would not build capacity for buyers who did not exist. Now the argument is about geography. Gulf crude is trapped behind the Strait of Hormuz, and the kingdom’s answer is to build around it. Prince Abdulaziz told the World Petroleum Congress that Saudi Arabia may lift its East-West pipeline capacity from about 7 million barrels a day to 10 million within three years, and he wants more international involvement. His logic is that the more countries have a stake in the line, the better it is protected. Both responses share one feature. Saudi Arabia cannot solve the crisis alone, and it ends up paying for the attempt. In 2008 it built rarely used spare capacity and has carried its cost ever since. A new pipeline will follow the same pattern. When the war ends it will not run full, and Riyadh will keep it as insurance. The oil market has also shifted. In 2008, OPEC was dominant and no one else could add meaningful supply. Some consumers searched for substitutes, and ethanol was an answer then. Today, it’s the electric vehicle. But neither remedy has removed the need for fossil fuels and no price spike has changed the thirst for oil. The biggest difference is Washington. In 2008, the US relied on OPEC’s oil. Today, it has plenty of its own, a reality that may not be felt by Americans paying more at the pump. If America needed OPEC barrels as badly as it did in 2008, the politics of this current crisis would look very different. Geopolitical risk has been the main factor driving $100 oil this year, with shipping and insurance comprising more than a third of the price of the global crude benchmark. Even if Hormuz is opened tomorrow, the new logistics of moving crude will weigh on producers. It will also change the relationship between states: Iraq is planning to build a pipeline through Syria to the Mediterranean, while Kuwait and Qatar may lean on their Gulf neighbors to reach ports outside the strait. Ultimately, much of the bill will go to the same address: Riyadh. The kingdom has carried the cost of a largely idle pipeline for decades, and will soon have to revert to its role as the global swing producer, keeping prices fair to producers paying for new infrastructure, and consumers who won’t tolerate high prices forever. Notable Saudi Arabia’s oil supply could still be threatened even after the end of the war. This report from the Center for Strategic and International Studies looks at what options there are. Despite the oil shock, the Saudi economy can remain resilient, according to t his briefing from the Atlantic Council .

events.title: Aldar's international unit plans to deliver 9,000 homes in next five years
events.summary: London Square, which is part of Abu Dhabi’s Aldar Properties , plans to deliver about 9,000 homes in the next five years in the UK capital with a total development value of £5 billion ($6.6 billion), as demand remains resilient. The homes will be built across about 30 sites, with the company targeting buyers in the affordable segment as well as international investors. More than 3,600 homes will be for sale, 1,538 will be for build-to-rent and another 3,575 will be in the affordable segment, in which government provides grants to registered developer to help it lease to tenants at affordable rental rate. London Square plans to start work on 12 sites this year with 65 per cent of those affordable, said chief executive Adam Lawrence. “There's always demand for affordable housing, it is a huge market and a huge need,” he told The National. There is also international demand from buyers in Turkey, Hong Kong and Middle East countries, he added. “Turkey is really strong at the moment. We've opened an office in Turkey, in Istanbul, recently, and we're seeing, within days of opening, we're into double-digit sales there. Hong Kong's been very quiet, but that looks like it's coming back.” The company, which was acquired by Aldar in 2023, has delivered 5,000 homes across 46 sites with a development value of £2.9 billion ($3.8 billion) since London Square was founded in 2010. “Under the Aldar banner, our sales have actually been better than they were historically and in the current market have been outperforming all of our peers,” said Scott Brown, chief financial officer of London Square. “Through our involvement with Aldar, we've not only been able to drive the capital but we've also been able to drive our sales.” London Square, which regenerates former industrial sites, is behind projects such as the Nine Elms development, which features more than 750 residential homes and 21,500 square feet of commercial and retail space. It is also transforming the former headquarters of Surrey County Council into a premium 292-home development, which includes the restoration of old structures. The company aims to complete 600 homes this year, up from 398 last year, with sales backlog to reach £1 billion by the end of 2026. “Most of this year will be on the affordable market rather than the build-to-sell market … about 30 per cent of what we're building is affordable,” Mr Brown told The National in London. He did not provide details on the total sales the company expects this year. London Square reported sales of £251 million for the first half of 2026, up 236 per cent year-on-year on the back of three new projects – Bermondsey Phase 3, Wimbledon Bridge House and Ransome’s Wharf. Sales from the Middle East account for 10 to 15 per cent of total international sales, with UAE buyers dominating sales activity, says Naomi Minegishi, London Square international sales director. “International demand is being driven by investment opportunity, safe haven of their capital and a strong legal framework,” Ms Minegishi said. “Families also want to have a second home to spend time in summer, as well as to have a home to support their children as they enrol them in school or universities to study in London.” London's property market has been affected by geopolitical uncertainty that is pushing inflation higher. In the third quarter, the average home price in London grew modestly by 0.4 per cent annually to £529,720, as demand remained subdued amid higher borrowing costs, according to the Nationwide Building Society. However, fundamentals remain strong on higher investment activity, lifestyle vibrancy and a diverse population, said Sharief Ibrahim, executive director and head of residential agency at CBRE. “There is real cause for optimism. There are countless examples of schemes that are performing really well, many in the London Square portfolio in terms of the volume of apartments being sold and the value being achieved,” he said. “London is a resilient place. It's been through economic downturns, shocks to the economy and the system and the appeal of London has endured throughout that period. It's a global powerhouse and one of the, if not the most, successful city in terms of inward investment globally.” It projects home transaction volumes to be around 6,000 to 7,000 this year and 7,500 to 8,000 next year.

events.title: New Mexico and El Paso Spent Millions on Climate Plans. Three New Data Centers Could Undo Them.
events.summary: Meta is building a massive data center on the northeast edge of El Paso, Texas, on the New Mexico border. Paul Ratje for ProPublica and The Texas Tribune Last December, New Mexico officials celebrated publication of a plan to address climate change, designed to dramatically reduce the state’s greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. A few months later, just across the state line in Texas, El Paso city officials adopted their own such plan with a similar ambition.  Each report cost millions of dollars to draft, but neither one took into account how the construction of data centers could upend climate goals in both places.  Work is underway in Doña Ana County in southern New Mexico on one of the largest data center developments in the country: Project Jupiter, built by Austin-based Oracle. Twenty miles away in El Paso, construction is underway on another massive data center, this one built by Meta Platforms.  A third, larger data center project is planned less than a 30-minute drive from the Meta site, on the Fort Bliss Army post in east El Paso. The data centers are “going to undo a lot of the very expensive and very meaningful work a lot of people are doing,” New Mexico state climatologist Dave DuBois told El Paso Matters. The sites are among a wave of data centers under construction across the country, driven by the rapidly escalating demand for artificial intelligence services like Claude and ChatGPT. Such projects have drawn intense scrutiny in recent months , as residents and elected officials have questioned their impact on communities’ water supplies, household electric bills and air quality. Texas alone has 596 data centers that are either in operation or planned across Texas as of early September, according to research by The Texas Tribune .  But the projects located in this population center of 1.2 million, which encompasses El Paso and parts of southern New Mexico, are particularly notable because of their combined scope. When fully built out, the three data centers, each with its own power plant, will emit millions of tons of greenhouse gas emissions, equivalent to the planet-warming emissions released by more than two million cars in a year. They will also release air pollutants like particulate matter and nitrogen oxides, which directly affect local air quality and human health. The Meta and Project Jupiter data centers are expected to release these kinds of pollutants at relatively low levels, according to paperwork submitted to state regulators. But even a small increase in air pollution can still negatively impact communities close to and downwind of the data center sites, said Shaolei Ren, a professor of electrical and computer engineering at University of California, Riverside.  “The health impacts can be significant for local communities,” Ren said. Because Project Jupiter, Meta and the Fort Bliss data centers are in two different states, and because there is no single federal regulation governing climate change or emissions, regulators have largely considered the projects’ impacts separately. “We’ve never had a national climate law passed by Congress,” said Ari Peskoe, director of the Electricity Law Initiative at Harvard Law School. “And so what we’ve had in this country are primarily state and local efforts.” The result is that officials in one state have little say over a project happening minutes away from them.  Texas and New Mexico also take different approaches to dealing with climate change. New Mexico has codified greenhouse gas reduction targets into state law; Texas has not. A truck sprays water for dust suppression at the construction site of Project Jupiter in Santa Teresa, New Mexico. New Mexico state Rep. Sarah Silva, a Democrat, represents the community of Chaparral, directly across the state line from Meta’s data center site in northeast El Paso. Her state has the power to regulate air quality and impose noise requirements, but only in New Mexico, not at a Texas construction site, even if it’s only a few hundred yards away.  Likewise, residents living in west El Paso across the state line from Project Jupiter have no say in the project despite sharing an aquifer that crosses the state boundary. Emissions do not remain within the state where they originate, Silva said. “This is why we need federal regulation,” said Silva. “How do we knit something together that makes sense for our region when actually this is the job of the federal government?” Though they profess a desire to mitigate the impacts of climate change, local governments in El Paso and Doña Ana counties green-lit these projects in a part of the country seeing rapidly rising temperatures. The counties offered Meta and Project Jupiter tax incentives in exchange for corporate investment in their communities, job creation and, hopefully, the ability to attract more technology companies to the region.  State officials have also provided incentives. More than a decade ago, Texas legislators approved a data center sales tax break , which exempts the facilities from paying sales tax on equipment they purchase, a decision that could now cost the state $3.2 billion in revenue over the next two years, according to The Texas Tribune.  New Mexico lawmakers declined to advance a bill creating a similar tax break for data centers in 2021. But in 2025, they passed an unrelated law allowing large facilities such as Project Jupiter to generate their own electricity using natural gas. The law exempts these private power systems, known as microgrids, from renewable energy requirements, even as New Mexico requires electric utilities to source 50% of the power they sell from clean energy by 2030.  The power plants that keep data centers running typically produce large amounts of emissions like carbon dioxide and methane that drive global climate change over time. Combined, the plants proposed for Project Jupiter and Meta’s data center could emit up to 10 million tons of planet-warming emissions annually. Comparatively, the region spanning El Paso County and neighboring Hudspeth County released 8.4 million tons of greenhouse gases in 2019 . (The Army has shared scant information about the Fort Bliss data center, so it’s not clear what level of emissions the facility will produce.)  “This does add to our greenhouse gas emissions in a massive way,” said Gunnar Schade, an associate professor of atmospheric sciences at Texas A&M University. “This is a huge source.” Homes in Chaparral, New Mexico, sit adjacent to Meta’s data center, just over the state border in El Paso, Texas. events.title: Political fallout from Trump’s Russian diesel deal overshadows price impact
events.summary: President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin’s deal to deliver Russian diesel to global markets may be sending shockwaves through the GOP — but don’t expect it to do the same to prices. Already, multiple House Republicans ; key GOP candidates ; and two bipartisan groups of senators have pushed back on the move. The planned imports will “have very little unnoticeable impact on domestic US diesel prices, even if it happens — and I think that’s a big if,” given legal complications and Russian constraints, Bloomberg economist Chris Kennedy, who served on the National Security Council during the Trump and Biden administrations, told Semafor. He said that the amount of diesel Russia has pledged to release for the month of November represents only “one day of US diesel demand.” He pointed to heating oil futures, observing that “traders appear to be pricing in very little near-term impact.” The White House pushed back: One official insisted to Semafor that “massive amounts of supply will lower costs for American farmers, truckers and workers.” “They’re not releasing that [diesel] to us, they’re releasing it to the entire world,” Trump told reporters Tuesday. “Because the world market suffered with high prices — and when you knock out diesel refineries, that’s not a great thing.” — Eleanor Mueller

events.title: Apple bets AI can finally make us want a smart home
events.summary: Apple's big new hardware bet for the AI era is here, and it's a ... smart display? Why it matters: Cue the time machine and let's head back to 2014, when Amazon's Alexa shocked the tech world and led us to imagine a Jetsons-style home would be ours in the near future. It wasn't, but Apple believes it could come soon. The iPhone maker is betting that modern AI can finally make good on that vision, unveiling a slew of new smart home devices Tuesday. Between the lines: While the smart home has largely failed to live up to its promise, modern AI could help address its biggest shortcoming: getting devices to just work without requiring users to become amateur IT experts. Apple's new products emphasize easy setup and integration with its existing ecosystem, while AI could help diagnose problems and coordinate devices. "The capabilities that AI would bring in helping make sure that these devices can solve their own problems and work together is really interesting to me," Paul Gagnon, a vice president at market research firm Circana, told Axios. Driving the news: Apple's announcements Tuesday included a new smart display, a revamped speaker, an updated streaming device and a collection of connected home accessories developed with partners. HomeView: Apple's new $299 smart display features a 7-inch screen and an AI-powered Siri that can respond to requests, control connected devices and recognize different household members to deliver personalized information. It will ship next month and comes in two versions, one that can hang on a wall and the other a tabletop device reminiscent of the iMac G4. Apple Home Collection: Apple worked with LG and Schneider Electric on smart locks, doorbells, cameras and thermostats designed to work together through Apple's Home app and Siri. The big picture: The AI hardware race is taking two different paths: making familiar devices substantially smarter and creating entirely new kinds of gadgets. Amazon and Google have been incorporating more capabilities into their respective assistants and accompanying smart home products, efforts that were three years in the making . Meanwhile, others are betting that the AI era needs new kinds of highly personal devices. OpenAI is expected to release its first AI device soon, and Meta recently teased plans for Charm , a Tamagotchi-like device meant to bring its Muse assistant to the masses. Reality check: Apple has a loyal customer base and a history of making complicated technology easier to use. But that doesn't guarantee consumers will spend more on a category that has struggled to generate sustained demand. U.S. smart speaker dollar sales fell 9% in 2024 and another 7% in 2025, and smart displays fared poorly as well before rebounding somewhat this year, according to Circana. "We have definitely been in a, we'll call it, an enthusiast phase or early adopters phase for quite a while now," said Circana's Gagnon. Zoom out: Better AI doesn't necessarily mean consumers will rush to buy more smart home devices, particularly when increasingly capable AI assistants are already available on smartphones. Apple could benefit from its large installed base of iPhone owners and its ability to simplify setup, but it's unclear whether those advantages will expand what has remained a niche market. "The new smart home products could appeal to consumers who have previously resisted buying smart home devices because they are perceived as difficult to set up and sometimes hard to use," Ben Wood, chief analyst of CCS Insight, told Axios. The bottom line: A decade ago, the smart home promised to change how we live. AI may finally make that possible. But Apple still has to convince consumers that the home needs another screen or speaker — not just a smarter phone.

events.title: Men Can’t Stop Faking How Much They Know About AI
events.summary: Say you’re a guy who reads WIRED—you know a thing or two about artificial intelligence . You recognize the names of well-known people developing AI, like OpenAI CEO Sam Altman . But do you know who Mira Murati is? What about Susan Milner? Craig Dalton? In a new survey of more than 5,400 Americans, 73 percent of male respondents told Harvard researchers they knew who Altman was. A little over half—53 percent—said they knew of Murati, Milner, and Dalton. There’s one problem. Murati is a real person: she’s the former CTO of OpenAI and the current CEO of Thinking Machine Labs. Milner and Dalton, on the other hand, do not exist. Compared to women , “we're seeing that men are more optimistic and more confident” across the board when it comes to AI, Harvard Kennedy School’s Shorenstein Center executive director Laura Manley tells WIRED. Sometimes, that veers into overconfidence—like claiming to recognize fictional AI executives. (For context, 40 percent of women claimed to know who Milner and Dalton were; 38 percent said they recognized Murati.) While Manley notes that men are more overconfident in general when surveyed, the report, published on Wednesday, digs into what the confidence gap on AI looks like, as well as the repercussions of gendered divides. Researchers found that men use AI more frequently and are, on average, better able to correctly answer factual questions about AI. But men and women answer questions incorrectly at around the same rate. The discrepancy is based on how often women said they weren’t sure of an answer—an average of 3.3 questions out of 12 compared to 2.3 questions for men. Researchers wondered if this predilection toward certainty colors coverage of AI. Across a year of media coverage, men were named in headlines about AI more than 14 times as often as women. Because top AI executives skew heavily male, researchers decided to reexamine coverage, looking solely at people who were quoted as subject experts. Three-quarters of these experts were men—a higher proportion than the actual AI talent pool, which is roughly 29 percent women. “Maybe there should be more women prominently featured as experts or given the platform to express: not sure,” Manley says. Besides intellectual bluster, Americans were generally in agreement that AI was freaking them out—men and women both rated “concern” as their top emotional response. However, female respondents were more concerned, fearful, and worried than their male counterparts. Men, meanwhile, rated every positive feeling—including curiosity, enthusiasm, and excitement—higher than women did. In the current discourse, “there's so much confidence in either doom or abundance,” Manley says. “It just drowns out all of the voices that should be saying ‘not sure.’” There are many unanswered questions on proper uses for and the future of AI. One gender is simply less likely to acknowledge such uncertainty. “We have to be able to be able to say ‘not sure’ more often,” Manley says. events.title: AI's extreme heat challenge is moving from prediction to protection
events.summary: Cities and researchers are using AI to map and predict extreme heat risk, but new research suggests it's used far more to identify where people are in danger than to help officials respond. Why it matters: As climate change intensifies extreme heat, better predictions won't protect vulnerable communities unless governments can turn them into action. U.S. deaths associated with high temperatures rose 53% from an annual average of 2,670 in 2000–2009 to more than 4,000 in 2010–2020, according to a 2025 Yale study . Driving the news: A study published in Climate Risk Management examined existing research on how AI and machine learning are being used to manage extreme heat. Of the research papers reviewed, 98.4% focused on prediction and 59.2% on prevention. That's compared with just 10.4% on response, 3.2% on recovery and 1.6% on preparedness — a disparity the authors call a "research-to-implementation gap." The research is heavily focused on using AI to forecast dangerous heat and identify who's at risk, with far less attention on how it can help officials decide what to do next. "Where AI can actually add value is where prediction is central to the decision-making, and that's in scale or providing more granularity," said Karishma V. Patel, a RAND policy researcher who co-authored the study. State of play: Turning sophisticated heat predictions into government action requires more than advanced models. Cornell researcher Jennah Gosciak told Axios that having "robust data systems" that can ingest data from a variety of sources and then make it usable to practitioners "is most of the battle here." Case in point: Google in June announced it had expanded its AI-powered Heat Resilience data from an initial 14-city pilot to more than 50 cities worldwide, giving urban planners building-level data to help target heat interventions. The data uses AI and high-resolution imagery to map roof reflectivity down to individual buildings. Google said data from the pilots helped inform decisions in several cities, including cool-roof ordinances and adaptation plans. Reality check: Better information doesn't necessarily equal better outcomes. Gosciak, who spent time as a Public Interest Technology Fellow with New York City Emergency Management, recently compared simpler heat-vulnerability indexes with more complex predictive algorithms for government heat decisions. She described one important distinction as "slow versus fast data." Predictive algorithms may be more useful for time-sensitive decisions "tied to a specific trigger event," while simpler indexes can be better suited to longer-term planning. One advantage of simpler indexes is that officials can explicitly choose which vulnerable populations to prioritize, added Gosciak, a Ph.D. student in Cornell's Information Science Department. What's next: The next frontier may be less about making heat forecasts incrementally better and more about connecting predictions to interventions. AI's value could lie in helping officials make "near real-time decisions" by integrating changing signals and providing "hyperlocal forecasting at granular levels," Patel said. That could help officials respond to heat risks in real time and better understand compound threats involving heat, air pollution, wildfire smoke and drought, she said. The bottom line: "What is important is not just that we can build AI-enabled technology, but it actually solves a problem or removes a bottleneck," Patel said.

events.title: Trump plays Russian roulette on eve of midterms
events.summary: President Trump is indulging his fondness for Vladimir Putin at a moment of acute political peril, forcing Republicans in the midterms to take cover as he showers Moscow with one-sided concessions. Why it matters: With just three weeks until the election, Trump is rekindling a decade-long, scandal-scarred relationship with a dictator reviled by most Americans — including his own supporters. Driving the news: Since speaking with Putin on Friday, Trump has embarked on a remarkable five-day campaign of diplomatic concessions and cover for Russia — sparking bipartisan blowback just as voters prepare to cast their ballots. On Friday, Trump announced a deal to unleash millions of tons of Russian diesel onto global markets, easing sanctions designed to starve Moscow's war revenues. On Saturday, Trump lashed out at Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky for striking Russian refineries and demanded that Kyiv replace its leader. On Sunday, Trump blindsided Zelensky by declaring an immediate "energy ceasefire." Russia has continued attacking Ukrainian energy infrastructure, with no apparent consequences from Washington. On Monday, Trump dismissed months of intelligence-based reports that Russia was enabling Iran's war effort by supplying information about U.S. military assets. On Tuesday, Trump doubled down on the diesel deal and brushed off concerns that the proceeds could finance Russia's war machine, even as GOP senators labeled it a "betrayal" and "a gift to our adversary." Between the lines: The benefits to Russia are clear. Far less apparent is what Trump's concessions accomplish for American security, European allies or his own political fortunes. For America: Energy analysts doubt the diesel deal will meaningfully ease fuel prices sent soaring by the Iran war. For Europe: Washington is breaking ranks with a NATO alliance confronting a historic threat environment , as Russia escalates its hybrid campaign of sabotage, cyberattacks and drone incursions. For Republicans: With control of Congress hanging in the balance, Trump is embracing a dictator viewed unfavorably by 81% of his own 2024 voters, according to a January YouGov poll . The big picture: Trump's warm relationship with Putin has haunted his political career since 2016, when Russia interfered in the presidential election to help him defeat Hillary Clinton. From the Mueller investigation to the Helsinki summit , Trump's deference toward Putin has long divided Republicans and put him at odds with his own national security establishment. A decade of investigations, scandals and Washington outrage has done little to shake that affinity. If anything, the scrutiny appears to have hardened Trump's determination to defy the foreign-policy consensus. What they're saying: On Monday, Trump again suggested that Russia was more interested in ending the war than the country it invaded, telling reporters: "I think, actually, Putin wants to make a deal more than Zelensky." "The President's diesel deal will help lower prices for farmers, truckers, and families across the nation as he simultaneously urges both sides of the Russia-Ukraine conflict to stop strikes against refineries, which are driving up costs and hurting American consumers," White House spokesperson Anna Kelly said in a statement. The bottom line: Losing control of Congress could paralyze Trump's legislative agenda and expose his administration to years of investigations and subpoenas. But as polling alarms pile up , the president appears increasingly willing to follow his raw political instincts, regardless of the consequences for Republicans fighting to keep him in power. In a Truth Social post Tuesday, Trump made clear that he sees himself as personally immune from the results of the midterms, writing: "I'm not running in the Elections, I've already won, IN A MASSIVE LANDSLIDE."

events.title: Exclusive: AI safety money floods into political races
events.summary: Advocates for AI safety and regulation are emerging as a force in U.S. elections, spending nearly $50 million this election cycle on candidates who favor regulation, a new analysis shared exclusively with Axios shows. Why it matters: The safety spending points to the unusual power dynamics in the AI race, where researchers shape policy and regulation in ways that differ at times from the priorities of the companies where they work. The researchers add to the advocacy and giving of an array of AI safety groups that have been well-funded for years, including from Coefficient Giving, a philanthropy with close ties to many top AI executives, especially at Anthropic. Driving the news: AI safety groups and individual donors have spent $48 million this cycle on Democratic and Republican races, according to new figures shared first with Axios. That includes donations from researchers, such as OpenAI's Juan Felipe Cerón Uribe and Redwood's Aryan Bhatt. It also includes Guardrails Alliance, a tech-worker-backed AI safety group that has raised $11.7 million between its super PAC and 501(c)(4). The big picture: Taking AI industry money has grown complicated due to viral warnings of catastrophic AI risk from the very same industry developing it and data center NIMBYism mobilizing communities in blue and red districts alike. OpenAI president Greg Brockman pulled a planned second $25 million donation from Leading the Future, a super PAC backed by tech execs and investors, in part because of an internal revolt at OpenAI. Forces favoring AI acceleration — who earlier in the year appeared to favor veiled threats to pro-regulation candidates — haven't spent as much as opponents expected, and safety advocates see an opportunity to fill the void. Zoom in: Jacob Eliosoff, who runs the cryptocurrency investment fund Calibrated Markets, said he decided to engage in political giving related to AI after he saw early fundraising and candidate advocacy from Leading the Future. Eliosoff, an active participant in New York's effective altruism community, said he didn't want to see a repeat of 2024, when crypto industry funding had outsized influence on the regulatory positions of most candidates. "If politicians feel like they can't say anything because there's a very deep-pocketed and ruthless political entity that's going to go after them, that motivates me to step in," Eliosoff said. Between the lines: Eliosoff has donated to Democrats and Republicans who he says appear to be open to taking AI risks seriously and could be well positioned to pass regulation. Donors told Axios they are not primarily motivated by party affiliation or specific policy positions but by fears that industry spending will silence candidates on an unpopular technology. The other side: Leading the Future had retained more than $31 million at the end of the second quarter and has supported more than 15 Democrats and more than 25 Republicans. In a statement, the group said AI regulation will need 60 votes to pass in the Senate, so anyone serious about safety "and harnessing the benefits of AI for all Americans should be focused on building a broad coalition for action." What's next: This cycle will be a test of whether candidates who take AI industry money and oppose real regulation lose and whether that is clearly understood as a central factor in their loss, Guardrails Alliance executive director Shaunna Thomas said. "Republican leadership and the Trump administration are on the other side of the majority of Americans on AI," Thomas said. "That's a very important place for Democrats to be stepping into — boldly." Yes, but: Guardrails faces pushback from some Democrats who warn its strategy, which includes opposing some Democrats, could help elect Republicans less inclined to regulate AI. The bottom line: Trump allies have opened a new front against Anthropic and safety advocates affiliated with the EA movement, but their political giving — as well as the insistence of AI insiders — shows that the political clout of pro-safety AI advocacy is set to grow.

events.title: Former Canadian official says Europe erred on Trump tariffs
events.summary: Europe made a “historic” blunder by caving to the Trump administration on tariffs during Trump’s second term, the former Canadian trade minister who helped negotiate the US-Mexico-Canada deal during the first Trump administration told Semafor. “A real problem for the Western alliance has been the decision by the UK and by the EU to give in to the Trump bullying on tariffs,” Chrystia Freeland said. “People thought appeasement would win a reprieve for us all.” The EU and UK have each negotiated with the administration following the imposition of unilateral tariffs, and the former agreed to a pact that went into effect this year. US trade relations with Canada, meanwhile, have broken down, and Ottawa has announced counter-tariffs following US pressure. Freeland, who is out with a new book , said it’s “possible” albeit difficult for the US and Canada to return to a constructive relationship. That might need to wait until Trump is out of office, though. “There would have to be a clear break because the problem is: How do you do a deal with someone who already broke the deal that you did with them?” she said.

events.title: AI task force readies for first meeting
events.summary: All eyes are on the first meeting of the White House’s AI task force this week as groups and members of Congress try to influence the newly formed body. Americans for Responsible Innovation, former Oklahoma Democratic Rep. Brad Carson’s nonprofit focused on federal AI safety regulation, is pushing the task force to “explore the need for Congress to develop new laws that provide for enforceable safety standards and public transparency” into AI development. Voluntary commitments will not be enough, the group argues, and the task force should make specific recommendations to Congress. Sens. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., also wrote to the task force asking for more resources for the National Institute of Standards and Technology and its in-house testing lab. They also want the task force to ensure that the Energy Department’s National Labs can test AI independently and to mobilize the technology to guard against cybersecurity incidents. Meanwhile, the FBI arrested a Saudi national Tuesday for allegedly secretly recording conversations at the offices of his employer, OpenAI. It’s still not clear what exactly will be discussed at the task force’s first meeting, as the group scrambles to organize following its formation earlier this month. Industry watchers are awaiting any official guidelines for enforcement of its new directive, which may come from the Office of Director of National Intelligence (headed by task force chair Jay Clayton) and the Federal Trade Commission. — Ashley Gold

events.title: OpenAI employee and Saudi suspect ‘came to the US with a dream’, lawyer says
events.summary: Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi citizen and OpenAI employee, has been arrested over accusations that he hid a recording device at the company's offices in San Francisco. The Justice Department said Mr Alfozan hid the device – a Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32-S3, manufactured by a company in China – behind a television in a conference room. The device has a “thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone and micro-SD storage”, the Justice Department said. Mr Alfozan had started working at OpenAI in July last year and worked on its product team. He was fired on the same day as his arrest, the company said. According to a court motion filed by prosecutors on October 8, actions taken by Mr Alfozan indicated he planned to quickly depart the US. "Indeed, the defendant, his wife, and a third family member have booked one-way tickets from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia (via Istanbul) .. and defendant has the means and the incentive to flee the US sooner if he learns about this case before he is arrested," the court filing reads. California lawyer William Pernik said that he is still waiting to see what other evidence the government has against his client, and that he plans on presenting all appropriate defences in court. “Like countless Americans, Mr Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream,” Mr Pernik told The National via email. “These allegations appear wholly out of character for him, and we will relentlessly investigate all evidence produced by the government in this case to understand what actually happened, who was responsible, and any possible reasons why.” He emphasised that his client has been charged with breaching a federal recording statute, not stealing trade secrets or working as a foreign agent. “There is no evidence to suggest otherwise at this time that has been shared with us,” he said. Mr Pernik implied that his client is already facing bias because he was not born in the US. “It is regretful that this is the one factor that seems to have caught the most attention,” he wrote. “Where someone was born is not evidence of anything and national origin is – and always should be – a protected status under our system of laws.” Who is Abdulrahman Alfozan? According to his LinkedIn profile, Mr Alfozan has lived in California since 2015 and started working at OpenAI as a lead engineer in 2025. Before his years in California, he was an intern at Meta, Microsoft and SAP. Mr Alfozan received his undergraduate degree from MIT in 2016 and then earned his master's degree in 2025 from the University of California-Berkeley. According to the Justice Department, he was arrested on October 9 and charged with using an electronic, mechanical or other device to intercept oral communications. He is scheduled to appear in court on October 19 for a detention hearing. “If convicted, Alfozan faces a maximum sentence of five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by three years of supervised release,” a press release from the Justice Department reads. OpenAI has faced a barrage of criticism from employees amid allegations that it has disregarded the need for regulations when developing AI technology. American AI companies such as OpenAI also face stiff competition from China, as Washington and Beijing vie for dominance in the technology race. Companies have gone to great lengths to protect intellectual property and trade secrets.

events.title: India's Bank of Baroda to 'defend interests' after BR Shetty's $15bn lawsuit
events.summary: India's Bank of Baroda on Wednesday ​said ​it would protect ​its interests, a day after UAE-based ⁠businessman and founder of NMC Health BR Shetty filed ⁠a $15 billion case against the lender and ​25 other defendants at Bombay High Court. Mr Shetty alleged ⁠the Bank of Baroda and several current and former employees helped facilitate a fraud that contributed to the collapse of the Middle East healthcare group, according to a ⁠court filing reviewed by Reuters. The firm, then the Gulf's largest private healthcare provider, ​was ⁠placed under administration in 2020 ‌after months of financial mismanagement and disclosed debts of $6.6 billion, way above previous estimates ​of $2.1 billion. Representatives for Mr Shetty did not immediately respond to requests for comment. In a stock exchange notification on Wednesday, the country's second-largest state lender said: “The bank has not been served with such a suit and cannot comment on the contents of pleadings, which are untested in court. If and when the bank is served, the bank will defend the suit firmly and take all steps necessary to protect its interests.” The Bank of Baroda added that it was pursuing recovery and enforcement proceedings in India and the UAE against Mr Shetty for outstanding dues of 28 billion rupees ($294.5 million) and had obtained several decrees against him. The lender will ​not bear any immediate liability until any order is ‌passed or until it ⁠is required to make a provision on ​account of potential damages, the lender said. Bank of Baroda ​shares dropped ‌2.6 per cent on Tuesday after the legal action was reported. The lawsuit, which centres on the bank's lending to ⁠NMC Health and affiliated entities in the UAE, comes three months after the lender agreed to pay $600 million to settle claims brought by administrators of NMC. Mr Shetty alleged that bank officials enabled round-tripping transactions, ignored repeated anti-money laundering warnings and ​accepted documents bearing forged signatures. He is seeking $5 billion in direct damages, $5 billion in consequential damages and an additional $5 billion for reputational harm, the filing showed.

events.title: Ossoff rejects 2028 buzz amid bruising night of Senate debates
events.summary: Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) delivered another debate performance tailor-made for social media Tuesday night, feeding the presidential speculation he insists is entirely misplaced. Why it matters: A darling of the Democratic internet and a favorite to win the party's nomination in 2028, Ossoff emphatically ruled out a White House bid and pledged to serve a full six-year Senate term if re-elected. "He is running. He's going to be your DSA candidate," Republican challenger Rep. Mike Collins countered, seeking to paint Ossoff as a socialist with ambitions beyond Georgia. The big picture: Georgia was one of three battleground states hosting Senate debates Tuesday night, with candidates in Iowa and Maine also clashing over President Trump's foreign policy, the cost of living and their records in Washington. In Georgia, Ossoff and Collins traded vicious personal attacks throughout their second and final debate, reprising a feud that has become a viral spectacle online. "Will you commit tonight that for the remainder of this campaign — it's just three weeks, Mike — you won't allow any more neo-Nazi propaganda to be produced from your house?" Ossoff demanded , referring to Collins' son-in-law, an alleged white nationalist influencer. Collins accused Ossoff of inciting threats against his family, then attacked him over campaign support from billionaire Reid Hoffman, who had ties to Jeffrey Epstein. "Mike, you really want to bring up the Epstein files?" Ossoff shot back , pointing to Collins' initial vote against releasing the documents — a position he reversed after Trump changed course. In Maine, Republican Sen. Susan Collins cast her independence from Trump as a political asset, arguing that her willingness to challenge the president — and work with him when necessary — has delivered for her state. Collins cited her nine votes to end the Iran war, opposition to Trump's Big Beautiful Bill and roughly $1.5 billion in federal funding secured for Maine projects. Democratic challenger Troy Jackson argued that Collins has spent years helping Trump advance policies that hurt Maine, only to express "concern" and claim credit for mitigating the damage. In his closing statement , Jackson invoked a fatal ICE shooting in Maine to accuse Collins of enabling Trump's immigration crackdown: "Sen. Collins paid for the bullets at Donald Trump's command. Now she wants credit for not pulling the trigger." In Iowa, GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson and Democratic challenger Josh Turek squared off in a race that has Republicans on edge , as Trump's tariffs and soaring farm costs threaten their grip on a state he carried by 13 points. Hinson broke with Trump over his deal to ease sanctions on Russian diesel , saying she believed there were ways to lower fuel prices without empowering Vladimir Putin and his war in Ukraine. Turek accused Hinson of helping drive Iowa toward a "second farm crisis" through her support for Trump's tariffs and votes against congressional efforts to end the Iran war. Hinson said the war should end "as quickly as possible" but rejected another congressional resolution, arguing Trump and the military could bring the conflict to a close themselves.

events.title: From Enterprise to Earthshot: UK’s Ecosystem Moves From Ambition to Application With NVIDIA
events.summary: NVIDIA Announces New Investments in the UK Startup Ecosystem Across industries, the U.K. is putting the full stack to work. T he scale of deployment is growing fast, from enterprises transforming their businesses to startups solving some of the planet’s hardest problems. NVIDIA is putting that principle into practice, including through a five-year, $250 million compute commitment to strengthen the U.K.’s agentic safety and security research. NVIDIA has been investing in the U.K. startup ecosystem, supporting companies including Basecamp Research , Ineffable Intelligence , Synthesia , Wayve and many more. Today, NVIDIA announced new planned investments in Boltz , Foresight , Hiverge, Prima Mente and Riverlane . Boltz , a London-based AI startup founded by MIT researchers, builds biomolecular models and AI agents that help scientists predict molecular structures and interactions, and design potential new medicines. Foresight, a London-based startup, helps owners of major infrastructure projects, including hyperscale data centers, predict completion dates, mitigate risks and accelerate time to revenue. Hiverge , a Cambridge-based AI startup founded by researchers from Google DeepMind and the University of Cambridge, builds an AI discovery engine that automatically writes and optimizes algorithms for tasks such as faster AI training and complex logistics planning. Prima Mente , a London-based AI biology startup, focuses on building biological foundation models to decode complex diseases and identify novel therapeutic targets, starting with Alzheimer’s, Parkinson’s and ALS. Riverlane, a Cambridge-based quantum computing startup, builds real-time error correction hardware and software that work across all major qubit types, helping quantum computers become reliable enough for practical use. In addition, NVIDIA is partnering with the Earthshot Prize , joining as a Global Alliance Founding Partner to bring compute and technical expertise to innovators working on solutions for the world’s greatest climate and sustainability challenges. Technology Leaders Pioneer Intelligent Solutions Across the UK In energy, Fuse Energy is moving its customer AI onto its own in-house infrastructure, built on NVIDIA B300 Blackwell Ultra, delivering faster, more responsive support to over 450,000 U.K. households. Meanwhile, sovereign AI company Locai Labs released Nemotron-Personas-UK — an open source dataset of one million synthetic personas representing the UK’s demographic, regional and cultural diversity — helping developers build fairer, more representative AI systems. In healthcare, OneAdvanced is deploying what it calls the U.K.’s first and most advanced fine-tuned LLM for Primary Care AI-triage — built with NVIDIA Agent Toolkit software and open models — supporting millions of National Health Service patients. Heidi has now integrated NVIDIA Nemotron open models to give clinicians faster access to trusted medical evidence. Speechmatics is deploying Oak, a multilingual medical speech recognition model, using NVIDIA Triton Inference — giving healthcare organizations control over where sensitive patient audio is processed. Apian , Synnovis and NVIDIA are teaming up to use advanced computing and digital simulations using NVIDIA Cosmos to help hospital robots handle the heavy lifting of moving lab samples, freeing up medical staff to focus on patient care. Danaher and NVIDIA are collaborating to advance autonomous science and help accelerate the pace of discovery by bringing accelerated computing, scientific and physical AI into laboratory workflows and instruments. Danaher’s recently announced AI-powered autonomous lab — designed to deliver up to 8x faster discovery of affinity reagents — is using NVIDIA BioNeMo open models within its AI-driven protein design workflows, data and automation technologies that connect design with experimental feedback. On the civic side, Liverpool City Region is building an NVIDIA-powered “City Brain” — a sovereign AI strategy designed as a blueprint for dozens of Unitary Authorities across the U.K. Digital Jersey , Innovation City Belfast and Tees Valley Combined Authority are each exploring how trusted AI compute can serve communities and public services. In financial services, LSEG and NVIDIA are bringing GPU-accelerated market analytics to global institutions. Revolut introduced PRAGMA earlier in the year — a foundation model for banking event sequences, pre-trained on 26 million anonymised user histories. PRAGMA has moved from research to real-time scaling. Lloyds Banking Group built ATUM , a transaction foundation model that converts billions of banking transactions into reusable AI. And Starling is developing a banking foundation model trained on Civo’s U.K. sovereign cloud infrastructure. NatWest is collaborating with NVIDIA on Nemotron Voice to better understand how banking customers across the U.K. speak, while Modulr is deploying a network of agents using Nemotron for distinct parts of payment operations. Quantum is moving from research to systems deployable alongside classical AI, and the U.K. is at the heart of this shift. Riverlane has shown how GPUs can accelerate decoder recalibration workflows used in quantum error correction, helping decoder performance keep pace with real-time changes in quantum hardware behaviour. The work forms part of a broader collaboration exploring how AI, accelerated computing and quantum error-correction technologies can work together to support future quantum systems. ORCA Computing unveiled PT-3, its latest photonic quantum accelerator, at the Digital Realty Innovation Lab , and used it to run the NVIDIA Proteina model for protein design. ORCA found that its hybrid quantum-classical extension improved identifying useful proteins by 20%. Together, these announcements showcase how enterprises, organizations and startups in the U.K. are fostering innovation across the nation. This includes more than 3,100 U.K. companies that are a part of the NVIDIA Inception program for cutting-edge startups. Tune in to NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang’s GTC Berlin keynote on Wednesday, Oct. 21, at 11 a.m. CEST. events.title: Saudi Ministry of Energy reports limited fire in building at Aramco compound targeted in attack
events.summary: The Saudi Ministry of Energy says a limited fire broke out in an administrative building in Aramco, one of the world’s largest oil facilities, that was targeted in the country's Eastern Province CAIRO -- A limited fire broke out Tuesday in an administrative building at Aramco, one of the world’s largest oil facilities, that was targeted in an attack in the country’s Eastern Province, Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Energy said. The ministry said no injuries were reported. The attack came as the Iranian-backed Houthis and the Saudi coalition fighting them exchanged attacks Tuesday night. The fighting marked a fresh escalation in the widening Middle East crisis and came shortly after the Saudi coalition reported a series of alerts for incoming missiles heading for the Eastern Province, a major oil-producing region, and the capital Riyadh. Saudi Arabia’s Civil Defense said debris from two intercepted Houthi missiles fell on residential areas in Riyadh, injuring four people and damaging 15 homes. The coalition of forces in Yemen led by Saudi Arabia carried out new airstrikes Tuesday on the Houthi rebel-held Yemeni capital, the Houthi-run broadcaster Al Masirah and residents said. The strikes came shortly after a coalition spokesman urged residents to evacuate the area for their safety. Witnesses reported hearing strong explosions in Sanaa hours after the coalition struck the Subaha fuel facility west of the city. In a rare statement earlier, the coalition had urged civilians in the Houthi-controlled capital to leave the Yemeni Oil Company site, on a hill overlooking the capital, and nearby storage areas ahead of a possible strike. Coalition spokesman Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki accused the Houthis of using the facility and its underground fuel depots for their arsenal of missiles and drones. Houthi officials appeared to have anticipated the attack. The oil company said its storage facilities were empty and that a Saudi strike would not affect oil reserves or supplies for residents. Still, witnesses in the city said lines of cars formed at some gas stations amid fears of a shortage. Shortly after the warning, Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said on Telegram that any Saudi attack on Sanaa would be met with a “firm and painful” response in the Saudi capital, Riyadh. Hours later, Saudi Arabia issued alerts for incoming missiles heading for Riyadh and the Eastern Province but quickly said the danger had passed. The coalition said it had intercepted a series of Houthi-launched ballistic missiles, drones and cruise missiles in multiple areas in the country, including Riyadh and the southern province of Wadi al-Dawasir. Riyadh residents reported hearing loud explosions. Airlines moved a number of their planes out of Riyadh on Tuesday on the advice of insurers and government officials because of the threat of additional attacks. They needed to transfer the planes to other airports in the country so they can keep flying passengers to their destinations, said Osprey Flight Solutions Chief Intelligence Officer Matthew Borie, whose company advises airlines, insurers and countries on flight threats. “It’s not abnormal for this to occur especially in this day and age with the types of conflict zone situations that have occurred in the region,” Borie said. More than 3,120 flights scheduled to depart from airports across Saudi Arabia since Oct. 8 have been canceled or listed as not operating, representing about 41% of scheduled departures, according to aviation analytics firm Cirium. That includes more than 300 flights that had been scheduled to depart Wednesday. Several airlines have suspended service to the kingdom because of the Houthi attacks on airports. It was unclear whether the Tuesday strike in Yemen was a signal of military escalation or a carefully measured response to recent deadly attacks on the Riyadh airport. The warning and the attack show “the Saudis’ aims of upping the ante and striking deep in the heart of Houthi-controlled territory while attempting to control the narrative by presenting themselves as more careful and humanitarian actors than the Houthis,” said Adam Baron, a fellow at the Washington-based New America institute. Teen shooter kills 3 children, 1 teacher at elementary school in Bend, Oregon: Police Woman accused of stabbing husband and son to death at Great Wolf Lodge: Complaint Hurricane Isaias: At least 4 dead as Isaias downgraded “It may be a warning — or it may be a sign of things to come," he said. Saudi Arabia is still scrambling to determine how its air defenses failed to intercept a barrage of missiles and drones fired by the Houthis , including an attack on Riyadh's international airport on Saturday that killed at least 13 people and wounded over 300.

events.title: NVIDIA Commits $250 Million to Advance UK Agentic Safety and Security Research Over the Next Five Years
events.summary: NVIDIA announces a compute donation valued at $250 million over five years to support U.K. agentic safety and security research. The program will support the wider U.K. research community, with a proportion of the commitment supporting BOLD, SOFAIR and Imperial College London across fundamental agentic foundation models and robotics safety. Compute access will be delivered through U.K.-based NVIDIA Cloud Partners, supporting the nation’s research capability and compute ecosystem. NVIDIA today announced a five-year compute donation valued at $250 million to strengthen the United Kingdom’s agentic safety and security research capability. The commitment will provide $50 million in compute access annually to support agentic safety and security research across the U.K. The majority will support the wider U.K. AI safety and security research community, with a proportion supporting work with the British Open-Ended Learning and Discovery Lab (BOLD), the Science of Fundamental AI Research Lab (SOFAIR) and Imperial College London. “AI capability and safety must advance together,” said Jensen Huang, founder and CEO of NVIDIA. “The U.K. brings world-class scientific rigor to this essential engineering challenge. With this $250 million commitment, NVIDIA will put accelerated computing in the hands of U.K. researchers to develop, test and strengthen safeguards for increasingly powerful AI. This is how the U.K. turns research leadership into real-world solutions — and scientific progress into a future that benefits everyone.” “This commitment is a vote of confidence in our world-leading strength and expertise in AI research — and, in particular, frontier AI safety that is becoming ever more important as AI’s capabilities develop,” said U.K. AI Minister Kanishka Narayan. “NVIDIA’s donation will help Britain’s AI innovators access the resources they need to bring their ideas to life — and, in the process, help build a distinctly British AI future that is safe, secure and that serves people’s best interests, objectives that will be central to the U.K.’s G20 presidency.” “To realise the opportunities of AI, people need to feel the technology is safe and secure. The government is committed to ensuring AI can be securely harnessed to fuel new discoveries and drive growth,“ said U.K. Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds. “NVIDIA’s investment will help British researchers continue to lead the world in that effort — accelerating the breakthroughs that build trust and help us deploy AI safely.” Strengthening UK Leadership in Agentic Safety and Security Compute provided through the initiative will be dedicated to agentic safety and security research. The program will connect complementary areas of U.K. research, including in AI safety and security. BOLD, led by the University of Oxford, is developing approaches that help AI systems learn, adapt and operate alongside people. SOFAIR, led by UCL, is exploring new open source AI architectures and more accessible ways to develop and deploy AI. Imperial’s work will include safety engineering and robotics. “We are experiencing a critical moment where AI safety as an afterthought is no longer appropriate for the open-ended, evolving world,” said Jakob Foerster, founding director of BOLD. “This compute will help us explore transparent and human-centric approaches to AI that allow us to collectively rise to the challenge by building in governance and human-AI co-improvement from the ground up.” “The next frontier of artificial intelligence is physical — robots, autonomous systems of agents that perceive, reason and act in the real world,” said Alessandra Russo, director of Imperial Frontier AI Research Lab and convening co-director of Human and AI, School of Convergence Science. “With NVIDIA and our industry partners, Imperial is working to ensure that safety and assurance is at the heart of this revolution, ensuring the U.K. leads not only in developing physical AI but in making it trustworthy for the communities and industries that will depend on it.” NVIDIA will fund compute access through U.K.-based NVIDIA Cloud Partners , with infrastructure hosted in the U.K. This will support the U.K. compute ecosystem and provide a domestic platform for research. Provider selection, technical architecture and commercial terms are to be agreed. As part of the wider initiative, research programs will focus on secure agents, open-model security and real-world threat mitigations. The work will support secure sandboxes, reproducible research and safety assessment benchmarks, including research conducted using NVIDIA OpenShell™ open, secure runtime software and the NVIDIA Sentry reference design . Findings are intended to inform safeguards across the wider computing ecosystem. The commitment builds on NVIDIA’s collaboration with the U.K.’s research community, including on the University of Bristol’s Isambard-AI supercomputer, powered by NVIDIA Grace Hopper Superchips.
