events.title: Russian diesel deal "a betrayal," bipartisan coalition says
events.summary: President Trump's deal to lift sanctions on Russia to increase diesel supplies "is a betrayal of the people of Ukraine" and "a gift to our adversary," a bipartisan coalition of senators wrote in a letter admonishing the agreement. Why it matters: The decision to turn to Vladimir Putin in an attempt to ease the diesel crunch is piling onto Republican headaches ahead of the midterms and fueling fresh friction between the U.S. and Ukraine. What they're saying: The deal "will not achieve just ends, nor will it benefit Americans," the senators warned, urging Trump to withdraw from it and ramp up the economic pressure on Russia as called for in a sanctions bill named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham that he signed into law last month. While record-shattering diesel and gas prices are squeezing key industries and American households, the lawmakers argued that "allowing Russian-origin diesel into global markets will offer limited to no relief to Americans." Analysts have expressed doubt that the levels Trump pitched will meaningfully sway prices, Axios' Ben Geman reports . However, the lawmakers argued that it will "undoubtedly finance" Russia's war "and advance its security cooperation with China, Iran, and North Korea." The fine print: The signers are Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Thom Tillis (R-NC), Jeanne Shaheen (D-NH), Susan Collins (R-Maine), Dick Durbin (D-Ill.), Alan Armstrong (R-Okla.), Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI), Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska), Jack Reed (D-RI), Chris Coons (D-Del.), Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) and John Cornyn (R-Texas). The White House directed Axios to the president's remarks to reporters Tuesday. He said described the agreement as a "diesel deal that's going to be released into the world for the world market because the world market suffers with high prices. And when you knock out diesel refineries, that's not a great thing, but they're not releasing that to us. They're releasing it to the entire world." Zoom out: That bipartisan coalition has fellow dissenters on the Hill, including members of the president's party who swiftly condemned the deal. Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) vowed over the weekend to force a vote to block Russian oil purchases, predicting that "it will pass overwhelmingly." Retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) told Axios' Andrew Solender he "already agreed" to sign the petition. Friction point: As lawmakers sound the alarm, the agreement reignited tensions between Kyiv and Washington. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told A xios' Barak Ravid the deal "looks like a happy birthday present for Putin." But Axios also reported that Trump decided to make the deal after Ukraine continued its highly effective attacks on Russian oil refineries , which contributed to spiking prices, despite the U.S. requesting that they halt such strikes. What we're watching: The administration's deadline to implement the sanctions law honoring Graham is Oct. 18 — but the legislation allows the president to waive key provisions. events.title: Companies are building with AI — and exposing new security risks
events.summary: The amount of AI-related infrastructure exposed to the public internet jumped 63% in nine months, according to new Censys data shared first with Axios. Why it matters: The AI boom isn't just creating new models and chatbots. It's creating a sprawling layer of software that companies will also need to inventory, patch and secure. Threat level: Many of these tools connect AI applications to sensitive corporate data and other services, creating potential entry points for hackers looking to access company systems. "It's a little bit beyond just like the tool itself, but these [tools] talk to some really sensitive systems," Emily Austin, a principal researcher at Censys and co-author of the report, told Axios. The big picture: Censys identified nearly 268,000 internet-facing systems running 44 different AI-related products as of July, up from roughly 164,000 in October 2025. These include the software used to connect AI models to databases, corporate applications and other services. Between the lines: The ease of building and hosting AI applications is making it harder for companies to keep track of what software employees are using and whether it's secure. Censys CEO Zakir Durumeric told Axios that companies were already struggling to keep track of their existing software even before employees started building their own AI applications. These new AI apps can often connect to sensitive company information, such as emails, financial records and internal databases. Zoom in: The most widely exposed product was n8n, a workflow automation platform that can connect AI agents to other applications and services. Censys found nearly 114,000 internet-facing deployments of n8n, including roughly 77,000 running software versions affected by at least one recently disclosed critical vulnerability. Researchers also found more than 54,000 exposed control panels for OpenClaw, an open-source AI agent that users can connect to personal accounts and other services. Yes, but: The findings don't establish whether those deployments are actually vulnerable to exploitation, but they highlight the risks of exposing software that can access sensitive company systems. The bottom line: Companies need to treat AI infrastructure like any other software they deploy, Austin said, including regularly reviewing, updating and securing the systems. events.title: White House pushes out Kimberly Guilfoyle after misconduct reports
events.summary: Kimberly Guilfoyle , the U.S. ambassador to Greece, announced her resignation Tuesday, shortly after the White House asked her to step down and following reports alleging misconduct before and during her diplomatic posting. Why it matters: The exit of the president's longtime political ally and former fiancée of his son Donald Trump Jr. follows a series of Wall Street Journal reports alleging she used her political connections to seek financial favors and promote private business interests. Guilfoyle has denied any wrongdoing. White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said Tuesday during her first press briefing that Guilfoyle was asked to resign. "She has been a wonderful asset to the team and we wish her well," Zacharia said. Driving the news: "My gratitude and respect for President Trump and Secretary Rubio remain unwavering," Guilfoyle wrote in a post on X on Tuesday. "I am proud of what we accomplished together, and I will always be a loyal supporter of President Trump and his mission to Make America Great Again." "While my time as Ambassador may be coming to an end, my commitment to President Trump, the America First movement, and the country I love will never end. It has been the honor of my lifetime to serve the United States of America." Guilfoyle's removal isn't entirely surprising, as Trump told reporters yesterday that he was "looking at" firing Guilfoyle following the allegations: "We're not happy," he said. Those comments follow a senior U.S. official telling AP that Trump and Rubio were "extremely pissed off" about the reports and were considering dismissing her. The U.S. Embassy in Athens and the State Department did not immediately respond to Axios' request for comment. Zacharia declined to answer additional questions about Guilfoyle and referred reporters to the president. Catch up quick: The WSJ's Oct. 8 report said that Guilfoyle allegedly sought $100,000 from a Trump donor to pay a credit card bill before her Senate confirmation hearing and offered access to Trump administration officials in return. The donor did not make the payment. An earlier investigation alleged she promoted the interests of a Greek construction and energy company and allowed its lobbyist into private diplomatic meetings. The WSJ also reported that recordings captured Guilfoyle allegedly discussing private jet travel and luxury hospitality provided by wealthy Greek businessmen. For the record: Guilfoyle's lawyer disputed the authenticity of messages the WSJ cited and the U.S. Embassy in Athens said she has followed State Department ethics and gift-reporting guidelines. Zoom in: In her statement, Guilfoyle once again said that the allegations against her are "false." "I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity. I have dedicated my professional life to fighting for justice, standing up for what is right, and defending the values that make America exceptional. I will not allow false accusations to define my decades of public service." Zoom out: Secretary of State Marco Rubio publicly defended Guilfoyle during a visit to Athens on Oct. 7, calling her "a strong ambassador." A day later, Rubio declined to address the allegations, saying he didn't know whether they were true. Flashback: Trump nominated Guilfoyle, a former Fox News host and California prosecutor, in December 2024. The Senate confirmed her in September 2025. What we're watching: The State Department's inspector general is reviewing the allegations, AP reported, citing an unnamed U.S. official. It is unclear whether a formal investigation has begun. Congressional Democrats have called for an investigation, with Rep. Gregory Meeks (D-N.Y.), the top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, requesting on Oct. 10 that Guilfoyle testify under oath. Editor's note: This story has been updated with more information.

events.title: Europe's alternative to Trump's China trade war
events.summary: Europe is testing a new response to China Shock 2.0 , betting that it can confront Beijing's export juggernaut without resorting to President Trump's tariff-heavy approach. Why it matters: More of the world is beginning to confront the threat that China's industrial overcapacity poses to their industries. But protecting individual sectors will not solve the bigger problem: China's factories are cranking out far more than its own economy can absorb. Driving the news: The European Union and China struck a preliminary deal on Friday to sharply limit Chinese hybrid vehicle exports to Europe. The EU plans to initially cap Chinese hybrid and plug-in hybrid imports at 350,000 annually, potentially starting as early as December. The cap would more than halve projected Chinese hybrid shipments, which were on track to reach roughly 800,000 this year, an EU official told reporters . Imports totaled 302,000 in 2025. (Chinese officials Monday noted that the deal still allows its automakers to increase shipments from last year's levels.) Vehicles exceeding the quota would be blocked rather than face additional tariffs. The backdrop: France and Germany last week proposed giving Brussels sweeping new powers to restrict market access over unfair trade practices, a striking shift for Germany, which opposed EU tariffs on Chinese EVs in 2024. European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen warned in her annual address last month that the bloc's trade deficit with China had reached a "tipping point." "Some say the second China shock is looming. But it's already here," von der Leyen said. What they're saying: EU leaders are considering tougher powers to confront Chinese trade practices, including one resembling the authority Washington has used to impose sweeping tariffs on Chinese goods. The agreement could dampen momentum for harsher measures, making member states "hesitant this week to rock the boat," Daniel Mullaney, an Atlantic Council senior fellow and former U.S. trade official, tells Axios. Washington is pushing trading partners to join forces against China's industrial overcapacity. "It's really hard for any one country to make progress on that if you don't have allies on your side," Mullaney says. By the numbers: Chinese automakers ramped up hybrid shipments to Europe after the EU imposed steep tariffs on fully electric vehicles in 2024. New data released yesterday shows that China's global passenger vehicle exports surged 64% in September, to 919,000, even as domestic sales fell 27%. What to watch: Europe's deal could shift pressure to other industries — or perhaps even other nations — without addressing the underlying imbalances driving China's export boom. Economist Michael Pettis argued over the weekend that the agreement would do little for European manufacturing overall. "EU producers of hybrids will be better off, but at the expense of other EU manufacturers," he wrote on X . The bottom line: Europe's deal may provide breathing room for its automakers. But China's industrial might — and the pressure it is inflicting on manufacturers around the world — is not going away.

Time: 10am – 11.30am | Location: Bank of England, 20 Moorgate, London, EC2R 6DA The Chair thanked members for attending and confirmed that the Minutes of the Money Markets Committee (MMC) June 2026 meeting had been published on the Bank’s website. footnote [1] The Chair updated on recent usage of the Bank’s market-wide repo facilities. Members were reminded that use of the Bank’s facilities, including against a broad range of eligible collateral, was consistent with the intended transition to a repo-led operating framework. The Chair provided a brief update on the Monetary Policy Committee’s (MPC’s) September decision on Quantitative Tightening footnote [2] , including the exchange of letters between the Governor and the Chancellor regarding QT and the APF. footnote [3] The Chair also noted the related announcements made by the Bank and HM Treasury that came out at the same time. footnote [4] Item 2 – Discussion on market conditions Members noted that money markets continued to function smoothly and that funding conditions remained stable, even during recent increased bond market volatility. Liquidity was reported to be ample, with limited signs of stress. Members also reported stable cross-currency funding conditions despite recent geopolitical developments and broader market volatility, with quarter-end and year-end conditions expected to remain orderly. While some highlighted the potential for volatility in outright asset markets to transmit into funding conditions through reduced risk appetite or position unwinds, the overall assessment was that money market functioning remained robust. Some nevertheless noted emerging funding pressures further out the euro curve as Eurosystem liquidity continued to decline. Members also discussed developments in European Commercial Paper (ECP) markets, noting increased issuance activity and growing use of these funding channels. Members also discussed the Financial Policy Committee’s proposed changes to the leverage ratio framework footnote [5] . Members generally welcomed the direction of the proposals but considered that leverage requirements are just one of a number of constraints on their activity including stress-testing assumptions, investor expectations and risk-weighted capital requirements. As a result, members considered that it was difficult to predict the extent to which the proposals would lead to a material increase in leverage or balance-sheet deployment in UK money markets in the near-term. Some noted that greater releasability of constraints in stress could support increased use of gilts and reverse repo within buffers. Members noted increasing competition for retail and corporate deposits. While this had not materially affected funding plans, some observed that sustained competition for deposits could increase wholesale funding requirements and funding costs over time. Members agreed this would remain an area to monitor. From a market infrastructure perspective, strong trading activity across gilt and international markets was reported, with no material change in cleared repo conditions. Members also welcomed the predictability provided by the MPC and Bank's recent balance sheet announcements and noted that the Bank's liquidity facilities continued to support confidence in firms' ability to manage reserves and liquidity needs.
